19:
How chicken rules actually work in Alabama

Alabama does not have one statewide rule for backyard hens. The real answer depends on where your property sits. If you live inside city limits, your city's zoning ordinance is what counts. If you live in an unincorporated part of the county, there may be very few rules at all, and many rural Alabamians keep flocks with no permit of any kind.

The tricky spot is the suburbs. A lot of newer subdivisions around Huntsville, Birmingham, Mobile and Montgomery have HOA covenants, and those covenants can ban poultry even when the city allows it. Read your deed restrictions before you buy a coop. The HOA can fine you even if the city never would.

Where to look

  • Your city's municipal code, usually under zoning or animal control. Search for "fowl" too.
  • The county commission or planning office if you are outside city limits.
  • Your HOA covenants and any recorded deed restrictions.

Heat, humidity and the long Alabama summer

Cold is rarely the problem here. Heat is. Summers run hot and sticky from late spring into fall, and humid air makes it harder for chickens to cool themselves by panting. Build for airflow first. Put the coop in afternoon shade, use plenty of high vents, and give the run a solid roof so it stays dry during summer storms.

Breeds with larger combs and lighter bodies handle this climate well. Heat-tolerant breeds like Leghorns and Easter Eggers are common picks. Heavy, fluffy birds can still work, but they need more shade and cool water through July and August.

What hunts chickens in Alabama

Raccoons, opossums, foxes, coyotes and hawks are all common. Snakes are a bigger deal here than in northern states. Rat snakes will slip through chicken wire and eat eggs and chicks, so use hardware cloth on vents and lower walls. Close the coop every night. Most losses happen after dark. The guide to predator proofing coops in Birmingham applies across most of the state.

Bird flu matters more in a big poultry state

Poultry is one of Alabama's largest farm industries, so the state takes bird flu seriously. The Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries and the State Veterinarian's office handle poultry disease reporting. If several birds die suddenly or show swelling, purple combs or breathing trouble, call them. Buy chicks from hatcheries that take part in NPIP, the National Poultry Improvement Plan, and keep wild birds away from feed and water.

Selling a few eggs

Many Alabama keepers sell extra eggs to neighbors. Small-scale sales are often allowed, but egg rules vary by state and can cover labeling, refrigeration and carton reuse. Check with the Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries before you set up a roadside stand.

Before you bring chicks home

  1. Confirm whether you are inside city limits or in the county.
  2. Read your HOA covenants.
  3. Plan shade and ventilation before insulation.
  4. Line the coop with hardware cloth, not chicken wire.
  5. Find a vet who sees poultry. The Alabama poultry vet list is a good start.

Common questions about chickens in Alabama

Can I keep chickens in the county without a permit?

Often yes in unincorporated areas, but some counties have zoning in certain districts. Call the county planning office to be sure.

Are roosters allowed in Alabama cities?

It depends on the city. Many cities that allow hens still ban roosters because of noise complaints.

Do chickens need heat lamps in Alabama winters?

Adult birds usually do not. A dry, draft-free coop is enough for most Alabama winters. Heat lamps are a fire risk.
1488:
Keeping hens where winter lasts half the year

Alaska is one of the hardest places in the country to keep chickens, and also one of the most rewarding. Rules are mostly set locally. Anchorage, Fairbanks, Juneau and the Mat-Su area each handle animals in their own way, and a big share of the state sits outside any city at all. If you live in a borough without zoning, you may have few rules beyond nuisance laws. In town, check the municipal code and your neighborhood covenants.

Many Alaska homes are on larger lots, but subdivisions near Anchorage and Wasilla often carry covenants. Read them. They are easy to miss and they can be stricter than the city.

Building a coop for deep cold

Alaska coops need to handle long stretches well below zero, heavy snow and short days. A few things matter most:

  • Insulation with ventilation. Insulate the walls, but keep vents up high. Moisture from breath and droppings causes frostbite faster than cold air does.
  • Snow load. Build a steep, strong roof. A flat run cover will collapse under wet spring snow.
  • Water that stays liquid. A heated waterer base is close to a must in most of the state.
  • Light. Hens slow down or stop laying in the dark months. Some keepers add a timed light. Others let the flock rest.

Pick cold-hardy breeds with small combs and dense feathers. The Chantecler was bred in Canada for this kind of winter, and Wyandottes and Brahmas also do well.

Predators are bigger here

Alaska keepers deal with foxes, weasels, mink, lynx, ravens, eagles, owls and loose dogs. Black and brown bears are a real issue in many areas, especially in spring and fall. Bears go after feed as much as birds, so store feed in sealed metal bins inside a building. Electric fencing is common around coops in bear country. Ravens are smart and will learn to steal eggs, so collect them often.

Bird flu and who to call

Wild waterfowl migrate through Alaska every year, which raises the risk of bird flu reaching backyard flocks. The Office of the State Veterinarian, part of the Alaska Department of Environmental Conservation, handles animal disease reporting. Keep ducks and geese away from your flock, cover the run and do not let your birds share water with wild birds. Buying from NPIP hatcheries helps you start clean. Shipping chicks to Alaska takes longer than to most states, so ask the hatchery how they handle it.

Selling eggs in Alaska

Fresh local eggs sell well in Alaska because so much food is shipped in. Small-scale sales are often allowed, but egg rules vary by state. Check with the state before you sell, and keep eggs clean and cold.

Checklist for new Alaska keepers

  1. Find out if your property falls under city or borough zoning.
  2. Read your subdivision covenants.
  3. Plan for snow load, heated water and bear-proof feed storage.
  4. Choose cold-hardy breeds and order early in spring.

Common questions about chickens in Alaska

Do chickens need a heated coop in Alaska?

Most healthy adult birds do fine without one if the coop is dry, insulated and well ventilated. Heated water matters more than heated air.

Will my hens lay through an Alaska winter?

Laying usually drops sharply in the dark months. Added light can keep some hens going, but many keepers let them rest.

How do I keep bears away from my chickens?

Store feed in sealed containers indoors, clean up spilled feed and use electric fencing around the coop and run.
1489:
Backyard flocks in a state built on poultry

Arkansas is one of the biggest poultry states in the country, and you can feel it. Chickens are normal here, and most rural landowners keep a flock without anyone asking questions. Inside cities it is different. Little Rock, Fayetteville, Springdale, Rogers, Fort Smith and Jonesboro each set their own rules through zoning and animal ordinances, and those rules change from time to time.

So the real question is not "does Arkansas allow chickens" but "what does my city or my HOA say". Many newer neighborhoods in Northwest Arkansas have covenants that ban livestock, including hens. Check those before you build anything.

Where the rules hide

  • City code. Look under animals, zoning or nuisances. Some cities treat chickens as pets, some as livestock.
  • County. Outside city limits, Arkansas counties often have little or no zoning, but some do. The county judge's office or planning office can tell you.
  • HOA. Covenants can override what the city allows.

Weather that swings both ways

Arkansas gets hot, humid summers and the odd hard freeze or ice storm in winter. Your coop has to handle both. Plan for shade and strong airflow first, since heat stress is the bigger killer here. Then make sure the coop is tight enough to block wind during a cold snap. Hardy, all-around birds like the Rhode Island Red and Australorp handle the swings well. Severe storms and tornadoes are part of spring, so anchor the coop and run so they do not move in high wind.

Predators to plan for

Raccoons, foxes, coyotes, opossums, bobcats, hawks and owls all live here. Snakes are a regular problem in the warm months and love eggs. In the Ozarks and the Ouachitas, black bears show up now and then. Hardware cloth, a buried apron around the run and a locked coop at night stop most losses. The guide to identifying predators can help you figure out what hit your flock.

Biosecurity in poultry country

Because so many commercial chicken houses are close by, bird flu or another disease in a backyard flock is a real concern for the whole area. The Arkansas Department of Agriculture handles poultry health through its livestock and poultry staff. Report sudden deaths quickly. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, do not swap birds at swap meets without a quarantine period, and keep your flock away from wild ducks and geese. If you work on a commercial poultry farm, ask about rules for keeping birds at home, since some companies restrict it.

Selling extra eggs in Arkansas

A backyard flock of six can outrun what one family eats by late spring. Selling the extras to coworkers or neighbors is common, and small sales are often allowed. Egg rules still vary by state, so ask the Arkansas Department of Agriculture what labeling and handling it expects before you take money for them.

Quick list before you start

  1. Check city code and HOA covenants.
  2. Plan shade, airflow and wind protection.
  3. Use hardware cloth and lock the coop every night.
  4. Source chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Common questions about chickens in Arkansas

Can I keep chickens if I work at a poultry farm?

Many integrators discourage or ban employees from keeping backyard birds because of disease risk. Ask your employer first.

Do Arkansas cities allow roosters?

Some do on larger lots, but many cities that allow hens ban roosters in residential areas.

What breeds do well in Arkansas heat?

Breeds with larger combs and good heat tolerance, plus steady layers like Rhode Island Reds, tend to do well with good shade.
1490:
Keeping chickens in the Arizona desert

Arizona is a heat state first and a law state second. Plenty of Arizona cities allow backyard hens, but the real challenge is keeping birds alive through summers where afternoons run well past 100 degrees for weeks at a time. Start with the rules, then build for the sun.

Who sets the rules

Cities and towns set most chicken rules through their zoning codes. Phoenix, Tucson, Mesa, Chandler, Scottsdale and Flagstaff each have their own. Lot size and distance from neighbors' homes often matter. Outside city limits, county zoning applies, and rural parcels in Maricopa, Pima and Pinal counties are often zoned for some animals. HOAs are very common in Arizona's newer suburbs, and many of them restrict or ban poultry. Read your CC&Rs. For examples of how two big cities handle it, see chicken laws in Phoenix.

Building for 110 degrees

  • Shade the whole run, not just the coop. Shade cloth and a solid roof both help.
  • Vent the coop on several sides and keep it out of direct afternoon sun.
  • Give more water than you think. Use several waterers and keep them in the shade so the water does not get hot.
  • Misters and frozen treats help on the worst days. Wet ground in dry air cools well here, unlike in humid states.
  • Do not insulate the coop like a cold-climate coop. Trapped heat kills.

Light-bodied, large-combed birds suit the low desert. Hot-climate breeds such as Leghorns, Minorcas and Egyptian Fayoumis are common choices. In the high country around Flagstaff and Prescott, you get real winters with snow, so cold-hardy birds make more sense there.

Desert predators

Coyotes are everywhere, even in town. Bobcats, hawks, owls, raccoons and skunks are common too. Snakes, including rattlesnakes, are drawn to coops by rodents and eggs, so keep feed sealed and the area tidy. In some areas, you may also deal with loose dogs. Hardware cloth on all openings and a covered run are worth the cost.

Bird flu and flock health

The Arizona Department of Agriculture handles animal disease issues, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian's office. Report sudden deaths or sick birds. Buy from NPIP hatcheries, quarantine new birds, and keep wild birds away from your feed.

Selling eggs in Arizona

Many people sell a few dozen eggs to neighbors. Small sales are often allowed, but egg rules vary by state. The Arizona Department of Agriculture can tell you what applies to you.

Before you buy chicks

  1. Check city zoning, lot size rules and HOA CC&Rs.
  2. Plan full shade and plenty of water.
  3. Time chick purchases so they are feathered before summer.
  4. Seal feed and keep the yard clear of rodents.

Common questions about chickens in Arizona

How hot is too hot for chickens?

Chickens start to struggle in the 90s and are at real risk past 100 without shade and water. Watch for panting with wings held out.

Can I keep chickens in an Arizona HOA?

Only if your CC&Rs allow it. Many do not, even where the city allows hens.

Do chickens lay in the Arizona summer?

Laying often slows in extreme heat. It usually picks back up when temperatures drop in fall.
1491:
Chicken rules across a very big state

California has hundreds of cities and dozens of counties, and each one can set its own rules for backyard birds. Many larger cities allow a small number of hens on a single-family lot, and many ban roosters. Some require setbacks from neighbors' homes. Others need a permit. Rules in a beach town, a Central Valley farm county and a Bay Area suburb can look nothing alike, so always start with your own city's municipal code.

If you live in an unincorporated area, look at the county zoning code. If you rent or live in an HOA, check your lease or CC&Rs too. San Diego and Bakersfield are two examples where you can see how the details play out, in our pages on San Diego chicken laws and Bakersfield.

Why California is strict about bird health

California has had serious poultry disease outbreaks tied to backyard birds. Virulent Newcastle disease spread through backyard flocks in Southern California from 2018 into 2020 and led to a large quarantine. Bird flu has also hit the state hard in recent years. That history is why the California Department of Food and Agriculture, known as CDFA, takes backyard flock reporting seriously.

  • Report sudden deaths, twisted necks, swelling or breathing trouble to CDFA or a vet.
  • Start with chicks from NPIP hatcheries.
  • Do not move birds between properties during a quarantine.
  • Keep wild birds and waterfowl away from feed and water.

One state, many climates

A coop in Fresno needs heavy shade and airflow. A coop in San Francisco needs to stay dry in fog and cool wind. A coop near Lake Tahoe needs to handle snow. Inland valleys and deserts get long stretches above 100 degrees. Pick birds for your region. Coast and Bay Area keepers do well with almost any common breed. In hot inland areas, lighter breeds like the Leghorn cope better. In the mountains, think cold-hardy.

Predators by region

Raccoons, skunks, opossums, hawks and owls are common almost everywhere. Coyotes live in most cities. Foxes, bobcats and, in foothill and mountain areas, mountain lions also show up. Rats are a constant issue around feed. Use hardware cloth, close the coop at night and store feed in metal bins.

Selling eggs in California

California has its own egg rules, and some of them are stricter than in other states. Small-scale sales are often allowed in some form, but the rules vary by state and California is not one to guess on. Check with CDFA before you sell any eggs.

What to do first

  1. Read your city or county code for hen limits, setbacks and permits.
  2. Check your HOA or lease.
  3. Match your breeds and coop to your region's climate.
  4. Set up a plan to report sick birds.

Common questions about chickens in California

Are roosters legal in California cities?

Many cities ban them in residential zones. Rules are set locally, so check your city's code.

Does California require registering backyard chickens?

Rules can change during disease outbreaks. Check with CDFA for current guidance for your area.

Can I let my chickens free range in California?

Only on your own property, and some cities require them to be confined. Free ranging also raises predator and disease risk.
1492:
How Colorado towns handle backyard hens

Colorado leaves chicken rules to cities and counties. Denver, Boulder, Fort Collins, Colorado Springs, Aurora and many smaller towns allow hens in some form, but the details vary a lot. Some require a permit or license. Some cap the number of hens. Most ban roosters in residential areas. Denver, for example, has used a permit system for food producing animals. Check the current version of your own city's code, because these rules get updated.

Unincorporated land falls under county zoning. Rural and agricultural zones often allow more birds. HOAs are common along the Front Range, and many have their own animal rules.

Altitude, sun and sudden storms

Colorado weather is hard on coops in ways people from other states do not expect.

  • Fast swings. It can be 60 degrees one day and snowing the next. Build a coop that handles both.
  • Snow load. Spring snow is heavy and wet. Run roofs need real support.
  • Hail. Summer hail can damage light run covers. Use solid roofing over at least part of the run.
  • Strong sun and dry air. UV is intense at altitude. Give the run shade, and keep water clean and full.
  • Wind. Chinook winds and plains wind can tip light coops. Anchor yours.

Most of the state favors cold-hardy breeds. Wyandottes, Australorps and Orpingtons are popular. On the eastern plains, summer heat matters too, so good ventilation is still key.

Predators from the plains to the mountains

Coyotes and foxes are common even in Denver. Raccoons, skunks, hawks and owls are everywhere. In foothill and mountain towns you may see bobcats, black bears and mountain lions. Bears are drawn to feed, so store it inside. The guide on predator proofing in Denver covers the Front Range well.

Bird flu in Colorado

Colorado has had large bird flu outbreaks in commercial flocks, and backyard birds are at risk too, especially near water where wild waterfowl gather. The Colorado Department of Agriculture handles animal disease reporting through the state veterinarian's office. If you see sudden deaths, call them. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries and keep wild birds away from your flock.

Selling eggs

Colorado has laws that allow some small-scale food sales, but egg rules vary by state and can change. Check with the Colorado Department of Agriculture before you sell eggs to the public.

Your starter list

  1. Check city code for permits, hen limits and setbacks.
  2. Read HOA rules.
  3. Build a coop that handles snow, hail and wind.
  4. Store feed where bears and rodents cannot reach it.

Common questions about chickens in Colorado

Do I need a permit for chickens in Denver?

Denver has used a permit for keeping food producing animals, including hens. Check the city's current rules before you start.

Does altitude affect chickens?

Healthy chickens adapt well. The bigger issues at altitude are strong sun, dry air and fast weather changes.

Can chickens handle Colorado winters outside?

Yes, cold-hardy breeds do fine in a dry, draft-free coop with good ventilation and unfrozen water.
1493:
In Connecticut, your town makes the call

Connecticut does not have county government the way most states do, so there is no county zoning layer to fall back on. Chicken rules come from your town or city, usually through the zoning regulations and sometimes through the local health department. That means two towns side by side can have very different rules. One might allow hens on any residential lot. The next might require a minimum lot size, a setback from the property line or a zoning permit.

The best first step is to call your town's zoning office or look up the zoning regulations online. Search for "poultry" and "accessory uses". If you live in a condo or a planned community, check the association rules too.

Built for New England weather

Connecticut winters are cold and damp, and coastal towns also get nor'easters, heavy wet snow and the occasional hurricane or tropical storm. A good Connecticut coop is:

  • Dry inside, with roof vents to let moisture out.
  • Strong enough to carry wet snow on the roof.
  • Raised off the ground so it stays dry in spring mud and storm runoff.
  • Anchored, so high winds cannot shift it.

Classic American breeds suit this climate. The Plymouth Rock was developed in New England and handles cold well. Wyandottes and Rhode Island Reds are also popular. For winter tips, our page on winter chicken care in Bridgeport fits most of the state.

Woods mean predators

Much of Connecticut is wooded, even in the suburbs. That means foxes, coyotes, raccoons, skunks, opossums and fishers. Bobcats and black bears are seen more often than they used to be, especially in the northern and western parts of the state. Hawks take free-ranging birds in daylight. Lock the coop at night, use hardware cloth and keep feed in sealed bins so bears are not drawn in.

Disease reporting

The Connecticut Department of Agriculture handles animal health issues, including bird flu. If you see several birds die quickly, or signs like swelling, purple combs or labored breathing, call the department or a vet. Start with chicks from NPIP hatcheries and quarantine any adult birds you bring in. Keep wild birds away from feed and water, especially near the shoreline and around ponds.

Eggs for sale

Lots of Connecticut keepers sell eggs at the end of the driveway. Small-scale sales are often allowed, but rules vary by state and can cover cartons, labels and refrigeration. Ask the Connecticut Department of Agriculture what applies before you start.

Five things to do first

  1. Call your town zoning office.
  2. Ask if you need a zoning or health permit.
  3. Check any HOA or condo rules.
  4. Plan for snow, wind and dampness.
  5. Find a poultry vet on the Connecticut vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Connecticut

Do I need a permit for chickens in Connecticut?

Some towns require one and some do not. Your town zoning office can tell you.

Can I keep a rooster in Connecticut?

Some towns allow roosters on larger lots. Others ban them in residential zones because of noise.

Do Connecticut chickens need heat in winter?

Cold-hardy breeds usually do not. Focus on a dry, ventilated coop and water that does not freeze.
1494:
Backyard birds next door to the broiler industry

Delaware sits in the middle of the Delmarva Peninsula, one of the busiest chicken-growing regions in the country. Sussex County in particular is lined with commercial broiler houses. That shapes what it means to keep a backyard flock here. Hens are welcome in many places, but disease control is taken very seriously, because one sick backyard flock can put nearby farms at risk.

State, county and town rules

Delaware has three counties, New Castle, Kent and Sussex, and each has its own zoning code for unincorporated land. Towns and cities like Wilmington, Dover and Newark set their own rules inside their limits. Many housing developments, especially the newer ones near the beaches and in Kent County, have HOA rules that limit or ban poultry.

  • Inside a town, read the town code.
  • Outside town limits, check your county's zoning.
  • In a development, read the deed restrictions.

Biosecurity is the big one

The Delaware Department of Agriculture handles poultry health, including bird flu. Delmarva has seen bird flu in commercial flocks, so the state watches closely. If your birds get sick or die suddenly, report it. Order from hatcheries that take part in NPIP. Keep your birds away from wild ducks and geese, which are common along the bays and marshes. Do not visit commercial farms and then go into your own coop. The USDA's Defend the Flock biosecurity guide is a good checklist.

Weather on the peninsula

Summers are hot and humid. Winters are mild compared with New England but bring cold snaps and the odd nor'easter. Coastal flooding and tropical storms are a real risk near the shore. Raise the coop off the ground, give it good airflow and make sure it will not float away in a storm surge or heavy rain.

The state's own chicken

Delaware's state bird is the Blue Hen chicken. The state also gave its name to the Delaware breed, a calm, white-bodied bird with black barring on the neck and tail. It was developed on Delmarva for the broiler trade and is now a good dual-purpose backyard bird that lays well and handles both heat and cold.

Predators

Red foxes, raccoons, opossums, skunks, hawks, owls and loose dogs are the usual problems. Near water, minks can get through small gaps. Use hardware cloth on every opening and close the coop at dusk.

Can you sell eggs in Delaware?

Usually in some form, at a small scale. The details on cartons, labels and keeping eggs cold vary by state, and Delaware sets its own. The Delaware Department of Agriculture is the place to ask before you put a cooler at the end of the driveway.

Getting started in Delaware

  1. Check town or county zoning and any HOA rules.
  2. Learn the signs of bird flu and how to report them.
  3. Raise the coop above flood risk.
  4. Look up a poultry vet on the Delaware vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Delaware

Is the Blue Hen a real breed?

The Blue Hen is a historic fighting bird tied to the state's history. It is not a common standard breed you can easily buy.

Can I keep chickens near a commercial poultry farm?

Often yes, but strict biosecurity is important. Some farm workers are asked not to keep backyard birds.

Should I let my chickens free range in Delaware?

Free ranging raises contact with wild birds. During bird flu alerts, keeping birds in a covered run is safer.
1495:
What Georgia keepers should know

Georgia grows more broiler chickens than almost any other state, and Gainesville likes to call itself the poultry capital of the world. Backyard flocks are part of that culture too. Even so, the state does not set one simple rule for backyard hens. Cities and counties decide through zoning, and HOAs add their own layer.

City, county and HOA

Atlanta, Savannah, Athens, Augusta, Columbus and Macon each handle chickens in their own codes. Many metro Atlanta suburbs and counties limit hens by lot size or zoning district. Rural counties are often much looser. In the big subdivisions around Atlanta, HOA covenants are the most common reason people cannot keep birds, so read yours before you buy a coop.

Heat and humidity come first

Georgia summers are long, hot and very humid. Heat stress kills more backyard chickens here than cold ever will. Shade the run, vent the coop up high on more than one side, and keep cool water in several spots. Do not build a sealed, insulated box like you would up north. Coastal areas near Savannah and Brunswick also need to plan for hurricanes and flooding, so raise the coop and anchor it well.

Good choices include heat-tolerant breeds like Leghorns and Easter Eggers. The page on breeds for Savannah weather covers coastal conditions in more detail.

Snakes, raccoons and hawks

Raccoons and opossums are the main night raiders in most of Georgia. Foxes, coyotes and bobcats are common too. Rat snakes are a constant problem in warm months and will eat eggs and chicks. Hawks pick off birds in open yards. Hardware cloth stops most of it. Our guide on predator proofing in Atlanta goes deeper.

Bird flu and NPIP in Georgia

With so much commercial poultry in the state, Georgia moves fast on bird flu. The Georgia Department of Agriculture and the State Veterinarian's office handle animal disease issues, and the Georgia Poultry Laboratory Network works closely with the poultry industry on testing and NPIP. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, keep your birds away from wild waterfowl and report sudden deaths right away. If you work in a commercial poultry operation, check your employer's rules about backyard birds.

Eggs, neighbors and a little extra cash

Plenty of Georgia keepers trade or sell eggs, and small sales are often allowed. Georgia has its own rules on things like candling, labeling and cold storage, though, and they differ from other states. Ask the Georgia Department of Agriculture what applies to a small flock before you sell.

Before chicks arrive

  • Check city or county zoning and your HOA covenants.
  • Plan shade, ventilation and water before anything else.
  • Protect against snakes with small mesh.
  • Buy from NPIP sources.

Common questions about chickens in Georgia

Can I keep chickens in metro Atlanta?

Many cities and counties in the metro allow hens with limits, but HOAs often do not. Check both.

What is the best coop design for Georgia heat?

An open, well-vented coop in shade, with a covered run and lots of airflow, works better than a closed box.

Do Georgia chickens need winter heat?

Usually not. A dry coop that blocks wind is enough for most Georgia winters.
1496:
Idaho rules, from Boise to the backcountry

Idaho has a strong farming culture and a lot of rural land, so backyard chickens are common. Rules are set at the city and county level. Boise, Meridian, Nampa, Idaho Falls, Pocatello and Coeur d'Alene each have their own codes. Some cap the number of hens on small lots, and many residential areas restrict roosters. Out in the county, agricultural zoning often allows larger flocks.

The fast growth in the Treasure Valley has brought a lot of new subdivisions with HOA rules. If you are in one, read the CC&Rs before you buy birds. They often say more about chickens than the city code does.

A dry state with real seasons

Idaho's climate changes a lot by region, but most of the state gets cold winters and hot, dry summers.

  • Winter. Cold snaps can drop well below zero, especially in the eastern part of the state and the mountains. Snow load matters in the north and at elevation.
  • Summer. The Snake River Plain and Treasure Valley get hot, dry summers. Shade and water matter.
  • Wind. Eastern Idaho can be very windy. Anchor coops and block drafts at roost level.

Cold-hardy breeds with small combs suit most of Idaho. The Wyandotte is a favorite for its rose comb and steady winter laying. Our page on breeds for Boise weather covers the Treasure Valley in more detail.

Western predators

Coyotes and red foxes are common across the state. Raccoons and skunks live in towns. Hawks, owls and golden eagles take free-ranging birds. In mountain areas, bobcats, mountain lions and black bears are possible. Weasels can squeeze through very small gaps, so use hardware cloth with small openings.

Who to call about sick birds

The Idaho State Department of Agriculture handles animal health, including bird flu reports, through the state veterinarian's office. Wild waterfowl use Idaho's rivers and reservoirs during migration, so keep your flock away from them and do not share water sources. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, and quarantine new adult birds for a few weeks before mixing.

Farm stand eggs in Idaho

Fresh eggs move fast at farmers markets and from porch coolers. Small-scale sales are often allowed, but each state sets its own egg rules on labels and storage. Check with the Idaho State Department of Agriculture first.

Idaho starter checklist

  1. Check city or county code for hen limits and rooster rules.
  2. Read HOA CC&Rs.
  3. Plan for snow, wind and summer heat.
  4. Find a vet on the Idaho poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Idaho

Can I keep chickens in Boise?

Boise has allowed backyard hens with limits. Check the current city code for numbers and rooster rules.

How do I keep water from freezing in an Idaho winter?

Use a heated waterer base or swap water out several times a day during cold snaps.

Are roosters allowed in rural Idaho?

Often yes on agricultural land, but nuisance rules can still apply if noise bothers neighbors.
1497:
Illinois chicken rules start with your town

Illinois has more units of local government than most states, and nearly all of them can write their own animal rules. That makes backyard chicken law here very local. A village in the Chicago suburbs might ban hens outright while the next village over allows four with a permit. Downstate, many small towns are open to chickens, and county zoning in rural areas often allows them by right.

How to find your answer

  • Look up your city or village code. Search "fowl", "poultry" and "hens".
  • If you live in an unincorporated area, check the county zoning ordinance.
  • Read your HOA covenants if you have them.
  • Ask whether a permit or neighbor consent is needed. Some Illinois towns have used both.

North versus south

Illinois runs a long way from north to south, and the climate changes with it. The Chicago area and northern Illinois get cold, windy winters with lake effect snow near Lake Michigan. Central Illinois is open prairie, so wind is the big issue. Southern Illinois is warmer and more humid, with longer summers.

Across the state, a good coop is dry, draft-free at roost level and vented up high. In the north, plan for heated water. In the south, plan for shade. Big, cold-hardy breeds like the Orpington do well in most of Illinois. For hot spells, our page on summer heat care in Springfield has practical tips.

Predators in farm and suburb

Raccoons are the top threat in most Illinois yards. Coyotes have moved into Chicago and its suburbs. Foxes, opossums, skunks, mink and weasels are common, and hawks and owls hunt open yards. Lock the coop each night and use hardware cloth, not chicken wire.

Bird flu and reporting

Illinois sits on a major migration path for ducks and geese along the Mississippi and Illinois rivers. That raises the risk of bird flu in spring and fall. The Illinois Department of Agriculture handles animal disease reporting. Report sudden deaths or signs like swelling and purple combs. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries and keep wild birds away from your feed.

Eggs and the farmers market

Small-scale egg sales are often allowed, but rules vary by state and may cover licensing, cartons and storage temperature. Ask the Illinois Department of Agriculture before you sell at a market or from home.

Your Illinois to-do list

  1. Check city or village code and HOA rules.
  2. Ask about permits and neighbor notice.
  3. Plan for wind, cold and summer heat.
  4. Read our guide to raising chickens in Peoria for a central Illinois example.

Common questions about chickens in Illinois

Can I keep chickens in the Chicago suburbs?

Some suburbs allow hens and some do not. Each village sets its own rules, so check your local code.

Do Illinois towns require neighbor permission for chickens?

A few towns have asked for neighbor consent as part of a permit. Check your local rules.

What breeds handle Illinois winters?

Heavy, cold-hardy breeds like Orpingtons, Wyandottes and Australorps do well with a dry, draft-free coop.
1498:
Raising chickens in the islands

Hawaii is different from every other state on this list. It is one of the few places where wild chickens are a normal part of daily life, especially on Kauai. It has no hard winters at sea level. And it has strict rules on bringing animals in from outside. All of that changes how you plan a backyard flock.

County rules, not city rules

Hawaii has no separate city governments below the county level. Honolulu, Hawaii County, Maui County and Kauai County handle zoning and animal rules. Each county decides how many birds you can keep in residential zones and how roosters are handled. Noise complaints about roosters are common in the islands, so check your county's rules before you add one. If you live in a planned community, check association rules too.

Bringing birds into Hawaii

The Hawaii Department of Agriculture controls what animals come into the state. Shipping chicks or hatching eggs from the mainland has its own rules and paperwork. Check with the department before you order, and buy from NPIP hatcheries when you can. Many keepers buy chicks from local farms and feed stores instead.

Heat, humidity and rain

Hawaii is warm all year at low elevation. Some areas get heavy rain, while leeward sides can be dry and hot. Upcountry areas on Maui and the Big Island get cool nights.

  • Build for airflow. Open, shaded coops work well.
  • Keep the coop dry on wet windward sides. Damp bedding leads to mold and foot problems.
  • Raise the coop and anchor it for storms.
  • Mosquitoes are around all year, and they can spread fowl pox. Reduce standing water near the coop.

Look at heat-tolerant breeds. The Naked Neck sheds heat well, and Leghorns and Easter Eggers do fine too.

Island predators

Hawaii has no raccoons, foxes or coyotes. Instead you deal with mongooses on most islands, feral cats, dogs and rats. Mongooses hunt in the day and eat eggs and chicks. Kauai is known for having few or no established mongooses, which is part of why its wild chickens do so well. Use hardware cloth with small openings, and keep feed sealed so rats do not move in.

Wild chickens and disease

Feral chickens can carry disease and parasites into your yard. Try to keep them away from your flock and its feed. Report sudden deaths or unusual illness to the Hawaii Department of Agriculture.

Selling eggs on the islands

Island eggs are in demand because so much food is shipped in. Small sales are often allowed, but egg rules vary from state to state. Ask the Hawaii Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Common questions about chickens in Hawaii

Can I bring chickens to Hawaii from the mainland?

Possibly, but import rules apply. Contact the Hawaii Department of Agriculture before you ship any birds or eggs.

Are roosters allowed in Hawaii neighborhoods?

It depends on your county and zone. Noise rules are often the deciding factor.

Do I need heat for chicks in Hawaii?

Yes, young chicks still need brooder heat for the first weeks, even in a warm climate.
1499:
Indiana backyard flocks, town by town

Indiana leaves backyard chicken rules to local governments. Indianapolis, Fort Wayne, Evansville, South Bend, Bloomington and smaller towns each decide whether hens are allowed, how many and under what conditions. Many towns that allow hens limit them by lot size and ban roosters. Outside town limits, county zoning applies, and agricultural zones usually allow chickens.

Indiana has a lot of new subdivisions around Indianapolis, especially in Hamilton and Hendricks counties. Most come with covenants. Many ban livestock, and some count chickens as livestock. Read yours before you build.

Who handles bird health in Indiana

Indiana is a little unusual. Animal health is handled by the Indiana State Board of Animal Health, often called BOAH, rather than the department of agriculture. BOAH is the agency to call about bird flu, sudden deaths or other poultry disease. Indiana has a large commercial egg, turkey and duck industry, so disease in backyard flocks gets attention quickly.

  • Get your chicks from an NPIP hatchery.
  • Quarantine new birds for several weeks.
  • Keep wild ducks and geese away from your flock.
  • Report sudden deaths or signs of illness to BOAH or a vet.

Midwest weather, all four seasons

Indiana gets cold winters with snow and ice, hot and humid summers and strong spring storms. Northern Indiana near Lake Michigan sees lake effect snow. Southern Indiana is warmer and more humid. A coop here should be dry, draft-free at roost level and vented near the roof. Anchor it for storm winds.

Dual-purpose American breeds do very well. The Buckeye, developed next door in Ohio, has a pea comb that resists frostbite and is a good forager. Plymouth Rocks and Orpingtons are also common.

Predators on the farm and in town

Raccoons, opossums, foxes, coyotes, skunks, hawks and owls are all common in Indiana. Mink and weasels live near creeks and can fit through tiny gaps. Lock the coop at night and cover vents with hardware cloth.

Before you sell a dozen

Selling a few dozen eggs a week is often allowed, but Indiana, like every state, has its own rules on licensing, labels and how eggs are stored. Ask the state before you set up at a market.

What to do first

  1. Check city and county code.
  2. Read your subdivision covenants.
  3. Save BOAH's contact information.
  4. Find chick sources, like our list of places to buy chicks near Fort Wayne.
  5. Find a poultry vet on the Indiana vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Indiana

Who do I report sick chickens to in Indiana?

The Indiana State Board of Animal Health handles poultry disease reports. A local vet can also help.

Can I keep chickens in Indianapolis?

Indianapolis has allowed hens under its animal rules. Check the current code for limits and setbacks.

Do chickens need a heated coop in Indiana?

Not usually. Cold-hardy breeds do fine in a dry, ventilated coop with unfrozen water.
1500:
Chickens in the top egg state

Iowa produces more eggs than any other state, and it learned a hard lesson in 2015 when bird flu swept through its commercial layer farms. That history still shapes how Iowa thinks about backyard birds. Hens are common and welcome in many towns, but biosecurity is not optional here.

Rules are local

Iowa cities set their own chicken rules. Des Moines, Cedar Rapids, Davenport, Iowa City, Ames and Sioux City each have a different approach. Some require a permit and a cap on hens. Many ban roosters. In rural areas, county zoning usually allows poultry on agricultural land. If you are in a newer subdivision, check the covenants. Our pages on chicken laws in Des Moines and Davenport show how two cities handle it.

Protecting Iowa's flocks

The Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship handles animal disease in the state, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Report sudden deaths, swollen heads, purple combs or a sharp drop in eggs right away.

  • Stick with NPIP hatcheries when you order chicks.
  • Keep wild birds out of the run with a cover.
  • Use dedicated boots for the coop.
  • Do not share equipment with other flocks.
  • If you work at a commercial egg or turkey farm, ask about rules for keeping birds at home.

Iowa State University has good material on this too. See the Iowa State small flock guide.

Cold, wind and humid summers

Iowa winters are cold and windy, with long stretches below freezing. Summers are hot and humid. That means your coop needs to block wind at roost level in winter and still move air in July. Vent high, insulate lightly if you like, and keep bedding dry.

Iowa has its own breed, the Iowa Blue, a hardy dual-purpose bird that handles cold well and forages actively. Wyandottes, Plymouth Rocks and Australorps are also good fits.

Predators

Raccoons are the top threat. Foxes, coyotes, skunks, opossums, mink and weasels are all common, along with red-tailed hawks and great horned owls. Bury hardware cloth around the run edge and lock the coop at night.

Selling your eggs

Small-scale egg sales are often allowed, but rules vary by state and may cover labeling and candling. Check with the Iowa Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship before selling.

Before you start

  1. Check city code and covenants.
  2. Plan for wind, cold and summer heat.
  3. Set up a biosecurity routine from day one.

Common questions about chickens in Iowa

Can I keep chickens in Iowa city limits?

Many Iowa cities allow hens with limits or permits. Check your city's code.

Why is Iowa so strict about bird flu?

Iowa has a huge commercial egg industry. A single outbreak can affect millions of birds, so early reporting matters.

What is the best breed for Iowa winters?

Cold-hardy breeds with small combs, like Iowa Blues and Wyandottes, handle Iowa winters well.
1501:
Wind, weather and local rules in Kansas

Kansas is farm country, and in most rural areas nobody blinks at a flock of hens. Inside cities, the rules come from local code. Wichita, Overland Park, Kansas City, Olathe, Topeka and Lawrence each have their own approach. Many cities allow a small number of hens and limit or ban roosters. Some ask for a permit or set distances from neighbors' homes.

Johnson County suburbs have lots of HOAs, and many of them do not allow poultry. If you have covenants, read them before you buy chicks. Our pages on chicken laws in Topeka and raising chickens in Wichita give two city examples.

The Kansas coop has to handle everything

Kansas weather can swing from over 100 degrees in summer to well below zero with wind chill in winter. Add hail, ice storms and tornadoes. A coop that works here is built tough.

  • Anchor it. Strong winds move light coops. Stake or bolt it down.
  • Block wind at roost height. Prairie wind in winter is harder on birds than still cold air.
  • Vent up high. Even in winter, moisture needs to escape.
  • Shade the run. Summer sun on open prairie is intense.
  • Use a solid roof. Hail can shred light run covers.

Hardy dual-purpose birds suit Kansas well. The Australorp handles heat and cold and lays steadily.

What goes after Kansas chickens

Coyotes are found across the state. Raccoons, skunks, opossums and foxes are common in towns and on farms. Red-tailed hawks and great horned owls hunt open land. Snakes, including bull snakes, raid nests for eggs. Use hardware cloth on vents and the lower run, and close the coop every night.

Bird flu and disease reporting

The Kansas Department of Agriculture handles animal health through its Division of Animal Health. Report sudden deaths or signs of bird flu to them or to a vet. Kansas sits under the Central Flyway, so wild ducks and geese move through every spring and fall. Keep your flock away from ponds they use, cover the run and buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Eggs at the end of the lane

An honor box at the end of a farm lane is a Kansas classic. Small sales like that are often allowed, but egg rules differ by state and can cover licensing and labels. The Kansas Department of Agriculture can tell you what you need.

Kansas checklist

  1. Check your city code or county zoning.
  2. Read any HOA covenants.
  3. Build for wind, hail and temperature swings.
  4. Have a plan for frozen water in winter.

Common questions about chickens in Kansas

Can I keep chickens in Wichita?

Wichita has allowed backyard hens under its code. Check the current rules for limits and permits.

How do I protect chickens during a Kansas tornado warning?

Anchor coops ahead of storm season. During a warning, take care of yourself first. Birds in a sturdy, anchored coop have the best chance.

Do chickens need shade in Kansas?

Yes. Summer heat is a major risk, so shade and lots of water are essential.
1502:
Kentucky flocks, from Louisville to the hills

Kentucky has a long history of farm flocks, and a big commercial broiler industry in the western part of the state. For backyard keepers, the rules are local. Louisville Metro and Lexington-Fayette each have their own codes, and smaller cities set their own as well. Many cities cap hens and restrict roosters. Rural counties often have little zoning that touches chickens at all.

Subdivisions around Louisville, Lexington and northern Kentucky often have deed restrictions. Check them, because they can ban birds even where the city says yes.

What the weather asks of your coop

Kentucky has hot, humid summers and cold but changeable winters. Ice storms happen. Spring brings heavy rain and severe storms. The best coop here moves a lot of air in summer, stays dry year round and blocks drafts at roost level in winter. Put it on high ground so spring rain does not flood the run.

Most common backyard breeds do fine in Kentucky. Heat is the tougher season, so give the run shade and keep water cool. Our page on summer heat chicken care in Lexington has practical tips.

Predators in the Bluegrass and beyond

Raccoons, opossums, foxes, coyotes and skunks are common across the state. Hawks and owls hunt open yards. Black rat snakes take eggs and chicks. In eastern Kentucky, black bears are now present in some counties. Hardware cloth, a buried apron and a locked coop at night stop most losses.

Bird flu and biosecurity

The Kentucky Department of Agriculture houses the Office of the State Veterinarian, which handles poultry disease reporting. Kentucky has a lot of commercial poultry, especially in the west, so report sudden deaths quickly. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, quarantine new adult birds and keep wild waterfowl away from your flock.

The University of Kentucky has good backyard flock resources. See our summary of the UK extension backyard flock resources.

Can you sell eggs in Kentucky?

Many people do. Small-scale egg sales are often allowed, but rules vary by state and can cover registration, labeling and storage. Ask the Kentucky Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Steps before your first chicks

  1. Check your city or county code.
  2. Read your deed restrictions.
  3. Plan for summer heat and spring rain.
  4. Find a vet on the Kentucky poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Kentucky

Can I keep chickens in Louisville?

Louisville Metro has allowed hens under its animal code. Check the current rules for limits and setbacks.

Are roosters allowed in Lexington?

Rules depend on zoning. Many urban residential areas restrict roosters. Check with Lexington-Fayette before you get one.

What do I do if my chickens die suddenly in Kentucky?

Wear gloves, keep the bodies cool and call the Office of the State Veterinarian or a vet.
1503:
Parishes, cities and Louisiana chicken rules

Louisiana is divided into parishes instead of counties, and that is where you look first if you live outside a city. Inside a city, the municipal code decides. New Orleans, Baton Rouge, Shreveport, Lafayette and Lake Charles each set their own rules. Many cities allow hens with limits and ban or restrict roosters. Rural parishes are usually more relaxed.

If you live in a subdivision, read your restrictions. Many south Louisiana neighborhoods have covenants that limit animals. For a city example, see our page on chicken laws in New Orleans.

Heat, humidity and hurricanes

Louisiana is one of the hottest and most humid places in the country to keep chickens. Summers are long and steamy, and heat stress is a constant risk. Hurricanes and flooding add another layer.

  • Open the coop up for airflow. Wire walls on one or two sides are common here.
  • Shade the run completely.
  • Raise the coop off the ground, ideally on legs or blocks, so it stays dry in heavy rain.
  • Anchor everything before hurricane season.
  • Make a plan to move birds if you have to evacuate.

Light, heat-tolerant breeds do well. See our page on breeds for Baton Rouge weather for picks that handle south Louisiana summers.

Swamp predators and more

Raccoons and opossums are the top threats. Snakes, including rat snakes and sometimes venomous species, are common around coops in warm months. Foxes, coyotes, bobcats, hawks and owls are present across the state. Near bayous and ponds, keep birds away from the water's edge, since alligators will take poultry. Mink can also be a problem near water. Our guide to predator proofing in Shreveport covers north Louisiana.

Bird health in Louisiana

The Louisiana Department of Agriculture and Forestry handles animal health, including bird flu reports, through the state veterinarian. Louisiana's marshes are winter home to huge numbers of ducks and geese, so keep wild birds away from your feed and water. Mites, lice and parasites build up fast in warm, damp weather. Check birds often and keep bedding dry.

Selling eggs in Louisiana

If your hens lay more than you can use, selling to neighbors is common and often allowed at a small scale. Louisiana sets its own rules, so ask the Louisiana Department of Agriculture and Forestry about cartons, labels and storage first.

Louisiana starter list

  1. Check city code or parish rules, plus your subdivision covenants.
  2. Build an open, raised, shaded coop.
  3. Plan for hurricanes and evacuation.
  4. Check for mites regularly.

Common questions about chickens in Louisiana

Can I keep chickens in New Orleans?

New Orleans has allowed backyard hens with rules. Check the current city code before you start.

What do I do with my chickens during a hurricane?

Plan ahead. Some keepers move birds to a sturdy building or take them along when they evacuate in crates.

Do Louisiana chickens need a closed coop?

Not really. A coop with good airflow and secure wire walls works better than a sealed box in this heat.
1504:
Maine towns write their own chicken rules

Maine is a state of small towns, and each town has wide power over local land use. So whether you can keep hens, and how many, is decided by your town's zoning ordinance. Portland, Bangor, Lewiston, South Portland and many other towns allow hens in some form, often with limits on numbers and roosters. In rural towns, chickens are often allowed by right.

Maine also passed a food sovereignty law that lets towns adopt local ordinances for direct food sales between neighbors. Some towns have done so. If you plan to sell eggs, ask your town whether it has one, and check with the state too.

Long winters shape everything

Maine winters are long, cold and snowy, especially inland and up north. Coops need to handle it.

  • Build a steep, strong roof for heavy snow.
  • Insulate if you want, but vent near the peak so moisture leaves.
  • Keep water from freezing with a heated base.
  • Give birds a covered run or cleared area so they get out on sunny days.
  • Expect laying to slow in the dark months.

Pick heavy, small-combed breeds. The Brahma has feathered feet and a pea comb and shrugs off cold. Wyandottes and Chanteclers are also good picks.

Woods full of predators

Maine's forests are home to foxes, coyotes, fishers, raccoons, skunks, weasels and mink. Bobcats and black bears are common in many areas. Hawks and owls hunt open yards, and eagles are around along the coast and lakes. Fishers and weasels can kill several birds in one night, so lock the coop and cover gaps with hardware cloth. See our guide to predator proofing in Portland, ME.

Disease and reporting

The Maine Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry handles animal health, including bird flu reports, through the state veterinarian's office. Maine's coast and lakes see lots of wild waterfowl during migration. Cover the run and keep wild birds away from feed. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries and quarantine new birds.

Egg sales

Small-scale egg sales are often allowed, but rules vary by state and by town under Maine's food sovereignty law. Ask the department and your town before you sell.

Before you begin in Maine

  1. Read your town zoning ordinance.
  2. Ask if your town has a local food ordinance.
  3. Plan for snow load and frozen water.
  4. Find a vet on the Maine poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Maine

Can I keep chickens in Portland, Maine?

Portland has allowed backyard hens with limits. Check the current city code.

Do Maine chickens need heat in winter?

Most cold-hardy breeds do not. A dry, ventilated coop and unfrozen water matter more.

Will hens lay in a Maine winter?

Laying usually drops in the darkest months. Some keepers use timed light to keep it going.
1505:
Maryland's county-driven chicken rules

In Maryland, counties carry a lot of weight. Most land use rules come from county zoning, and many counties have detailed rules on poultry in residential zones. Baltimore City is its own jurisdiction with its own rules, and incorporated towns like Annapolis, Frederick and Rockville have their own codes too. Lot size, setbacks and hen limits are common. Roosters are often restricted.

Montgomery, Howard, Anne Arundel and Baltimore counties all handle this differently. Look up your county or city code, then check your HOA. Many Maryland HOAs restrict poultry.

A small state with big poultry

The Eastern Shore is part of the Delmarva broiler region, one of the busiest in the country. That is why the Maryland Department of Agriculture takes bird flu and backyard flock health so seriously. Report sudden deaths or illness to the department or a vet. Choose a hatchery that is in the NPIP program. The Chesapeake Bay draws huge numbers of wintering ducks and geese, so keep wild birds away from your feed and water.

Climate from the bay to the mountains

Central Maryland has hot, humid summers and mild to cold winters. Western Maryland is higher and colder, with real snow. The Eastern Shore is flat, humid and low lying, so flooding and storm surge are concerns near the water.

  • Vent the coop well for humid summers.
  • Raise it off the ground in low areas.
  • Plan for snow load in the western counties.

Most common backyard breeds do well in central Maryland. The Sussex is a calm, friendly bird that handles heat and cold well and suits suburban yards.

Predators

Red foxes, raccoons, opossums and hawks are the most common threats. Coyotes are now spread across the state. Black bears live in western Maryland. Near the bay, mink and river otters can raid coops close to water. Lock up at night and use hardware cloth. Our guide on predator proofing coops in Baltimore covers city and suburb issues.

A note on egg sales

Maryland keepers often sell a few dozen at work or from home. Small-scale sales are often allowed, but egg rules differ between states, and Maryland may expect registration. Ask the Maryland Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Checklist for Maryland keepers

  1. Find your county or city zoning rules for poultry.
  2. Read your HOA covenants.
  3. Plan for heat and humidity, and for snow in the west.
  4. Read our guide to raising chickens in Annapolis for a local example.

Common questions about chickens in Maryland

Can I keep chickens in Baltimore City?

Baltimore City has allowed hens with rules and limits. Check the current city code before you start.

Does Maryland require registering backyard chickens?

Maryland has had registration rules for poultry owners. Check with the Maryland Department of Agriculture for current requirements.

Are roosters allowed in Maryland suburbs?

Many counties restrict roosters in residential zones. Check your county code.
1506:
Massachusetts and the board of health

In Massachusetts, chickens are mostly a town matter, and the local board of health often plays a big role. Many towns require a permit from the board of health to keep animals, including hens. Zoning bylaws may also set lot size, setbacks and limits. Boston, Cambridge, Somerville, Worcester and Springfield each have their own rules, and smaller towns can be very different from one another.

So start with two calls. Ask the town's board of health whether you need a keeping permit. Then ask the building or zoning office about setbacks and coop rules. If you live in a condo or HOA, check those rules too. Our page on raising chickens in Boston shows how one city approaches it.

Old breeds for a cold state

Massachusetts gave the world the Plymouth Rock, one of the classic American breeds. It is still one of the best birds for New England. Barred Rocks lay well, handle cold, and are calm in a backyard. Rhode Island Reds, Wyandottes and Buff Orpingtons are also common choices.

Weather on the coast and inland

Winters are cold and snowy, especially in central and western Massachusetts. The coast gets nor'easters, heavy wet snow and the odd hurricane. Summers can be hot and humid for a few weeks.

  • Build a roof that can hold wet snow.
  • Vent high so the coop stays dry.
  • Block drafts at roost level.
  • Have a heated waterer for January and February.

New England predators

Foxes, coyotes, raccoons, skunks and fishers are found across the state, even in suburbs. Hawks and owls are common. Black bears are spreading east from the western part of the state. Bobcats show up too. Lock the coop at night, use hardware cloth and do not leave feed out.

Bird flu and who to call

The Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources, called MDAR, handles animal health at the state level, including bird flu. Report sudden deaths or signs of illness to MDAR or a vet. The coast and inland ponds draw wild ducks and geese, so keep your flock away from them. Buy from NPIP hatcheries and quarantine new birds.

Egg money in Massachusetts

Selling eggs from a small flock is often allowed, but rules vary by state and your town may have its own say. Ask MDAR and your local board of health before you sell.

Massachusetts steps

  1. Call your board of health about permits.
  2. Check zoning setbacks and limits.
  3. Find chicks, for example from sources near Worcester.
  4. Plan for snow, cold and predators.

Common questions about chickens in Massachusetts

Do I need a permit to keep chickens in Massachusetts?

Many towns require a board of health permit. Some also require zoning approval. Ask your town.

Can I keep chickens in Boston?

Boston has allowed hens in some areas with rules. Check the current city zoning and permits.

What breeds handle a Massachusetts winter?

Plymouth Rocks, Wyandottes and Rhode Island Reds all do well in a dry, draft-free coop.
1507:
Michigan, Right to Farm and backyard hens

For years, some Michigan keepers argued that the state's Right to Farm Act protected backyard flocks from local bans. That changed in 2014, when the state updated its siting standards for livestock. Since then, Right to Farm protections generally do not cover animals in primarily residential areas. In practice, that means your city or township ordinance is what decides whether you can keep hens in a neighborhood.

Michigan has cities, villages and townships, and each can write its own rules. Ann Arbor, Lansing, Grand Rapids, Detroit and many suburbs allow hens in some form, often with a permit, a hen limit and no roosters. Townships with agricultural zoning usually allow more. Our page on chicken laws in Lansing shows a city example.

Where to check

  • Your city, village or township code.
  • The zoning map, to see if your lot is residential or agricultural.
  • Your HOA or condo rules.
  • The Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development, called MDARD, for state animal health rules.

Lake effect winters

Michigan winters are cold and long, and areas near the Great Lakes get heavy lake effect snow. The Upper Peninsula is colder still. Build a coop with a strong roof, high vents and draft-free roosts. Keep water from freezing with a heated base. Cold-hardy breeds like the Chantecler, bred in Canada for brutal winters, do very well. Wyandottes and Buckeyes are also great choices. See our tips on winter chicken care in Detroit.

Predators in the Great Lakes State

Raccoons, foxes, coyotes, skunks and opossums are common. Mink and weasels live near water and can slip through small gaps. Hawks and owls are year round threats. In northern Michigan and the UP, black bears, bobcats and fishers add to the list. Lock up at night and use hardware cloth.

Bird flu and MDARD

MDARD handles poultry disease reporting, including bird flu. Michigan's lakes and wetlands draw lots of wild waterfowl. Keep them away from your flock and its water. Report sudden deaths to MDARD or a vet. Buy from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling eggs

Plenty of Michigan keepers sell a few dozen eggs a week. Small-scale sales are often allowed, but rules vary by state and can cover licensing, cartons and storage. Check with MDARD before selling.

Michigan quick list

  1. Check city, village or township code.
  2. Confirm your zoning district.
  3. Plan for snow and frozen water.

Common questions about chickens in Michigan

Does Right to Farm protect backyard chickens in Michigan?

Generally not in primarily residential areas since the 2014 change. Local ordinances decide.

Can I keep chickens in Detroit?

Detroit's rules have changed over time. Check the current city code and any permit requirements.

What breeds handle Michigan winters best?

Small-combed, cold-hardy breeds like Chanteclers, Wyandottes and Buckeyes.
1508:
Missouri hens, cities and the Ozarks

Missouri leaves chicken rules to its cities and counties. Kansas City, St. Louis, Springfield, Columbia and Independence each have their own codes. Many cities allow a few hens and limit or ban roosters. Some ask for a permit or set distances from neighbors' homes. St. Louis City and St. Louis County are separate governments with separate rules, which surprises a lot of newcomers. Outside cities, many Missouri counties have little or no zoning that affects backyard birds.

Subdivisions often have covenants that restrict poultry. Read yours before you buy a coop. For a city example, see chicken laws in Springfield, MO.

Built for Missouri's mix of weather

Missouri gets hot, humid summers and cold winters with ice storms. Spring storms and tornadoes are part of life, especially in the southwest. The coop has to do a lot.

  • Shade and lots of air in summer.
  • Draft-free roosts and dry bedding in winter.
  • Solid anchoring for spring storms.
  • Good drainage, since Ozark and river valley soils can get muddy fast.

The Dominique, one of America's oldest breeds, is a smart pick. It has a rose comb that resists frostbite, handles heat reasonably well and forages hard.

Predators

Raccoons and opossums are the top night raiders. Coyotes, foxes, bobcats, skunks and mink are common. Hawks work open yards by day and owls take over at night. Snakes take eggs in summer. In southern Missouri, black bears are growing in number. Our guide to predator proofing in St. Louis covers the basics.

Bird flu and the state veterinarian

The Missouri Department of Agriculture handles animal health through the state veterinarian's office. Report sudden deaths or signs of bird flu. Missouri is on the Mississippi Flyway, and wild ducks and geese pass through each spring and fall. Keep them away from your flock. Missouri has commercial turkey and broiler farms too, so early reporting protects them as well. NPIP hatcheries are the safest place to buy chicks.

Thinking about selling eggs?

Small sales to neighbors are often allowed. Missouri has its own rules on licensing and labeling, and they are not the same as in nearby states. Ask the Missouri Department of Agriculture before you start.

Missouri start list

  1. Check your city or county rules. Remember St. Louis City and County are separate.
  2. Read HOA covenants.
  3. Plan for heat, ice and storms.
  4. Line the coop and run with hardware cloth.

Common questions about chickens in Missouri

Can I keep chickens in Kansas City, Missouri?

Kansas City has allowed hens with rules. Look up the latest version of the city code.

Are roosters legal in Missouri?

There is no simple statewide answer. Many cities ban roosters while rural counties usually allow them.

Do I need a permit for chickens in Missouri?

Some cities require one. Rural areas usually do not. Check with your city or county.
1509:
Minnesota cities and the permit question

Minnesota leaves backyard poultry to cities and townships. A lot of Minnesota cities allow hens, but many of them want a permit first. Minneapolis and St. Paul have both used permit systems, and some suburbs have asked for neighbor notice or consent as part of the process. Hen limits and rooster bans are common. Rural townships and county agricultural zones are usually more relaxed.

Read your city code, then your HOA or townhome rules. Our page on raising chickens in St. Paul gives a good example of how a big Minnesota city handles it.

The real test is January

Minnesota winters are long and hard. Temperatures can stay below zero for days, especially up north. Chickens can handle this, but only in the right coop.

  • Dry beats warm. Moisture causes frostbite. Vent near the roof, even in deep cold.
  • No drafts at the roost. Air should move above the birds, not across them.
  • Wide roosts. A flat 2x4 lets birds cover their toes with their feathers.
  • Heated water. Most Minnesota keepers use a heated base.
  • Deep litter. Many keepers use the deep litter method for extra warmth.

The University of Minnesota has strong advice on this. See our summary of U of M guidance on chickens in cold weather. Small-combed, heavy breeds do best. The Icelandic is a hardy landrace bred for cold, and Wyandottes and Brahmas are popular too.

Predators

Raccoons, foxes, coyotes, skunks, weasels and mink are all common. Great horned owls hunt in winter, and hawks hunt year round. In northern Minnesota, fishers, bobcats, wolves and black bears are present. Hardware cloth and a locked coop stop most problems.

Turkey country and bird flu

Minnesota raises more turkeys than any other state, and it was hit hard by bird flu in 2015 and again in later years. The Minnesota Board of Animal Health handles poultry disease in the state and is the agency to call about sick or dead birds. Minnesota also runs NPIP through the Board. Buy from NPIP sources, keep wild ducks and geese away and do not share equipment with other flocks.

Eggs and the rules around them

Selling a few dozen to friends is common, and small sales are often allowed. Minnesota has its own rules on licensing, grading and labels, and they differ from other states. Ask the Minnesota Department of Agriculture what applies to your flock.

Getting started in Minnesota

  1. Check city code and permit rules.
  2. Ask whether neighbor consent is needed.
  3. Build for dry, draft-free winter housing.
  4. Choose cold-hardy breeds.

Common questions about chickens in Minnesota

Do I need a permit for chickens in Minneapolis?

Minneapolis has required a permit for backyard poultry. Check the city's current rules and fees.

How cold is too cold for chickens in Minnesota?

Healthy cold-hardy birds can handle below zero if the coop is dry and draft-free. Watch combs and wattles for frostbite.

Should I heat my coop in a Minnesota winter?

Most keepers do not. Heaters are a fire risk. Focus on ventilation, dry bedding and unfrozen water.
1510:
Backyard chickens in Mississippi

Mississippi is a big poultry state, with a large commercial broiler industry. Backyard flocks are part of everyday life in much of the state, especially in rural areas where there may be no zoning at all. Inside cities like Jackson, Gulfport, Hattiesburg, Southaven and Tupelo, your city code decides. Many cities cap hens and restrict roosters. A few want a permit first.

Subdivisions often come with covenants that ban poultry, especially in suburbs around Jackson and along the coast. Check those first.

Who to call about sick birds

Mississippi handles livestock and poultry health through the Mississippi Board of Animal Health, which is the agency for bird flu reporting. Because the state has so many commercial chicken houses, early reporting of backyard illness matters a lot. Buy from NPIP hatcheries. Quarantine new birds. If you work in a commercial poultry operation, check whether your employer allows backyard birds.

Mississippi State University has helpful guides too. See our summary of MSU's guide to starting a flock.

Built for heat

Mississippi summers are long, hot and very humid. Heat stress is the biggest weather risk. A good coop here:

  • Sits in shade, ideally under trees on the west side.
  • Has big vents or wire walls for airflow.
  • Keeps bedding dry, since humidity breeds mold and mites.
  • Is anchored for storms. The coast faces hurricanes, and tornadoes happen statewide.

Light, active breeds handle the heat well. The Andalusian and Leghorn are good examples. See our page on breeds for Jackson weather for more ideas.

Predators

Raccoons and opossums are the main night threats. Snakes are common in the warm months and love eggs. Foxes, coyotes, bobcats, hawks and owls round out the list. Near water, watch for mink. Hardware cloth and a locked coop are the best defense.

Fire ants are a smaller but real problem. They can attack chicks, sick birds and hens sitting on eggs. Keep brooders off the ground, treat mounds near the coop with a product labeled for use around animals, and follow the label.

Selling eggs from a backyard flock

Many Mississippi keepers sell a few dozen to church friends or neighbors. Small sales are often allowed, but egg rules vary by state. The Mississippi Department of Agriculture and Commerce can tell you what applies to labels and storage.

Mississippi checklist

  1. Check city code or county rules, and your covenants.
  2. Save the Board of Animal Health contact info.
  3. Plan for shade, airflow and storms.
  4. Use small mesh against snakes.

Common questions about chickens in Mississippi

Can I keep chickens in Jackson, Mississippi?

Rules depend on the current city code and your zoning. Check with the city before you start.

Do Mississippi chickens need heat lamps?

Adult birds rarely need them, and they are a fire risk in a dusty coop. Chicks do need brooder heat for their first weeks.

How do I keep snakes out of my chicken coop?

Use hardware cloth with small openings, seal gaps and collect eggs every day.
1511:
Two very different Nevadas

Most Nevadans live in one of two places. Las Vegas and Henderson sit in the low Mojave Desert, with brutal summers and mild winters. Reno, Sparks and Carson City sit in the high desert, with hot dry summers and cold, snowy winters. Your coop and breed choices depend on which one you live in.

How the rules work

Cities and counties set chicken rules in Nevada. Clark County, Las Vegas, Henderson, North Las Vegas, Reno, Sparks and Washoe County each have their own approach. Lot size and zoning district often decide how many birds you can keep, and roosters are often restricted in residential zones. Some areas require a permit.

HOAs are everywhere in southern Nevada. Many ban poultry outright. Read your CC&Rs before you buy chicks.

Las Vegas heat

Summers in the Las Vegas valley regularly pass 110 degrees. That is dangerous for chickens. To keep birds alive:

  • Shade the entire run, not just part of it.
  • Give several large waterers and refill with cool water often.
  • Use misters. In dry desert air they cool well.
  • Open the coop for airflow. Do not insulate it shut.
  • Pick heat-tolerant breeds like Leghorns or Egyptian Fayoumis.

Our page on summer heat care in Las Vegas goes into detail.

Reno and the high desert

Northern Nevada needs a coop that handles both heat and cold. Summer days get hot, but nights cool off fast. Winters bring snow, freezing nights and strong wind. Build a coop that vents well, blocks wind at roost level and has a roof that can hold snow. Cold-hardy breeds suit this area better. See our coop ideas for Reno backyards.

Desert predators

Coyotes live in and around every Nevada city. Hawks, owls and ravens are common. Bobcats and foxes appear on the edges of town, and raccoons and skunks live in Reno. Snakes, including rattlesnakes, come for rodents and eggs. Keep feed sealed and use hardware cloth.

Bird health

The Nevada Department of Agriculture handles animal disease, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Report sudden deaths. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries and keep wild birds away from water and feed.

Eggs for sale in Nevada

Selling a few dozen to neighbors is often fine, but Nevada writes its own egg rules, so ask the Nevada Department of Agriculture before you take money. Keep eggs cool, since a Nevada summer will spoil them fast.

Common questions about chickens in Nevada

Can I keep chickens in Las Vegas?

It depends on your zoning, lot size and HOA. Some areas allow hens and many HOAs do not.

How do I keep chickens cool in a Nevada summer?

Full shade, misters, lots of cool water and an open coop. Watch for panting and wings held away from the body.

Do Reno chickens need winter protection?

Yes. A dry, draft-free coop and unfrozen water get them through Reno winters.
1512:
Chickens in big sky country

Montana has a lot of open land and a lot of people who keep chickens on it. If you live outside city limits, county zoning often allows poultry, and in some areas there may be no zoning at all. In towns like Billings, Missoula, Bozeman, Great Falls, Helena and Kalispell, the city code decides. Many towns allow a limited number of hens and restrict roosters. Some ask for a permit.

Fast growth around Bozeman and the Flathead Valley has brought many new subdivisions with covenants. Some ban poultry. Read your covenants before you buy birds.

Bears change the plan

In much of western Montana, bears are the predator that matters most. Black bears are common, and grizzlies range across parts of the state. Chickens and their feed can draw bears onto your property, which is bad for you and for the bear. In bear country:

  • Store feed in sealed containers inside a locked building.
  • Use electric fencing around the coop and run.
  • Clean up spilled feed and do not leave scraps out.
  • Follow any local bear rules. Some communities have their own.

Other predators include coyotes, foxes, raccoons, skunks, weasels, mink, bobcats, mountain lions, hawks, owls and golden eagles. Our page on predator-proofing basics is a good start.

Winter that means it

Montana winters bring deep cold, wind and snow. East of the mountains, chinook winds can raise temperatures fast and then drop them again. Coops need to be dry, draft-free at the roost and vented high. Plan for snow load and heated water. Choose cold-hardy breeds with small combs, like Wyandottes, Brahmas or Chanteclers.

Bird flu and the Department of Livestock

In Montana, animal health falls under the Montana Department of Livestock rather than a general agriculture department. It handles poultry disease reporting, including bird flu. Montana's rivers and wetlands host many migrating ducks and geese, so keep wild birds away from your flock. Pick NPIP hatcheries and keep newcomers separate at first.

Selling eggs in Montana

Fresh eggs sell well in small towns where the grocery store is a long drive away. Small sales are often allowed, but each state sets its own egg rules, and they can change. Check with the state before you sell at a market or from home.

Before you start in Montana

  1. Check city code or county zoning, plus covenants.
  2. If you are in bear country, plan feed storage and electric fencing first.
  3. Build for snow, cold and wind.
  4. Find a vet on the Montana poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Montana

Will chickens attract bears in Montana?

They can, mostly because of feed. Sealed feed storage and electric fencing reduce the risk a lot.

Who do I report sick chickens to in Montana?

The Montana Department of Livestock handles animal disease reports. A local vet can help too.

Can chickens survive a Montana winter outside?

Cold-hardy breeds can, with a dry, draft-free coop, wide roosts and water that does not freeze.
1513:
Nebraska rules for city and farm flocks
