Nebraska is farm country, and in rural areas chickens are often allowed with few rules. In town, the city code decides. Omaha, Lincoln, Bellevue, Grand Island and Kearney each have their own approach. Many Nebraska cities allow a small number of hens. Some require a permit. Roosters are often restricted in residential areas.

Suburban developments around Omaha and Lincoln often have covenants that limit animals. If you have an HOA, read the rules before you start.

Prairie weather

Nebraska weather is hard on coops. Winters are cold and windy, with blizzards that drift snow. Summers are hot, and storms can bring hail and tornadoes.

  • Wind is the enemy. Face the coop door away from the north and west, and block drafts at roost height.
  • Snow drifts. Place the coop where drifts will not bury the door.
  • Hail. Use a solid roof over the run.
  • Summer heat. Add shade and keep water cool.
  • Anchoring. Tie the coop down for storm season.
  • Ice. Freezing rain can seal pop doors and waterers, so check them each morning.

Our page on breeds for Omaha weather covers good picks. Hardy dual-purpose birds like Plymouth Rocks, Wyandottes and Australorps are popular.

Prairie predators

Raccoons, coyotes, foxes, skunks, opossums, mink and weasels are common. Hawks and owls hunt open land. Bull snakes raid nests. Use hardware cloth, bury an apron around the run and lock the coop every night. See our guide to predator proofing in Lincoln.

Bird flu on the Central Flyway

Nebraska sits under the Central Flyway, and huge numbers of geese, ducks and cranes pass through each spring, especially along the Platte River. That raises bird flu risk. The Nebraska Department of Agriculture handles animal health, including bird flu reporting, through the state veterinarian. Cover the run, keep your flock off ponds and report sudden deaths. Nebraska also has commercial egg farms, so early reports matter. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Your extra eggs

Nebraska keepers often sell to coworkers and neighbors, and small sales like that are usually allowed. Some sellers may need a license, though, and rules differ from state to state. Ask the Nebraska Department of Agriculture first.

Nebraska starter list

  1. Check city code and any permit rules.
  2. Read HOA covenants.
  3. Plan for wind, snow drifts and hail.
  4. Find chick sources, like our list of places to buy chicks near Lincoln.

Common questions about chickens in Nebraska

Can I keep chickens in Omaha?

Omaha has allowed backyard hens under its rules. Check the current city code for limits and permits.

Do Nebraska chickens need a heated coop?

Usually not. Block the wind, keep the coop dry and use a heated waterer. Healthy, fully feathered birds handle Nebraska cold well.

Why does bird flu hit Nebraska in spring?

Spring migration brings huge numbers of wild waterfowl through the state, and they can carry the virus.
1514:
New Hampshire towns, zoning and hens

New Hampshire is known for local control, and backyard chickens are no exception. Each town and city sets its own rules through zoning. Many rural towns allow chickens by right. Larger places like Manchester, Nashua, Concord, Portsmouth and Dover have more detailed rules on hen limits, setbacks and roosters. In some places you need a permit. Our page on chicken laws in Manchester gives a city example.

If your town has a planning or zoning board, call them first. Ask about poultry in your zone. Then check any HOA or condo rules.

The state's own bird

The New Hampshire Red was developed here from Rhode Island Reds, bred for faster growth and early laying. It is a hardy, friendly, dual-purpose bird that handles cold winters well. It is a natural choice for a New Hampshire flock, along with Plymouth Rocks, Wyandottes and Buff Orpingtons.

Winter in the Granite State

Winters are long and snowy, especially in the White Mountains and the north. Even the seacoast gets cold snaps and nor'easters. Build a coop that:

  • Has a steep, strong roof for snow.
  • Vents near the peak so moisture leaves.
  • Keeps drafts off the roost.
  • Has a heated waterer for the coldest months.

Mud season in spring is real too. Put the coop and run on high, well drained ground.

Forest predators

New Hampshire is heavily wooded. Foxes, coyotes, raccoons, skunks, fishers, weasels and mink are all common. Black bears are widespread and drawn to feed, so store it inside. Bobcats are seen in many towns. Hawks and owls hunt in daylight and at dusk. Lock the coop at night and cover openings with hardware cloth.

Disease and reporting

The New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food handles animal health through the state veterinarian. If birds die suddenly or look like they have bird flu, report it. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, and keep wild ducks and geese away from your flock. UNH Extension has solid advice too. See our summary of UNH's guide to small poultry flocks.

Before you sell eggs

A small flock often lays more than one family can eat, and selling the extras is commonly allowed. Each state sets its own egg rules, though, so ask the New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food what labels and storage it expects.

New Hampshire checklist

  1. Call your town zoning office.
  2. Check HOA or condo rules.
  3. Plan for snow, mud season and bears.
  4. Pick cold-hardy birds.

Common questions about chickens in New Hampshire

Do I need a permit for chickens in New Hampshire?

Some towns require one and many rural towns do not. Ask your town zoning office.

What is the difference between a New Hampshire Red and a Rhode Island Red?

New Hampshire Reds were bred from Rhode Island Reds. They are usually lighter in color and mature a bit faster.

How do I keep bears away from my chickens?

Store feed indoors in sealed bins and use electric fencing around the coop.
1515:
Chickens at altitude in New Mexico

New Mexico has a long tradition of backyard and small farm flocks, especially in rural and village communities. Rules are local. Albuquerque, Santa Fe, Las Cruces, Rio Rancho and Roswell each set their own limits through city code. Many cities allow a few hens. Roosters are often restricted or need special permission. County zoning covers unincorporated land, and rural parcels are often zoned for animals.

Newer developments, especially around Albuquerque and Rio Rancho, often have HOAs that restrict poultry. Read your covenants. Our page on raising chickens in Albuquerque covers the state's biggest city.

Sun, wind and cold nights

Much of New Mexico sits at high elevation. That means strong sun, dry air, wind and big swings between day and night. Summers in the south and the low valleys get very hot. The north and mountains get real winters with snow.

  • Shade the run. UV at altitude is strong.
  • Vent the coop for hot days, but block wind at the roost for cold nights.
  • Keep plenty of water out. Dry air dehydrates birds fast.
  • Dust bathing is easy here, so give birds a dry spot to do it.
  • Anchor the coop. Spring winds are strong.

In the southern deserts, heat-tolerant birds like the Egyptian Fayoumi or Leghorns work well. In the north, cold-hardy dual-purpose breeds are a better fit.

Predators

Coyotes are found everywhere. Bobcats, foxes, raccoons, skunks, hawks and owls are common. Snakes, including rattlesnakes, come for rodents and eggs. In mountain areas, black bears and mountain lions are present. Seal feed, use hardware cloth and close the coop at night.

Bird flu and animal health

Animal health in New Mexico is handled by the state veterinarian through the New Mexico Livestock Board. If you see sudden deaths or signs of bird flu, report it or call a vet. Wild ducks, geese and cranes winter along the Rio Grande, so keep your birds away from them. Source new birds from NPIP hatcheries.

Eggs and the market

Fresh eggs sell well at markets in Santa Fe, Albuquerque and small towns alike. Small sales are often allowed, but the rules vary by state. Ask the New Mexico Department of Agriculture first.

Start here

  1. Check city or county rules and your HOA.
  2. Plan for sun, wind and cold nights.
  3. Seal feed and protect against snakes.
  4. Find a vet on the New Mexico poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in New Mexico

Can I keep a rooster in Albuquerque?

Rooster rules depend on the current city code and any permit requirements. Check with the city before you get one.

Does altitude affect chicken health?

Healthy birds adapt. Strong sun and dry air are the bigger issues, so give shade and lots of water.

What breeds do well in New Mexico?

Heat-tolerant breeds suit the south. Cold-hardy dual-purpose breeds suit the north and mountains.
1516:
Over 500 towns, over 500 sets of rules

New Jersey has more than 500 municipalities, and each one can write its own animal rules. That makes the Garden State one of the most local places in the country for chicken law. Some towns welcome hens with a simple permit. Others ban them outright on small lots. Many set limits on numbers, require a coop setback from property lines and ban roosters.

The easiest way to find your answer is to search your town's code for "poultry" and "fowl", or call the town clerk. Then check any HOA, condo or co-op rules.

The Jersey Giant

New Jersey gave its name to the Jersey Giant, one of the largest chicken breeds. It was developed in the state as a meat bird. Today it is a calm, gentle backyard bird that lays brown eggs and handles cold well. It needs more space and stronger roosts than smaller breeds, so plan for that if you want one.

Weather from the shore to the hills

New Jersey summers are hot and humid, especially in the south and along the I-95 corridor. Winters are cold, with snow that gets heavier in the northwest. The shore deals with nor'easters, hurricanes and flooding.

  • Vent high and shade the run for summer.
  • Raise the coop and anchor it in flood or storm zones.
  • Plan for snow load in the north.

Our tips on summer heat care in Trenton cover the hottest weeks.

Predators, even in dense suburbs

Raccoons, red foxes, opossums and skunks are common in almost every New Jersey town. Hawks are a big daytime threat in suburbs. Black bears are common in the northwest and have been seen across much of the state. Coyotes are spreading too. Rats are a constant issue in dense areas. See our guide to predator proofing in Jersey City.

Bird flu and the state

The New Jersey Department of Agriculture handles animal health, including bird flu. Report sudden deaths or illness. New Jersey's marshes and bays draw lots of wild waterfowl, so cover your run and keep wild birds away from feed. Choose NPIP sources and quarantine birds from swaps or sales.

Can I sell my eggs in New Jersey?

Often yes, at a small scale. New Jersey has its own egg rules on cartons and storage, which are not always the same as in New York or Pennsylvania. Check with the New Jersey Department of Agriculture before you sell.

New Jersey to-do list

  1. Search your town code or call the clerk.
  2. Check HOA, condo or co-op rules.
  3. Plan for heat, storms and bears.
  4. Store feed so rats cannot get in.

Common questions about chickens in New Jersey

Are backyard chickens legal in New Jersey?

It depends on your town. Many allow hens with limits and some do not allow them at all.

Do I need a permit for chickens in New Jersey?

Some towns require one. Your town clerk or code can tell you.

Are Jersey Giants good for small yards?

They are calm, but very large. They need more space than standard breeds.
1517:
From the mountains to the Outer Banks

North Carolina stretches from the Blue Ridge to the coast, and keeping chickens looks different at each end. The rules are local everywhere. Charlotte, Raleigh, Durham, Greensboro, Asheville, Wilmington and Winston-Salem each set their own limits, permits and rooster rules. Counties handle unincorporated land, and many rural counties are relaxed about poultry. HOAs in the fast-growing suburbs around Charlotte and the Triangle often restrict or ban birds, so read your covenants.

For examples of city rules, see our pages on chicken laws in Wilmington and Winston-Salem.

Three climates, three coop plans

Mountains

Western North Carolina gets real winters, with snow and ice at higher elevations. Coops need draft-free roosts, high vents and roofs that hold snow. Cold-hardy birds do well. Black bears are common, so store feed indoors.

Piedmont

The middle of the state has hot, humid summers and mild winters with occasional ice storms. Shade and airflow come first. Our page on summer heat care in Raleigh covers the worst weeks.

Coast

Eastern North Carolina is hot, humid and exposed to hurricanes and flooding. Raise the coop off the ground, anchor it and have an evacuation plan for your birds.

Who is hunting your hens

Raccoons, opossums, foxes, coyotes and hawks are common statewide. Rat snakes are a regular threat to eggs and chicks. Bobcats live in rural areas. Black bears range across the mountains and much of the coastal plain. Use hardware cloth and lock up at night. See our guide to predator proofing in Charlotte.

Bird flu in a top poultry state

North Carolina is one of the biggest poultry states in the country, with large turkey and broiler industries. The North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, through the state veterinarian, handles poultry disease. Report sudden deaths or signs of bird flu right away. Buy from NPIP hatcheries and keep wild waterfowl away from your flock, especially in the east where many ducks and geese winter.

Egg sales in North Carolina

Selling a few dozen from home is common. Small sales are often allowed, but North Carolina may require a license or specific labeling, and rules differ by state. Check with the North Carolina Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services before you sell.

Before chicks come home

  1. Check city or county code and your HOA.
  2. Plan for your region's climate.
  3. Seal feed if you live in bear country.
  4. Know how to report sick birds.

Common questions about chickens in North Carolina

Can I keep chickens in Charlotte?

Charlotte has allowed hens with rules on numbers and coop placement. Read the current code before you build.

Do I need a permit for chickens in North Carolina?

Some cities require one and many rural areas do not. Ask your city or county.

What do I do with chickens during a hurricane?

Anchor the coop, move birds to a secure building if you can, and plan ahead if you need to evacuate.
1518:
Keeping chickens on the northern plains

North Dakota has some of the coldest winters in the lower 48 and a lot of wind to go with them. It also has a strong farm culture, so chickens are common on rural land. Inside cities like Fargo, Bismarck, Grand Forks, Minot and West Fargo, the city code decides. Many cities allow a limited number of hens and restrict roosters. Some require a permit or a minimum distance from neighbors' homes. Outside city limits, county and township zoning applies, and agricultural land usually allows poultry.

New subdivisions in growing cities often have covenants. Check them before you buy chicks.

What a North Dakota winter demands

Below zero for days on end, blizzards and strong wind are normal. Chickens can handle it, but they need help.

  • Block the wind. Face the door and run away from the prevailing wind. Add a windbreak if you can.
  • Keep it dry. Vent near the roof. Wet air is what causes frostbite.
  • Wide, flat roosts. Birds can cover their feet while they sleep.
  • Heated water. A heated base is close to required.
  • Snow. Place the coop where drifts will not bury the door.

Small-combed, heavy breeds do best. The Wyandotte has a rose comb and dense feathers. Brahmas, Chanteclers and Buckeyes are also good picks.

Summers are short but can still get hot, so the coop needs to open up for airflow in July too.

Predators

Red foxes, coyotes, raccoons, skunks, weasels and mink are all common. Great horned owls and hawks hunt year round. Our guide to predator proofing in Fargo covers the basics for the Red River Valley.

Bird flu and reporting

North Dakota is on a major migration path, and its prairie potholes and wetlands host huge numbers of ducks and geese. That makes bird flu a real risk for backyard flocks in spring and fall. The North Dakota Department of Agriculture handles animal health through the state veterinarian. Report sudden deaths. Keep your flock away from wild waterfowl, cover the run and buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling a few eggs

Selling extras to neighbors is common and usually allowed on a small scale. North Dakota sets its own rules, so ask the North Dakota Department of Agriculture what applies before you sell.

Your checklist

  1. Check city code or county zoning, and covenants.
  2. Build for wind, snow and deep cold.
  3. Plan for heated water.
  4. Find a vet on the North Dakota poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in North Dakota

Can chickens survive a North Dakota winter?

Yes, with cold-hardy breeds, a dry, draft-free coop and unfrozen water.

Can I keep chickens in Fargo?

Fargo has allowed backyard hens under its rules. Look at the current code for hen limits and any permit.

Should I use a heat lamp in my North Dakota coop?

Most keepers avoid them because of fire risk. Good ventilation, dry bedding and wind protection work better.
1519:
New York City is not the rest of New York

New York may be the most varied state on this list for chicken keeping. In New York City, hens are allowed, but roosters are not. Upstate, rules change from city to city and town to town, and plenty of rural towns allow chickens by right. Long Island towns and villages set their own rules, often with lot size and setback limits.

New York has cities, towns and villages, and a village inside a town can have different rules from the town around it. To find your answer, look up your local code, then check any HOA, condo or co-op rules. Our page on chicken laws in Yonkers gives one example.

Weather by region

  • Western and central New York. Lake effect snow off Lake Erie and Lake Ontario can bury coops. Build a strong roof and keep the door clear. See our page on breeds for Rochester weather.
  • North Country and Adirondacks. Some of the coldest temperatures in the Northeast. Cold-hardy breeds and heated water are a must.
  • Hudson Valley and Long Island. Milder winters, humid summers and coastal storms.
  • New York City. Heat in summer, limited space and lots of rats.

Predators from Brooklyn to the Adirondacks

In the city, rats and raccoons are the main problems, and hawks hunt from rooftops. Upstate, add foxes, coyotes, fishers, weasels, mink, skunks, owls and black bears. Lock the coop each night and use hardware cloth with small openings. Store feed in metal cans with tight lids. Our guide to predator proofing in New York covers city coops.

Bird flu and the state

The New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets handles animal health, including bird flu reports, through the state veterinarian. New York has commercial poultry and many live bird markets, so the state watches disease closely. Call the department about sudden deaths or sick birds. Start with NPIP chicks and keep new adult birds apart for a few weeks. Keep wild waterfowl away from your flock.

Farm stand eggs

Farm stands are common upstate, and small egg sales are often permitted. The rules are set state by state, though. Ask the Department of Agriculture and Markets what applies before you sell at a stand or market.

Starting out in New York

  1. Find out if you are in a city, town or village, and read that code.
  2. In NYC, plan for hens only.
  3. Check HOA, co-op or lease rules.
  4. Build for your region's snow and cold.

Common questions about chickens in New York

Can I keep chickens in New York City?

Yes, hens are allowed in New York City. Roosters are not. Your building, lease or co-op may still forbid them.

Do I need a permit for chickens in upstate New York?

Some cities and villages require one. Many rural towns do not. Check your local code.

How do I handle lake effect snow with chickens?

Build a strong, steep roof, keep paths and the coop door shoveled and give birds a covered run.
1520:
Oklahoma chickens and the weather that tests them

Oklahoma has a deep farm culture, and backyard flocks are common across the state. The rules are local. Oklahoma City, Tulsa, Norman, Broken Arrow, Edmond and Lawton each have their own code for hens, roosters and coops. Many cities allow a few hens with limits and restrict roosters. A permit is required in some cities. Rural areas outside city limits are usually far more relaxed.

Suburbs around OKC and Tulsa often have HOAs that limit poultry. Read your covenants. Our page on chicken laws in Tulsa gives a city example.

Heat, ice, wind and storms

Oklahoma throws everything at a coop. Summers often pass 100 degrees. Winters bring ice storms and hard freezes. Spring is tornado season. Wind blows most of the year.

  • Summer. Full shade, lots of airflow and several waterers. See our tips on summer heat care in Oklahoma City.
  • Winter. Draft-free roosts and a plan for frozen water during ice storms.
  • Storms. Anchor the coop and run. Use a solid roof for hail.
  • Wind. Block the north side in winter.

Active, heat-tolerant breeds like the Ancona and Leghorn handle Oklahoma summers well. Dual-purpose breeds like Australorps and Rhode Island Reds handle the swings too.

Predators

Coyotes are found statewide, even in cities. Raccoons, opossums, skunks, foxes and bobcats are common. Red-tailed hawks and great horned owls hunt open land. Snakes take eggs in warm months. Coyotes will dig, so bury hardware cloth along the run edge or lay a wire apron on the ground. Use hardware cloth on vents and lock the coop every night.

Expect laying to dip in the worst of July and August. That is normal in Oklahoma heat, and most hens pick back up when fall arrives.

Bird flu and disease reporting

The Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry handles animal health, including bird flu reports, through the state veterinarian. Oklahoma has commercial poultry, especially in the eastern part of the state, so early reports matter. Report sudden deaths. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries and keep wild waterfowl away from your flock.

What about selling eggs?

A few dozen to neighbors is usually fine. Oklahoma has its own rules on licensing and labeling, which may differ from what a friend in Texas or Kansas follows. Check with the Oklahoma Department of Agriculture, Food and Forestry first.

Oklahoma first steps

  1. Check city code or county rules, plus HOA covenants.
  2. Build for heat, ice, wind and hail.
  3. Anchor the coop before storm season.
  4. Save the state veterinarian's contact info.

Common questions about chickens in Oklahoma

Can I keep chickens in Oklahoma City?

Oklahoma City has allowed hens under its rules. The current city code lists the limits and permit rules.

How do I keep chicken water from freezing in an Oklahoma ice storm?

A heated waterer base works well. If power goes out, bring fresh water out several times a day.

What breeds handle Oklahoma heat?

Lighter, large-combed breeds like Anconas and Leghorns, plus hardy dual-purpose birds with good shade.
1521:
Ohio, home of the Buckeye chicken

Ohio is one of the top egg-producing states, and it has its own breed. The Buckeye was developed in Ohio in the late 1800s by Nettie Metcalf, and it is still one of the best birds for a cold Midwestern backyard. It has a pea comb that resists frostbite, it forages well and it lays brown eggs.

City, village and township rules

Ohio has cities, villages and townships, and each can have its own rules on poultry. Columbus, Cleveland, Cincinnati, Toledo, Akron and Dayton each handle chickens differently. Many allow a small number of hens with limits on placement and coop size. Some make you get a permit. Roosters are often restricted. Townships may allow more birds on larger lots. Our page on chicken laws in Columbus shows one example.

Suburban HOAs are common and often restrict poultry, so check yours.

Ohio weather and your coop

Ohio winters are cold and gray, with lake effect snow in the northeast near Lake Erie. Summers are warm and humid. Spring is wet and muddy.

  • Build on high ground or add drainage for wet springs.
  • Vent near the roof to keep the coop dry in damp winters.
  • Use a heated waterer in January and February.
  • Add shade for July and August.

Wet Ohio springs are also when coccidiosis tends to show up in young birds. Keep brooder and run bedding dry, and call a vet if chicks get bloody droppings or stop eating.

Our tips on winter chicken care in Toledo fit most of northern Ohio.

Predators

Raccoons are the top threat. Foxes, coyotes, opossums, skunks, mink and weasels are common. Hawks and owls hunt yards and fields. Lock the coop each night and use hardware cloth, not chicken wire.

Bird flu and the Ohio Department of Agriculture

Because Ohio has so many commercial egg and poultry farms, the Ohio Department of Agriculture takes backyard flock health seriously. It handles animal disease reporting through the state veterinarian. Call in sudden deaths or signs of bird flu quickly. Buy from NPIP hatcheries, quarantine new birds and keep wild waterfowl away.

Selling eggs in Ohio

Ohio is a big egg state, and it has its own rules for sellers on licensing, candling and labels. Small backyard sales are often allowed, but check with the Ohio Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Before getting chicks in Ohio

  1. Find out if you are in a city, village or township.
  2. Read your local code and HOA rules.
  3. Plan drainage, ventilation and heated water.
  4. Consider a Buckeye or two.

Common questions about chickens in Ohio

Can I keep chickens in Columbus, Ohio?

Columbus has allowed hens with rules and permits. Confirm with the city's current code.

Are Buckeye chickens good for beginners?

Yes. They are hardy, calm and good foragers, and they handle cold winters well.

Do Ohio townships allow chickens?

Many do, especially on larger lots. Township zoning varies, so check yours.
1522:
Oregon chicken rules, west and east of the Cascades

Oregon is friendly to backyard chickens in many cities, but rules are still local. Portland, Eugene, Salem, Bend, Medford and Corvallis each set their own limits and permit rules. Many allow a small number of hens without much fuss and restrict roosters. Some require a permit for larger flocks. County zoning covers rural land, and farm and forest zones usually allow poultry.

Check HOA rules too, especially in Bend and the newer suburbs around Portland. For city examples, see our pages on raising chickens in Portland and chicken laws in Eugene.

Two climates

West of the Cascades

The Willamette Valley and coast are mild but very wet from fall through spring. Mud and damp bedding are the main problems. Give the run a solid roof, raise the coop off the ground and use deep, dry bedding. Mold and respiratory issues are more common in wet coops, so good ventilation matters even in winter.

East of the Cascades

Central and eastern Oregon are dry, with cold winters and hot summers. Bend and the high desert get snow and freezing nights. Plan for heated water and wind protection, plus shade for summer.

Most common breeds do well in western Oregon. Australorps, Barred Rocks and Easter Eggers are popular.

Predators

Raccoons are the top threat in western Oregon cities. Coyotes, foxes, skunks, opossums, hawks and owls are common. Rats are drawn to feed. In rural and forested areas, add bobcats, cougars and black bears. Use hardware cloth and lock the coop each night.

Bird flu and the Oregon Department of Agriculture

The Oregon Department of Agriculture handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Oregon has had bird flu cases in backyard flocks. Report sudden deaths. Wild ducks and geese winter in the Willamette Valley and on eastern wetlands, so keep them away from your flock. When you order, pick an NPIP hatchery.

Oregon State University Extension has useful guides. See our summary of OSU's guide to raising chickens.

Selling eggs in Oregon

Oregon keepers often sell eggs from a porch cooler or at a weekend market. That is usually allowed at a small scale, but the state writes its own egg rules. Check with the Oregon Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Oregon checklist

  1. Check city or county rules and your HOA.
  2. West side, plan for rain and mud. East side, plan for cold and heat.
  3. Store feed so rats cannot reach it.
  4. Buy from NPIP sources.

Common questions about chickens in Oregon

Can I keep chickens in Portland?

Portland has allowed a small number of hens, with a permit for larger flocks. Check the current city rules.

How do I keep my coop dry in the Oregon rain?

Roof the run, raise the coop, use deep bedding and vent high so moisture can escape.

Are roosters allowed in Oregon cities?

Many cities restrict them. Rural zones usually allow them.
1523:
Pennsylvania's patchwork of local rules

Pennsylvania has thousands of local governments, including cities, boroughs and townships. Each one can set its own rules on backyard poultry. Philadelphia, Pittsburgh, Allentown, Erie, Lancaster and State College all differ. A borough may ban chickens while the township around it allows them. Many places limit hens and restrict roosters. Some require a permit or a minimum lot size.

Start by finding which municipality you are in. Then read its zoning ordinance. Search "poultry", "fowl" and "animal husbandry". Check your HOA too. Our pages on raising chickens in Philadelphia and Erie show how two cities approach it.

A big farm state with a lot of poultry

Pennsylvania has a large poultry and egg industry, centered in Lancaster County and the south central part of the state. Bird flu has hit Pennsylvania commercial flocks hard in recent years. That makes backyard biosecurity a community issue here, not just a personal one.

  • Report sudden deaths or illness to the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture or a vet.
  • Look for the NPIP label when you buy chicks.
  • Keep wild ducks and geese away from your flock.
  • Do not share equipment with other flocks.
  • Use separate boots for the coop.

Penn State Extension has excellent resources. See our summary of Penn State's biosecurity guide for small flocks.

Weather

Pennsylvania winters are cold, with more snow in the north, the mountains and near Lake Erie. Summers are warm and humid, especially in the southeast. Build a coop that is dry, draft-free at roost level and vented high. Plan for snow load and frozen water. Classic dual-purpose breeds like Plymouth Rocks, Wyandottes and Orpingtons do well statewide.

Spring mud is a real issue in much of Pennsylvania. If your yard is heavy clay, put the run on high ground and add wood chips or gravel so birds are not standing in muck for weeks.

Predators

Raccoons, foxes, coyotes, opossums and skunks are common across the state. Mink and weasels live near streams. Raptors pick off birds in open yards. Black bears are widespread in much of Pennsylvania, so store feed inside and consider electric fencing in bear country. Lock the coop each night and use hardware cloth.

Selling eggs in Pennsylvania

Roadside egg stands are everywhere in rural Pennsylvania. Small sales are often allowed, but the state has its own rules on registration and labeling. Check with the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture first.

Pennsylvania checklist

  1. Confirm your city, borough or township.
  2. Read the zoning ordinance and HOA rules.
  3. Set up a biosecurity routine.
  4. Plan for snow, cold and bears.

Common questions about chickens in Pennsylvania

Can I keep chickens in Philadelphia?

It depends on your zoning and the city's animal rules, which can be strict on small lots. Check both before you start.

Do Pennsylvania townships allow chickens?

Many do, especially in agricultural or rural residential zones. Check your township's zoning.

Why is Pennsylvania strict about bird flu?

The state has a big commercial poultry industry, and outbreaks can spread quickly between farms.
1524:
The state that named a breed

Rhode Island is the smallest state, but it gave the world one of its most famous chickens. The Rhode Island Red was developed here in the 1800s, and it is the official state bird. It is hardy, a strong layer of brown eggs and a great first bird for new keepers.

How Rhode Island handles chickens

Rhode Island has no county government, so the rules come from its cities and towns. Providence, Warwick, Cranston, Pawtucket, Newport and the rural towns to the west each have their own approach. Many allow hens with limits on numbers and placement. Others want a permit before the first bird arrives. Roosters are often restricted in denser areas.

Call your city or town zoning office, or read the local code. Check condo or HOA rules too. Our page on chicken laws in Providence covers the capital.

Coastal weather

Rhode Island is mostly coastal, with cold, damp winters, humid summers and exposure to nor'easters and hurricanes. Salt air and wind are hard on coop materials.

  • Raise the coop and anchor it.
  • Use materials that hold up to salt air.
  • Vent high to keep the coop dry in damp weather.
  • Plan for heated water in the coldest weeks.
  • Shade the run for hot summer days.

For hot weather tips, see our page on summer heat care in Providence.

Predators

Raccoons, foxes, coyotes, skunks and opossums are common. Fishers have returned to many wooded areas. Hawks and owls hunt yards. Rats are drawn to feed in denser neighborhoods. Near the shore, gulls and crows will steal eggs and small chicks from open runs, so cover the top. Shut the coop every night and skip chicken wire in favor of hardware cloth.

Lots are small and close together in much of the state. Put the coop where it will not bother neighbors, keep it clean and share a few eggs. It goes a long way.

Bird flu and the state

In Rhode Island, agriculture and animal health fall under the Department of Environmental Management, through its Division of Agriculture and the state veterinarian. Report sudden deaths or signs of illness. The bays and salt marshes host many wild ducks and geese, so keep them away from your flock. Buy only from NPIP sources.

A word on egg sales

Selling a dozen here and there is often allowed. Each state has its own egg rules, so ask the Department of Environmental Management's Division of Agriculture before you sell.

Rhode Island to-do list

  1. Check your city or town code.
  2. Check condo or HOA rules.
  3. Build a coop that handles salt, wind and storms.
  4. Consider adding a few Rhode Island Reds.

Common questions about chickens in Rhode Island

Is the Rhode Island Red really the state bird?

Yes. Rhode Island adopted the Rhode Island Red as its state bird.

Can I keep chickens in Providence?

Providence has allowed hens with rules. Read the latest code for numbers and permits.

Who regulates chickens in Rhode Island?

Local zoning covers whether you can keep them. The state Division of Agriculture covers animal health.
1525:
South Carolina flocks, from the Upstate to the Lowcountry

In South Carolina, the rules for backyard hens are set by cities and counties. Columbia, Charleston, Greenville, Rock Hill, Myrtle Beach and Spartanburg each have their own code. Many allow a few hens and restrict roosters. A handful require a permit. Rural counties often have little zoning that affects chickens. HOAs are very common in the suburbs and coastal developments, and many of them ban poultry. Read your covenants first.

A different kind of state veterinarian

In South Carolina, the state veterinarian's office sits at Clemson University, through Clemson Livestock Poultry Health. That is the place to report sudden deaths or signs of bird flu. South Carolina has a big commercial poultry industry, including broilers and turkeys, so early reporting matters. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, keep wild waterfowl away and quarantine new birds.

Built for heat and storms

South Carolina summers are long, hot and humid. The Lowcountry is also exposed to hurricanes and flooding. The Upstate is a bit cooler and sees the occasional ice storm.

  • Shade the run and coop, especially in the afternoon.
  • Use large vents or wire walls for airflow.
  • Raise the coop off the ground near the coast.
  • Anchor everything before hurricane season.
  • Keep bedding dry. Humidity brings mites and mold.

Pick heat-tolerant breeds like Leghorns, Easter Eggers or Naked Necks for the Midlands and the coast.

Predators

Raccoons and opossums are the main night raiders. Foxes, coyotes, bobcats, hawks and owls are common. Snakes are a big problem in warm months. Near water, alligators and mink can take birds. Fire ants can attack chicks. Hardware cloth plus a nightly lockup stops most predators.

Mosquitoes are active for much of the year in South Carolina, and they can spread fowl pox. It shows up as dark scabs on combs and wattles. Cut down standing water near the coop and ask a vet if you see it.

Eggs to sell?

You can often sell a few dozen at a small scale, but South Carolina sets its own rules on labeling and storage. Ask the South Carolina Department of Agriculture before you sell, and keep eggs cool in the heat.

South Carolina first steps

  1. Check your city or county rules and HOA covenants.
  2. Save the Clemson Livestock Poultry Health contact info.
  3. Plan for heat, humidity and storms.
  4. Find chicks, like our list of places to buy chicks near Columbia.
  5. Find a vet on the South Carolina poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in South Carolina

Who do I call about sick chickens in South Carolina?

Clemson Livestock Poultry Health, home of the state veterinarian, handles poultry disease reports.

Can I keep chickens in Charleston?

Rules depend on the current city code and your zoning. Ask the city before you get birds.

How do I protect chickens from fire ants?

Keep brooders off the ground, treat mounds near the coop with a product labeled for use around animals, and follow the label.
1526:
Tennessee rules from Memphis to the mountains

Tennessee runs about 500 miles from the Mississippi River to the Smoky Mountains, and its backyard chicken rules are just as spread out. Memphis, Nashville, Knoxville, Chattanooga, Clarksville and Murfreesboro each have their own code. Many cities allow hens with limits and restrict roosters. Some require a permit or set distances from neighbors' houses. Rural counties are usually more relaxed. Our page on chicken laws in Chattanooga gives one city example.

Middle Tennessee suburbs around Nashville have grown fast, and most new subdivisions have HOAs. Many restrict poultry. Read the covenants before you spend money on a coop.

Climate by region

West Tennessee is hot and humid, with flat land and strong storms. Middle Tennessee has hot summers and mild winters with the occasional ice storm. East Tennessee is cooler in the mountains, with more snow at higher elevations.

  • Plan for summer heat statewide. Shade and airflow come first.
  • Block drafts at the roost for winter cold snaps.
  • Anchor the coop for spring storms and tornadoes.
  • In the mountains, build for snow load.

Expect egg production to dip in the short days of December and again in the worst summer heat. Both are normal in Tennessee, and hens usually bounce back when conditions ease.

The Welsummer is a good fit for much of Tennessee. It forages well, handles both heat and cold and lays dark brown speckled eggs.

Predators

Raccoons, opossums, foxes, coyotes and skunks are common. Hawks and owls watch open yards for easy meals. Snakes take eggs and chicks in warm months. In East Tennessee, black bears are common and drawn to feed, so store it inside. Bobcats live statewide. Use hardware cloth and lock the coop at night.

Bird flu and the state veterinarian

The Tennessee Department of Agriculture handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Tennessee has commercial broiler farms, so report sudden deaths or illness quickly. Wild ducks and geese use the state's rivers and lakes, especially in the west along the Mississippi Flyway. Keep them away from your flock and buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling eggs in Tennessee

Many keepers sell their extras to friends and neighbors, and that is commonly allowed at a small scale. Tennessee has its own egg rules, so check with the Tennessee Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Tennessee starter list

  1. Check city code or county zoning, plus HOA rules.
  2. Plan for heat, storms and winter cold snaps.
  3. In bear country, store feed indoors.
  4. Find a vet on the Tennessee poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Tennessee

Can I keep chickens in Nashville?

Nashville has allowed hens in some areas with rules. Check the current Metro code before you start.

Are roosters allowed in Tennessee?

Many cities restrict them, while rural counties usually allow them.

Do Tennessee chickens need winter heat?

Usually not. A dry, draft-free coop is enough for most Tennessee winters.
1527:
South Dakota hens, prairie to the Black Hills

South Dakota is mostly farm and ranch land, and rural keepers often face few rules beyond common sense and nuisance law. In towns, the city code decides. Sioux Falls, Rapid City, Aberdeen, Brookings, Watertown and Pierre each have their own approach. Many cities allow a small number of hens and restrict roosters. Some require a permit or a minimum distance from neighbors' homes. Our page on chicken laws in Sioux Falls covers the biggest city.

New subdivisions in growing towns often have covenants. Read them before you buy chicks.

The South Dakota winter coop

Winters are cold, windy and long. Blizzards on the open prairie can drift snow against anything in their path. West River and the Black Hills see big temperature swings when chinook winds blow.

  • Face the door and pop hole away from the north and northwest wind.
  • Add a windbreak of bales, fencing or a building.
  • Vent near the roof so moisture escapes.
  • Use wide, flat roosts so birds can cover their feet.
  • Run a heated waterer from late fall to spring.

Heavy, cold-hardy breeds do well. The Orpington is calm, fluffy and steady through cold weather. Wyandottes and Brahmas are also good choices. For more, see our tips on winter chicken care in Sioux Falls.

Summers can still get hot, and hail is common. Add shade and a solid roof over part of the run.

Predators

Coyotes, red foxes, raccoons, skunks, mink and weasels are all common. Great horned owls and hawks hunt year round. In the Black Hills, bobcats and mountain lions are present. Cover openings with hardware cloth and shut the coop every evening.

Bird flu and the Animal Industry Board

In South Dakota, animal health is handled by the South Dakota Animal Industry Board, home of the state veterinarian. Report sudden deaths or signs of bird flu to them or a vet. South Dakota's prairie wetlands host huge numbers of ducks and geese in spring and fall, and the state has a big commercial turkey industry. Keep wild birds away from your flock and buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling eggs in South Dakota

Small-town buyers love farm eggs, and selling a few is often allowed. The rules differ by state, so check with the South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources before you sell.

Checklist for South Dakota

  1. Check city code or county rules and covenants.
  2. Plan for wind, drifts and deep cold.
  3. Set up heated water before the first freeze.
  4. Save the Animal Industry Board's contact info.

Common questions about chickens in South Dakota

Who do I report sick chickens to in South Dakota?

The South Dakota Animal Industry Board handles animal disease reports. A poultry vet is another good first call.

Can I keep chickens in Rapid City?

Rules depend on the current city code and your zoning. Call the city first.

Do chickens need heat in a South Dakota winter?

Most cold-hardy breeds do not, if the coop is dry and out of the wind. Heated water matters more.
1528:
Texas is big, and so are the differences

Texas has hundreds of cities, and each one writes its own animal rules. Houston, Dallas, San Antonio, Austin, Fort Worth and El Paso all handle backyard hens differently. Many Texas cities allow a few hens, often with rules on how far the coop must sit from a neighbor's house. Roosters are often restricted inside city limits. In unincorporated areas, Texas counties have limited power over land use, so rural keepers usually have few rules.

HOAs are everywhere in Texas suburbs, and many of them limit or ban poultry. Read your deed restrictions. For city examples, see our pages on chicken laws in Austin and Dallas.

Who to call about bird health

In Texas, animal disease is handled by the Texas Animal Health Commission, or TAHC. That is the agency to call about bird flu or sudden deaths. Texas has a big commercial poultry and egg industry, especially in East Texas, so early reports matter. Use NPIP hatcheries, and isolate any new adults before they join the flock. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension has strong backyard resources. See our summary of AgriLife's backyard poultry resources.

Climate across Texas

Gulf Coast

Houston and the coast are hot and very humid, with hurricanes and flooding. Raise the coop, give it open sides and anchor it. See our page on raising chickens in Houston.

Central and North Texas

Long, hot summers, mild winters and the occasional hard freeze or ice storm. Shade and water first, but have a plan for frozen pipes and waterers.

West Texas and the Panhandle

Dry heat, strong wind, dust and real winter cold in the Panhandle. Block wind at the roost and shade the run.

Heat-tolerant breeds like Leghorns, Naked Necks and Easter Eggers do well in most of the state.

Texas predators

Raccoons, opossums, coyotes, foxes, bobcats, skunks, hawks and owls are common. Snakes, including rat snakes and venomous species, are attracted to coops. Fire ants will go after chicks. Feral hogs can wreck runs in rural areas. Hardware cloth and a closed coop at night handle most of these.

Egg sales in Texas

Texas has its own egg licensing rules that may apply even to small sellers, though small sales are often allowed. Check with the Texas Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Texas checklist

  1. Check city code and HOA deed restrictions.
  2. Plan for heat and your region's storms.
  3. Save TAHC's contact info.
  4. Protect against snakes and fire ants.

Common questions about chickens in Texas

Can I keep chickens in Houston?

Houston has allowed hens with rules about coop distance from neighbors. Rules change, so check the current code.

Who handles bird flu in Texas?

The Texas Animal Health Commission handles animal disease reports, including bird flu.

How do I keep chickens cool in a Texas summer?

Full shade, an open, well-vented coop, several waterers and frozen treats on the worst days.
1529:
Virginia's cities, counties and towns

Virginia has an unusual setup. Its independent cities are separate from the counties around them. So Richmond, Norfolk, Virginia Beach, Alexandria and Roanoke each make their own rules, apart from nearby counties. Counties like Fairfax, Loudoun, Chesterfield and Henrico have their own zoning, and towns inside counties can add their own rules on top.

Many Virginia localities allow hens with limits on numbers, setbacks and lot size. Roosters are often restricted in residential zones. Some also require a permit. Northern Virginia HOAs often restrict poultry. Start with your city or county zoning ordinance, then check your HOA.

Coast, Piedmont and mountains

Hampton Roads is hot and humid, with hurricanes and flooding. The Piedmont has hot summers and mild winters. The Shenandoah Valley and southwest mountains get real cold and snow.

  • On the coast, raise and anchor the coop.
  • Statewide, shade and ventilate for humid summers.
  • In the mountains, plan for snow load and frozen water.

Low, flat parts of Hampton Roads can hold water for days after a storm. If your run stays soggy, raise the floor with sand or gravel or move the coop to higher ground.

For coastal heat, see our page on summer heat care in Norfolk. For western Virginia, see our coop ideas for Roanoke.

Predators

Raccoons, foxes, opossums and hawks are the most common threats. Coyotes are found statewide. Black bears are common in the mountains and parts of the Piedmont, and they come for feed. Snakes take eggs. Mink live near water. Hardware cloth and a locked door at dusk are your best tools.

Bird flu in Virginia

The Virginia Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, or VDACS, handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. The Shenandoah Valley has a big commercial poultry industry, especially turkeys and broilers, so the state acts fast on disease. Report sudden deaths. Keep wild ducks and geese away from your flock and buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling eggs in Virginia

A small egg business on the side is often possible. Virginia sets its own rules on labels and storage, so check with VDACS before you sell.

A good starter breed for Virginia

Most common breeds do well in Virginia. Easter Eggers, Barred Rocks and Australorps are all popular. On a small Northern Virginia lot with close neighbors, a few quiet hens and no rooster will keep the peace. See our page on raising chickens in Charlottesville for a central Virginia example.

Virginia steps

  1. Find out if you are in an independent city, a county or a town.
  2. Read that locality's zoning ordinance.
  3. Check HOA rules.
  4. Plan for your region's weather and bears.

Common questions about chickens in Virginia

Why do Virginia cities and counties have different chicken rules?

Virginia's independent cities are separate from counties, so each sets its own zoning.

Can I keep chickens in Fairfax County?

Fairfax County sets its poultry rules through its zoning ordinance, and lot size matters. Check the current ordinance.

Are roosters allowed in Virginia?

Many localities restrict them in residential zones, while rural areas usually allow them.
1530:
Vermont, where chickens are part of the landscape

Vermont has a strong small-farm and homesteading tradition, and backyard flocks are common. Rules are set by towns and cities through zoning. Burlington, South Burlington, Montpelier, Rutland and many small towns each have their own rules. Rural towns often allow chickens by right. Denser towns may set limits on numbers and restrict roosters. Our page on chicken laws in Burlington covers the state's biggest city.

Call your town zoning administrator or read the bylaws. Then check any HOA or condo rules.

Built for a Vermont winter

Vermont winters are long, cold and snowy, with mud season after. Coops need to be tough.

  • Snow load. Build a steep, strong roof.
  • Moisture. Vent near the peak. Dry air prevents frostbite.
  • Drafts. Keep the roost out of moving air.
  • Water. A heated waterer is close to required.
  • Mud season. Put the coop on high ground with good drainage.

Pick cold-hardy breeds with small combs and dense feathers. The Faverolles has a beard, muffs and feathered feet, and it handles cold well. Wyandottes, Chanteclers and Buckeyes are also good picks. See our tips on winter chicken care in Burlington.

Predators in the Green Mountains

Foxes, coyotes, raccoons, skunks, fishers, weasels and mink are all common. Black bears are widespread and drawn to feed. Bobcats live statewide. Hawks and owls hunt yards. In winter, weasels turn white and are called ermine, and they can slip through a gap about an inch wide. Lock the coop each night, use hardware cloth and keep feed in sealed bins inside.

Fresh snow is a free predator camera. Walk around the coop the morning after a snowfall and read the tracks to see what has been visiting.

Bird flu and the Agency of Agriculture

The Vermont Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Sick birds or sudden deaths should be reported. Lake Champlain and Vermont's many ponds draw wild ducks and geese during migration. Keep them away from your flock. Order from NPIP sources and quarantine anything new.

Driveway egg stands

Many Vermont keepers sell eggs at the end of the driveway, and that is often allowed at a small scale. Each state writes its own egg rules, so check with the Agency of Agriculture, Food and Markets first.

Vermont starter list

  1. Read your town's zoning bylaws.
  2. Plan for snow, cold, mud and bears.
  3. Set up heated water before the first freeze.
  4. Choose cold-hardy breeds.

Common questions about chickens in Vermont

Do I need a permit for chickens in Vermont?

Some towns require one and many rural towns do not. Ask your town zoning administrator.

Will hens lay through a Vermont winter?

Laying usually drops in the dark months. Some keepers add timed light. Others let hens rest.

How do I keep bears away from my Vermont coop?

Store feed indoors in sealed bins, clean up spills and use electric fencing around the coop.
1531:
Utah backyard flocks

Utah has a strong self-reliance culture, and backyard chickens are popular along the Wasatch Front and in rural towns. Rules are local. Salt Lake City, Provo, Orem, Ogden, St. George and Logan each have their own code. Many cities allow hens with limits based on lot size and restrict roosters. Some require a permit or setbacks from neighbors' homes. County zoning applies outside city limits, and agricultural zones are common in rural areas.

Many Utah neighborhoods have HOAs, especially newer developments. Some allow chickens and many do not. Read your CC&Rs before you buy birds.

Desert, mountains and inversions

Utah is dry, with big swings in temperature. Northern Utah gets cold, snowy winters and hot, dry summers. St. George and southern Utah are low desert, with very hot summers and mild winters.

  • North. Plan for snow load, frozen water and cold nights. Block wind at the roost.
  • South. Plan for heat. Full shade, misters and lots of water.
  • Everywhere. Dry air dehydrates birds fast. Keep water clean and full.
  • Winter inversions. Valley air can get stale in winter. Keep the coop well vented.

The Easter Egger handles heat and cold well and lays blue or green eggs, which makes it a popular pick. See our page on breeds for Provo weather for more.

Predators

Raccoons and skunks live in most Utah cities. Coyotes and red foxes are common on the edges of town. Hawks, owls and golden eagles hunt open land. In canyon and foothill areas, bobcats, mountain lions and black bears are possible. Rattlesnakes come for rodents and eggs in the south. Close the coop at dusk and use hardware cloth on every opening.

Bird flu in Utah

The Utah Department of Agriculture and Food handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Utah has commercial egg and turkey farms, and the Great Salt Lake wetlands draw huge numbers of migrating birds. Report sudden deaths. Keep wild birds off your feed and start with NPIP chicks.

Selling eggs

Utah has laws that allow some homemade food sales, but egg rules vary by state and can be separate. Check with the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food before you sell.

Utah first steps

  1. Check city or county code and your CC&Rs.
  2. Plan for your region's heat or cold.
  3. Keep plenty of water out.
  4. Find a vet on the Utah poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Utah

Can I keep chickens in Salt Lake City?

Salt Lake City has allowed hens with rules. Check the current city code for limits and setbacks.

How do I keep chickens cool in St. George?

Full shade, misters, several waterers and an open, well-vented coop.

Are roosters allowed in Utah?

Many cities restrict them, while agricultural zones usually allow them.
1532:
Chickens in the Mountain State

West Virginia is rugged and rural, and plenty of families keep chickens the way their grandparents did. Outside city limits, there is often very little zoning that touches backyard flocks. Inside cities like Charleston, Huntington, Morgantown, Parkersburg and Wheeling, the city code decides. Many cities allow a few hens and restrict roosters. Some cities add a permit step. If you rent or live in a subdivision, check your lease or covenants.

Weather in the hills and hollows

West Virginia gets cold, snowy winters, especially at higher elevations. Summers are warm and humid. Hollows can stay damp and shaded, and heavy rain can cause flash flooding.

  • Put the coop on high ground, away from creeks that flood.
  • Keep bedding dry. Damp hollows breed mold and respiratory problems.
  • Vent high and block drafts at the roost.
  • Build a strong roof for snow in the mountains.
  • Use a heated waterer in deep winter.

Hardy American breeds are a good fit. The Java is one of the oldest American breeds, a good forager and tough in cold weather. Plymouth Rocks and Rhode Island Reds also do well. See our tips on winter chicken care in Charleston.

Bears, foxes and more

West Virginia has a large black bear population, and bears are drawn to chicken feed. Store feed in sealed bins inside a building, and consider electric fencing around the coop. Foxes, coyotes, raccoons, opossums, skunks, weasels and mink are all common. Bobcats live statewide. Hawks and owls hunt from the trees. Black rat snakes take eggs. Our guide on predator proofing in Charleston covers what works.

Bird flu and the state

The West Virginia Department of Agriculture handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. The Eastern Panhandle and Potomac Highlands have commercial poultry farms, so early reporting matters. Report sudden deaths. Buy chicks from NPIP hatcheries, quarantine new birds and keep wild ducks and geese away.

Selling a few dozen

Selling extras is common and often allowed on a small scale. West Virginia has its own egg rules, so check with the West Virginia Department of Agriculture before you sell.

West Virginia starter list

  1. Check city code if you live in town.
  2. Pick a dry, high spot for the coop.
  3. Bear-proof your feed storage.
  4. Choose hardy, cold-tolerant breeds.

Common questions about chickens in West Virginia

Do I need a permit for chickens in West Virginia?

Rural areas usually do not. Some cities require one. Check with your city if you live in town.

How do I keep bears away from my chickens?

Store feed indoors in sealed bins, pick up spills and use electric fencing around the coop.

What breeds handle West Virginia winters?

Hardy American breeds like Javas, Plymouth Rocks and Rhode Island Reds do well in a dry, draft-free coop.
1533:
Wisconsin, premises registration and local rules

Wisconsin has one rule that surprises many new keepers. The state requires livestock premises registration, and poultry counts as livestock. That can include a small backyard flock. Registration helps the state reach owners quickly during a disease outbreak. Check with the Wisconsin Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection, known as DATCP, for how it applies to you.

Beyond that, chicken rules are local. Milwaukee, Madison, Green Bay, Kenosha, Racine and Appleton each have their own code. Many cities allow hens with a permit and limits on numbers, and ban roosters. Towns and counties set rules for rural land, and agricultural zones usually allow poultry. Our page on chicken laws in Milwaukee shows one example.

Wisconsin winters

Wisconsin winters are long and cold, with lake effect snow near Lake Michigan and Lake Superior. The north woods are colder still.

  • Build a strong roof for snow.
  • Vent high so moisture escapes.
  • Keep drafts off the roost.
  • Use a heated waterer.
  • Give birds a covered or cleared run so they can get out on sunny days.

Big single combs are the most likely to get frostbite in a Wisconsin cold snap, so roosters and Leghorns need extra watching. Look for black or white tips on combs and wattles, and keep the coop dry.

Cold-hardy breeds like Wyandottes, Buckeyes, Brahmas and Chanteclers do well. See our page on raising chickens in Green Bay for northeast Wisconsin tips.

Predators

Raccoons, foxes, coyotes, skunks, opossums, mink and weasels are common. Hawks and owls hunt year round. In the north, fishers, bobcats, wolves and black bears are present. A locked coop and hardware cloth stop most losses. Spring thaw softens the ground, and that is when diggers try to get under the run, so bury wire or lay an apron around the edge.

Bird flu and DATCP

DATCP handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Wisconsin has commercial egg and turkey farms, and its lakes and marshes host many migrating ducks and geese. Report sudden deaths. Keep wild birds away and order from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling eggs in Wisconsin

Backyard egg sales are often allowed at a small scale, but Wisconsin has its own rules and some sellers may need a license. Check with DATCP before you sell.

Wisconsin checklist

  1. Check DATCP's premises registration rules.
  2. Read your city, town or county code and any HOA rules.
  3. Plan for snow, cold and heated water.
  4. Find chicks, like our list of places to buy chicks near Milwaukee.

Common questions about chickens in Wisconsin

Do I need to register my backyard chickens in Wisconsin?

Wisconsin requires livestock premises registration, and poultry is included. Check DATCP's current rules for backyard flocks.

Can I keep chickens in Milwaukee?

Milwaukee has allowed hens with a permit. Check the current city rules for limits.

What breeds handle Wisconsin winters?

Cold-hardy breeds with small combs, like Wyandottes, Buckeyes and Chanteclers.
1534:
Washington, wet side and dry side

Washington is split by the Cascades. West of the mountains, Seattle, Tacoma, Olympia and Bellingham are mild and wet. East of the mountains, Spokane, Yakima and the Tri-Cities are dry, with hot summers and cold winters. Your coop plan depends on which side you live on.

How the rules work

Cities and counties set chicken rules. Many Washington cities allow hens with limits on numbers and restrict roosters. Some require a permit or setbacks from property lines. County zoning covers unincorporated land, and rural zones usually allow poultry. HOAs in the Puget Sound suburbs often have their own rules. Our page on chicken laws in Tacoma gives a city example.

Coops for the wet side

Rain, mud and damp air are the main issues in western Washington. Mold and respiratory problems are more common in wet coops.

  • Roof the whole run.
  • Raise the coop off the ground.
  • Use deep, dry bedding and change wet spots often.
  • Vent high, even in winter.

See our coop ideas for Seattle backyards for designs that handle the rain.

Coops for the dry side

Eastern Washington needs a coop that handles summer heat and winter cold. Add shade and lots of water for summer, and block wind at the roost in winter. Use a heated waterer for freezing months. Wildfire smoke can be heavy in late summer, so keep birds calm and give them clean water.

The Barnevelder is a good fit for much of the state. It is calm, handles cold and damp well and lays dark brown eggs.

Predators

Raccoons are the top threat in western cities. Coyotes, foxes, opossums, skunks, hawks, owls and bald eagles are common. Rats are drawn to feed. In rural and forested areas, add bobcats, cougars and black bears. Use hardware cloth and lock up at night.

Bird flu and WSDA

The Washington State Department of Agriculture, or WSDA, handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Washington has had bird flu cases in backyard flocks. Report sudden deaths. Puget Sound and eastern wetlands host many wild ducks and geese, so keep them away from your flock. Buy from NPIP hatcheries.

Selling eggs in Washington

You can often sell a few dozen from a small flock, but Washington may require a license for some sellers. Check with WSDA first.

Washington checklist

  1. Check city or county code and HOA rules.
  2. West side, plan for rain. East side, plan for heat and cold.
  3. Store feed so rats cannot get in.
  4. Save WSDA's contact info.

Common questions about chickens in Washington

Can I keep chickens in Seattle?

Seattle has allowed backyard hens with limits and no roosters. The city's current code has the details.

How do I keep my coop dry in western Washington?

Roof the run, raise the coop, vent high and use deep, dry bedding.

Who do I report sick chickens to in Washington?

WSDA handles animal disease reports. A vet who treats birds can also help.
1537:
Wind, cold and open space in Wyoming

Wyoming has the fewest people of any state and a lot of open land, so many keepers live on rural parcels with few rules. In towns like Cheyenne, Casper, Laramie, Gillette and Sheridan, the city code decides. Many towns allow a limited number of hens and restrict roosters. You may also need a permit. Outside city limits, county zoning applies, and agricultural land usually allows poultry. Subdivisions often have covenants, so read yours.

Building for Wyoming weather

Wyoming is high, dry and windy. Winters are cold and long, and the wind can be relentless, especially in the southeast around Cheyenne and Laramie.

  • Block the wind. Use a windbreak and face the door away from the prevailing wind.
  • Anchor everything. Light coops and run covers will blow away.
  • Dry, ventilated coop. Vent near the roof, not at roost height.
  • Heated water. Water freezes fast in wind and cold.
  • Sun. UV is strong at altitude. Shade part of the run.

Choose cold-hardy breeds with small combs. Wyandottes, Brahmas, Chanteclers and Buckeyes are good choices.

Predators on the high plains

Coyotes and red foxes are found statewide. Raccoons and skunks live in towns. Hawks, owls and golden eagles hunt open land. In mountain areas, bobcats, mountain lions, black bears and grizzlies are present. In bear country, store feed indoors and use electric fencing. Our guide on predator proofing in Cheyenne covers the basics.

Bird flu and the Livestock Board

In Wyoming, animal health is handled by the Wyoming Livestock Board, which works with the state veterinarian. Do not wait to report sudden deaths or bird flu signs. Wild ducks and geese use Wyoming's rivers and reservoirs during migration, so keep them away from your flock. Get NPIP chicks and give new birds a quarantine period.

Selling eggs in Wyoming

Wyoming's Food Freedom Act is known as one of the most open direct-to-consumer food laws in the country. It may cover some egg sales from your home or farm, but rules can change and details matter. Check with the Wyoming Department of Agriculture before you sell.

Wyoming checklist

  1. Check city code or county rules, plus covenants.
  2. Plan for wind first, then cold.
  3. Bear-proof feed in mountain areas.
  4. Find a vet on the Wyoming poultry vet list.

Common questions about chickens in Wyoming

Can I sell eggs under Wyoming's Food Freedom Act?

Some direct sales may be covered. Check with the Wyoming Department of Agriculture for the current details.

How do I protect chickens from Wyoming wind?

Anchor the coop, add a windbreak and keep drafts off the roost while venting near the roof.

Who handles sick chickens in Wyoming?

The Wyoming Livestock Board handles animal disease reports. A vet who sees birds can help as well.
1754:
Florida flocks and the Florida climate

Florida is one of the few states where cold is almost never the problem. Heat, humidity, storms and predators are. And the rules are very local. Miami, Tampa, Orlando, Jacksonville, St. Petersburg, Gainesville and Tallahassee each handle hens differently, and so do the counties around them. Many allow a few hens with limits and ban roosters. A permit can be part of the deal. Others do not allow chickens on residential lots at all.

HOAs and deed restrictions are very common in Florida, and many ban poultry. Check yours before buying anything. Our page on chicken laws in Jacksonville gives one example.

Hurricane season and your coop

Hurricane season runs from June through November. Plan ahead.

  • Anchor the coop and run with ground anchors or straps.
  • Raise the coop off the ground in flood-prone areas.
  • Have a plan to move birds into a garage or secure building, or to take them with you if you evacuate.
  • Keep extra feed and water stored in a dry place.

Heat and humidity

Florida summers are long, hot and very humid. Open coops with wire walls, deep shade and plenty of cool water work best. Do not insulate the coop. Keep bedding dry, since humidity brings mold, mites and other parasites. Light, heat-tolerant breeds do well. Leghorns, Easter Eggers and Naked Necks are popular.

Florida predators

Raccoons and opossums are the top threats. Snakes, including rat snakes and venomous species, are common around coops. Foxes, coyotes, bobcats, hawks and owls hunt across the state. Fire ant mounds near a brooder are a danger to chicks. Near water, alligators will take poultry. Use hardware cloth and lock the coop each night. See our guide to predator proofing in Cape Coral.

Bird flu and FDACS

The Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services, or FDACS, handles animal health, including bird flu, through the state veterinarian. Florida hosts huge numbers of wintering ducks and other wild birds, so keep them away from your flock and its water. Report sudden deaths. Order chicks from an NPIP participant. UF/IFAS Extension has good guidance. See our summary of UF/IFAS bird flu advice for backyard flocks.

Selling eggs in Florida

Selling extras to neighbors is often allowed. Florida writes its own egg rules, so check with FDACS before you sell, and keep eggs cold in the heat.

Florida checklist

  1. Check city or county code and HOA rules.
  2. Plan for hurricanes before June.
  3. Build an open, shaded, raised coop.
  4. Protect against snakes, fire ants and raccoons.

Common questions about chickens in Florida

Can I keep chickens in Miami?

Rules depend on the current city or county code and your zoning. Check before you start.

What do I do with chickens during a Florida hurricane?

Move them to a secure building or take them with you in crates. Anchor the coop ahead of time.

Why are there wild chickens in Key West?

Key West has free-roaming chickens that descend from birds kept there long ago. They are a well-known part of the island.
17:
What the Altsteirer is like to keep

The Altsteirer is an old breed from Styria in southeastern Austria. The name means "old Styrian." It was kept as a farm bird that could forage for much of its own food, lay a fair number of eggs and still put something on the table. It is rare outside Austria and Germany, and very rare in the United States.

The two best known colors are white and a wild-type color, often called wheaten or partridge in English sources. Many birds carry a small tuft of feathers at the back of the head, which helps tell them apart from other light farm breeds.

Day to day

  • Light, active birds that forage well and do best with space.
  • Alert and often flighty, especially when young.
  • Good fliers, so a covered run or tall fence helps.
  • Light colored eggs, generally white to cream.

Their background as farm foragers means they are happiest when they can range. In a small, bare run they can become restless. Give perches, scratch areas and space to keep them busy.

Climate and coop

Altsteirers come from a region with cold winters, and keepers generally describe them as hardy. They have a single comb, so in very cold, damp weather the comb can get frostbite. A dry, well-ventilated coop is more important than added heat. The cold climate breed list has other hardy options if you cannot find Altsteirers.

Who they suit

They suit keepers who want to help preserve a rare European breed and who have room for active birds. They are not a good fit for someone who wants a calm lap chicken or a guaranteed supply of eggs from a small coop.

Where to find them

In the US, finding Altsteirers is hard. Your best bet is rare breed groups and specialty breeders, and it may take time. Similar active European breeds that are easier to find include the Appenzeller.

Common questions about Altsteirers

Are Altsteirers good layers?

They are known as fair layers of light colored eggs, kept for practical farm use.

Are Altsteirers friendly?

They tend to be active and somewhat flighty rather than cuddly.

Where do Altsteirers come from?

Styria, a region of southeastern Austria.
887:
Living with Ameraucanas day to day

Ameraucanas are the breed people mean when they say they want a "real" blue egg layer. They are not the same thing as the mixed blue egg birds sold at feed stores, and that difference matters if you care about predictable looks, egg color and temperament.

Day to day, most Ameraucanas are alert, a bit reserved and not especially cuddly. They will follow you around for treats, but many do not love being picked up. They are active foragers and do well free ranging, and their muffs and beard give them a round, owlish face that keepers tend to love.

Who they suit

  • Keepers who want true blue eggs and a bird that breeds true to type.
  • People interested in showing, since the breed has a written standard.
  • Mixed flocks, since they are usually middle of the pecking order.

Who might be disappointed

If you want maximum egg numbers, a production brown layer will outlay them. If you want a lap chicken for small kids, a calmer heavy breed may be a better fit. Ameraucanas are also harder to find and cost more than hatchery Easter Eggers.

Eggs through the year

Expect a steady but moderate supply of medium blue eggs. Pullets often start a little later than production breeds. Like most heritage birds, they slow down or stop in the short days of winter and during the fall molt, then pick back up in spring. Laying tapers a bit each year after the second or third season. The blue color goes all the way through the shell, so it does not wash or rub off, though shade can vary between hens and lighten slightly over a long laying season.

Space, coop and climate

Plan on standard large fowl space, around 4 square feet per bird inside the coop and about 10 in the run. The coop size per bird guide walks through the math. Ameraucanas have a pea comb and small or no wattles, which makes them quite cold-hardy and less prone to frostbite than single comb breeds. They handle heat reasonably well with shade and water. Their beards can get messy at the waterer in winter, so check for ice buildup on very cold days.

Quirks to know about

  • Beards and muffs can hide mites and lice, so part the feathers when you do health checks.
  • Some hens go broody, but it is not a defining trait of the breed.
  • They can fly better than heavier breeds, so a covered run or taller fence helps.

Ameraucana vs Easter Egger and Araucana

An Easter Egger is a mixed bird that may lay blue, green or even brown-tinted eggs and has no set look. The Easter Egger vs Ameraucana comparison goes deeper. The Araucana is a separate Chilean breed that is rumpless with ear tufts. Ameraucanas have a full tail, no tufts, a beard and muffs.

Where to get them

True Ameraucanas mostly come from breeders and poultry shows rather than big hatcheries. Many hatchery chicks labeled "Ameraucana" are really Easter Eggers, so ask about the parent stock, recognized color varieties and slate legs. Expect to pay more and to wait for hatching season.

Common questions about Ameraucanas

Are hatchery Ameraucanas real Ameraucanas?

Often not. Many are Easter Eggers sold under the name. A breeder working from the standard is the surest source.

Do Ameraucanas lay blue eggs every time?

A purebred Ameraucana hen lays blue eggs. The shade varies a little between hens, but a true Ameraucana should not lay brown or green.

Are Ameraucanas friendly?

They are usually calm and easy to manage, but many are independent. Handling them as chicks helps them settle with people.
890:
What the 55 Flowery Hen is

The 55 Flowery Hen is a hatchery-developed layer, not a historic standard breed. The "flowery" name refers to its mottled, speckled feathering, which can make a flock look like a bunch of tiny flower-print birds. Because it is a commercial line, detailed public information about its exact background is limited, and you should treat seller descriptions as the main source on its parent stock.

Not the same as the Swedish Flower Hen

The name invites confusion with the Swedish Flower Hen, an old Swedish landrace known for white-tipped, flowery feathers. They are different birds. If you want the heritage landrace, look for breeders of Swedish Flower Hens specifically.

What to expect

  • A backyard layer chosen for color and eggs together.
  • Variation between birds, as with many hatchery lines.
  • Standard space needs for a medium chicken.

Since there is no breed standard, temperament and output can vary from bird to bird. Give them standard care. That means about 4 square feet each inside the coop, a secure run, a good layer feed and oyster shell. In cold areas, check the comb in hard freezes, and in summer give shade and water.

Where to get them

Look for this exact name in hatchery catalogs. Because it is a specific commercial line, supply depends on the seller. If you hatch eggs from your own hens, the chicks may not look like the parents.

If you want a colorful, predictable mixed flock, an Easter Egger is another easy choice.

Common questions about the 55 Flowery Hen

Is the 55 Flowery Hen a Swedish Flower Hen?

No. They are different birds that share a similar name.

Will 55 Flowery Hen chicks look like their parents?

Not reliably. Hatchery lines often do not breed true.

Are they good layers?

They are sold as backyard layers, but output varies by bird. Ask the seller what to expect.
894:
Living with Anconas

Anconas are a Mediterranean breed from Italy, named after the port city of Ancona. They are black with white tips on many feathers, which gives a mottled, speckled look. They lay white eggs and are known for being active, alert and good at taking care of themselves.

Day to day, Anconas are busy birds. They range widely, fly well and are quick to dodge danger. Many are flighty and do not like being caught. They are generally not aggressive, just energetic.

Who they suit

  • Free range setups where an alert, hardy forager is useful.
  • Keepers who want white eggs from a non-hybrid breed.
  • People who enjoy watching active birds rather than holding them.

They are a poor fit for small enclosed runs, for families wanting a lap chicken, or for keepers who want hens to go broody.

Laying across the year

Anconas are good layers of white eggs. Like most Mediterranean breeds, they mature fairly early and are rarely broody, so laying is not interrupted for chicks. They lay best in spring and summer, slow in the short days of winter, and taper with age.

Space and climate

Anconas need room. In a small run they can get restless and start feather pecking. A covered run keeps them in. Single combed Anconas have a large comb that is prone to frostbite in cold climates.
