Rose combed Anconas exist too and are a better choice in cold areas. They tolerate heat fairly well thanks to their light build.

Ancona vs Leghorn

The Leghorn is the best known Mediterranean layer. White Leghorns usually lay more, but Anconas are often described as hardier and more independent. Another Mediterranean option is the Andalusian, which has the blue color.

Where to buy

Several hatcheries sell Anconas, and they are listed as a conservation breed in the US. Breeders offer show lines with better mottling.

Common questions about Anconas

Are Anconas good layers?

Yes. They are good layers of white eggs.

Are Anconas noisy?

They are active and can be vocal, but not unusually loud.

Do Anconas get more white with age?

Many keepers find mottling increases after molts, so birds often show more white as they age.
895:
What makes the Amrock different

The Amrock is a barred breed that descends from American Plymouth Rocks taken to Germany in the early 20th century. German breeders kept those birds as practical utility layers and did not follow later American show trends. The result is a bird that looks like a Barred Rock but is often described as closer to the older, working type.

Amrocks are recognized in Germany as their own breed. In the US, they are mostly found through breeders who have imported or kept Amrock lines.

Amrock vs Barred Rock

Side by side, the two look very similar. The Plymouth Rock in show lines is often bred for size and very crisp barring. Amrocks are often described as slightly lighter in build, with a focus on laying. Hatchery Barred Rocks vary a lot, so the gap between an Amrock and a hatchery Rock may be small. The barring pattern also makes them easy to confuse with the rose-combed Dominique, but Amrocks have single combs.

Day to day

  • Calm, friendly and easy to handle.
  • Steady layers of light brown to medium brown eggs.
  • Active foragers, but also fine in a run.
  • Hardy in cold weather, though the single comb can frostbite in deep freezes.

They fit standard large fowl space. Barring is sex-linked, and some keepers say Amrock chicks can be sexed by head spot size and down color, but this is not as reliable as a true autosexing breed or sex link.

Who they suit

Amrocks suit anyone who wants a dependable, friendly brown egg layer with a classic look. They are a good choice for families and first flocks.

Where to find them

Amrocks are uncommon in the US. A few breeders and specialty hatcheries sell them. If you mainly want the look and temperament, a Barred Rock is far easier to find.

Common questions about Amrocks

Is an Amrock just a Barred Rock?

They share ancestry, but Amrocks were bred separately in Germany as a utility line.

Are Amrocks good layers?

Yes. They are kept as productive brown egg layers.

Can you sex Amrock chicks at hatch?

Sometimes, by head spot and down color, but it is not fully reliable.
896:
What Andalusians are like

Andalusians are a Mediterranean breed associated with Andalusia in Spain, developed into their modern form with help from British breeders. They are best known for their blue color, a slate gray with darker lacing on each feather. They are light, upright and active, and they lay white eggs.

The blue color problem

Blue Andalusians do not breed true. A bird with one copy of the blue gene is blue. Two copies make splash, a pale bird with flecks. No copies make black. Breeding two blues gives roughly half blue, a quarter black and a quarter splash. Breeding black to splash gives nearly all blue chicks. That is useful to know if you plan to hatch your own, since blacks and splashes are still Andalusians.

Day to day

  • Active, alert and good foragers.
  • Often flighty. They fly well, so a covered run helps.
  • Good layers of white eggs, rarely broody.
  • Generally not aggressive, but not usually cuddly.

Their large single combs are prone to frostbite in cold climates. They do well in heat with shade, since they are light and lean. They are a good choice for the hot climate breed list.

Andalusian vs Ancona and Leghorn

All three are Mediterranean white egg layers. The Ancona is black with white tips, and the Leghorn is the top layer of the group. Andalusians are chosen mostly for their color and as a heritage breed.

Where to find them

Several hatcheries sell Blue Andalusians, though shipments may include blacks and splashes. Breeders offer better lacing and color. They are considered a conservation breed in the US.

Common questions about Andalusians

Why did my blue Andalusians hatch black chicks?

Blue does not breed true. Blue to blue pairings produce some black and splash chicks.

Are Andalusians good layers?

Yes. Expect a good supply of white eggs.

Are Andalusians good in cold weather?

They can manage, but their big single combs need protection from frostbite.
898:
What keeping Araucanas is really like

Araucanas are one of the most distinctive birds you can keep. They are rumpless, so there is no tail, and many have tufts of feathers sprouting near the ears. They lay blue eggs, came originally from Chile, and are a true breed with a written standard. They are also one of the harder breeds to raise well, and that is worth knowing before you order.

In the yard they are lively, quick and independent. Many are good foragers and some hens are protective broodies. They are not usually aggressive with people, but they are not the calm, sit-on-your-lap type either.

The tuft gene and hatching problems

The ear tuft trait is tied to a gene that is lethal when a chick gets two copies. In practice, when you breed two tufted birds together, a share of the embryos die late in the shell. Breeders often pair a tufted bird with a clean-faced bird to get around this, accepting that only some chicks will carry tufts. If you plan to hatch your own, expect lower hatch rates than with most breeds and do not assume something is wrong with your incubator.

Rumplessness can also make fertility harder in some lines, because the feathers around the vent are not held out of the way by a tail. Some breeders trim vent feathers on breeding birds for that reason.

Who Araucanas suit

  • Keepers who want a rare, unusual blue egg breed and enjoy a challenge.
  • People who want to show or preserve a breed.
  • Free range setups where an active, alert bird is an asset.

They are a poor pick if you want a cheap, easy, high-output layer for a first flock. For that, see the best breeds for beginners.

Laying across the seasons

Araucanas lay a moderate number of medium blue eggs. Egg size tends to be on the smaller side compared with big production breeds. They lay best in spring and early summer, slow down in the fall molt, and many take a break in winter without extra light. Output drops gradually after the first couple of years, as it does with most heritage breeds.

Space, coop and climate

Give them normal large fowl space and a run with cover. They are light enough to fly over low fences. Their pea comb is a real plus in cold weather because it resists frostbite much better than a tall single comb. In heat, shade and ventilation matter more than anything breed-specific.

Araucana vs Ameraucana

These two get confused all the time. The Ameraucana was developed in the United States from Araucana-type birds and has a full tail, a beard and muffs, and no ear tufts. It is easier to breed and easier to find. The Araucana is the tailless, tufted bird. Both lay blue eggs. If tufts and no tail are not important to you, the Ameraucana is the easier keep.

Where to find them

True Araucanas are uncommon. Some hatcheries list "Araucana" chicks, but these are often mixed birds with tails, so look at photos of the parent stock. Breed clubs, poultry shows and breeders who focus on rumpless tufted birds are the best sources. Be ready to wait and pay more.

Common questions about Araucanas

Do Araucanas have tails?

No. A true Araucana is rumpless, meaning it lacks the tail. Birds with tails sold as Araucanas are usually Easter Eggers or Ameraucanas.

Why do so many Araucana chicks die before hatching?

The ear tuft gene is lethal in double dose, so tufted to tufted pairings lose some embryos late in incubation.

What color eggs do Araucanas lay?

Blue. The shade varies from pale to deeper blue between hens.
899:
What Appenzellers are like

Appenzellers are a Swiss breed from the Appenzell region. There are two forms. The Appenzeller Spitzhauben has a forward-pointing crest, often compared to a lace bonnet, and a small V-shaped comb. The Appenzeller Barthuhn is the bearded type, with a rose comb and no crest. Both are light, hardy birds that lay white eggs.

Day to day

  • Very active foragers that enjoy space.
  • Strong fliers. Expect them to roost high and clear low fences.
  • Alert and often flighty. Some become tame with handling.
  • White eggs, and fair to good laying for a heritage breed.

They come from a mountain region and are generally considered hardy in cold weather. The small comb of both types helps with frostbite. The Spitzhauben's crest should still be checked in wet, cold weather, since wet crests can freeze.

Who they suit

Appenzellers suit keepers with room for an active flock and an interest in rare breeds. They are not a good match for small runs without a roof, or for anyone who wants a slow, calm pet.

Crest care for Spitzhauben

The crest is smaller than a Polish crest, so vision problems are less common, but it still benefits from care. Check for mites and lice in the crest. Keep waterers from soaking the crest. Watch for other birds pulling crest feathers.

Where to find them

Spitzhauben are the more common type in the US, and a few hatcheries and breeders carry them. The bearded Barthuhn is much harder to find. If you like crested birds that lay white eggs but cannot find Appenzellers, the Houdan is another option, though it is heavier and calmer.

Common questions about Appenzellers

What is the difference between Spitzhauben and Barthuhn?

Spitzhauben have a forward crest and V comb. Barthuhn have a beard and rose comb.

Are Appenzellers cold-hardy?

Generally yes. Their small combs help.

Do Appenzellers fly?

Yes. They are strong fliers.
901:
What it is like to keep Aseel

The Aseel is an old game breed from the Indian subcontinent. The name is often translated as "pure" or "of long pedigree." It was bred for fighting, and that shapes everything about keeping it. Aseel are short, extremely muscular birds with hard, tight feathers, a pea comb, small wattles and a fierce look.

Many Aseel are calm and even friendly with their keepers. The issue is other chickens. Aseel can be very aggressive toward other birds, and in many lines both roosters and hens will fight.

Who they suit

  • Experienced keepers interested in preserving an old game breed.
  • People who can house them separately or in small single-breed groups.
  • Anyone who wants a strong broody hen and protective mother.

They do not suit mixed backyard flocks, beginners or keepers who want eggs.

Eggs and broodiness

Aseel hens lay few eggs, usually small to medium and tinted or light brown, mostly in warm months. They go broody readily and are excellent mothers. The breed also matures slowly.

Space and climate

Give them enough room that birds can avoid each other. Low, sturdy roosts suit their heavy, compact build. Aseel are generally heat-tolerant. Their tight feathering gives less insulation in cold weather, so a dry, draft-free coop matters. The pea comb resists frostbite well.

Handling notes

Introductions need care. Even young Aseel can start serious fights. Keep an eye out for injuries and separate birds early if fighting starts. The wound care page covers what to do with injuries. Many Aseel tolerate handling well, which makes health checks easier.

Colors and availability

Many colors exist. The Black Breasted Red Aseel is one of the more familiar. Aseel are uncommon in the US. A few hatcheries list them, and game breeders keep them. Buy from sources who can tell you about temperament in their lines.

Common questions about Aseel chickens

Can Aseel hens live together?

Sometimes, but even hens can fight, so watch closely and have a backup pen.

Are Aseel good for eggs?

No. They lay few eggs.

Are Aseel friendly to people?

Many are calm with their keepers. Their aggression is mostly toward other chickens.
902:
What it is like to keep Australorps

The Australorp is one of the easiest chickens to recommend. It is calm, sturdy, a strong brown egg layer and generally easy to handle. Most people know the black variety, with glossy feathers that shine green in the sun, but you may also see blue and white in some places.

In the yard, Australorps tend to be steady and unbothered. They are not usually the bossy birds or the flighty ones. Many will come running for scratch and tolerate being picked up, which makes them a good fit for families. Their dark eyes and black legs give them a clean, simple look that is easy to tell apart from other black chickens.

Where the breed came from

Australorps were developed in Australia from Orpington stock, bred with more focus on laying than on show fluff. The name is a mix of "Australian" and "Orpington." They became famous for laying records in the 1920s, including a widely repeated record of 364 eggs in 365 days by a single hen. Treat that as a record, not what to expect from a backyard bird.

Laying pattern by season and age

  • Pullets usually start laying around the same age as other heavy breeds, often a bit earlier than many show lines.
  • Spring and summer are peak season, with medium to large light brown eggs most days.
  • Many Australorps keep laying better into fall and winter than lighter heritage breeds, though they still slow down in the molt.
  • Expect a gradual drop after the second year, but hens often stay useful layers for several more seasons.

Hatchery birds are generally bred for production and may lay more than show-line birds, which tend to be larger and fluffier.

Space, coop and climate

Australorps are a standard large fowl. Give them around 4 square feet per bird inside and about 10 in the run, and more if they are confined. The coop size for 6 chickens page is a handy start for a typical backyard flock. They are cold-hardy thanks to their size and dense feathers, but their single comb can get frostbite in very cold, damp coops, so keep ventilation good and moisture low.

Black feathers soak up heat, so in hot summers they need shade, airflow and plenty of cool water. They cope fine in warm climates with that support.

Health and handling notes

Australorps are a robust breed without major breed-specific problems. A few things to watch:

  • Some hens go broody, and they make good mothers when they do.
  • They like to eat, so too many treats can make them overweight, which can affect laying.
  • Check the single comb in hard freezes for darkened tips, a sign of frostbite.

Australorp vs Orpington and Plymouth Rock

An Orpington is usually bigger and fluffier, with a reputation as more of a pet, while the Australorp is a little sleeker and generally lays more. The Australorp vs Plymouth Rock comparison covers another common choice. Rocks are similar in temperament and output and come in barred and other patterns, so it often comes down to looks.

Where to get Australorps

Black Australorps are easy to find. Most large hatcheries carry them, and feed stores often stock them in spring. If you want birds closer to the show standard, look for breeders at poultry shows. Blue and white are less common and are more likely to come from breeders.

Common questions about Australorps

Are Australorps good for beginners?

Yes. They are calm, hardy and good layers, which is why they show up on so many beginner lists.

Do Australorps lay in winter?

Many keep laying better than lighter breeds in winter, but egg numbers still drop with short days and during the molt.

Are Australorps noisy?

Hens are usually fairly quiet, with some egg song. Roosters crow like any other rooster.
904:
What an Austra White is

The Austra White is a hybrid layer made by crossing a Black Australorp with a White Leghorn. The idea is to blend the Leghorn's laying power with some of the Australorp's calm nature and body size. Most Austra Whites are white, sometimes with small black flecks, and they have a single comb.

How it compares with its parents

  • Lighter than an Australorp, heavier than a Leghorn.
  • Usually calmer and friendlier than a typical Leghorn.
  • Strong layers. Eggs are usually light, from cream to lightly tinted.
  • Less broody than an Australorp.

Because it is a first generation cross, results vary. Some birds lean toward the Leghorn side and are more active and flighty. Others are steadier like an Australorp.

Day to day care

Austra Whites are active foragers and do well free ranging. They fit normal coop space. Their single comb is fairly large, so in cold climates watch for frostbite and keep the coop dry and ventilated. Their lighter build and white feathers help in the heat, as long as they have shade.

Like other high-output layers, they tend to lay most in their first years. A good layer feed and oyster shell help keep shells strong.

Breeding and availability

They do not breed true. Mating two Austra Whites gives unpredictable chicks. Several hatcheries sell them, but they are less common than sex links.

Common questions about Austra Whites

What color eggs do Austra Whites lay?

Usually cream to lightly tinted.

Are Austra Whites flighty?

Some are, especially if they take after the Leghorn side. Many are calmer.

Are Austra Whites good for small backyards?

Yes, if they have enough space and something to do, since they are active.
906:
What keeping Ayam Cemani is really like

The Ayam Cemani is an Indonesian breed from the island of Java and is famous for being black almost everywhere. Its feathers, skin, comb, wattles, beak, legs and even much of its internal tissue are dark. This comes from a genetic trait called fibromelanosis, which causes extra pigment throughout the body.

What it does not do is lay black eggs. Ayam Cemani eggs are cream to lightly tinted, like many other breeds. That is one of the most common myths about them.

Temperament and daily life

  • Active and alert, and often flighty.
  • Usually not aggressive toward people.
  • Good fliers, so covered runs help.
  • Not top layers. Expect a modest number of eggs, with breaks.

They are kept mainly for looks, rarity and interest, not production.

Climate notes

As a tropical breed, Ayam Cemani handle heat well with shade and water. Black feathers do absorb sun, so shade is still important. In cold climates, give them a dry, draft-free coop. Their single comb can get frostbite in hard freezes.

Buying tips

Ayam Cemani are expensive compared with most breeds. Because of the price, mixed birds sometimes get sold as purebred. Check for dark tongues, mouths and combs, and ask breeders about their lines. Birds with red in the comb or mouth are not true to type.

They are often compared with the Silkie, which also has dark skin from the same trait, though Silkies have fluffy feathers and very different personalities. If egg color matters to you, the cream egg page lists other breeds in the same range.

Where to find them

Specialty breeders and a few hatcheries sell them. Supply is better than it once was, but prices remain high.

Common questions about Ayam Cemani

Do Ayam Cemani lay black eggs?

No. Their eggs are cream to lightly tinted.

Why are Ayam Cemani so expensive?

They are still uncommon, and breeding true to type takes careful selection.

Are Ayam Cemani good layers?

Not really. They lay a modest number of eggs.
909:
What Ayam Kampung really means

Ayam Kampung means "village chicken" in Indonesian and Malay. It is not one standardized breed like a Wyandotte or an Orpington. It is a broad name for the free ranging, mixed native chickens kept around homes and villages in Indonesia and Malaysia. Because of that, birds called Ayam Kampung vary widely in color, size and comb type.

That makes it hard to say exactly what one will look like. What they share is a practical background. These chickens are used to finding much of their own food, surviving heat and humidity, and raising their own chicks.

What to expect if you keep them

  • Hardy, self-reliant birds that forage well.
  • Often good fliers and alert to predators.
  • Modest egg numbers, with frequent broodiness.
  • Highly variable looks, even within one group.

They are well suited to hot, humid climates. In colder places, they need a dry, draft-free coop, and single combs can get frostbite.

Availability outside Southeast Asia

Outside their home region, birds sold as Ayam Kampung are rare and hard to verify. Because there is no single breed standard, you are relying on the seller's knowledge of where the stock came from. If you want a standardized Indonesian breed, the Ayam Cemani is the best known, though it is a very different bird.

If you simply want a hardy, heat-tolerant backyard bird, the hot climate breed list has options that are easier to buy in the US.

Common questions about Ayam Kampung

Is Ayam Kampung a breed?

Not in the standardized sense. It is a general name for village chickens in Indonesia and Malaysia.

Are Ayam Kampung good layers?

They usually lay a modest number of eggs and go broody often.

Can I buy Ayam Kampung in the US?

They are rare and hard to verify. Ask sellers about the origin of their stock.
910:
What to know about Barbezieux chickens

The Barbezieux is a French breed from the area around the town of Barbezieux in western France. It is often described as one of the tallest French chicken breeds. Birds are black with a green sheen, with a large single comb and long legs. It was historically valued as a table bird and also lays well-sized white eggs.

It nearly disappeared in the 20th century, and today it is kept mostly by French breed enthusiasts. Outside France it is rare, and in the United States it is very hard to find.

Keeping them

  • Tall, fairly heavy birds that need generous space and wide doors.
  • Large single combs that can get frostbite in hard winters.
  • Black feathers that soak up sun, so summer shade matters.
  • Large white eggs.

Detailed information about temperament and laying patterns is limited in English sources, so expect a heavy, active farm bird and plan your coop around its size. Higher doors, sturdy roosts and roomy nest boxes help.

Similar breeds that are easier to find

If you like the look of a big black French bird, the La Fleche is another French table breed in black. For a tall, black, white egg layer that is easier to buy in the US, the Minorca is worth a look, though it comes from Spain rather than France.

Where to find them

Barbezieux are rarely offered in the US. Rare breed groups and imported lines are the main sources, and supply may be close to none in a given year.

Common questions about Barbezieux

What color eggs do Barbezieux lay?

White eggs, usually large for the breed's size.

Are Barbezieux good meat birds?

They were historically raised as a quality French table bird.

Can I buy Barbezieux in the US?

It is very difficult. They are rare outside France.
911:
What Barnevelders are like to keep

Barnevelders are a Dutch breed named after the town of Barneveld, best known for dark brown eggs and beautiful double-laced feathers. In person, a well-marked hen looks like she is wearing layered rows of brown and black. They are a heavy, calm bird that suits a relaxed backyard flock.

Most Barnevelders are gentle and steady. They are not usually the first ones in your hand, but they settle easily and are rarely flighty. They forage well and do not mind confinement if the run is roomy.

Who they suit and who they do not

  • Good for keepers who want dark eggs in the basket and a calm, attractive bird.
  • Good in cooler climates and mixed flocks.
  • Not the best pick if your top goal is the highest egg count. Many keepers are surprised that output is moderate, not huge.

Eggs, color and the seasons

Barnevelders lay medium to large brown eggs, and in good lines they are a rich, dark brown. Two things catch new keepers off guard. First, the color varies a lot between strains, and hatchery birds may lay lighter eggs than breeder birds. Second, egg color usually lightens over the laying season, then darkens again after the molt and rest. That is normal and not a health problem. You can see more breeds in this range on the dark egg color page.

Laying slows in fall and winter and during the molt. Hens tend to lay well for the first two seasons, then taper.

Space, coop and climate

Treat them like any heavy large fowl, with about 4 square feet per bird in the coop and 10 in the run. They are cold-hardy because of their size and dense feathering. They have a single comb, so in very cold weather keep the coop dry and well ventilated to lower the risk of frostbite. They handle moderate heat well if they have shade and water.

Health and handling quirks

There are no big breed-specific problems. Some practical notes:

  • They can be on the heavy side, so do not overdo treats.
  • Broodiness is occasional, not constant.
  • Low roosts help heavy hens avoid foot strain when jumping down, which can help prevent bumblefoot.

Barnevelder vs Welsummer and Barred Rock

If dark eggs are the draw, the Welsummer is the usual alternative. Welsummers tend to be more active foragers and lay terracotta brown eggs, often speckled. Barnevelders are a little heavier and calmer. The Barred Plymouth Rock vs Barnevelder comparison is worth a read if you are choosing between a reliable layer and a prettier, darker egg.

Varieties and where to buy

The double-laced pattern is the classic. You may also see blue double-laced, silver and black, depending on the country and breeder. Many hatcheries sell Barnevelders, but breeders are your best bet for dark eggs and correct lacing. Ask what color eggs the parent hens lay. Expect to pay more for breeder stock than for hatchery chicks.

Common questions about Barnevelders

Why are my Barnevelder eggs getting lighter?

Brown pigment is added at the end of shell formation, and many hens lay lighter as the season goes on. Color often darkens again after a rest.

Are Barnevelders good layers?

They are fair to good, not top production layers. Expect a moderate supply of dark brown eggs.

Are Barnevelders friendly?

They are usually calm and easy to handle, though not always lap chickens.
914:
About the Basque hen

The Basque hen, known in Basque as Euskal Oiloa, comes from the Basque Country of northern Spain. It is a dual-purpose farm breed that was developed and preserved there as a local breed. It lays brown eggs and has a solid, medium to heavy body.

Several color varieties exist in the breed. The red type is one of the best known. Outside Spain, the Basque is rare, and in the US only a few breeders keep it.

What they are like to keep

  • Usually calm and practical farm birds.
  • Good foragers that also tolerate a run.
  • Brown eggs in reasonable numbers for a heritage breed.
  • Single comb, so watch for frostbite in very cold weather.

They need standard large fowl space. Because detailed English-language information is limited, ask any breeder about the temperament and laying of their specific line.

Climate notes

The breed comes from a green, rainy part of Spain, so a coop that stays dry inside matters more than extra heat. Muddy runs are the bigger problem in wet regions, so add drainage or deep litter. In hot summers, give shade and cool water.

Who they suit

Basque hens suit keepers who want a dual-purpose heritage bird and are interested in a rare breed. They are a good conversation piece for anyone who likes regional breeds with a story. If you want something similar that is easy to buy, look at the dual-purpose breed list, or at a common brown egg layer like the Rhode Island Red.

Where to find them

Basque hens are uncommon in the US. A small number of breeders have imported lines, and supply is limited. Expect higher prices and waiting lists.

Common questions about Basque hens

What color eggs do Basque hens lay?

Brown eggs.

Are Basque chickens friendly?

They are generally described as calm, but temperament varies by line.

Where do Basque chickens come from?

The Basque Country of northern Spain.
916:
Belgian Antwerp Danvers, one breed under many names

If you see "Belgian Antwerp Danvers" in a hatchery list, it is the same bird as the Belgian d'Anvers. "Danvers" is a run-together spelling of d'Anvers, which is French for "of Antwerp." You may also see Antwerp Belgian, Barbu d'Anvers or Bearded d'Anvers. All of these point to one small, bearded Belgian bantam.

How to check you are getting the right bird

Because names get mixed up, it helps to know the key traits.

  • True bantam size, with no large fowl version.
  • Full beard and muffs.
  • Rose comb, not a single comb.
  • Clean, unfeathered legs.
  • Upright, chest-forward stance, especially in roosters.

If the birds you receive have feathered feet and single combs, you probably have d'Uccles instead. Those have their own page under Mille Fleur d'Uccle. If they have feathered feet but no beard, that points to a Booted Bantam.

What they are like to keep

Most are lively, alert and easy to tame with handling. They suit small coops and runs. Hens lay small, light-colored eggs and some go broody. Their rose combs do well in cold weather, while beards need watching in winter, since water can freeze in them. They can fly over low fences, so a roof on the run is a good idea.

Where to buy

A few hatcheries sell them under this name, often in quail, mille fleur, porcelain or self blue. Bantam breeders and poultry shows offer a wider range of colors and closer to standard birds.

Common questions about Belgian Antwerp Danvers

Is "Danvers" a different breed?

No. It is another spelling of d'Anvers, meaning from Antwerp.

How big do they get?

They are true bantams, so they stay small, much smaller than standard hens.

Are they noisy?

Hens are fairly quiet. Roosters crow like any rooster.
917:
What the Belgian d'Anvers is like

The Belgian d'Anvers, also called the Antwerp Belgian or Barbu d'Anvers, is a true bantam from the Antwerp area of Belgium. There is no large version. It has a full beard and muffs, a small rose comb, clean legs and a proud, chest-out posture. Roosters in particular strut with their tails held high and their heads pulled back.

How it differs from the d'Uccle

The d'Anvers is often mixed up with the bearded d'Uccle. Both are small, bearded Belgian bantams, and both come in patterns like mille fleur and porcelain. The easy way to tell them apart is the feet and comb. The d'Uccle has heavily feathered feet and a single comb. The d'Anvers has clean legs and a rose comb. If you like the look of a Mille Fleur d'Uccle but hate muddy foot feathers, the d'Anvers is worth a look.

Daily care

  • Small size means little space and feed, which suits small yards.
  • Small cream to white eggs in modest numbers. People keep them for charm, not production.
  • Beards get wet and dirty at open waterers. Cups or nipples keep faces cleaner.
  • Check under the beard for mites and lice during health checks.
  • They fly well for their size, so a covered run is useful.

The rose comb holds up well in cold weather. Like all bantams, they need protection from predators that larger hens might fend off.

Quail is the classic color, and many others exist. Most come from bantam breeders, and some hatcheries carry a few colors.

Common questions about Belgian d'Anvers

Is a d'Anvers the same as a d'Uccle?

No. The d'Anvers has clean legs and a rose comb. The d'Uccle has feathered feet and a single comb.

Are Belgian d'Anvers friendly?

Many are tame and easy to handle, though roosters can be bold for their size.

Do d'Anvers lay many eggs?

No. Hens give a modest number of small eggs.
921:
What Bielefelders are like to keep

The Bielefelder is a modern German breed developed in the 1970s around Bielefeld by breeder Gerd Roth. It is large, calm and autosexing, which means chicks can be sexed by down color at hatch, and that keeps working generation after generation. Its full German name is Bielefelder Kennhuhn.

Adult hens show a barred, crele-type pattern with gold and salmon tones. Roosters are big, showy birds with orange and barred feathers. Most Bielefelders are gentle and easy to handle, and many keepers describe them as friendly.

Who they suit

  • Keepers who hatch their own chicks and want to know which are hens.
  • Families who want a calm, large bird.
  • Cold climate keepers.

They are less ideal for very small coops because of their size, and they cost more than hatchery breeds.

Laying pattern

Bielefelders are good layers of large brown eggs. Like other heavy breeds, they can take a while to start. They lay best in spring and summer and slow in winter and during the molt. Some hens go broody.

Sexing chicks

Female chicks generally have darker down with clear chipmunk-style stripes. Male chicks are generally lighter, with fuzzier markings and often a light spot on the head. Compare chicks side by side, as differences are clearer that way.

Space and climate

Give them generous space, low roosts and large nest boxes. They handle cold well. Their single comb can get frostbite in harsh winters, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. In heat, they need shade and water like any heavy breed.

Compared with similar breeds

The Cream Legbar is another autosexing breed, lighter and crested, laying blue eggs. If you mainly want easy sexing for a laying flock, a hybrid like the Black Sex Link works too, but it will not breed true.

Where to buy

Bielefelders are uncommon but growing in the US. Breeders and a few hatcheries sell chicks and hatching eggs.

Common questions about Bielefelders

Are Bielefelders friendly?

Most are calm and gentle.

How big do Bielefelders get?

They are a large breed, with roosters noticeably bigger than hens.

Do Bielefelders lay well?

Yes. They are good layers of large brown eggs.
922:
What Kennhuhn means

Bielefelder Kennhuhn is the full German name of the Bielefelder. Kennhuhn roughly means a chicken you can recognize or identify, which points to the breed's main selling point. It is autosexing. You can tell male chicks from female chicks by their down color at hatch, without crossing two breeds.

It is the same breed, not a separate strain. Some sellers use the long name, some the short one.

How autosexing works here

The breed carries a barred, crele-type pattern. Day-old females generally show darker down with clear chipmunk-like stripes down the back. Males are generally lighter, with blurrier markings and often a light spot on the head. Sexing takes a little practice, and comparing chicks side by side helps a lot.

Unlike sex link hybrids such as the Black Sex Link, a Bielefelder bred to a Bielefelder keeps producing autosexing chicks. That makes it useful if you hatch your own.

What adult birds are like

  • Large, heavy and usually calm.
  • Good layers of large brown eggs.
  • Cold-hardy thanks to size and dense feathers.
  • Roosters are big and showy, with orange, red and barred tones.

They need standard large fowl space and low, sturdy roosts. Single combs can frostbite in very cold weather, so keep the coop dry and well ventilated.

Where to get them

Bielefelders are still uncommon in the US but easier to find than they used to be. Breeders and a few hatcheries sell them, often under either name.

Common questions about Bielefelder Kennhuhn

Is Bielefelder Kennhuhn different from Bielefelder?

No. Kennhuhn is part of the full German name for the same breed.

Can I sex Bielefelder chicks at hatch?

Yes, by down color and markings, though it takes some practice.

Are Bielefelders good layers?

Yes, they are known as solid layers of large brown eggs.
923:
What sets the Birchen color apart

Birchen is one of the darker Old English colors, and it is easy to spot once you know what to look for. On a Birchen rooster, the hackle and saddle feathers are silvery white with black striping, and the black breast carries narrow silver edging toward the top. Hens are mostly black with silver lacing around the neck. Birchens usually have dark faces and dark eyes.

If you have seen a Brown Red, a Birchen is close to its silver counterpart. Where a Black Breasted Brown Red shows lemon or orange in the hackle, the Birchen shows silver.

How it relates to the Old English Game

"Standard Old English" is the name many hatcheries use for large fowl Old English Game, as opposed to the more common bantams. The color does not change the bird underneath. A Birchen behaves, lays and needs care exactly like any other Old English Game.

  • Hardy, active and an excellent forager.
  • Small, cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers.
  • Hens go broody readily and are protective mothers.
  • Good fliers, so expect them to roost high or clear low fences.

Keeping Birchens in a backyard flock

The game background matters more than the color. Roosters of this breed will fight other roosters, sometimes seriously, so most keepers run one male per group. Their tight feathering sheds rain well but insulates less than fluffy breeds, so give them a dry, draft-free coop in winter. Single combs can get frostbite in hard freezes.

Birchens are less common than red-based colors. Look to game breeders at shows and hatcheries with large fowl Old English.

Common questions about Birchen Old English

Is Birchen the same as Brown Red?

No. They are related patterns, but Birchen uses silver where Brown Red uses lemon or gold.

Do Birchen Old English hens lay well?

They lay a modest number of small eggs and spend a lot of time broody.

Can I keep two Birchen roosters together?

It is risky. Males often fight, so one per flock is safer.
927:
The Black Breasted Brown Red look

Brown Red is one of the classic dark game colors. The rooster is mostly black with lemon to orange hackle and saddle feathers striped with black, and the breast is black. Hens are largely black with lemon in the hackle. Brown Reds are known for dark faces, often described as purple or gypsy-faced, along with dark eyes and dark legs. The name "Black Breasted" here points to a cleaner black breast, as opposed to the more heavily laced Brown Breasted Brown Red.

How it fits the Old English Game breed

This is a color of the large fowl Old English Game, which some hatcheries sell as "Standard Old English." Every color shares the same tight-feathered, upright game body and the same temperament. Individual lines vary more than colors do.

What to expect day to day

  • Active birds that forage hard and prefer room to roam.
  • Strong fliers. A covered run or tall fence keeps them home.
  • Small cream or tinted eggs, mostly in spring and summer.
  • Very broody hens that make fierce, attentive mothers.

Roosters are the main management issue. Game males fight other males and can be quick to do it, so plan on one rooster per group or separate pens. Hens tend to get along.

Climate and coop

Tight feathers mean they handle wet weather well but have less fluff for cold. A dry, ventilated coop without drafts is enough for most winters. Watch single combs for frostbite in deep cold. They tolerate heat well with shade.

Where to find them

Brown Reds are popular with game breeders, and some hatcheries offer them in large fowl.

Common questions about Black Breasted Brown Red Old English

Why do Brown Red Old English have dark faces?

Dark skin pigment around the face is a normal trait of the Brown Red color.

Are Brown Red hens good mothers?

Yes. Old English hens are known for going broody and protecting chicks.

Are they good for eggs?

Not really. They lay small eggs in modest numbers.
928:
What the Jungle Fowl strain means

This listing is a Black Breasted Red Old English sold as a "Jungle Fowl" type. The idea is a bird that looks close to the wild red junglefowl, the ancestor of domestic chickens. Roosters show red to orange hackles and saddles, red shoulders, a black breast and a black tail with green sheen. Hens are brown and finely stippled, with a lighter salmon breast, which is a camouflage pattern suited to sitting on a hidden nest.

This is still a domestic chicken, a color strain of Old English Game. It is not a captive wild junglefowl. The name describes the look.

How it differs from the standard Black Breasted Red

The Black Breasted Red Old English shares the same basic color. A Jungle Fowl listing is usually aimed at keepers who want the wild-type appearance rather than strict show color. Exact differences depend on the hatchery or breeder, so look at photos of their adult birds before you order.

Keeping them

  • Alert, active and quick. They do best with space to forage.
  • Good fliers that often roost in trees if allowed.
  • Hens are frequent broodies and protective mothers.
  • Small cream to tinted eggs, mostly in warm months.

Roosters will fight other roosters. One male per flock is the safe plan. Their tight feathers shed rain but give less warmth, so keep the coop dry and out of drafts in winter.

Where to get them

Some hatcheries sell this exact listing as part of their large fowl Old English range. Game breeders may offer similar wild-type birds under their own names.

Common questions about Jungle Fowl Old English

Is this a real wild junglefowl?

No. It is a domestic Old English Game bred to look like the wild red junglefowl.

Will the hens hatch their own chicks?

Very often. They go broody readily and are good mothers.

Can they live in a small backyard?

They can, but they are active and fly well, so a covered run is best.
929:
The Black Breasted Red Aseel

Black Breasted Red is a classic color in the Aseel, the old game breed from the Indian subcontinent. Roosters show red hackles and saddles over a black breast and tail. Hens are usually brown with darker markings. The color sits on the Aseel body, which is short, very muscular and tight-feathered, with a pea comb, small wattles and a hard, intense face.

How it relates to the parent breed

Color does not change what an Aseel is. The breed was developed for fighting, and that history drives how you keep it.

  • Aseel can be aggressive toward other chickens, and both roosters and hens may fight.
  • Many are surprisingly calm and tolerant with people.
  • Hens lay few eggs, usually small and tinted to light brown.
  • Hens are strongly broody and are excellent, protective mothers.
  • They mature slowly.

Because of the aggression toward other birds, many keepers house Aseel separately or in small groups of their own breed, rather than in a mixed backyard flock.

Climate and coop

Aseel generally handle heat well. Their tight feathering gives less insulation in cold weather, so a dry, draft-free coop matters in winter. The pea comb resists frostbite. Give them sturdy, low roosts and enough space to avoid conflict.

A similar, better-known game choice is the Black Breasted Red Old English, which is lighter and more active but still a game bird.

Where to find them

Aseel are uncommon in the US. Some hatcheries list them, and game fowl breeders keep them. Buy from sources that can show adult birds.

Common questions about Black Breasted Red Aseel

Can Aseel live with other chickens?

Often not well. They tend to fight other birds, so separate housing is common.

Are Aseel friendly to people?

Many are calm with their keepers. Their aggression is mostly aimed at other chickens.

Are Aseel good egg layers?

No. They lay few eggs but are great mothers.
932:
The classic Black Breasted Red

Black Breasted Red is the most familiar color in Old English Game, and it is the picture most people have of a fighting rooster from old paintings. The rooster has bright red to orange hackles and saddle feathers, deep red shoulders, a black breast and a black tail. Hens are brown with fine stippling and a salmon breast.

Why this color is so common

This pattern is close to the wild type, so it shows up easily and has been kept for centuries. It is often the first color a hatchery lists under "Standard Old English," which is the large fowl version of the breed. It is usually the easiest Old English color to find.

What daily life looks like

  • Alert birds that forage well.
  • Small cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers.
  • Hens often go broody and raise chicks without help.
  • Strong fliers, so clip wings or cover the run if you need to keep them in.

The game background shows up most in roosters. Males fight each other and may fight to serious injury, so one rooster per group is the standard advice. Hens are generally manageable, and many become tame with regular handling.

Climate notes

Hard, tight feathering sheds water well but traps less heat, so a dry coop matters more than extra heat. Single combs can be nipped by frost in very cold climates. They handle hot summers well when they have shade.

Similar colors

The Crele is basically a barred version of this color. The Jungle Fowl listing is a strain aimed at the wild look.

Common questions about Black Breasted Red Old English

Why do the hens look so different from the roosters?

Hens carry a brown, camouflaged version of the pattern, while roosters show the bright red and black.

Are Black Breasted Red Old English good layers?

No. They lay a modest number of small eggs.

Are the roosters aggressive?

They are usually aggressive with other roosters. Temperament with people varies by bird and line.
934:
What makes the Black Japanese Bantam special

The Black Japanese Bantam is a solid black version of one of the most unusual chicken shapes around. Japanese Bantams have very short legs, a large upright single comb and a tall tail that sweeps up almost to the head. In black, the feathers carry a green sheen that sets off the red comb.

Black breeds true, so two black parents give black chicks. That makes it a straightforward color to keep and breed compared with diluted colors like blue.

How it relates to the Japanese Bantam breed

Color is the only thing that changes. Everything that makes the Japanese Bantam tricky to breed applies here too. The short legs come from a gene that is lethal when a chick gets two copies. When two short-legged birds are bred, about a quarter of the embryos die in the shell. Breeders often use a longer-legged bird in pairings, knowing some chicks will not have show leg length.

Day to day care

  • Their low build means tails and wings drag in mud. Keep runs dry and clean.
  • The big single comb is prone to frostbite. A warmer, draft-free coop helps in cold areas.
  • They are small and lay small cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers.
  • Many hens go broody.

Black birds absorb more heat, so in summer they need good shade. Japanese bantams are usually friendly and suit small yard setups.

Where to find them

Black is a common Japanese color. Some hatcheries sell it, and many bantam breeders keep it.

Common questions about Black Japanese Bantams

Why do some Black Japanese chicks have long legs?

Breeders often pair short and long-legged birds to avoid the lethal short leg combination, so some chicks have longer legs.

Are Black Japanese Bantams good layers?

Expect small eggs, and not many of them. They are kept for looks and personality.

Do they need a special coop?

They need a dry floor and protection from cold drafts to keep combs and tails in good shape.
935:
What makes the Black Laced Red different

Black Laced Red is a Wyandotte variety with deep red to mahogany feathers, each edged in black. It looks like a darker, redder cousin of the Golden Laced Wyandotte. In good light the contrast is rich, and roosters are especially bright on the hackle and saddle. Lacing quality varies a lot between sources, and hatchery birds often show less even lacing than breeder stock.

How it relates to the parent breed

Under the color it is a standard Wyandotte, an American breed with a rounded body and a low rose comb.

  • Calm and easy to handle, though some hens are a bit bossy.
  • Good layers of light to medium brown eggs.
  • Very cold-hardy, helped by the rose comb that resists frostbite.
  • Some hens go broody.

Day to day

Treat them like any large fowl, with about 4 square feet each in the coop and more in the run. Dark feathers soak up sun, so summer shade matters. Thick feathering around the vent can collect droppings, so check now and then. Wyandottes also sometimes take a while to start laying, so do not worry if your pullets start a little later than the production birds.

Where to find them

Black Laced Red is less common than Silver or Golden Laced but is sold by some hatcheries and breeders. If you want strong lacing, ask breeders for photos of adult hens.

Common questions about Black Laced Red Wyandottes

Are Black Laced Red Wyandottes good layers?

Yes. Like other Wyandottes, they are dependable layers of brown eggs.

Do they handle cold winters?

Yes. The rose comb and dense feathering make them very cold-hardy.

How are they different from Golden Laced?

The ground color is a deeper red or mahogany instead of gold.
937:
What a Black Red Star is

Black Red Star is one of several hatchery names for a black sex link hybrid. You may also see Black Star or Black Sex Link. The usual cross is a red rooster, such as a Rhode Island Red or New Hampshire, over a barred hen, such as a Barred Plymouth Rock. Exact parent lines depend on the hatchery.

Why people buy them

The big draw is sexing at hatch. Because barring passes from the mother to sons, the chicks are easy to tell apart. Male chicks usually have a white spot on the head and grow up barred. Female chicks are solid black and grow into black hens, often with red or gold on the neck and breast. That means you are much less likely to end up with a surprise rooster.

What they are like to keep

  • Strong layers of brown eggs, bred mainly for production.
  • Usually friendly, calm and easy to handle.
  • Hardy in cold weather thanks to solid size and dark, dense feathers.
  • Rarely broody, which keeps eggs coming.

They need standard large fowl space. Dark feathers absorb heat, so give shade in summer. Single combs can frostbite in harsh winters.

Breeding them on

Sex links do not breed true. If you hatch eggs from Black Red Star hens, you will not get the same autosexing chicks. To get more, you need to repeat the original cross.

They are easy to find at hatcheries and often at feed stores in spring.

Common questions about Black Red Stars

Is Black Red Star the same as Black Sex Link?

Yes, broadly. Both names describe the same type of red over barred cross, though lines differ by hatchery.

Do Black Red Stars lay a lot of eggs?

Yes. They are bred as productive brown egg layers.

Can I breed my Black Red Stars?

You can, but the chicks will not be true sex links.
940:
Solid black Old English Game

The Black Old English is exactly what the name says. It is a solid black bird with a strong green sheen in good light. Combined with the tight, upright game build, it is a sleek, clean-looking chicken. Most have dark legs and dark eyes, with a red face and comb that stand out against the feathers.

One practical plus is that black breeds true. Two black parents give black chicks, unlike the Blue Old English, which splits into blue, black and splash.

Relationship to the parent breed

"Standard Old English" is a hatchery name for large fowl Old English Game. The black variety shares everything with other colors except the feathers. Expect a hardy, active bird with strong instincts.

  • Good foragers and quick to spot danger.
  • Small cream to tinted eggs, mostly in spring and summer.
  • Very broody hens with strong mothering instincts.
  • Able fliers who often roost higher than other breeds.

Living with Black Old English

Black feathers absorb heat, so in hot summers they need shade and airflow more than lighter colors do. In winter, their tight feathering gives less insulation than fluffy breeds, so a dry, well-ventilated coop without drafts is key. Watch the single comb in very cold snaps.

Roosters are the challenge, as with all Old English. They fight other roosters, so plan one per pen. Hens get along with most flock mates and can become quite tame.

Black is a less flashy color, so it is usually easy to source from hatcheries that carry large fowl Old English, and breeders sometimes have extra stock.

Common questions about Black Old English

Does Black Old English breed true?

Yes. Black to black produces black chicks.

Do Black Old English do well in heat?

They handle heat fairly well but absorb more sun than light colors, so shade is important.

Are they good mothers?

Yes. Old English hens are famous for going broody and protecting chicks.
941:
How the Black Sex Link cross works

A Black Sex Link is a first generation hybrid made by crossing a red or gold rooster, most often a Rhode Island Red or New Hampshire, with a Barred Plymouth Rock hen. The barring gene sits on the sex chromosome, and a hen passes it only to her sons. So all the sons are barred, and the daughters are not.

At hatch, that shows up as a simple color code. Males are black with a white or light spot on the head. Females are black without the spot. Adult hens are mostly black, often with red or gold tones on the neck and chest. Adult roosters are barred.

What daily life with them looks like

Black Sex Links are practical birds. They are known for:

  • Strong laying of brown eggs from an early age.
  • Calm, friendly temperaments.
  • Good cold tolerance thanks to their size and feathering.
  • Low broodiness, so laying is rarely interrupted.

Like many high-output layers, they tend to lay hardest in their first couple of years, then slow down. Feed a good layer ration and offer oyster shell, which the grit and oyster shell guide covers.

Climate and coop

Give standard large fowl space. Their single comb can get frostbite in bitter cold, and dark feathers mean they need shade in hot weather.

Breeding and buying

They do not breed true. Offspring from two Black Sex Links will be mixed and not reliably sexable. Hatcheries and feed stores sell them widely, sometimes as Black Star or Black Red Star.

Common questions about Black Sex Links

How do I sex Black Sex Link chicks?

Males have a white or light spot on the head. Females do not.

Are Black Sex Links good for beginners?

Yes. They are hardy, calm and productive.

Do Black Sex Links go broody?

Rarely. They are bred for laying.
943:
The Black Tailed Buff variety

Black Tailed Buff Japanese Bantams have a warm golden buff body with a black tail. The contrast is striking against the breed's tall, upright tail and large red comb. Wings may show some black too. The color looks simple, but getting an even buff body without patchy or washed out areas takes careful breeding, so quality varies between sources.

How it relates to the Japanese Bantam

This is a color variety of the Japanese Bantam, a true bantam with no large fowl version. Shape, size and temperament are the same as other colors. It is closely related to the Black Tailed White, which follows the same pattern on a white body.

Keeping them well

  • Short legs mean they sit low, so mud and wet bedding quickly dirty their feathers.
  • The big comb needs protection from hard frost.
  • Buff feathers can fade in strong sun. Shade helps keep color even if you plan to show.
  • Hens lay small eggs in modest numbers and often go broody.

Breeding has the same catch as all Japanese. The short-leg gene is lethal in double dose, so short to short pairings lose some embryos. Expect variable leg length in your chicks if you hatch.

Who they suit

They are a good fit for small yards and for keepers who enjoy ornamental birds. Most are friendly and easy to tame. They are not a choice for egg production or for wet, muddy, free range setups.

How common are they?

Black Tailed Buff is less common than Black Tailed White. Look for bantam breeders and poultry shows, and some hatcheries offer them seasonally.

Common questions about Black Tailed Buff Japanese Bantams

Do Black Tailed Buff Japanese breed true?

Color is fairly consistent between good birds, but leg length varies because of the short-leg gene.

Are they friendly?

Most are calm and easy to handle, especially if handled young.

Can they live outside in winter?

Yes, with a dry, draft-free coop. Watch their large combs in hard frost.
946:
The most recognized Japanese Bantam color

Black Tailed White is the variety many people picture when they hear "Japanese Bantam." The body is white, the tail is black, and the tail feathers usually carry white edging. Set on a very short-legged bird with a tall upright tail and a big red comb, it is one of the most eye-catching bantams at any show.

How it relates to the parent breed

This is a color of the Japanese Bantam, also known in Japan as Chabo. All the breed traits come along with it.

  • A true bantam, with no large fowl version.
  • Short legs from a gene that is lethal in double dose, so short to short pairings lose about a quarter of embryos.
  • Small cream or tinted eggs in modest numbers.
  • Friendly temperament and frequent broodiness.

Keeping the white clean

White birds show dirt quickly, and Japanese sit so low that their feathers almost touch the ground. Dry bedding, a well-drained run and regular cleaning keep them looking good. If you plan to show, many keepers keep them on clean shavings for weeks beforehand. Strong sun can yellow white feathers in some birds, so give shade.

Climate and coop

The big single comb is the weak spot in cold weather. A coop that is dry, ventilated and out of drafts lowers frostbite risk. They handle warm weather well with shade. Their size suits small coops and small yards.

Where to find them

This is the easiest Japanese color to find. Many hatcheries sell it, and most Japanese breeders keep it.

Common questions about Black Tailed White Japanese Bantams

Are Black Tailed White Japanese good with kids?

Usually yes. They are small, calm and easy to tame.

Why are some of my chicks long-legged?

Breeders often cross short and long-legged birds to avoid the lethal short-leg combination.

How many eggs do they lay?

A modest number of small eggs, with breaks for broodiness.
947:
How the Blue color works in Old English

Blue Old English are a soft slate gray, often with darker edging on the feathers and darker hackles and tails on roosters. The color is attractive, but it has a genetic quirk every keeper should know about. Blue does not breed true.

The blue gene dilutes black. A bird with one copy is blue. A bird with two copies is splash, which is pale with gray or blue flecks. A bird with no copies is black. Breed two blues together and you get roughly half blue, a quarter black and a quarter splash. Breed black to splash and nearly all chicks come out blue.

Relationship to the parent breed

This is a color variety of large fowl Old English Game, sold by some hatcheries as "Standard Old English." Shape, temperament and care do not change with the color. The Black Old English is the closest relative and the one you would use to make more blues.

What to expect from them

  • Hardy, alert, active foragers.
  • Small cream or tinted eggs, laid mostly in warm months.
  • Hens go broody easily and mother well.
  • Strong fliers that need a covered run or tall fence.
  • Roosters fight other roosters, so keep one male per pen.

Climate and coop

Their tight feathers are good in rain but less warm in deep cold, so give them a dry, ventilated coop without drafts. Single combs can get frostbite in harsh cold. They handle heat well with shade.

Where to find them

Some hatcheries and game breeders offer blue. Ask whether you will get blues only, or a mix of blue, black and splash.

Common questions about Blue Old English

Why did my blue chicks hatch black and splash?

Blue does not breed true. Blue to blue pairings produce some black and some splash chicks.

How do I get all blue chicks?

Pair a black bird with a splash bird. Nearly all chicks will be blue.

Are Blue Old English different from other colors in temperament?

No. Temperament depends on the bird and its line, not the color.
949:
Living with Booted Bantams

The Booted Bantam, known in the Netherlands as the Sabelpoot, is a true bantam with no large version. Its trademark is heavy foot feathering plus stiff feathers growing down from the hocks, called vulture hocks. The result is a tiny bird that looks like it is wearing big feathery boots.

Many keepers find them friendly and easy to tame. They are small enough for kids to hold, and they do well in small spaces.

Booted Bantam vs d'Uccle

The Booted Bantam and the Mille Fleur d'Uccle look a lot alike. Both have feathered feet, single combs and colors like mille fleur and porcelain. The key difference is the face. A d'Uccle has a beard and muffs. A Booted Bantam does not. The Belgian d'Anvers has a beard but clean legs.

Care for feathered feet

  • Keep bedding dry and change it often, since foot feathers pick up mud and droppings.
  • In winter, check for mud or ice balls stuck in foot feathers.
  • Look under the leg feathers for scaly leg mites during checks.
  • Low roosts and soft landing areas help protect foot feathers from breaking.
  • Grass runs or dry sand work better than wet dirt.

Eggs and personality

Hens lay small cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers. Many go broody and make good mothers for small clutches. They are mostly calm, though roosters can be bold for their size.

Climate notes

Their size makes them more sensitive to deep cold than big birds, and their single comb can frostbite. A dry, draft-free coop is important. They handle mild heat well with shade.

Where to buy

Booted Bantams are less common than d'Uccles in the US. Bantam breeders and poultry shows are the most reliable sources, and some hatcheries carry a few colors.

Common questions about Booted Bantams

Do Booted Bantams have beards?

No. Beards are what separate d'Uccles from Booted Bantams.

Are Booted Bantams good with kids?

Usually yes. They are small and often tame.

How do I keep their foot feathers clean?

Dry bedding, clean runs and avoiding mud make the biggest difference.
951:
What Brabanters are like

The Brabanter is an old crested breed from the Low Countries, associated with the Brabant region of the Netherlands and Belgium. It has a distinctive upright crest that is narrow side to side and stands up rather than spreading into a ball like a Polish crest. It also has a full beard and muffs and a small V-shaped comb. Hens lay white eggs.

Brabanters nearly vanished in the 20th century and were later rebuilt by Dutch breeders. They remain uncommon, especially in the US.

Day to day

  • Active and alert birds that like to forage.
  • Generally not aggressive, though some can be flighty.
  • White eggs, with fair to good laying for a heritage breed.
  • Usually not strongly broody.

Crest and beard care

The upright crest tends to block vision less than a big round crest, but it still needs care.

  • Part the crest and beard to check for mites and lice.
  • Use waterers that keep beards and crests from soaking.
  • Watch for flock mates pulling crest feathers.

The small V comb is a plus in cold weather. In wet winters, keep crests dry so they do not freeze.

Compared with similar breeds

The Polish has a much larger round crest. The Appenzeller Spitzhauben has a forward crest and V comb but no beard. The Brabanter sits in between, with an upright crest plus a beard.

Where to find them

Brabanters are rare in the US. A few breeders keep them. Rare breed clubs and shows are the best leads.

Common questions about Brabanters

What color eggs do Brabanters lay?

White eggs.

Do Brabanters see well with their crests?

Their upright crest blocks vision less than larger crests, but check that it stays clean and trimmed if needed.

Are Brabanters rare?

Yes. They are uncommon, especially in the US.
953:
What life with Brahmas is really like

Brahmas are big, slow, feather-footed chickens with a calm nature. They are one of the largest breeds you can keep, and a full-grown rooster can look startling next to a normal hen. Most people find them gentle, and many keepers call them gentle giants.

Day to day they tend to move at their own pace, walking rather than running. They are easy to catch and usually tolerate handling well, so they are a good choice around kids, as long as the kids can manage a heavy bird. They are not great fliers, which makes them easy to contain with a modest fence.

Who Brahmas suit

  • Cold climate keepers who want a hardy bird.
  • Families who want a calm, easy to handle chicken.
  • People who like a striking bird and do not need the most eggs.

They are a weaker fit for small coops, muddy yards or keepers who want maximum egg numbers. They also take a long time to mature.

Laying across seasons and age

Brahmas are slow to mature, and many pullets start laying later than lighter breeds. They lay medium brown eggs. One thing keepers like is that many Brahmas lay fairly well in fall and winter compared with lighter breeds, though nothing lays at full speed in the short days. Output is moderate overall, and some hens go broody, especially in spring.

Space, coop and climate

Size changes your coop plan. Brahmas need more room than average, wider pop doors, larger nest boxes and lower, sturdy roosts. Heavy birds jumping off a high roost can injure their feet, which is a common cause of bumblefoot. Give them more than the usual 4 square feet per bird inside if you can.

Their pea comb, small wattles and heavy feathering make them excellent in cold weather. Heat is the bigger challenge. In hot summers, give deep shade, good airflow and cool water, and watch for panting with wings held out.

Feathered feet and other quirks

  • Feathered feet pick up mud and manure. Dry bedding and a well-drained run make a big difference.
  • In winter, mud on foot feathers can freeze into balls, so check feet on cold, wet days.
  • Scaly leg mites can hide under foot feathers. Look closely at the scales when you do health checks.
  • Brahmas eat more than smaller breeds, which is worth factoring into feed costs.

Brahma vs Cochin and Jersey Giant

A Cochin is also big and feather-footed but is rounder and fluffier, usually lays less and is more often broody. The Jersey Giant is a very large clean-legged American breed. The Brahma vs Jersey Giant comparison goes into size, growth and eggs side by side.

Varieties and where to buy

Light, Dark and Buff are the classic varieties, and others show up from breeders. Hatchery Brahmas are easy to find and fine for backyard use, though they are often smaller than show-line birds. For bigger birds closer to the standard, look for breeders and poultry shows. Bantam Brahmas are also popular if you like the look but have less space.

Common questions about Brahmas

How big do Brahma chickens get?

They are one of the largest breeds. Roosters are noticeably bigger than hens, and show lines are larger than most hatchery birds.

Do Brahmas lay eggs in winter?

Many keep laying better in winter than lighter breeds, but expect fewer eggs in the shortest days.

Are Brahmas good with kids?

Yes, they are usually calm and gentle. Their weight means small children may struggle to hold them.
954:
Braekel and Brakel, the same Belgian breed

Braekel is the Flemish spelling of the breed most English sources call the Brakel. It is one bird, named after the Brakel area of East Flanders in Belgium. If you are comparing listings or searching for breeders, try both spellings, since European sellers often use Braekel and American sellers more often use Brakel.

What makes a Braekel a Braekel

Braekels are a light, active Belgian layer with a barred, penciled pattern and a solid colored hood over the neck. Silver and gold are the best known colors. Roosters are cock-feathered, with normal long hackles and sickle feathers. That is one of the main differences from the closely related Campine, where roosters are hen-feathered and look more like the hens.

Keeping them

  • Active, alert foragers that enjoy room to roam.
  • Can be flighty and are good fliers, so a covered run helps.
  • White eggs, with good laying for a light heritage breed.
  • Rarely broody.
  • Single comb, so watch for frostbite in hard winters.

They are not a lap chicken. They suit keepers who like busy, self-reliant birds and have space for them to move. In a tight urban run they can get bored and noisy.

How rare are they?

Braekels are uncommon in the US and more often seen in Belgium, the Netherlands and other parts of Europe. In America, you will mostly find them through specialty breeders, some of whom imported newer lines. Expect a waiting list and higher prices.

Common questions about Braekels

Is a Braekel different from a Brakel?

No. They are two spellings of the same Belgian breed.

How do I tell Braekels from Campines?

Braekel roosters are cock-feathered with full hackles and sickles. Campine roosters are hen-feathered.

Do Braekels lay well?

They are fair to good layers of white eggs for a heritage breed.
956:
What it is like to keep Bresse

The Bresse comes from the Bresse region of eastern France and is famous as a table bird. In France, poultry raised in the Bresse area under strict rules carries a protected name, and the birds are prized by chefs. The classic white Bresse looks like the French flag, with a red comb, white feathers and steel blue legs.

In the US, keepers raise Bresse lines descended from imported birds, often called American Bresse. They cannot use the French protected name for meat, but the breed itself is the same idea, a fast-growing heritage bird with fine meat.

Who they suit

  • Homesteaders raising their own meat who want a heritage breed that grows faster than most.
  • Keepers who want a dual-purpose bird that also lays well.
  • Free range setups, since Bresse are active foragers.

They are not the best pick for keepers who want a very calm lap chicken, as many Bresse are active and a bit flighty.

Eggs and growth

Bresse hens are good layers of cream to lightly tinted eggs. For meat, they grow faster than most heritage breeds but slower than commercial Cornish Cross broilers. Many keepers raise them on pasture and finish them on a richer diet before processing, following the French tradition in a looser way.

Space and climate

Bresse do best with room to forage. In a run, give generous space to avoid boredom. Their single comb needs protection in very cold, damp weather. They handle moderate heat well if shade is available.

Compared with other meat breeds

The heritage Cornish is heavier and slower, and it lays poorly. The Delaware is an American dual-purpose choice that lays brown eggs. For a broader list, see the best breeds for meat.

Where to buy

Several US breeders and some hatcheries sell American Bresse. Prices are higher than for common dual-purpose breeds. Ask about growth rate and egg production in the breeder's line.

Common questions about Bresse chickens

Why do Bresse have blue legs?

Blue legs are a breed trait and part of the classic Bresse look.

Are Bresse good layers?

Yes. Hens lay a good number of cream to tinted eggs.

How fast do Bresse grow?

Faster than most heritage breeds, but much slower than commercial broilers.
957:
What Brakels are like to keep

The Brakel is a Belgian breed from the region around Brakel in East Flanders. It is a light, active layer with fine barring on the body and a solid colored hood over the head and neck. Silver and gold are the main colors. You may also see it spelled Braekel, which is the Flemish spelling of the same breed.

Brakels are busy, alert birds. They are good foragers and like to range. Many are flighty and avoid being caught, though some calm down with regular handling.

Brakel vs Campine

The Campine is the Brakel's close cousin and the two are often confused. The easiest difference is in the roosters. Brakel roosters are cock-feathered, with normal long, pointed hackles and curved sickle tail feathers. Campine roosters are hen-feathered, so they look much like the hens. Brakels are also often described as a little sturdier.

Eggs and seasons

  • White eggs, with good laying for a light heritage breed.
  • Rarely broody, so laying is steady in season.
  • Lay best in spring and summer, with a slowdown in winter.

Space and climate

Give Brakels room. In small runs, active breeds can get bored and start pecking at each other. A covered run keeps them in, since they fly well. Their single comb is prone to frostbite in harsh winters, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. They handle warm weather well.

Who they suit

Brakels suit keepers who like independent birds, want white eggs from a heritage breed and have space. They are not ideal for small urban coops or families who want a calm pet. For that, the family breed list is a better guide.

Where to buy

Brakels are rare in the US. A few breeders keep them, sometimes from newer imports. Expect to search and to pay more.

Common questions about Brakels

Are Brakel and Braekel the same breed?

Yes. They are two spellings of one Belgian breed.

Are Brakels good layers?

They are good layers of white eggs for a heritage breed.

Are Brakels friendly?

They are more active and independent than cuddly.
959:
What Brown Breasted Brown Red means

Brown Red is a dark game color with lemon to orange accents on a black base. The "Brown Breasted" version carries more color through the breast, so instead of a mostly clean black chest you see lacing or brown tones there. It is a less common variation of the more familiar Black Breasted Brown Red. Like other Brown Reds, these birds usually have dark faces, dark eyes and dark legs.

Markings vary between breeders, so ask to see adult birds first.

How it relates to Old English Game

Hatcheries use "Standard Old English" for the large fowl Old English Game. Color is the only thing that changes here. Brown Breasted Brown Reds have the same upright stance, hard feathering and strong instincts as any Old English.

Keeping them well

  • Give them space. They are active and forage widely.
  • Plan for flying. A covered run or tall fence works best.
  • Expect small eggs, cream to tinted, mostly in spring and summer.
  • Expect broody hens, which are useful if you want to hatch chicks naturally.

Roosters will fight other roosters, sometimes badly. Keep one male per group. Hens are easier to manage.

Climate notes

Old English handle heat well with shade. In cold weather, their tight feathers do not trap as much warmth as fluffy breeds, so a dry, draft-free coop is important. Watch single combs in hard freezes.

How rare is it?

This is one of the less common Old English listings. A few hatcheries and game breeders carry it, and supply can be limited.

Common questions about Brown Breasted Brown Red Old English

What is the difference from Black Breasted Brown Red?

The brown breasted type shows more color or lacing on the breast, while the black breasted type has a cleaner black chest.

Do they lay many eggs?

No. Expect small eggs in modest numbers and frequent broody breaks.

Are they good free range birds?

Yes. They are alert, active foragers, though they still need a secure coop at night.
961:
What life with Buckeyes is like

The Buckeye was developed in Ohio in the late 1800s by Nettie Metcalf and is often noted as the only American Poultry Association breed known to have been developed by a woman. It was bred as a practical, cold-hardy dual-purpose bird. It has a pea comb, a solid, muscular body and rich mahogany red feathers, named for the color of the buckeye nut.

Buckeyes are active and curious. Many keepers say they are good at catching mice and other small critters in the yard. They are generally calm with people and do well in mixed flocks, though roosters can be assertive.

Who they suit

  • Cold climate keepers, thanks to the pea comb.
  • Homesteads wanting a dual-purpose heritage breed.
  • Free range setups where an active forager is useful.

They are less suited to tiny runs with nothing to do, since they like to move.

Eggs and laying

Buckeyes lay brown eggs at a moderate to good rate for a heritage breed. Many keep laying reasonably into the cold months, though short days still slow them down. Some hens go broody.

Space and climate

Give them standard large fowl space and plenty to do. The pea comb resists frostbite very well, so Buckeyes are a top choice for cold climates. In hot summers, shade and water are the main needs.

Buckeye vs Rhode Island Red

Buckeyes are often confused with the Rhode Island Red. The Rhode Island Red usually lays more eggs and has a single comb. The Buckeye has a pea comb, is broader and more muscular, and is a better meat bird. Another close look-alike in mahogany is the New Hampshire Red, which is lighter in color.

Where to buy

Buckeyes are a conservation breed. Several hatcheries and many heritage breeders sell them. Breeder birds are usually closer to the standard in shape and color.

Common questions about Buckeyes

Are Buckeye chickens cold-hardy?

Yes. Their pea comb and solid build make them very cold-hardy.

Are Buckeyes good layers?

They are moderate to good layers of brown eggs.

Are Buckeyes friendly?

They are usually calm with people and curious, though roosters can be pushy.
962:
What a Brussbar is

The Brussbar is one of the British autosexing breeds developed in the mid 20th century, a group that also includes the Rhodebar and the Cream Legbar. These breeds were made by adding the barring gene to an existing breed so that chicks could be sexed by down color at hatch. The Brussbar is based on the Sussex.

It is one of the rarest of the group. Detailed, reliable information about the breed today is limited, especially outside Britain, so this page sticks to what is well established.

How autosexing works

In an autosexing breed, males carry two copies of the barring gene and females carry one. That makes male chicks lighter, with blurred markings, and female chicks darker, with clearer markings. Unlike sex link hybrids, autosexing breeds keep this trait when you breed them to each other.

What to expect

  • A Sussex-type body, so a medium to heavy dual-purpose bird.
  • Barred feathers over the base color.
  • A single comb that needs protection from hard frost.

Temperament and laying will depend on the line, but the Sussex background suggests a calm, practical bird.

If you do find some, quarantine them before they join your flock, as with any new birds.

Where to find them

Brussbars are extremely hard to find. In the US, you may not find any for sale. In Britain, rare breed groups are the best place to start. If you want an autosexing heritage bird that is easier to buy, the Cream Legbar or the Bielefelder are more realistic options.

Common questions about Brussbars

Is a Brussbar a Sussex?

It is an autosexing breed based on the Sussex, with the barring gene added.

Can you sex Brussbar chicks?

Yes. As an autosexing breed, chicks can be sexed by down color.

Can I buy Brussbars in the US?

They are very rare and may not be available.
964:
The Buff Brahma Bantam

The Buff Brahma Bantam is a small version of the Brahma in the buff color. It keeps the big breed's shape, with a broad body, pea comb and heavily feathered feet, at a fraction of the size.
