The buff pattern is a warm golden body with black in the hackle, wings and tail, which gives a soft color with a dark frame around the neck.

How it differs from the large Brahma

  • Much smaller, so it needs less space and less feed.
  • Lays small light brown eggs instead of medium ones.
  • Easier for kids to pick up and hold.
  • Same calm, gentle nature in most birds.

If you love the look of Brahmas but have a small yard, the bantam is the practical answer.

Feathered feet and daily care

Like the large Brahma, bantams have feathered feet that pick up mud and droppings. Keep bedding dry and the run free of standing water. In winter, check for mud or ice balls on the foot feathers. Look under the leg feathers for scaly leg mites during health checks.

The pea comb holds up well in cold weather. In hot weather, all that feathering makes shade and water important. Some hens go broody, and bantam Brahmas can be good mothers for small clutches.

Buff color notes

Buff can fade in strong sun, and getting an even shade takes careful breeding. If you plan to show, give them shade and pick breeder stock with even color.

Where to find them

Buff Brahma Bantams are fairly easy to find. Many hatcheries sell them, and bantam breeders carry show lines. They are a common choice for families. You can also compare them with Cochin bantams, which are rounder and fluffier.

Common questions about Buff Brahma Bantams

How big do Buff Brahma Bantams get?

They stay small, far smaller than standard Brahmas.

Are Buff Brahma Bantams good with kids?

Yes. They are usually calm and easy to handle.

Do they lay eggs?

Yes, small light brown eggs in moderate numbers.
966:
What Campines are like to keep

The Campine is a Belgian breed from the Kempen region. It is light, active and lays white eggs. It has a solid colored hood over the head and neck with fine barring on the body, in silver or gold. The unusual trait is that Campine roosters are hen-feathered. They lack the long, pointed hackle and sickle feathers most roosters have, so they look much like the hens.

Campines are busy, alert and often flighty. They forage well, like to explore and are usually not interested in being held. They are generally not aggressive.

Campine vs Brakel

The Brakel is the closest relative. Brakel roosters are cock-feathered, with normal long hackles and sickles. That is the easiest way to tell the breeds apart. Brakels are also often described as a little heavier.

Who they suit

  • Keepers who want white eggs from an active heritage breed.
  • Free range or large covered runs.
  • Fans of unusual breeds and rare bird conservation.

They are not a good match for small enclosed runs or for anyone wanting a calm pet.

Eggs and climate

Campines are fair to good layers of white eggs and rarely go broody. They lay best in warm months. In bitter cold the single comb is at risk of frostbite, and a dry, ventilated coop is the best defense. They handle heat well with shade.

Where to buy

Campines are rare in the US and are a conservation breed. Some breeders keep them, and a few hatcheries offer them. If you like the barred look but want something easier to find, the Hamburg is a similar light, active white egg layer.

Common questions about Campines

Why do Campine roosters look like hens?

Campine males are hen-feathered, so they lack long hackles and sickles.

Do Campines lay well?

They are fair to good layers of white eggs.

Are Campines friendly?

They are active and independent, not usually cuddly.
967:
What the California Grey is like

The California Grey was developed in California in the 1930s by poultry breeder Horace Dryden. It came from crossing Barred Plymouth Rocks with White Leghorns. The goal was a bird that lays white eggs well but has more body than a Leghorn. The result is a barred, medium-sized bird with a single comb that lays white eggs.

California Greys are rarely seen today, but they have a loyal following among keepers who want a calm white egg layer.

What to expect day to day

  • Barred gray and white feathers, similar to a Barred Rock but often lighter in build.
  • White eggs in good numbers for a backyard bird.
  • Many keepers describe them as calmer than typical Leghorns.
  • Usually not very broody.

Some hatcheries and breeders have used California Greys as a parent in crosses, including with White Leghorns, to make white laying birds.

Space and climate

Treat them as a medium large fowl. They fit standard coop space and do well in a run or free ranging. Their single comb can get frostbite in cold climates, so keep the coop dry. They handle heat reasonably well with shade.

Compared with its parents

A Leghorn lays more but is lighter and more nervous. A Plymouth Rock is heavier and calmer, but lays brown eggs. The California Grey sits between them.

Who they suit

They suit keepers who want white eggs and a calmer bird than a Leghorn, and anyone interested in American breeds with a clear history.

Where to find them

California Greys are uncommon. A small number of hatcheries and breeders keep them.

Common questions about California Greys

What color eggs do California Greys lay?

White eggs.

Are California Greys good layers?

Yes, they are known as good layers of white eggs.

Is the California Grey a Barred Rock?

No. It was developed from Barred Rocks and White Leghorns, but it is its own bird.
969:
What Catalanas are like to keep

The Catalana, often called the Buff Catalana or Catalana del Prat, comes from Catalonia in Spain, near Barcelona. It is a Mediterranean type bird, buff colored with a black tail, a single comb and an upright, active build. It was developed as a practical bird for both eggs and meat in a warm climate.

Catalanas are active foragers and generally do well free ranging. They can be flighty, though many are calmer than Leghorns. They are usually not aggressive.

Heat tolerance

Catalanas are one of the better breeds for hot climates. Their lean build and single comb help them shed heat. They still need shade, airflow and cool water on the hottest days. If you live where summer is tough, see the hot climate breed list for more options.

Eggs and laying

  • Good layers of cream to lightly tinted eggs.
  • Rarely broody.
  • Lay best in warm months and slow down in winter.

Climate and cold

Their large single comb is the weak spot in cold climates. Frostbite is a real risk in hard freezes. A dry coop with good ventilation and no drafts helps. If you live in a very cold area, they may not be the best choice.

Compared with similar breeds

Catalanas are often compared with the Leghorn as a heat-tolerant layer. Leghorns lay more white eggs. Catalanas are heavier, with more meat. Another Spanish choice is the Penedesenca, known for very dark eggs.

Where to buy

Catalanas are uncommon in the US. A few hatcheries and breeders sell them.

Common questions about Catalanas

Are Catalanas good in hot weather?

Yes. They are known for handling heat well.

What color eggs do Catalanas lay?

Cream to lightly tinted eggs.

Are Catalanas good for cold climates?

Not ideal. Their large combs are prone to frostbite.
970:
What Chanteclers are like to keep

The Chantecler is a Canadian breed developed in the early 1900s by Brother Wilfrid Chatelain, a monk at the Oka abbey in Quebec. His goal was a dual-purpose bird built for harsh Canadian winters. The answer was a chicken with a small cushion comb and tiny wattles, so there is very little for frost to bite.

White and Partridge are the best known colors. Chanteclers are generally calm and steady, and most keepers find them easy to manage.

Built for the cold

Few breeds handle cold as well as the Chantecler. The cushion comb sits low and tight on the head, and the wattles are very small. Dense feathers add insulation. In very cold areas, they are one of the top choices on any cold climate breed list. A dry, ventilated coop is still important.

Heat is the bigger challenge. In hot summers, give deep shade, airflow and water.

Eggs and laying

  • Good layers of brown eggs for a heritage breed.
  • Many keep laying into the cold months better than lighter breeds.
  • Some hens go broody.

Who they suit

Chanteclers suit northern keepers and homesteaders who want a hardy dual-purpose bird. They also suit anyone interested in heritage breeds with a clear story. They are less suited to very hot, humid climates.

Compared with similar breeds

The Buckeye is another cold-hardy North American breed, with a pea comb and mahogany color. The Wyandotte uses a rose comb and is easier to find. The Chantecler's comb is the smallest of the three.

Where to buy

Chanteclers are rare and listed as a conservation breed in the US. Some hatcheries and breeders offer them. Breeder birds are usually closer to the standard.

Common questions about Chanteclers

Are Chanteclers good in cold weather?

Yes. They were bred for Canadian winters and have very small combs and wattles.

Are Chanteclers good layers?

Yes. They are good layers of brown eggs.

What is a cushion comb?

A small, low, rounded comb that sits close to the head and resists frostbite.
972:
Chabo, the Japanese name for the Japanese Bantam

Chabo is the Japanese name for what English speakers usually call the Japanese Bantam. It is the same bird. The name shows up most often in European breed listings and among keepers who want to point to the breed's roots in Japan.

A Chabo is a true bantam, with no large version. It has very short legs, a deep upright tail that rises above the head, large wings carried low and a big single comb. The overall look is a tiny bird that seems to sit right on the ground.

What to know before keeping Chabo

  • The short legs come from a creeper type gene. Two copies are lethal, so short to short pairings lose about a quarter of embryos in the shell.
  • Low wings and tails drag in mud. Dry ground matters more for Chabo than for most breeds.
  • The large comb can get frostbite in hard winters.
  • Hens lay small eggs in modest numbers and go broody often.

Most Chabo are calm and friendly. They are popular for small backyards and with kids, as long as the setup stays clean and dry. The small yards breed list has other options in the same space.

Colors and frizzled types

Chabo come in many colors, and there are also frizzled and silky-feathered types. On this site, colors like Black Tailed White have their own pages. Not every color is recognized in every country.

Where to get them

Under the Chabo name, you are more likely to find them through bantam breeders and clubs. Under the Japanese Bantam name, several hatcheries carry common colors.

Common questions about Chabo

Is a Chabo the same as a Japanese Bantam?

Yes. Chabo is the Japanese name for the same breed.

Why do Chabo have such short legs?

A gene for very short legs is part of the breed. It is lethal in double dose, which affects hatch rates.

Are Chabo good layers?

No. Egg numbers are low and the eggs are small.
974:
What it is really like to keep Cochins

Cochins are the big, round, feather-footed chickens that look like walking pillows. They are known for calm, friendly personalities, and many keepers get them as pets more than as egg machines. That is the right mindset going in.

Day to day, Cochins are slow, easy to catch and usually fine being held. They do not range far and are happy in a run. They rarely fly, so they are easy to contain. Because they are so docile, they can end up low in the pecking order in a flock of bossy breeds, so watch them at the feeder.

Who Cochins suit

  • Families, kids and anyone who wants a calm pet chicken.
  • Keepers who want a reliable broody hen to hatch eggs.
  • Cold climates, where their heavy feathering helps.

They are a poor choice if eggs are your main goal, or if your run turns to mud every spring.

Laying and broodiness

Cochins lay a modest number of light to medium brown eggs. Many pullets are slow to start. The bigger factor is broodiness. Cochins go broody often, and a broody hen stops laying for weeks. That makes them great natural mothers, and keepers often use them to hatch eggs from other breeds. If you do not want chicks, you will need to break broodiness now and then. Laying slows in winter and drops more with age.

Space, coop and climate

Standard Cochins are large, so plan on generous coop space, wide doors and larger nest boxes. Low roosts are a good idea since they are heavy and not agile. Bantam Cochins are much smaller and very popular for small yards. They handle cold well, but they can struggle in strong heat because of all that feathering. Shade, airflow and water are essential in summer.

Feathered feet and health quirks

  • Foot feathers get caked with mud and droppings. Keep bedding dry and the run well drained.
  • Check under foot feathers for scaly leg mites, which can raise and crust the scales.
  • Dense, fluffy vent feathers can collect droppings. Some keepers trim them for cleanliness.
  • Cochins gain weight easily. Limit rich treats and keep them moving.
  • In winter, wet foot feathers can freeze, so look at feet after cold, wet days.

Cochin vs Silkie and Brahma

A Silkie is smaller with fur-like feathers and is even more famous for going broody. The Silkie vs Cochin comparison covers that choice in detail. A Brahma is also big and feather-footed, but is taller, with a pea comb, and usually lays a bit better.

Varieties and where to buy

Cochins come in many colors, including buff, black, blue, partridge, white and frizzled types. Bantam Cochins are especially common. Most hatcheries sell both large and bantam Cochins. Show-quality birds with huge feathering come from breeders and poultry shows.

Common questions about Cochins

Are Cochins good egg layers?

Not really. They lay a modest number of brown eggs and take breaks when they go broody.

How do I stop my Cochin from going broody?

Remove her from the nest often, collect eggs quickly and, if needed, put her in a wire-floored crate with food and water for a few days.

Can Cochins live in hot climates?

They can, but heavy feathering makes heat hard on them. Provide shade, airflow and cool water all summer.
975:
What a Cinnamon Queen is

Cinnamon Queen is a red sex link hybrid. It is made by crossing a gold or red rooster, usually from Rhode Island Red or New Hampshire lines, with a silver hen, such as a white or silver laced type. Each hatchery uses its own parent lines. The result is a bird bred for brown eggs and easy sexing at hatch.

Female chicks hatch in red or buff tones, and male chicks hatch white or cream. As adults, hens are a warm cinnamon red, often with lighter feathers in the tail or neck. Roosters are mostly white with some red.

How it compares with other sex links

Cinnamon Queen sits in the same family as Golden Comet, Red Sex Link and ISA Brown. All are red hens bred for production, and the differences come down to the parent lines each company uses. In a backyard flock you will see similar behavior and output.

Daily life

  • Early, strong layers of brown eggs.
  • Friendly, curious and often very tame.
  • Rarely broody.
  • Medium sized, so they fit standard coops easily.

High production layers often lay hard in the first two years and then taper off sooner than heritage breeds. Good feed and calcium matter. If shells get thin, read up on thin shell eggs.

They handle both cold and heat reasonably well with standard care. Their single combs can frostbite in severe cold.

Breeding and buying

Cinnamon Queens do not breed true. Hatcheries and feed stores sell them widely each spring.

Common questions about Cinnamon Queens

Are Cinnamon Queens good layers?

Yes. They are bred for steady brown egg production.

Are Cinnamon Queens friendly?

Most are calm and people-friendly.

How long do Cinnamon Queens lay?

They lay heavily for about two years, then production usually drops.
977:
What a Columbian Rock is

"Columbian Rock" usually refers to the Columbian variety of the Plymouth Rock. The Columbian pattern is a white body with black striping in the hackle, black in the tail and black in the wing feathers. It is the same pattern you see on Light Brahmas and Delawares, laid over a Plymouth Rock body. Some hatcheries also use similar names for crosses, so check the listing for parent stock if that matters to you.

How it relates to the Plymouth Rock

The Barred Rock is the best known Plymouth Rock. The Columbian is the same breed in a different color. You can expect the usual Rock traits.

  • Calm, friendly and easy to handle.
  • Reliable brown egg layers, light to medium in shade.
  • Solid dual-purpose size.
  • Cold-hardy, with a single comb that needs watching in hard freezes.

Day to day

Columbian Rocks are an easy backyard bird. They do well in a run or free ranging, and they fit standard coop space for large fowl. The white body shows dirt more than barred feathers do, so a clean, dry run keeps them looking good. They are a good fit for families and first flocks, and they appear on lists of dual-purpose breeds.

The Delaware looks very similar. It is a separate breed developed in part from Plymouth Rock stock, known for faster growth.

Where to find them

Columbian Rocks are less common than Barred Rocks, but some hatcheries and breeders carry them.

Common questions about Columbian Rocks

Is a Columbian Rock a Plymouth Rock?

Usually, yes. It is the Columbian color of the Plymouth Rock, though some sellers use the name for crosses.

Are Columbian Rocks good layers?

Yes. They lay brown eggs reliably, like other Rocks.

How do I tell a Columbian Rock from a Delaware?

They look alike. Delawares tend to show barring in the black areas, while Columbians show solid black striping.
978:
What keeping Cornish chickens is like

The Cornish is a heavy, broad, muscular breed from Cornwall in England, where it was known as Indian Game. It was built for meat, not eggs, and it looks like it. A good Cornish has a wide chest, thick legs set far apart and tight, hard feathering.

It is important to separate the heritage Cornish from the Cornish Cross broiler. The Cornish Cross is a fast-growing commercial meat hybrid that reaches butcher weight in weeks and is not meant to live long. A heritage Cornish grows much more slowly, lives a normal chicken life and can breed naturally, though not always easily.

Temperament and day to day care

Heritage Cornish can be calm with people but some lines are assertive with other chickens, which reflects their game bird background. Roosters in particular can be pushy. They are not great fliers, and their heavy build makes them less active than lighter breeds. They are more likely to stand around than to range far.

Who they suit and who they do not

  • Good for people raising heritage meat birds or breeding their own meat crosses.
  • Good for keepers interested in showing a striking, uncommon type.
  • Not a good choice if you want eggs. Hens lay few eggs, and they are small to medium and brown to tinted.

Eggs and broodiness

Cornish hens are poor layers by backyard standards, and laying is seasonal, mostly spring and summer. Many hens do go broody and can be protective mothers. Their build can make natural mating less successful in some lines, which is one reason they are not the easiest breed to keep going.

Space, coop and climate

Cornish are heavy for their height, so use low roosts and give them room. Their tight, short feathering gives less insulation than fluffy breeds, so they need a draft-free coop in cold winters. Their pea comb helps with frostbite. In heat, they can suffer because of their heavy body, so shade and water are important.

Health and handling notes

  • Heavy birds are more prone to leg and foot strain, including bumblefoot, especially with high roosts or hard landings.
  • Keep them fit. Free choice rich feed can make them too heavy.
  • Watch new roosters with flock mates and separate if fighting gets serious.

Cornish vs other meat breeds

If your goal is a dual-purpose bird that also lays, look at a breed like the Delaware, which grows reasonably fast and still lays well. For a heritage French option known for flavor, the Bresse is popular. The best breeds for meat page lays out more choices.

Varieties and where to buy

Dark Cornish is the classic. White, White Laced Red and Buff also exist, along with bantams. Many hatcheries sell Dark Cornish chicks. For true heritage type, look to breeders and shows, since hatchery birds vary. Do not confuse them with Cornish Cross listings, which are a different product.

Common questions about Cornish chickens

Is a Cornish chicken the same as a Cornish Cross?

No. The Cornish is a heritage breed. The Cornish Cross is a commercial meat hybrid that grows very fast.

Do Cornish hens lay many eggs?

No. They lay a small number of brown to tinted eggs, mostly in warmer months.

Are Cornish chickens aggressive?

They are often calm with people, but some can be assertive with other chickens because of their game background.
979:
What life with Cream Legbars is like

The Cream Legbar was developed in Britain, at Cambridge, in the mid 20th century. It was bred from Leghorns, Barred Rocks and Araucana-type birds to combine three things. It is autosexing, so chicks can be sexed at hatch. It lays blue eggs. And it carries a small crest at the back of the head.

Adult hens are a soft mix of cream, gray and salmon, with a small crest. Roosters are lighter, barred and cream with a taller crest. Most Cream Legbars are active, alert and good foragers. Some are flighty, especially young birds, but many settle into friendly backyard birds.

Autosexing chicks

This is the biggest selling point. Female chicks usually have a clear dark brown stripe down the back with defined edges, like a chipmunk. Male chicks are lighter, with a blurred, faded stripe and often a light head spot. It takes a little practice, so compare chicks side by side.

Eggs through the year

  • Good layers of blue to blue-green eggs.
  • Egg size is usually medium.
  • Broodiness is rare, so hens keep laying through the season.
  • They lay best in spring and summer and slow in winter.

Egg color varies between lines. Some lay a clear sky blue, others more of a green tint. The blue egg page lists other breeds in the same range.

Space and climate

Give them standard large fowl space and room to roam. They fly well, so cover the run if needed. Their single comb is prone to frostbite in very cold, damp weather, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. Summer heat is manageable with shade and cool water.

Cream Legbar vs Ameraucana

The Ameraucana is another blue egg breed. It has a pea comb, beard and muffs, which makes it better in cold weather. Cream Legbars are usually more productive and autosexing, which Ameraucanas are not. Hatchery quality varies, so if autosexing matters, buy from a breeder who selects for it.

Where to buy

Cream Legbars have grown popular in the US. Many breeders and some hatcheries sell them. Prices are higher than for common layers.

Common questions about Cream Legbars

Do Cream Legbars lay blue eggs?

Yes. They lay blue to blue-green eggs.

Can I sex Cream Legbar chicks?

Yes. Females have a dark, defined back stripe. Males are lighter and blurrier.

Are Cream Legbars friendly?

Many are friendly, though some are flighty, especially when young.
981:
What makes a Crele different

Crele is a barred version of the red-based game colors. Take a Black Breasted Red and add the barring gene, and you get a Crele. Roosters show barred hackles and saddles in orange to straw tones over a barred body, so the bright red and black of a Black Breasted Red softens into stripes. Hens are barred too, often with a salmon tone in the breast.

The barring gene is sex-linked, and males usually carry two copies while females carry one. That is why Crele roosters often look lighter and more washed out than the hens.

Relationship to Old English Game

This is a color of large fowl Old English Game, often sold as "Standard Old English." Body type, behavior and care are the same as any Old English.

  • Lively, alert foragers that do well free ranging.
  • Strong fliers. Expect them on fence tops if the run is open.
  • Eggs are small and cream to tinted, and most come in spring and summer.
  • Broody hens that are very protective of chicks.

Keeping Creles

Roosters fight other roosters, which is the biggest management point with any game breed. Keep one rooster per group or house males separately. In winter, give a dry coop with good ventilation, since tight feathers hold less warmth. Single combs can frostbite in deep cold. Heat is less of a problem with shade and water.

Crele is also a known pattern in other breeds. The Bielefelder, for example, uses a crele-type pattern for autosexing, though it is a very different, heavy bird.

Where to find them

Creles are fairly popular with game fanciers. Some hatcheries offer them in large fowl, and they show up at poultry shows.

Common questions about Crele Old English

Why do Crele roosters look lighter than hens?

Roosters usually carry two copies of the barring gene, which lightens their color more.

Is Crele a separate breed?

No. It is a color pattern within Old English Game and some other breeds.

Are Crele hens good mothers?

Yes. Like other Old English hens, they go broody often.
984:
What you get in a Crested "Top Hat" Special

The Crested "Top Hat" Special is a hatchery assortment, not a breed. It is a mix of crested chickens, usually drawn from breeds like the Polish and Houdan, and sometimes other crested types, depending on the hatchery and the season. You cannot usually choose which breeds or colors you get, and you may get a range of sizes and egg colors.

The appeal is variety. A box of top hat chicks grows into a flock of birds with puffball heads in different colors and patterns.

Living with crested birds

Crests are fun but bring specific care needs.

  • Big crests can block vision, so crested birds may startle easily. Talk to them as you approach.
  • Wet crests can freeze in winter or get dirty. Nipple waterers or cups help keep heads dry.
  • Mites and lice hide in crests. Part the feathers during health checks.
  • Other chickens sometimes pull at crest feathers. Watch for bullying.
  • Limited vision makes them easier targets for hawks. A covered run helps, and the aerial predators guide has more ideas.

Eggs and temperament

Most crested breeds lay white eggs, and many are fair layers rather than top producers. Temperaments range from calm to a bit nervous. Since the assortment mixes breeds, expect variation in both.

Who it suits

It is a good pick for keepers who want an eye-catching, mixed flock and do not need high egg numbers. It is not ideal for wet, cold climates without extra care, or for free ranging where hawks are common.

Common questions about the Crested Top Hat Special

Can I choose which breeds come in the assortment?

Usually not. The hatchery picks from what it has available.

Are crested chickens hard to keep?

Not hard, but crests need extra checks for mites, wetness and vision problems.

Do crested chickens lay well?

Most lay a fair number of white eggs.
985:
What to know about Crevecoeurs

The Crevecoeur is one of the oldest French breeds, from Normandy. It is solid black with a full crest, a beard and muffs, and a V-shaped comb. Historically it was raised as a table bird, prized for fine meat. Hens lay white eggs.

Today it is one of the rarest breeds in the US and is listed as a conservation priority by heritage breed groups.

Temperament and daily care

  • Usually calm and gentle.
  • Not very active foragers, so they tolerate runs well.
  • Fair layers of white eggs.
  • Not strongly broody.

Crest and beard care

Crested birds have particular needs. The crest can limit vision, so approach calmly and talk to them. Wet crests and beards can freeze in winter, so use waterers that keep heads dry. Check crests and beards for mites and lice. Flock mates may peck at crest feathers, so watch for bullying.

Limited vision also means they are easier targets for hawks, so a covered run is a good idea.

Climate notes

The V comb is small and resists frostbite reasonably well. The crest is the bigger winter concern if it gets wet. Black feathers absorb heat, so shade matters in summer.

Compared with similar breeds

The Houdan is another crested, bearded French breed, usually mottled and with five toes. The Polish has a much larger crest and is easier to find. If you like the Crevecoeur look but cannot find one, a black Polish or Houdan is a closer alternative.

Where to buy

Crevecoeurs are very rare. A few breeders and hatcheries offer them some years. Expect small supply and higher prices.

Common questions about Crevecoeurs

Are Crevecoeurs rare?

Yes. They are one of the rarest breeds in the US.

What color eggs do Crevecoeurs lay?

White eggs.

Are Crevecoeurs friendly?

They are usually calm and gentle.
987:
What Cubalayas are like to keep

The Cubalaya was developed in Cuba from Asian game birds and is the breed most closely tied to that country. Its trademark is the "lobster tail," a long, full tail that sweeps down and back rather than up. It has a pea comb and the upright, alert build of a game bird.

Many keepers describe Cubalayas as calmer and more people-friendly than many game breeds. Roosters can still fight with other roosters, so watch them closely.

Heat tolerance and climate

Cubalayas come from a hot climate and handle heat well. Shade, airflow and water are still important. Their pea comb resists frostbite, but their tight game feathering gives less insulation than fluffy breeds, so in cold areas a dry, draft-free coop matters.

Day to day

  • Good foragers that like to range.
  • A fair number of light brown to tinted eggs.
  • Hens often go broody and are protective mothers.
  • Slow to mature.

Their tails need care. Keep perches high enough that tails do not drag, and keep runs dry and clean.

Who they suit

Cubalayas suit keepers in warm climates who like game breeds with a calmer temperament. They also suit anyone interested in rare breeds. They are not a production layer.

Compared with similar breeds

The Sumatra is another game type with long, flowing tail feathers. The Phoenix is known for very long upward tails.

Where to buy

Cubalayas are rare in the US and listed as a conservation breed. A few breeders keep them.

Common questions about Cubalayas

What is a lobster tail?

It is the Cubalaya's long, full tail that sweeps down and back instead of up.

Are Cubalayas good in heat?

Yes. They come from Cuba and handle heat well.

Are Cubalayas aggressive?

Many are calm with people, but roosters may fight each other.
990:
Keeping a breed as rare as the Dampierre

The Dampierre is a rare breed, and reliable information about it in English is very limited. You will find few photos, fewer breed descriptions and almost no sellers in the US. Rather than guess at details, this page focuses on what you can do if you come across Dampierres or want to find them.

Check what you are buying

With very rare breeds, mislabeled birds are common. Before buying, ask the seller:

  • Where their stock came from and how many generations they have bred it.
  • For photos of adult roosters and hens, not just chicks.
  • What egg color their hens lay.
  • Whether the line is related to a breed standard or club in another country.

Good breeders of rare birds are usually happy to talk about their lines. Vague answers are a warning sign.

General care for rare heritage birds

Most rare heritage breeds need the same basics as any backyard chicken. That means about 4 square feet per bird in the coop for standard size birds, a secure run, good ventilation, a layer feed and clean water. Quarantine any new birds for several weeks before adding them to a flock, since rare stock may come from small breeders with different disease history. The biosecurity basics page explains how.

Helping preserve a rare breed

If you get Dampierres, keeping records helps. Note hatch rates, egg color, laying and temperament. Share with other breeders. Small populations lose genetic diversity quickly, so avoid breeding closely related birds whenever possible.

If you cannot find this breed, the breeds encyclopedia lists many rare European breeds that are easier to find.

Common questions about Dampierre chickens

Can I buy Dampierre chickens in the US?

They are very rare. You may need to search rare breed groups or go without.

Why is there so little information about Dampierres?

Very rare breeds are kept by few people, and little is published about them in English.

How do I avoid buying mislabeled birds?

Ask for adult photos, the history of the line and egg color, and buy from breeders who answer clearly.
991:
The Cuckoo color in Old English

Cuckoo Old English have irregular gray and dark barring over the whole body, similar to the look of a Dominique but on a slim, upright game frame. The barring gene works on a black base, so instead of crisp black and white stripes you get a softer, blurred pattern. Roosters are usually lighter than hens because the barring gene is sex-linked and males often carry two copies.

How it relates to the parent breed

"Standard Old English" is the hatchery name for large fowl Old English Game. The cuckoo color does not change behavior or needs. Cuckoo birds are as hardy, alert and broody as any other color.

Why some keepers pick cuckoo

  • The gray barred look blends into brush and leaf litter, which may help free ranging birds stay less visible.
  • It is a quieter color than the bright reds, if you prefer a subtle bird.
  • Barring is sex-linked, which matters if you breed crosses.

Daily care

Expect active foragers that fly well and like to roost high. Hens lay small cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers and go broody often. Roosters fight other roosters, so plan one male per group.

Their tight, hard feathers handle rain well. In cold climates, keep the coop dry and draft-free, and watch the single comb in very cold weather. They do well in heat with shade.

Where to find them

Cuckoo is offered by some hatcheries in large fowl Old English and by game breeders. It is less common than Black Breasted Red but not unusual.

Common questions about Cuckoo Old English

Is Cuckoo the same as barred?

They come from the same barring gene. Cuckoo usually describes a less crisp, more irregular barred look.

Can I sex Cuckoo chicks?

Not reliably within the pure color. Sex-linked barring helps mainly in planned crosses.

Do Cuckoo Old English lay well?

They lay modest numbers of small eggs, like other Old English.
993:
What the Deathlayer actually is

Deathlayer is the English take on the Westfalische Totleger, an old breed from Westphalia in Germany. The odd name means "dead layer" and comes from the claim that hens keep laying until the day they die. Treat that as folklore about a steady, long-lived layer rather than a promise.

It sits in the same family of light, penciled European layers as the Friesian and the Hamburg. Gold and silver are the main colors, with fine penciling on the body.

What they are like to keep

  • Small, light birds that eat little and forage well.
  • Active and alert. Many are flighty and fly well.
  • Small to medium white eggs.
  • Rose comb, which helps resist frostbite.
  • Not usually broody.

They do best with room to roam and are not a cuddly breed. In a small run they can become restless, so give them perches, scratching areas and space. A covered run keeps them in and keeps hawks out.

Climate

Their rose comb and hardy background make them a decent choice for cold weather, provided the coop is dry and draft-free. Their light bodies also handle warm summers well with shade.

How rare are they?

Deathlayers are rare in the United States. A small number of breeders and specialty hatcheries offer them, and supply can be limited. Expect to pay more than for common breeds and to wait.

Common questions about Deathlayer chickens

Do Deathlayers really lay until they die?

The name reflects a reputation for long laying life, not a guarantee.

What color eggs do Deathlayers lay?

White eggs, usually small to medium.

Are Deathlayers a hybrid?

No. They come from an old German breed, the Westfalische Totleger.
994:
What Dominiques are like to keep

The Dominique is often called America's oldest chicken breed. It was common on farms in the 1800s and nearly vanished in the 20th century before preservation work brought it back. Dominiques are barred black and white, with a rose comb and a medium, practical body.

They are calm, friendly and easy to keep. Many keepers say they are good at foraging and handle themselves well in a free range flock.

A day with Dominiques

Dominiques are practical birds. They spend the day scratching through leaves and grass, and they are good at finding bugs and seeds on their own. Their barring helps them blend into the ground, which is one reason old farm keepers liked them. They are usually quiet and steady, and hens rarely cause trouble in a mixed flock. Roosters are generally manageable, though like any rooster they should be watched around small kids.

Dominique vs Barred Rock

The two look alike, but there are clear differences. The Barred Plymouth Rock has a single comb. The Dominique has a rose comb. Dominique barring is often described as less crisp, more of a cuckoo look. Dominiques are also usually smaller. The Amrock is another barred breed, but it has a single comb like a Rock.

Eggs and seasons

  • Reliable brown egg layers, light to medium in shade.
  • Eggs are usually medium in size.
  • Some hens go broody and make good mothers.

Space and climate

Dominiques fit standard coop space. Their rose comb resists frostbite, making them good for cold climates. They also handle heat fairly well with shade. Their barred feathers are good camouflage when free ranging.

Who they suit

Dominiques suit beginners, families and anyone wanting a hardy heritage breed. They do well in mixed flocks.

Laying across the years

Pullets usually start at a normal age for a medium heritage breed. Expect the best laying in the first two seasons, with a gradual decline after that. Hens often keep laying at a lower rate for several more years, which suits keepers who do not want to replace birds often.

Where to buy

Dominiques are a conservation breed, but they are fairly easy to find. Many hatcheries and breeders sell them.

Common questions about Dominiques

How can I tell a Dominique from a Barred Rock?

Look at the comb. Dominiques have a rose comb. Barred Rocks have a single comb.

Are Dominiques good layers?

Yes. Yes, they lay brown eggs well.

Are Dominiques cold-hardy?

Yes. Their rose comb helps prevent frostbite.
995:
What Delawares are like to keep

The Delaware was developed in Delaware in the 1940s from Barred Plymouth Rock and New Hampshire stock. Light colored birds with dark markings appeared in those crosses and were bred into a new breed. It was a popular meat bird in the Delmarva region for a short time, before Cornish Cross broilers took over.

Delawares are white with black barring in the hackle, tail and wing tips. They are calm, friendly and easy to handle, and they grow fairly fast for a heritage breed.

Who they suit

  • Homesteaders wanting a dual-purpose heritage bird.
  • Families who want a calm, easy breed.
  • Keepers who want brown eggs and decent meat from one flock.

Eggs and growth

Delawares are good layers of brown eggs, usually medium to large. They grow faster than many heritage breeds, which made them popular for meat in their time. Some hens go broody, but it is not common.

Space and climate

They fit standard large fowl space. Single combs can freeze in a hard winter. Dry air and good ventilation matter more than heat. With shade, they cope with hot weather fairly well.

Raising Delawares for the table

If you plan to raise some for meat, Delawares make a good homestead option. They grow faster than most heritage breeds, and their light feathers leave fewer dark pin feathers on the carcass, which makes for a cleaner look after plucking. Many keepers keep the hens for eggs and raise the extra cockerels for the freezer.

Compared with similar breeds

A Columbian Rock looks similar but has solid black striping instead of barring. A New Hampshire Red is one of the Delaware's parent breeds and is red rather than white. The dual-purpose breed list covers more options.

Where to buy

Delawares are a conservation breed, but several hatcheries and breeders sell them. Hatchery birds are often smaller than breeder birds.

Common questions about Delawares

Are Delawares good layers?

Yes. Yes. Expect a steady supply of brown eggs.

Are Delawares good for meat?

Yes. They grow fairly fast for a heritage breed.

Are Delawares friendly?

Most are calm and easy to handle.
996:
What Dorkings are like to keep

The Dorking is one of the oldest British breeds and has been linked to Roman Britain, though its early history is hard to pin down. It was developed as a table bird, and it shows. Dorkings have a long, low, rectangular body, short legs and five toes on each foot. Despite their red earlobes, they lay white to lightly tinted eggs.

Dorkings are calm, gentle and easy to handle. They are not fast or flighty, and they do well around families.

Who they suit

  • Homesteaders wanting a heritage table bird that also lays.
  • Families who want a calm, docile breed.
  • Keepers interested in rare, historic breeds.

They are not the best choice for high egg production.

Eggs and broodiness

Dorkings are fair layers of white to tinted eggs. Many hens go broody and are good mothers. They are slow to mature compared with production breeds.

Space and climate

Their short legs and long bodies need room, so do not crowd them. Low roosts help. Dorkings handle mild and cool climates well. Their large single comb, especially in roosters, can get frostbite in harsh cold, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. They do best in a well-drained run, since their low bodies get dirty in mud.

Five toes and foot care

The extra toe is normal. Check feet now and then for injuries or bumblefoot, especially on heavy birds.

Compared with similar breeds

The Faverolles also has five toes and is said to have Dorking in its background. It is fluffier, with a beard and feathered feet. The Sussex is another British table breed, easier to find and a better layer.

Where to buy

Dorkings are a conservation breed. You can find them through a handful of hatcheries and breeders. Silver-gray, red, white and colored are known varieties.

Common questions about Dorkings

Why do Dorkings have five toes?

It is a normal breed trait.

What color eggs do Dorkings lay?

White to lightly tinted, even though they have red earlobes.

Are Dorkings friendly?

Yes. They are known for being calm and gentle.
997:
What Easter Eggers are like day to day

Easter Eggers are not a breed in the strict sense. They are mixed chickens that carry the blue egg gene, usually with some Ameraucana or Araucana in their background. That is why no two look quite the same. Some have beards and muffs, some have tails like any other chicken, and colors range from gray to brown to partridge to white.

That variety is part of the fun. Most Easter Eggers are friendly, curious and easy to keep. They tend to be sturdy, low-maintenance birds that do well in backyards and mixed flocks.

Who they suit

  • Beginners who want colorful eggs without paying breeder prices.
  • Families who want friendly, hardy birds.
  • Anyone who likes a flock where every hen looks different.

They are not a good pick if you want to show, since there is no standard, or if you need every egg to be the exact same shade.

Egg color and laying through the year

Most Easter Eggers lay blue or green eggs, and the exact shade depends on the hen. Some lay pale blue, some sea green, and some lay olive or even tinted eggs. A hen lays the same general shade her whole life, though it may lighten a little over a long season. You will not know the color until she starts laying. The green egg page lists other breeds in that range.

Laying is solid for a backyard bird. Expect regular medium to large eggs in spring and summer, a slowdown in fall and winter, and a gentle decline after the first two years. Some hens go broody, but most are not strongly broody.

Space, coop and climate

Easter Eggers are medium-sized and fit standard coop guidelines of about 4 square feet per bird inside. Many have pea combs inherited from Ameraucana stock, which helps a lot in cold weather. Some have single combs, so check yours. They handle heat about as well as any average backyard bird when they have shade and water.

Health and handling notes

  • Bearded birds can hide mites and lice under their muffs, so part feathers during health checks.
  • Because they come from mixed stock, they are usually hardy without breed-specific problems.
  • Some are good fliers. A covered run helps if yours like to go over fences.

Easter Egger vs Ameraucana and Olive Egger

An Ameraucana is a standardized breed that lays blue eggs and breeds true to type. The Easter Egger vs Ameraucana comparison explains why hatchery "Ameraucanas" are often Easter Eggers. An Olive Egger is a cross between a blue egg layer and a dark brown egg layer, bred for olive shells. See the Easter Egger vs Olive Egger comparison for more.

Where to get them

Easter Eggers are easy to find. Almost every major hatchery and many feed stores sell them each spring, sometimes under the names "Ameraucana" or "Americana." They are usually affordable. Because they are mixed, there is no real rarity issue and no breed club standard.

Common questions about Easter Eggers

Are Easter Eggers good layers?

Yes. Most lay well for a backyard bird and do so for several years.

Can I tell what egg color a chick will lay?

Not reliably. You will usually find out when she lays her first egg.

Are Easter Eggers friendly?

Most are friendly and curious, especially when handled as chicks.
999:
What Dutch Bantams are like to keep

The Dutch Bantam is a true bantam from the Netherlands, so there is no large version. It is one of the smallest chicken breeds. Dutch Bantams have a single comb, white earlobes and an upright, lively stance. They come in many colors, with light brown, silver and gold types among the best known.

They are active, alert birds. Many become tame with handling, and their small size makes them easy for kids to hold. They are good fliers for their size.

Who they suit

  • Keepers with small yards who want a few birds.
  • Families wanting small, friendly chickens.
  • Anyone wanting good broody hens for small clutches.

They are not a good pick for egg production or for open areas with lots of hawks.

Eggs and broodiness

Dutch Bantams lay small cream to white eggs in modest numbers. Many hens go broody and are protective mothers.

Space and climate

They need little space, but they do fly, so cover the run. Their small size makes them vulnerable to predators, so use secure hardware cloth. Their single comb can get frostbite in harsh cold. A dry, draft-free coop is important. They handle heat well with shade.

Handling tips

Dutch Bantams tame best when handled young. Sitting quietly in the run with treats helps. Adult birds that were not handled may stay wary, so set expectations if you buy grown stock.

Compared with similar bantams

The Sebright is another tiny true bantam, laced and with a rose comb. The Serama is even smaller and more upright. Dutch Bantams are usually hardier than Seramas.

Where to buy

Dutch Bantams are popular with bantam breeders and at shows. Some hatcheries sell them.

Common questions about Dutch Bantams

How small are Dutch Bantams?

They are one of the smallest breeds, much smaller than standard hens.

Do Dutch Bantams fly?

Yes. They are good fliers for their size.

Are Dutch Bantams good mothers?

Yes. Many hens go broody and are protective.
1000:
What Egyptian Fayoumis are like to keep

The Egyptian Fayoumi comes from the Faiyum region of Egypt, near the Nile. It is a small, light breed with a silvery white neck and a body of fine black and white penciling. It has a single comb and an upright, alert posture. You will also see it listed simply as Fayoumi.

Fayoumis are very active and flighty. They are quick, alert and wary of people and predators. They forage well and do best with space.

Early maturing

Fayoumis mature early. Hens often start laying before many other breeds, and roosters may start crowing young. Their eggs are small and range from off-white to a light tint.

Hardy reputation

Fayoumis have been studied for disease resistance, and keepers often describe them as hardy. That does not make them immune to illness. Biosecurity, clean housing and health checks still apply.

Handling and temperament

Fayoumis are one of the harder breeds to tame. Even when raised by hand, many stay jumpy and will scatter when you enter the run. They are not mean, just nervous and quick. If you want to handle them, start with chicks and keep sessions short and calm.

Who they suit

  • Keepers in hot climates, where they do very well.
  • Free range setups.
  • Anyone who wants an independent, hardy bird.

They do not suit families wanting a calm pet, or small runs without a roof.

Space and climate

Fayoumis are excellent in heat. In cold climates, their single comb and small body need a dry, draft-free coop. They fly well and often roost high, so cover the run. See the hot climate breed list for other heat-tolerant breeds.

Where to buy

Several hatcheries sell Egyptian Fayoumis, and they are not hard to find.

Common questions about Egyptian Fayoumis

Are Egyptian Fayoumis good layers?

They start laying young and give a fair number of small eggs.

Are Fayoumis good in heat?

Yes. They handle heat very well.

Are Fayoumis friendly?

Usually not. They are flighty and wary.
1002:
About the Empordanesa

The Empordanesa is a rare breed from the Emporda area of Catalonia in northeastern Spain. It is best known for laying dark red-brown eggs, which makes it interesting to keepers who like dark egg breeds. It is a local Catalan breed that has been kept going by Spanish breeders.

Detailed information in English is limited, and the breed is very rare outside Spain. This page sticks to what is well known.

What to expect

  • Dark brown eggs, a main reason people seek the breed out.
  • A Mediterranean type bird, generally light and active.
  • Suited to a warm climate.

Like other dark egg layers, egg color may lighten during the laying season and darken again after a rest. That is normal.

Climate and coop

Catalonia has a Mediterranean climate, so the breed is suited to warm weather. In cold climates, a dry, draft-free coop is important, and combs should be watched in hard freezes.

Buying tips

With rare breeds, mislabeled birds are common. Ask for photos of adult birds and their eggs, and ask where the line came from.

Compared with similar breeds

The Penedesenca is another Catalan breed known for very dark eggs and is easier to find in the US. For more dark egg layers, see the dark egg page.

Where to find them

Empordanesas are very rare in the US. Rare breed groups and specialty importers are the main leads.

Common questions about Empordanesas

What color eggs do Empordanesas lay?

Dark red-brown eggs.

Where do Empordanesas come from?

The Emporda area of Catalonia, Spain.

Can I buy Empordanesas in the US?

They are very rare. You may need to look to rare breed groups.
1003:
What life with Faverolles is like

Faverolles are a French breed named after the village of Faverolles, developed as a table and egg bird. Today most backyard keepers know them as the fluffy, bearded, feather-footed chickens with a gentle personality and a funny, chatty way of following you around.

The salmon variety is the best known. Hens are a soft mix of cream and salmon brown. Roosters look quite different, with straw-colored hackles, a black beard and breast and mahogany on the back. That makes it fairly easy to sex salmon chicks as they feather out.

Temperament and who they suit

Faverolles are usually calm, curious and friendly. They are often the first chickens to walk up to you. That gentleness comes with a downside. They tend to sit low in the pecking order and can get picked on by bossy breeds.

  • Good for families, kids and keepers who want a personable bird.
  • Good in cold climates.
  • Better with other gentle breeds than with aggressive or very active ones.

Eggs and the seasons

Faverolles lay a moderate number of light brown to tinted eggs. Many keepers find they lay reasonably well into the cooler months compared with lighter heritage breeds, but they still slow down in winter and during the molt. Expect a steady decline after the first couple of seasons. Some hens go broody.

Space, coop and climate

They are a medium to heavy breed and fit normal large fowl space. Their beards, muffs and feathered feet help them in cold weather. In hot climates, they need shade and good ventilation, as with any heavily feathered bird.

Breed quirks to know

  • Faverolles have five toes on each foot, an extra toe that is normal for the breed.
  • Feathered feet collect mud. Dry bedding and a drained run help.
  • Beards and muffs get wet and dirty at waterers. Nipple waterers or cups can keep faces cleaner.
  • Check under beards and foot feathers for mites and lice during health checks.
  • Watch for bullying if they share space with dominant breeds. Extra feeders help.

Faverolles vs Houdan and Dorking

The Houdan is another French breed with five toes and a beard, but it has a crest and clean legs. The Dorking, a British table breed with five toes, is often mentioned in Faverolles history. Faverolles are generally the more pet-friendly of the three.

Varieties and where to buy

Salmon is the standard US variety. White, blue salmon and other colors are kept by breeders and in other countries. Many hatcheries sell salmon Faverolles, and bantams are available too. For birds closer to the standard, look at breeders and poultry shows. Faverolles are not rare in the US, but quality breeder stock is less common than hatchery birds. You may also see them listed as Faverolle, which is just a spelling variation.

Common questions about Faverolles

Are Faverolles good layers?

They are fair layers of light brown eggs, not high production birds.

How can I tell Faverolles roosters from hens?

In the salmon variety, young males show darker, black feathers on the breast and beard, while hens stay creamy salmon.

Why does my Faverolles have five toes?

It is a normal breed trait. Faverolles have an extra toe on each foot.
1005:
Faverolle or Faverolles?

Faverolle and Faverolles are the same breed. The breed is named after the French village of Faverolles, so the proper name keeps the final "s" even for a single bird. Many people drop it in casual use, and some hatcheries list it both ways. Searching both spellings is the easiest way to find more breeders.

A quick guide to the breed

If you are looking at a Faverolle listing, here is what to expect from the bird itself.

  • Bearded and muffed face, feathered feet and five toes on each foot.
  • Salmon is the common US color. Hens are cream and salmon, roosters are darker with black beards and breasts.
  • Gentle, chatty and friendly, often low in the pecking order.
  • Fair layers of light brown to tinted eggs.
  • Good cold tolerance thanks to heavy feathering.

Care tips specific to the breed

The beard and muffs dip into water and get messy, so cups or nipple waterers help. Feathered feet pick up mud, so dry bedding matters. Because they are mild-mannered, they can be bullied in mixed flocks with assertive breeds. Pair them with other gentle birds if you can, like Orpingtons or Cochins.

Sexing salmon chicks

As salmon chicks feather out, young males usually show darker or black feathers on the breast and wings, while young hens stay light. That makes salmon Faverolles easier to sex than many breeds by a few weeks of age.

Faverolles are fairly available from hatcheries, and breeders offer show lines and other colors. Bantams are available too.

Common questions about Faverolle chickens

Is Faverolle a different breed from Faverolles?

No. It is just a spelling variation.

Are Faverolle chickens good for kids?

Yes. They are known for being gentle and friendly.

Do Faverolles have extra toes?

Yes. Five toes on each foot is normal for the breed.
1008:
Fayoumi, the short name for the Egyptian Fayoumi

A "Fayoumi" listing is the same breed as the Egyptian Fayoumi, named for the Faiyum region of Egypt. It is a small, light breed known for early maturity, toughness and a very alert, flighty nature. The common color is silver penciled, with a silvery white neck and a body of fine black and white barring.

What makes them different from most backyard breeds

  • They mature early, both in laying and in roosters starting to crow.
  • They lay small eggs that are off-white to lightly tinted.
  • They are very active, fly well and often roost high.
  • They are wary of people and predators.
  • They handle heat very well.

Fayoumis have been studied by researchers for their disease resistance, and backyard keepers often describe them as hardy. That does not mean they cannot get sick, so standard biosecurity and health checks still apply.

Who they suit

They suit hot climates, free range setups and keepers who like independent birds. They are a poor match for families who want calm pets, or for small runs without a roof. In those cases, the family-friendly breeds list is a better start.

Climate notes

Fayoumis are at their best in heat. In cold areas, their single combs and small bodies mean they need a dry, draft-free coop in winter.

Where to find them

Several hatcheries sell them, often as Egyptian Fayoumi, and they are not hard to find in the US.

Common questions about Fayoumi chickens

Are Fayoumi and Egyptian Fayoumi the same?

Yes. Fayoumi is the short name.

Are Fayoumis friendly?

Usually not very. They are flighty and wary, though some tame down with handling.

Do Fayoumis lay many eggs?

They lay a fair number of small eggs and start young.
1009:
What the Friesian chicken is like

The Friesian, sometimes spelled Friesan, is a small, light breed from Friesland in the northern Netherlands. It is one of the old Dutch farm breeds, kept for laying. Birds are finely penciled or spotted, with gold, silver and other colors. They have a single comb and white earlobes, and they lay white eggs.

Friesians are active, alert and good foragers. They are light on their feet and fly well. Many are flighty, though some become tame with handling.

Who they suit

  • Keepers who want a small, active white egg layer.
  • Free range setups with room to roam.
  • Rare breed fans.

They are not ideal for small runs without a roof or for families wanting calm pets.

Eggs and seasons

Friesians are fair to good layers of small to medium white eggs. They are not usually broody. They lay best in spring and summer.

Space and climate

Their small size means they eat less feed than large breeds. They fly well, so cover the run. Their single comb can get frostbite in harsh cold, so keep the coop dry. They handle heat well with shade.

Good for small flocks

Because Friesians are small, they eat less than large breeds, and they work well for keepers who want white eggs without big birds. A flock of small, active hens can find much of its own food when free ranging. They do still need secure housing at night, since small birds are easy prey.

Compared with similar breeds

The Hamburg is a similar light, spangled or penciled layer, with a rose comb. The Deathlayer is another old penciled European breed.

Where to buy

Friesians are rare in the US. A few breeders keep them.

Common questions about Friesian chickens

What color eggs do Friesians lay?

White eggs.

Are Friesians good layers?

They are fair to good layers for their size.

Are Friesians flighty?

Many are. They are active and fly well.
1011:
What it is like to keep Frizzles

A Frizzle has feathers that curl outward and forward instead of lying flat. The effect is a bird that looks like it walked through a wind tunnel. In the US, the Frizzle is treated as a breed by the American Poultry Association. In many other places, frizzling is treated as a feather type that can appear in many breeds, such as Cochins, Polish and Japanese Bantams.

Frizzles are usually calm and friendly, and they are popular with families.

How frizzling is inherited

The frizzle gene is incompletely dominant. A bird with one copy is a frizzle. A bird with two copies is often called a frazzle, or over-frizzled, with brittle feathers that break easily and can leave bald patches. A bird with no copies has smooth feathers. Breeding frizzle to frizzle gives roughly a quarter frazzle, half frizzle and a quarter smooth. Breeding frizzle to smooth avoids frazzles.

Care needs

  • Frizzled feathers insulate less and shed rain poorly, so keep birds dry and out of drafts.
  • They may struggle in cold, wet weather more than smooth breeds.
  • Curled feathers make them poor fliers, so they are easy to contain.
  • Check for mites and lice, which can hide in the feathers.

Eggs and temperament

Egg color, size and number depend on the breed the frizzle is in. Most frizzled birds are kept for looks and personality rather than production.

Climate

Frizzles do best in mild, dry climates. In cold areas, give a dry coop with good ventilation and no drafts. In heat, give shade.

Compared with similar birds

Silkies also have unusual feathers. A cross between a Silkie and a Frizzle is sometimes called a Sizzle. See the Silkie page for more. Frizzled Cochins are among the most common frizzles.

Where to buy

Many hatcheries sell frizzles, often as bantam Cochins or as a mixed listing.

Common questions about Frizzles

Is a Frizzle a breed?

In the US, yes. In many places, it is a feather type found in several breeds.

What is a frazzle?

A bird with two copies of the frizzle gene, with brittle feathers that break easily.

Can Frizzles fly?

Not well. Their curled feathers make flying hard.
1014:
About the Gallina di Saluzzo

The Gallina di Saluzzo is a traditional Italian breed from the area around Saluzzo in Piedmont, in northwestern Italy. It is part of a group of local Piedmont breeds that were kept on farms for eggs and meat, and that Italian breed groups have worked to preserve. The best known type is white, often called the Bianca di Saluzzo.

Detailed information in English is limited, and the breed is very rare outside Italy. This page sticks to the basics.

What to expect

  • A traditional dual-purpose farm bird.
  • A breed suited to foraging and outdoor life.
  • Rare, with small populations.

Because it is so rare, ask any seller about the origin and adult appearance of their birds.

Climate and coop

Piedmont has cold winters and warm summers, so a well-built coop that stays dry in winter and has shade in summer suits the breed. Give standard space, a good feed and secure housing. The coop ventilation guide covers how to keep air moving without drafts.

Quarantine new birds for several weeks before adding them to your flock, since rare stock often comes from small, scattered breeders.

Helping preserve it

If you keep this breed, records of hatch rates, egg production and temperament help other breeders. Avoid breeding close relatives when you can.

If you cannot find Gallina di Saluzzo, the breeds encyclopedia lists other rare European breeds that are easier to find.

Common questions about Gallina di Saluzzo

Where does the Gallina di Saluzzo come from?

The area around Saluzzo in Piedmont, Italy.

Is the Gallina di Saluzzo rare?

Yes. It is very rare, especially outside Italy.

Is it a meat or egg breed?

It is a traditional dual-purpose farm bird.
1015:
The Ginger Red color

Ginger Red is one of the warmer, lighter game colors. Hens are a ginger to buff red, often with darker markings in the tail and hackle. Roosters are richer red with darker tails. It is a softer look than the high-contrast Black Breasted Red, where hens are brown and stippled. Exact shades vary a lot between lines, so use breeder photos as your guide.

How it relates to Old English Game

Ginger Red is a color of large fowl Old English Game, sold by some hatcheries as "Standard Old English." The body, stance and instincts are the same as every other color. Choosing ginger is about looks, not a different kind of bird.

What to expect

  • Small cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers, mainly spring and summer.
  • Strong broody instincts and protective mothering.
  • Active foraging and good predator awareness.
  • Good flying ability, so cover the run if they need to stay in.

As with all Old English, roosters fight other roosters. Keep one male per flock or pen males apart. Hens can become quite tame, especially if raised with regular handling.

Climate and coop

Lighter feathers reflect a bit more sun than black, and the breed generally handles heat well with shade. Their tight feathering is less insulating in cold weather, so a dry, ventilated, draft-free coop is important. Check single combs for frostbite after very cold nights.

How common is it?

Ginger Red is offered by some hatcheries that carry large fowl Old English and is kept by game breeders. It is not as easy to find as Black Breasted Red.

Common questions about Ginger Red Old English

Are Ginger Red Old English good for beginners?

Hens are manageable, but game roosters and strong flying make them a better fit for keepers with some experience.

Do they lay in winter?

Usually very little. They are seasonal layers.

Will ginger hens hatch eggs?

Yes. Old English hens go broody readily.
1017:
The Golden Duckwing Phoenix

Golden Duckwing is one of the classic colors of the Phoenix, a long-tailed breed developed in Europe from Japanese long-tailed fowl. Roosters show golden to straw hackles and saddles, a black breast and a steely band across the wing that gives the "duckwing" name. Hens are much quieter in color, with gray to brown tones and a salmon breast. On a mature rooster, the long flowing tail makes the color even more striking.

How it relates to the Phoenix and Onagadori

The Phoenix descends from Japanese breeds like the Onagadori, which is famous for tails that can grow for years without a normal molt. Most Phoenix do molt their tails, and their tails are shorter than top Onagadori, but well-bred Phoenix roosters still grow very long tails.

Keeping long-tailed birds

  • Use high perches so tails do not drag on the floor.
  • Keep the coop and run clean and dry to protect tail feathers.
  • Avoid crowding, since other birds may step on or pull tails.
  • Give them room to range. They are active and fly well.

Hens lay small cream to tinted eggs in modest numbers and often go broody. Phoenix are generally alert and can be flighty, though some become quite tame. Their single combs need protection in hard winters.

Where to find them

Golden Duckwing is one of the easier Phoenix colors to find. Some hatcheries offer it, and long-tail breeders keep better lines. Silver duckwing and other colors are also kept.

Common questions about Golden Duckwing Phoenix

How long do Phoenix tails grow?

Long, often several feet in good lines, but length varies a lot between birds and lines.

Do Phoenix hens lay well?

Not really. They are not egg birds. Eggs are small and few.

What does duckwing mean?

It describes the colored band on the rooster's wing, which looks like the wing markings of a duck.
1020:
The Golden Laced Wyandotte look

Golden Laced Wyandottes have rich gold feathers, each outlined in black. On a good bird, the lacing is crisp and even across the breast and back, giving a scaled look. Roosters have bright gold hackles striped with black and a black tail. It is one of the most popular Wyandotte colors and an easy bird to pick out in a mixed flock.

How it relates to the Wyandotte

The Wyandotte is an American breed known for a round body, a low rose comb and good laying. Golden Laced is a color variety, and it shares all the breed traits. It is closely related to Silver Laced, which has the same pattern with white instead of gold, and to the deeper red Black Laced Red.

What daily life is like

  • Dependable layers of light to medium brown eggs.
  • Calm overall, though hens can be assertive in the pecking order.
  • Rose comb resists frostbite, so they are great for cold climates.
  • Fluffy rear feathering can collect droppings, so check vents.
  • Some hens go broody, especially in spring.

They need standard large fowl space and do well both free ranging and in a run. In hot climates, provide shade and water. Laying slows in winter and during the molt, then returns in spring.

Where to get them

Golden Laced Wyandottes are easy to find from hatcheries and feed stores. Hatchery lacing is often less sharp. For show quality, look to breeders. Bantams are also popular.

If you are torn between breeds, the Wyandotte vs Orpington comparison lays out the differences.

Common questions about Golden Laced Wyandottes

Are Golden Laced Wyandottes good for beginners?

Yes. They are hardy, calm and good layers.

What color eggs do they lay?

Light to medium brown.

Are Golden Laced Wyandottes aggressive?

Not usually toward people, but hens can be bossy with other chickens.
1021:
About the Gournay

The Gournay is a French breed from Normandy, named after the town of Gournay-en-Bray. It is black and white mottled, with a single comb and a compact, practical body. It looks a bit like a Houdan without the crest, beard or fifth toe. It was historically kept as a farm and market bird for eggs and meat.

It is rare, especially outside France.

What to expect

  • A dual-purpose farm bird.
  • White eggs.
  • Generally calm and practical.

Mottled feathers can show more white after each molt, a common trait in mottled breeds.

Space and climate

Give them standard large fowl space. Their single comb can get frostbite in harsh cold, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. Warm weather is fine as long as there is shade.

Who they suit

Gournays suit keepers interested in rare French breeds who want a practical bird for eggs and meat. Since so few are kept, buying them means taking part in preserving the breed. Ask breeders for photos of adult birds and about the history of their line.

Compared with similar breeds

The Houdan is the obvious comparison, as both are mottled black and white French birds from the same general area. The Ancona is another mottled breed, a Mediterranean layer that is lighter and more flighty.

Where to buy

Gournays are very rare in the US. Rare breed groups and specialty breeders are the main leads.

Common questions about Gournay chickens

What color eggs do Gournays lay?

White eggs.

Is a Gournay a Houdan?

No. They look similar, but the Gournay has no crest, beard or fifth toe.

Are Gournays rare?

Yes, very rare outside France.
1023:
The Gray Japanese Bantam

Gray is one of the less common colors in Japanese Bantams. It mixes darker body tones with lighter, silvery edging, especially around the neck and back of roosters. Exact markings vary a lot between breeders and countries, so treat photos of the parent stock as your best guide to what your birds will look like.

How it relates to the parent breed

Gray is a color variety of the Japanese Bantam, sometimes called Chabo. Body type and care are the same as any color. You still get the short legs, upright tail and large single comb. The color changes nothing about temperament.

The short-leg gene still applies. It is lethal in double dose, so pairing two short-legged birds means some embryos will not hatch. Breeders often use one longer-legged parent.

Daily care

  • Keep the run dry. Their low bodies pick up mud quickly.
  • Protect the big comb from frost with a dry, draft-free coop.
  • Expect small eggs in modest numbers and plenty of broodiness.
  • Give shade in summer and fresh water all day.

Japanese are friendly and easy to keep in a small space. They suit keepers who enjoy ornamental bantams. They are not a production layer and are not ideal for wet free range land.

How rare is Gray?

Gray is a hard color to find. It is mostly in the hands of bantam breeders and shows up at shows. If you want one, joining a bantam club or asking at shows is the most reliable route. If you just want the breed, Black Tailed White is far easier to source.

Common questions about Gray Japanese Bantams

Is Gray a recognized Japanese color?

Gray is kept and shown in some places, but standards differ between countries, so check with your local breed club.

Are Gray Japanese Bantams hardy?

They are hardy enough with a dry coop, but their combs need protection in hard frost.

Where can I buy them?

Mostly from bantam breeders and at poultry shows.
1026:
What Houdans are like to keep

The Houdan is a French breed from the town of Houdan, near Paris. It has a full crest, a beard and muffs, and five toes on each foot. In the US it has a V-shaped comb. It is usually mottled black and white, and there is also a white variety. It was kept in France as a table bird and also lays white eggs.

Houdans are calm, gentle and friendly. They are not fast or flighty, and they do well in runs.

Who they suit

  • Families wanting a calm, friendly breed.
  • Keepers who love crested birds.
  • Small flocks in runs.

They are not the best pick for free ranging where hawks are common, since crests limit vision.

Crest care

  • Approach calmly, as the crest can limit their vision.
  • Use waterers that keep crests and beards dry.
  • Check for mites and lice under the crest and beard.
  • Watch for flock mates pulling at crest feathers.

Eggs and climate

Houdans are fair layers of white eggs. They handle cold well, as the V comb is small. Wet crests can freeze, so keep them dry. They do fine in heat with shade.

Five toes and foot checks

The extra toe is normal for Houdans. Check feet now and then for injuries or swelling, and keep roosts at a sensible height, since heavier birds can hurt their feet jumping down. Houdans can also be low in the pecking order because of their calm nature, so keep an eye out for bullying.

Houdan vs Polish

The Polish has a bigger crest, four toes and is lighter. Houdans are heavier and calmer. See the Polish vs Houdan comparison for more.

Where to buy

Houdans are a conservation breed. Some hatcheries and breeders sell them.

Common questions about Houdans

Why do Houdans have five toes?

It is a normal breed trait.

Are Houdans good layers?

They are fair layers of white eggs.

Are Houdans friendly?

Yes. They are known as calm and gentle.
1027:
What Hamburgs are like to keep

The Hamburg is a light, elegant breed with a rose comb, white earlobes and slate blue legs. Despite the German-sounding name, its roots are usually traced to the Netherlands as well as Germany and Britain. Silver Spangled is the best known color, with black spots on a white body. Golden spangled, penciled and black also exist.

Hamburgs are active, flighty and fast. They forage well, fly well and often roost in trees if allowed. They are not cuddly, but they are fun to watch.

Who they suit

  • Free range setups with room to roam.
  • Keepers wanting white eggs from a small, hardy bird.
  • Anyone wanting a striking, active breed.

They are a poor fit for small runs, families wanting pets or keepers who want broody hens.

Eggs and seasons

Hamburgs are good layers of small to medium white eggs. They are rarely broody. Spring and summer are their best laying months.

Space and climate

Hamburgs need space. In small runs they can get stressed. Cover the run, since they fly very well. The rose comb resists frostbite, and they are generally hardy in cold. They handle heat well with shade.

Living with flighty birds

Hamburgs do not like being caught. Train them to come in at dusk with a little scratch, and close them in for the night. A fully covered run saves a lot of chasing. Because they are so active, they also get bored in bare runs, so give them perches and areas to scratch.

Compared with similar breeds

The Campine is another light, active white egg layer with barring. The Friesian is a small Dutch breed with similar penciled patterns and a single comb.

Where to buy

Many hatcheries sell Silver Spangled Hamburgs. Other colors are harder to find. Bantams are also available.

Common questions about Hamburgs

Are Hamburgs good layers?

Yes. Yes, white eggs and plenty of them for a heritage bird.

Do Hamburgs fly?

Yes. They fly very well.

Are Hamburgs friendly?

Not usually. They are active and flighty.
1028:
About the Holland chicken

The Holland is an American breed developed in the 1930s, partly from stock imported from the Netherlands. The goal was a dual-purpose bird that laid white eggs, since many American dual-purpose breeds lay brown eggs. White and barred are the recognized varieties.

Hollands are calm and practical birds, and they are rare today.

What to expect

  • White eggs, laid at a fair to good rate.
  • A medium to heavy dual-purpose body.
  • Calm temperament.
  • Single comb.

Space and climate

Give standard large fowl space. A dry, airy coop protects the single comb from frostbite in severe cold. Give shade in summer and they do fine.

Who they suit

Hollands suit keepers who want a calm, practical bird that lays white eggs, and anyone interested in rare American breeds. They are a good fit for small homesteads that want eggs and the option of meat from one flock.

Helping preserve the breed

Because Hollands are rare, keepers who breed them help keep the breed going. Keep records of laying and temperament, select good birds to breed, and avoid pairing close relatives when you can.

Compared with similar breeds

A Barred Holland can look like a Barred Plymouth Rock, but it lays white eggs instead of brown. The California Grey is another American barred breed that lays white eggs.

Where to buy

Hollands are a conservation breed and are hard to find. A few breeders keep them.

Common questions about Holland chickens

What color eggs do Hollands lay?

White eggs.

Are Hollands rare?

Yes. They are a rare American breed.

Are Hollands good for meat?

They are a dual-purpose bird, so they can be used for both eggs and meat.
1029:
What Icelandic chickens are like to keep

Icelandic chickens are a landrace that came to Iceland with Norse settlers more than a thousand years ago. Because the island was so isolated, the birds stayed mostly free of outside breeding and were shaped by farm life and a harsh climate, not by a show standard. In Iceland they are called the settlers' hen. The breed was in real danger in the 1900s as modern layers took over, and conservation work in Iceland helped bring it back.

No two look alike

There is no single look. Icelandics come in almost every color and pattern, with single, rose or other combs, and some have small crests. Breeders who keep the landrace true avoid selecting for one color, since the variety is part of what makes it an Icelandic.

Day to day

They are small to medium, lively and very independent. Icelandics are some of the best foragers you can keep, and they do well on free range where they find a lot of their own food. They are alert and quick to dodge predators. Most are not lap birds, but many get used to their keepers. Roosters tend to be watchful flock guards.

Eggs and broodiness
