Hens lay white to light-tinted eggs, small to medium in size, at a fair rate. Many go broody and raise chicks well, which suits keepers who want a self-sustaining flock.

Climate

Icelandics handle cold very well. Larger single combs can still get frostbite in hard freezes, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. They cope with heat with shade, though they are clearly built for cool weather.

How they compare

The Swedish Flower Hen is another Nordic landrace with lots of color variety. It is a bit larger and lays tinted to light brown eggs.

Where to get them

Icelandics are rare in the US and mostly come from small breeders who keep separate lines. Ask about the source of the stock, since keepers care about keeping the lines pure.

Common questions about Icelandic chickens

Are Icelandic chickens good layers?

They are fair layers of small to medium white or lightly tinted eggs.

Are Icelandic chickens cold-hardy?

Very. They were shaped by Icelandic winters.

Why do Icelandic chickens look so different from each other?

They are a landrace, so color and comb vary naturally. Breeders keep that variety on purpose.
1030:
What owning ISA Browns is really like

The ISA Brown is a commercial hybrid, not a breed. It was developed in France in the late 1970s, and the name comes from the company that created it. Today it belongs to the poultry genetics firm Hendrix Genetics. ISA Browns are sex-linked, so hens hatch red or brown and males hatch white or cream, which makes ordering pullets very reliable.

Huge first year, shorter career

ISA Browns are bred for one job. A healthy young hen lays brown eggs almost every day, often starting younger than heritage breeds. The catch is that this pace takes a lot out of the bird. Most slow down noticeably after their second year, and many keepers find they have a shorter life than heritage hens. Reproductive problems such as egg yolk peritonitis, tumors and internal laying are commonly reported in older hybrid layers. If a hen stands upright like a penguin, has a swollen belly or stops eating, call a vet.

Day to day

Most ISA Browns are very friendly and easy to handle, which surprises people who expect a factory bird. They are curious, follow you around, and do well with kids. They are rarely broody. Feed a good layer ration with oyster shell on the side, since all those eggs need calcium.

Space and climate

They are medium-sized and fine on standard space. They handle both cold and heat fairly well. Their single combs can get frostbite in deep cold.

How they compare

The Lohmann Brown and Golden Comet are close equivalents from other companies. See the ISA Brown vs Golden Comet comparison for how they line up.

Common questions about ISA Browns

How long do ISA Browns lay?

They lay heavily for about two years, then production drops. Many keep laying a little after that.

Are ISA Browns good for beginners?

Yes, for egg production and friendliness. Just know they tend to have shorter lives than heritage breeds.

Can you breed ISA Browns?

You can hatch their eggs, but the chicks will not be ISA Browns or sex-linked in the same way.
1032:
Keeping Iowa Blues on a homestead

The Iowa Blue was developed in the early 1900s around Decorah, Iowa. It is a dual-purpose farm bird and despite the name, it is not blue. Hens have a white or silvery neck and a body of dark, penciled feathers that can look bluish gray from a distance. Roosters have silver-white necks and saddles over darker bodies. Chicks hatch in a brown, chipmunk-striped down.

Day to day

Iowa Blues are known as active, alert foragers that do best with space. They are a good choice for free-range homesteads. Keepers often describe them as calm and practical, and many tame down well. Old stories say Iowa Blue hens would fight off hawks. Treat that as farm lore, not something to rely on. A covered run is still the best protection.

Laying and broodiness

Hens lay brown eggs at a moderate rate. They are a heritage farm breed, so expect the usual slowdown in winter and during the molt. Some hens go broody and are good mothers.

Space and climate

They are medium-heavy birds and do well on standard space. Bred in the Midwest, they handle cold winters. Watch single combs in hard freezes. In summer, give shade and fresh water.

How they compare

If you like the look but want something easier to find, the Plymouth Rock is a similar sized American dual-purpose bird. For winter laying in a cold Midwest climate, see our cold climate breeds.

Where to get them

The Iowa Blue is rare. It is not recognized by the American Poultry Association. A handful of breeders and a few hatcheries sell them. Ask about the line, since some birds sold under the name can vary in type.

Common questions about Iowa Blues

Are Iowa Blue chickens actually blue?

No. The color is a dark penciled pattern that can look bluish gray.

What color eggs do Iowa Blues lay?

Brown eggs.

Are Iowa Blues good for free range?

Yes. They are active foragers that do well with room to roam.
1033:
Isbar, Silverudd Blue and the name confusion

The Isbar is a Swedish breed developed in the mid 1900s by Martin Silverudd, a breeder who created several laying breeds in Sweden. Many sellers use Isbar and Silverudd Blue for the same bird, which is why both pages exist. If you are buying, the name alone does not tell you much. Ask what the birds look like and what color eggs the hens lay.

What most Isbars look like today

Most birds sold as Isbars in the US come in blue, black and splash. Blue to blue matings give a mix of all three, since blue does not breed true. They are medium-sized, fairly light-bodied birds with single combs.

Eggs

Isbars are known for green-tinted eggs, from light mint green to deeper shades depending on the hen. They are good layers for a non-production breed.

The bar in the name

The ending follows the same naming style as British autosexing breeds like the Rhodebar and the Legbar, where chicks can be sexed by color at hatch. Some older sources describe the Isbar as autosexing. The blue, black and splash birds sold today are generally not sexed this way, so do not count on it unless the seller confirms it.

Living with them

Keepers describe them as active and friendly. They forage well and are cold-hardy, though single combs can get frostbite in very cold weather. They are not common, and most come from small breeders.

Common questions about Isbars

Are Isbar and Silverudd Blue the same?

The names are commonly used for the same bird. Ask the seller to be sure.

What color eggs does an Isbar lay?

Green-tinted eggs, in shades from pale mint to deeper green.

Can you sex Isbar chicks at hatch?

Generally not. Wait for combs and feathers to tell hens from roosters.
1035:
What to know about Ixworth chickens

The Ixworth is a British breed created in the 1930s by Reginald Appleyard in Ixworth, Suffolk. Appleyard was also known for his duck breeds. He wanted a white table chicken with good meat that could also lay a fair number of eggs. The Ixworth was the result, a white bird with a pea comb and a deep, broad body.

A table bird first

The Ixworth was bred for meat quality, with white skin and a good breast. It grows much slower than a modern meat hybrid, so it is a heritage table bird for keepers who want to raise their own meat at a slower pace. Hens lay tinted or cream eggs at a moderate rate.

Day to day

Ixworths are generally described as active and fairly calm birds. They forage well. Their white feathers show dirt, and like any white bird they are easier for predators to spot.

Climate

The pea comb is small and resists frostbite well, which suits cold winters. They are a sturdy British breed suited to cool, damp weather.

Rarity

The Ixworth almost disappeared after modern meat hybrids took over, and it is still rare, even in the UK. It is rarely seen in the US. If you find one, it will usually be through a specialist breeder. If you want a similar role from an easier to find breed, the Dorking is another old British table bird, and the Delaware is an American dual-purpose choice.

Common questions about Ixworth chickens

Are Ixworths good meat birds?

They were bred as table birds and have good meat, but they grow much slower than modern meat hybrids.

What color eggs do Ixworths lay?

Tinted or cream eggs.

Can you get Ixworths in the US?

It is very hard. They are rare even in Britain.
1038:
Living with Java chickens

The Java is one of the oldest American chicken breeds, often called the second oldest after the Dominique. Its exact origin is unclear, but it was well established in the US by the mid 1800s. The Java helped create other American breeds, including the Plymouth Rock and the Jersey Giant. Black and Mottled are the classic colors, with White also recognized.

Day to day

Javas are large, long-bodied birds with a calm, steady temperament. They are excellent foragers and were built to find food on free range farms. Most keepers find them friendly enough, though not as cuddly as an Orpington. Roosters are usually reasonable.

Laying through the year

Hens lay brown eggs at a good rate for a heritage breed. They are known for laying fairly well in winter. Some hens go broody and make good mothers. They mature slower than production breeds.

Space and climate

They are big birds, so give them a bit more room. They handle cold well, though single combs on roosters can still get frostbite. Black Javas need shade in hot summers, since dark feathers soak up heat.

Look for the green sheen

Good Black Javas have a beetle-green sheen in the sun. Mottled Javas are black with white tips, and like other mottled birds they often get whiter with each molt.

Rarity and where to buy

Javas nearly disappeared in the 1900s and have appeared on the Livestock Conservancy priority list. A few hatcheries sell them, and breeders who focus on heritage American breeds are the best source. The Dominique is a good companion breed if you want to keep two of the oldest American breeds together.

Common questions about Java chickens

Are Java chickens good layers?

Yes, for a heritage breed. They lay brown eggs and hold up fairly well in winter.

Are Javas good meat birds?

They are large and were used as dual-purpose birds, but they grow slowly.

Are Java chickens rare?

Yes. They are uncommon, but a few hatcheries and breeders keep them.
1039:
What keeping Japanese Bantams is really like

Japanese Bantams, also called Chabo, are true bantams from Japan, meaning there is no large version. They have been kept as ornamental birds for centuries. You notice them right away for their very short legs, a large upright tail that rises above the head, and a big single comb. Common colors include black-tailed white, black-tailed buff, black, white, gray and mottled, and the breed comes in plain, frizzled and silkie-feathered types.

The short leg gene

The short legs come from a gene that is lethal in a double dose. When two short-legged birds are bred, about a quarter of the embryos die in the shell. That is why hatch rates for this breed look poor even with good eggs and a good incubator. Some chicks also hatch with normal legs. Breeders often pair short to long legged birds to help with this.

Day to day

Japanese Bantams are calm and friendly, easy to tame, and good with gentle kids. They are poor fliers and stay close to the ground. Because of that, their wings and tail drag in mud and wet grass. Give them a dry, covered run and clean bedding. They do not dig or range far, which suits small gardens.

Eggs and broodiness

Hens lay small cream or tinted eggs. They go broody often and make attentive mothers, though they can only cover a few eggs.

Climate

They do well in warm weather with shade. Cold is harder. They are small, they sit low on cold ground, and their combs are large for their size, so frostbite is a real risk. In cold areas, give them a draft-free coop with deep dry bedding.

Colors with their own pages

See the Black Tailed Buff and Mottled Japanese Bantam for details on individual colors.

Common questions about Japanese Bantams

Why do so many Japanese Bantam eggs fail to hatch?

The short leg gene is lethal in a double dose, so a share of eggs from two short-legged parents will not hatch.

Are Japanese Bantams good pets?

Yes. They are small, calm and easy to tame.

Do Japanese Bantams need heat in winter?

Not usually, but they need a dry, draft-free coop and close watch on their combs in cold weather.
1040:
Living with Jersey Giants day to day

Jersey Giants are the biggest American chicken breed, and you feel that the first time you pick one up. A grown rooster can weigh around 13 pounds and a hen around 10. They were developed in New Jersey in the late 1800s, mostly from Javas, Langshans and Brahmas, with the idea of making a large roasting bird. The Cornish cross later took over that job because it grows so much faster, which is why the Giant is now mostly a backyard and homestead bird.

Day to day, most keepers find them calm and easygoing. They are not quick, they are not flighty, and many hens will let you scoop them up without much fuss. Roosters are usually mellow for their size, though a 13 pound bird that does decide to be rude is a lot to handle, so it pays to choose a gentle one.

Slow to grow, slow to lay

The thing that surprises new owners is how long Jersey Giants take to mature. They put on frame first and fill out later, and many need well over six months before they look finished. Pullets often start laying later than lighter breeds. Once they start, expect large brown eggs at a steady but not record pace. They tend to keep laying fairly well through cooler months, then slow down during the molt and in their later years like any heritage breed.

Space, roosts and nest boxes

Plan your coop around their size, not the average hen. Give them more floor space per bird than you would for a standard breed, wider pop doors, and roomy nest boxes so they are not squeezing in and cracking eggs. Keep roosts low. Heavy birds jumping down from a high bar land hard, and that is one of the ways leg and foot problems like bumblefoot start. A broad, flat roost is easier on their feet than a thin round dowel. Fences can be lower than for flighty breeds, since Giants rarely fly.

Climate notes

Their size and thick feathering make them very cold-hardy. Big single-combed roosters can still get frostbite in hard freezes, so good ventilation without drafts matters. Heat is the bigger concern, especially for the black variety. In hot summers give them deep shade, airflow and plenty of cool water.

How they compare

The breed most often lined up against the Giant is the Brahma. Both are big and gentle, but Brahmas have feathered feet and usually a pea comb, while Giants are clean-legged with a single comb. There is a full Brahma vs Jersey Giant comparison if you are choosing between them. If you mainly want eggs from a calm black bird, an Australorp matures faster and usually lays more.

Where to get them

Black Jersey Giants are easy to find from big US hatcheries, and white ones are fairly common too. Blue birds are offered by some hatcheries and breeders. If you want birds close to the show standard in size and type, look for a breeder who exhibits at poultry shows. Hatchery birds are often smaller than the standard describes. The breed has appeared on the Livestock Conservancy priority list in the past, so buying from heritage breeders helps keep good lines going.

Common questions about Jersey Giants

Are Jersey Giants good layers?

They are fair layers of large brown eggs. They are not in the same league as production breeds, and they start later than most, but they are steady once going.

How long until a Jersey Giant is full grown?

Much longer than most breeds. Many keep filling out until they are close to a year old, especially roosters.

Are Jersey Giants good with kids?

Usually yes. Hens tend to be calm and tolerant. Just teach kids to support the whole body, since these birds are heavy and can hurt themselves if dropped.
1044:
Keeping Lakenvelders

The Lakenvelder comes from the border area of Germany and the Netherlands and has been around since at least the 1800s. Its pattern is striking, a white body with a solid black neck and tail. The Dutch name is often explained as a shadow on a sheet, which fits the look.

Day to day

Lakenvelders are a light, active breed. They are alert, quick and fairly flighty, and they do not usually enjoy being handled. Many keepers like them for exactly that reason. They are great foragers and often avoid predators well. They fly better than heavy breeds, so a covered run or tall fence helps.

Laying

Hens lay white or lightly tinted eggs, small to medium, at a good rate. They rarely go broody. Like other light breeds, they may start earlier than heavy breeds and lay well in their first couple of years.

Climate

Their light build handles heat well. Their single combs can get frostbite in cold weather, so keep the coop dry and well ventilated.

Show quality is hard

The pattern is tricky to breed well. Clean white bodies with sharp black necks and tails take careful selection, and many birds show some smudging. That is fine for a backyard bird, but it matters if you want to show.

How they compare

The Vorwerk has the same black neck and tail pattern on a buff body and is a bit calmer and heavier. The Leghorn is a similar light, productive layer that is much easier to find.

Rarity

Lakenvelders are uncommon in the US and have appeared on the Livestock Conservancy priority list. A few hatcheries and breeders keep them.

Common questions about Lakenvelders

Are Lakenvelders good layers?

Yes. They are steady layers of white or lightly tinted eggs.

Are Lakenvelders friendly?

They are usually shy and flighty, though some tame with regular handling.

Do Lakenvelders go broody?

Rarely.
1045:
What La Fleche chickens are like

La Fleche is an old French breed named after the town of La Flèche in the Sarthe region. It was famous in France as a table bird. Today it is best known for its comb, two spikes that stick up in a V shape like horns. That comb has earned it the nickname devil bird. The common color in the US is a glossy black.

Day to day

La Fleche are active, alert and often flighty. Many keepers describe them as wary and hard to catch. They are good foragers and do well with room to range. They fly well for their size, so plan on a covered run or tall fence.

Laying

Hens lay white eggs, usually large for the size of the bird. They are not known for broodiness.

Comb and climate

The V comb is fairly small, which helps in cold weather, though it is not immune to frostbite in very hard cold. They handle heat reasonably with shade.

How they compare

The Crevecoeur is another old French breed, black with a V comb, but it also has a crest and beard. The Houdan is a crested French bird with a calmer nature. Both share some history with La Fleche.

Rarity

La Fleche is rare in the US. A few hatcheries and specialist breeders sell them. Because numbers are small, ask about the health and history of the stock before you buy.

Who they suit

La Fleche suit keepers with space who enjoy an unusual, active bird and do not need it to be tame. They are a poor fit for small yards or families who want hens to handle.

Common questions about La Fleche chickens

Why do La Fleche chickens have horns?

It is their V-shaped comb. It is just two spikes of comb, not real horns.

What color eggs do La Fleche lay?

White eggs.

Are La Fleche chickens friendly?

Usually not very. They tend to be wary and flighty.
1046:
Living with Langshans

The Langshan comes from China and reached England in the 1870s. In Britain, one line became known as the Croad Langshan after the family who imported it. Langshans are tall, deep-bodied birds with lightly feathered legs and a U-shaped profile, with the tail held high. Black is the classic color, with white and blue also kept. The breed played a part in the making of the Orpington and the Australorp.

Day to day

Langshans are calm, gentle and fairly quiet. They are big but graceful, and many are easy to handle. They forage well but also cope with confinement. Roosters are usually mellow for their size.

Laying

Hens lay brown eggs, and some lines lay eggs with a plum or purplish bloom. They are known as decent winter layers. Some go broody. They mature slower than production breeds.

Space and roosts

Langshans are tall, long-legged birds. Give them a coop with enough head room, and keep roosts at a sensible height so they do not land hard coming down. Leg feathers need a dry run, and check them for scaly leg mites.

Climate

They handle cold well. Roosters' single combs are the part to protect in a hard freeze. Black birds need shade in summer heat.

How they compare

Against the Brahma, the Langshan is taller and leaner with fewer leg feathers, and the two breeds share a similar calm nature. Langshans are easier on feed than Brahmas for their size.

Rarity

Langshans are uncommon in the US and have appeared on the Livestock Conservancy priority list. A few hatcheries and breeders keep them. In the UK, the Croad Langshan has its own breed club.

Common questions about Langshans

What color eggs do Langshans lay?

Brown eggs, sometimes with a plum colored bloom.

Are Langshans good with kids?

Usually, yes. They are calm and gentle.

Are Langshans cold-hardy?

Yes. Watch roosters' single combs in very cold weather.
1047:
What keeping Leghorns is really like

Leghorns are the breed behind most white eggs sold in stores, and that tells you what they were built for. They came from Italy, named after the port of Livorno, and were refined in the US and Britain into lean, efficient layers. In the backyard they give you a lot of white eggs from a small, light bird that eats less than the heavy breeds.

What they do not give you is a lap chicken. Most Leghorns are alert, quick and nervous around people. They run when you walk in, they are hard to catch, and many are loud, especially when something startles them. Some keepers love that busy energy. Others find it stressful. If you want birds your kids can carry around, look elsewhere.

Laying through the seasons

Good Leghorn strains often start laying earlier than heavy breeds and keep a strong pace through their first couple of years. They are rarely broody, so they do not take weeks off to sit on eggs. Production drops during the fall molt and slows with shorter days like any breed. After the second or third year you will notice fewer eggs, though many hens keep laying at a lower rate for years. Because they put so much into eggs, keep oyster shell available and feed a proper layer ration.

Space and fencing

Leghorns are small but they need room to move. A cramped Leghorn flock is more likely to peck each other. They forage well and do best with a good run or free range time. They also fly. A four foot fence will not hold most of them, so plan on a covered run, a tall fence, or clipping one wing. They tend to roost high if you let them.

Combs, heat and cold

The big single comb is the breed's weak spot in winter. Roosters' combs and hens' floppy combs are prone to frostbite in hard cold, so keep the coop dry and well ventilated. Rose comb Leghorns exist and handle cold better. In heat, Leghorns are excellent. That big comb helps shed heat, and their light build suits hot climates well.

Hatchery Leghorns vs show Leghorns

Most backyard Leghorns come from hatcheries and are bred for laying. Show strains, especially in the US, can be bigger birds with larger combs and often lay less. If eggs are the goal, hatchery or production stock is usually the better choice. If you want a specific color like brown, buff or exchequer, you may need a breeder. The white variety has its own page at White Leghorn.

How they compare

Next to a Rhode Island Red, the Leghorn lays white eggs instead of brown, eats less, and is far more flighty. The Leghorn vs Rhode Island Red comparison covers that matchup in detail. The Ancona is a close cousin with a similar build and laying style, in a mottled black and white coat.

Where to get them

White Leghorns are one of the easiest breeds to buy. Nearly every US hatchery sells them, often as sexed pullets. Brown and other colors are widely available too. Exhibition lines come from breeders you can meet at poultry shows.

Common questions about Leghorns

How many eggs does a Leghorn lay?

Good laying strains are among the best layers you can keep, often laying most days in their first year. Show strains lay less.

Are Leghorns friendly?

Some become tame with daily handling, but most stay wary and quick. They are better suited to keepers who mainly want eggs.

Can Leghorns live in a cold climate?

Yes, but watch the combs. Dry, well ventilated housing helps prevent frostbite, and rose comb birds are the safer pick for very cold winters.
1050:
What sets the Lavender Orpington apart

A Lavender Orpington is an Orpington in a pale, silvery gray-blue color. It has the same big, soft body, calm temperament and light brown eggs as other Orpingtons. The difference is one gene. Lavender is a recessive dilution that turns black pigment into that soft dove gray.

It breeds true

Because lavender is recessive, a lavender bird carries two copies of the gene. Breed two lavenders together and all the chicks will be lavender. That is different from the more common Blue Orpington, where blue to blue matings give a mix of blue, black and splash chicks. If you want a whole flock of matching gray birds, lavender is the easier color to keep consistent.

Feather quality and sun

Some lavender lines have weaker feathers that fray or look ragged, especially in the tail and wings. Breeders have worked on this for years, so quality varies a lot between flocks. Look at the adult birds before you buy. Strong sun can also bleach lavender feathers to a brassy or tan shade. Shade in the run helps keep the color even, which matters most if you plan to show.

Living with them

Care is the same as any Orpington. They are cold-hardy, struggle more in heat, and need extra checking for mites in their thick fluff. Hens go broody fairly often and are gentle mothers.

Where to get them

Lavender Orpingtons are mostly sold by breeders, and some hatcheries offer them too. They usually cost more than Buff Orpingtons. Also see the Wyandotte vs Orpington comparison if you are still choosing a heavy breed.

Common questions about Lavender Orpingtons

Are Lavender Orpingtons good layers?

They lay about as well as other Orpingtons, a fair number of light brown eggs.

What is the difference between blue and lavender Orpingtons?

Blue is a different gene that does not breed true. Lavender is recessive, so lavender to lavender gives all lavender chicks.

Why do some lavender chickens look tan?

Sun can bleach the feathers. Shade helps keep them a cleaner gray.
1051:
Keeping Lohmann Browns at home

The Lohmann Brown is a commercial brown egg hybrid from Lohmann, a German poultry breeding company. Like other modern brown layers, it is sex-linked. Female chicks are brown or red and males are white, so pullets can be sorted at hatch with high accuracy. Lohmann Browns are widely used on egg farms around the world, and retired farm hens often end up in backyard flocks as rescues.

What they are good at

Lohmann Browns are built to lay a lot of large brown eggs on a moderate amount of feed. In a backyard flock, a young hen can lay most days for her first laying year. They mature early and rarely go broody. Most are friendly, calm and easy to handle.

What to watch for

That high output has a cost. Like the ISA Brown, Lohmanns often slow sharply after the second year, and reproductive problems are common in older hens. Keep calcium available, watch for soft shells, and know the signs of trouble like a swollen belly or upright posture. Our soft shell eggs guide covers one of the most common issues.

Rescue hens

Ex-farm Lohmanns may arrive with patchy feathers, pale combs and little experience of the outdoors. They usually feather back after a molt and learn to scratch and dust bathe quickly. Give them a quiet space to settle in, and introduce them slowly to an existing flock.

How they compare

Lohmann Browns are close to the ISA Brown and Red Shaver in looks, laying and lifespan. Most keepers cannot tell them apart. If you want a longer laying life, a heritage breed like a Rhode Island Red will lay fewer eggs per year but often keeps going longer.

Common questions about Lohmann Browns

Are Lohmann Browns and ISA Browns the same?

No. They come from different breeding companies, but they are very similar birds.

How long do Lohmann Browns live?

Many live a few years. Their lifespan is often shorter than heritage breeds because of the heavy laying.

Are Lohmann Browns friendly?

Most are very friendly and easy to handle.
1053:
What we know about the Lyonnaise

The Lyonnaise is a French breed linked to the region around Lyon. It is rare even in France, and almost unknown in North America. Because so few birds exist outside Europe, reliable details on how it performs in a backyard flock are hard to come by. We would rather give you a short, honest page than fill it with guesses.

If you are thinking about keeping them

Rare French breeds are mostly kept by small numbers of dedicated breeders and conservation groups. If you want Lyonnaise, the best route is through a French or European breed club or a breeder who keeps registered stock. Ask for photos of adult birds and details on egg color and laying from that breeder's own flock, since that is more useful than general claims.

Importing is not simple

Bringing birds or hatching eggs into the US involves federal import rules and health requirements. It is usually expensive and slow, and many hobby keepers find it is not practical. Talk to your state's animal health office before you plan an import.

Similar options

If you like French breeds and want something you can find in the US, look at the Faverolles, a calm, bearded dual-purpose bird, or the Marans, famous for its dark eggs. Both are well documented and easy to buy.

Common questions about the Lyonnaise

Can you buy Lyonnaise chickens in the US?

Very rarely, if at all. Most birds are in France.

Is the Lyonnaise a good layer?

Ask a breeder who keeps them. Reliable figures for backyard flocks are scarce.

Are there French breeds like it that are easier to find?

Yes. Faverolles and Marans are widely available and well known.
1055:
Keeping Marans for those dark eggs

Most people buy Marans for one reason, the deep chocolate brown eggs. The breed comes from the area around the town of Marans in western France, where it was developed as a sturdy farm bird. Today the Black Copper is the most famous variety, but you will also see Cuckoo, Wheaten, Blue Copper, Splash, Black, White and others.

Living with them is easy. Most Marans are calm, quiet and practical birds. They are not usually cuddly, but they are not wild either. They forage well, handle confinement fine, and get along in mixed flocks. Roosters vary, so pick a calm one if you plan to keep a male.

Why the egg color changes

The dark color is a coating laid down at the very end of shell formation, and it is not constant. Most hens lay their darkest eggs when they first start laying and again after a break, like the molt. As the laying season goes on, the color often fades a shade or two. This is normal and not a sign of illness. Egg color is also strain-dependent. Many hatchery Marans lay a medium brown, while breeder lines selected for color lay the near-black shades you see in photos. Keepers often grade shells on a numbered color chart, with higher numbers being darker. If dark eggs matter to you, ask the seller what their hens actually lay.

Laying pattern and age

Marans are moderate layers. Expect fewer eggs than a production hen, but large ones. Like most heritage breeds they slow down in winter and during the molt, and lay less each year after their first two seasons. Some hens go broody.

French and English types

You will hear about French and English Marans. In the US, the standard calls for lightly feathered shanks, which follows the French style. In the UK, Marans are clean-legged. Feathered legs need a bit more care. Check for scaly leg mites, which hide easily under leg feathers, and keep the run from getting muddy so the feathers do not clump with dirt.

Climate and space

Marans are solid, medium-heavy birds and handle cold well. Roosters' single combs can still get frostbite in deep cold. They tolerate heat reasonably when they have shade and water. Standard coop and run space for a large fowl breed is fine.

How they compare

The other famous dark egg breed is the Welsummer, which lays terracotta brown eggs, often speckled, while Marans eggs are darker and more chocolate. The Marans vs Welsummer comparison goes through the differences. The Penedesenca from Spain also lays very dark eggs but is a much flightier bird.

Where to get them

Black Copper and Cuckoo Marans are sold by many US hatcheries. For the darkest eggs and the best type, look to breeders who work with egg color and show their birds. Hatching eggs from good lines are often sold online. Ask to see egg photos from the actual breeding hens.

Common questions about Marans

Why are my Marans eggs not dark?

Color depends on the strain and fades during the laying season. Many hatchery lines simply lay medium brown eggs.

Are Marans good layers?

They are moderate layers. You get fewer eggs than from a production breed, but each egg is large and well colored.

Are Marans cold-hardy?

Yes. They are sturdy birds that handle cold well. Give roosters a draft-free, ventilated coop to protect their combs.
1056:
What keeping Malays is really like

The Malay is one of the tallest chicken breeds. It comes from Asia and has been kept in Britain since the 1800s. Malays stand very upright, with long necks and legs, a short sloping tail, hard tight feathers and a heavy brow over the eyes that gives them a stern look. They have a small, lumpy strawberry comb. Malay blood went into breeds like the Rhode Island Red and the Cornish.

A game bird at heart

Malays are game birds. Roosters often fight each other hard, and hens can be aggressive too. Most keepers pen males separately or keep only one. With people, many Malays can be calm when handled from young, but they are not a family pet breed.

Laying and growth

Hens are poor layers, with small numbers of brown or tinted eggs, mostly in spring and summer. Hens can go broody. Malays grow and mature slowly, and they take a long time to fill out.

Space and housing

Because they are so tall, they need high coop ceilings, tall pop doors and roosts set at a reasonable height. Their hard feathers do not insulate as well as fluffy breeds, so they need a dry, draft-free coop in winter. They are more comfortable in heat than cold.

How they compare

The Shamo from Japan has a similar upright game shape and a similar fighting nature. The Aseel is shorter and stockier but just as game.

Rarity

Malays are rare in the US. They are mostly kept by game bird breeders and exhibitors. The breed has been listed by the Livestock Conservancy as a conservation priority.

Common questions about Malays

How tall is a Malay chicken?

Very tall for a chicken. Large roosters can stand well above most breeds.

Are Malays good layers?

No. They lay few eggs and are kept for their look and history.

Can Malays live with other chickens?

Hens can, with care. Roosters usually should not be kept with other males.
1058:
Keeping the rare Marsh Daisy

The Marsh Daisy is a British breed from Lancashire, developed in the late 1800s. Breeds such as Old English Game, Malay, Hamburg and Sicilian Buttercup are commonly listed in its background. It has a rose comb, white earlobes and willow green legs, and wheaten is the best known color.

Day to day

Marsh Daisies are active foragers and do well where they can range. Keepers describe them as hardy and practical. They are a light to medium breed and fly better than heavy birds.

Eggs

Hens lay tinted eggs at a moderate rate.

Climate

The rose comb is low and less likely to get frostbite than a big single comb. They were developed in a wet, cool part of England and suit that kind of climate.

Rarity

The Marsh Daisy is very rare, even in Britain, and is kept mostly by a small number of breeders who work to keep it going. It is almost unknown in the US. If you want a hardy rose combed forager that you can actually buy, the Hamburg or Redcap are related options, though both lay white eggs.

Common questions about Marsh Daisies

Where can I buy Marsh Daisy chickens?

Mainly from specialist breeders in the UK. They are very hard to find elsewhere.

What color eggs do Marsh Daisies lay?

Tinted eggs.

Are Marsh Daisies good foragers?

Yes. They are active, hardy birds that like to range.
1060:
What to expect from Minorcas

The Minorca is the largest of the Mediterranean breeds, named after the Spanish island of Menorca. It was developed further in Britain and the US in the 1800s. Black is the classic color, with white and buff also known. Minorcas have long bodies, big white earlobes, and very large combs. They lay large white eggs, often bigger than you would expect from a light breed.

Day to day

Minorcas are active and alert. Many are flighty, though usually a bit calmer than Leghorns. They are good foragers and prefer space. Handling from young helps them settle. They are not often broody.

Laying

Expect a good number of large white eggs, with the strongest laying in spring and summer and in their first two years.

Combs and cold

The biggest care issue is the comb. Minorca combs, especially on roosters, are huge and prone to frostbite. In cold climates, the rose comb variety is a safer choice. Good ventilation without drafts helps keep moisture down in winter.

Heat

Minorcas handle heat well. Black birds still need shade, but the big comb and long body help shed heat. They suit warm climates better than very cold ones.

How they compare

The Leghorn lays a similar egg but is smaller and lighter. The White Faced Black Spanish is a close relative with a large white face instead of just white earlobes.

Rarity

Minorcas are uncommon but sold by a few US hatcheries, and some breeders keep show lines. The Livestock Conservancy has included Minorcas on its conservation list.

Common questions about Minorcas

Do Minorcas lay big eggs?

Yes. They lay large white eggs.

Are Minorcas good in cold weather?

They are fine if their combs are protected. Rose comb birds do better in hard cold.

Are Minorcas friendly?

Some are, but many are wary. Handling from a young age helps.
1061:
What makes the Mille Fleur d'Uccle special

Mille Fleur is a color variety of the Belgian d'Uccle, a true bantam developed in the early 1900s in the town of Uccle, near Brussels. Mille fleur means a thousand flowers in French. Each feather is orange-red with a black band and a white tip, so the bird looks covered in tiny spots. It is the most popular d'Uccle color in the US.

What the breed brings

Like all d'Uccles, Mille Fleurs have a beard and muffs, a single comb, and heavily feathered legs and feet with stiff feathers at the hocks. They are calm, friendly, and often very tame, which makes them a favorite with families and small yards. Hens lay small cream or tinted eggs and many go broody.

Spots change with age

The white tips often get bigger after each molt, so older birds can look much lighter and more speckled than they did in their first year.

Foot feather care

Those feathered feet need a dry run. Mud and wet snow can ball up around the toes and lead to frostbite or sores. Check for scaly leg mites, which can hide under the feathers. Many keepers use sand or dry bedding to keep feet clean.

How it relates to similar birds

The Porcelain d'Uccle is the same pattern in a pale, lavender-diluted version. The Booted Bantam is closely related but has no beard. The Belgian d'Anvers has a beard but clean legs and a rose comb.

Common questions about Mille Fleur d'Uccles

Are Mille Fleur d'Uccles friendly?

Very. They are one of the gentlest bantams and often enjoy being handled.

Do Mille Fleur d'Uccles lay eggs?

Yes, small cream eggs at a modest pace, with breaks when hens go broody.

Can Mille Fleur d'Uccles live in cold climates?

Yes, if their feet stay dry. Wet, muddy runs are the main problem.
1064:
What the mottled color means for Japanese Bantams

The Mottled Japanese Bantam is a color variety of the Japanese Bantam, also called the Chabo. The birds are black with white tips on many feathers, giving a speckled look. Underneath the color it is the same tiny, short-legged bantam with a big upright tail and a large single comb.

Mottling changes with age

Mottled birds often look darker when young and gain more white tips after each molt. A three year old bird can look much whiter than a pullet. This is normal for mottled breeds and does not mean anything is wrong.

Living with them

Japanese Bantams are mostly kept as pets and show birds. They are friendly, small and easy to tame. They lay small cream or tinted eggs and hens go broody often. Their very short legs mean their wings and tail nearly touch the ground, so a muddy run makes them dirty fast. Keep them on dry ground with good drainage.

The short leg gene

Short legs in Japanese Bantams come from a gene that is lethal when a chick gets two copies. When you breed two short-legged birds, part of the eggs will not hatch, and some chicks will have longer legs. That is normal for the breed, not a problem with your birds. The Scots Dumpy carries a similar short leg trait.

Climate notes

They tolerate heat well, but their small bodies and big single combs make them vulnerable to cold. Give a dry, draft-free coop and watch for frostbite on the comb.

Common questions about Mottled Japanese Bantams

Do Mottled Japanese Bantams get whiter?

Yes. White tips usually increase after each molt.

Are Japanese Bantams good layers?

Not really. They lay small eggs at a modest pace and are kept mostly for looks.

Why are some of my chicks long-legged?

Not every chick inherits the short leg gene. Long-legged chicks are normal in this breed.
1065:
What keeping Modern Game is really like

Modern Game were developed in Britain in the 1800s, after cockfighting was banned, from Old English Game stock. Breeders selected purely for show, aiming for very long legs and neck, short tight feathers and an upright stance. The result looks almost like a wading bird. Most Modern Game in the US are bantams, though large fowl exist. Colors include birchen, black breasted red, brown red, silver duckwing and many more.

A show bird first

Modern Game are not productive birds. Hens lay few small cream or tinted eggs. They are kept for exhibition and for their unusual look. Many are surprisingly friendly and tame, which helps on the show table.

Cold is a problem

Their short, tight feathers and slim bodies give very little insulation. They do not handle cold well. In cold areas, they need a well-insulated, draft-free coop, and many keepers give extra protection in winter. Their single combs are also prone to frostbite. They do better in warm climates.

Roosters

Like other game breeds, males can fight. Most keepers pen roosters separately.

Space and handling

They need little space but a tall coop for their height. Pick them up carefully, supporting the body and legs. They are not great foragers compared with hardier breeds.

How they compare

The Old English Game shares the same roots but is much hardier and more practical. The Malay is another tall bird, but heavy and much more aggressive.

Where to get them

Most Modern Game come from bantam breeders and exhibitors, and they are a common sight in game bantam classes at shows. A few hatcheries sell them. If you plan to show, buy from a breeder whose birds already do well on the table.

Common questions about Modern Game

Are Modern Game good layers?

No. They lay few eggs and are kept mostly for show.

Can Modern Game live outside in winter?

Only with good protection. They have little feather insulation.

Are Modern Game friendly?

Many are tame and easy to handle, especially hens.
1066:
Living with Naked Necks

Naked Necks are often called Turkens because people thought they were a cross between a chicken and a turkey. They are not. The bare neck comes from a single dominant gene in a normal chicken. The breed was developed in Transylvania, in present day Romania, which is why it is sometimes called the Transylvanian Naked Neck.

Fewer feathers, more heat tolerance

Naked Necks have far fewer feathers than most breeds, not just on the neck. That makes them good at handling heat, and they are a popular choice for hot climates. Fewer feathers also make plucking easier if you raise them for meat. The bare skin turns red in the sun, and pale-skinned birds can sunburn, so give them shade.

Cold is fine with shelter

Many people expect them to freeze, but Naked Necks handle cold better than you might think. Give them a dry, draft-free coop and they usually do fine. Watch single combs in hard freezes.

Day to day

They are calm, sturdy and friendly. Most keepers find them easy to handle. They forage well. They are a good dual-purpose bird, with brown eggs at a decent rate and a good carcass. Some hens go broody.

Love them or hate them

Their look divides people. Visitors either think they are ugly or love them. If you are building a flock for looks, decide if you will enjoy them. If you care about practical traits, they are hard to beat in heat.

Where to get them

Many US hatcheries sell Naked Necks in several colors. They are easy to find. For more birds that do well in warm areas, see the Fayoumi, a light, heat-tolerant breed.

Common questions about Naked Necks

Are Naked Necks part turkey?

No. They are fully chicken. The bare neck comes from a single gene.

Do Naked Necks get cold in winter?

They cope well with a dry, draft-free coop.

Are Naked Necks good layers?

Yes, decent layers of brown eggs.
1070:
What keeping Nankin bantams is like

The Nankin is one of the oldest true bantam breeds, meaning it has no large counterpart. It has been kept in England for centuries. Nankins are a warm buff or chestnut color, with darker tails in roosters. They come with single or rose combs. The Nankin is often said to have helped create the Sebright.

Day to day

Nankins are calm, friendly little birds. Many become very tame. They are good for small yards and gentle kids. They fly better than large breeds, so a covered run helps keep them safe.

Great broody hens

Nankin hens are well known for going broody and raising chicks well. Many keepers keep them for hatching. They lay small cream or tinted eggs at a modest pace.

Climate

Their small size means they lose heat faster than large birds. Give them a dry, draft-free coop. Single combed birds are more likely to get frostbite in hard cold than rose combed ones.

Rarity

Nankins are rare. The Livestock Conservancy has listed them among breeds that need help. A handful of breeders keep them, and some hatcheries sell them occasionally. Buying from breeders who keep good records helps keep lines healthy.

How they compare

The Rosecomb Bantam is another old English true bantam, kept mostly for show. Nankins are generally better mothers.

Single or rose comb

Both comb types are accepted. Rose combed birds are the better pick if your winters are harsh, while single combed birds are a little more common in some lines. Ask the breeder which type their flock carries before you buy hatching eggs.

Common questions about Nankin bantams

Are Nankins good broody hens?

Yes. They are known as excellent mothers.

Are Nankin bantams rare?

Yes. They are one of the rarer bantam breeds.

What color eggs do Nankins lay?

Small cream or tinted eggs.
1071:
Keeping New Hampshire Reds

New Hampshire Reds started as Rhode Island Reds. Farmers in New Hampshire in the early 1900s selected their RIRs for fast growth, early maturity and strong bodies, and over time the birds became different enough to be their own breed. The American Poultry Association recognized the New Hampshire in the 1930s. Officially the breed is just called the New Hampshire, but most people add Red.

They are a lighter, more chestnut red than the dark mahogany of a heritage RIR. Hens often have a golden tone around the neck.

Day to day

New Hampshires are active, practical birds. Many are friendly and curious, though they can be competitive at the feeder. Like RIRs, they can be near the top of the pecking order. Roosters vary, from calm to pushy. They forage well and are happy on free range or in a run.

Laying through the seasons

Expect a good number of brown eggs. They usually start laying fairly early for a heavy breed, since that was one of the traits they were selected for. They tend to keep laying into winter better than many breeds, though shorter days and the molt will slow them. They are more likely than production RIRs to go broody, and they make decent mothers. The best laying years are the first two or three.

A meat and egg bird

Because they were bred to grow fast and feather out quickly, New Hampshires were once an important meat breed in the US before the modern broiler took over. Today they are still a good dual-purpose choice if you want a bird that does both jobs. They are on our list of dual-purpose breeds.

Space and climate

Standard large fowl space works. They are cold-hardy and do reasonably well in heat. The single comb is fairly large, especially on roosters, so frostbite is a risk in very cold winters. A dry, ventilated coop helps a lot.

Their role in sex links

New Hampshire roosters are one of the common fathers of red sex link hybrids. When crossed with certain silver or white hens, the chicks can be sexed by color at hatch. The Red Sex Link page covers those crosses. They were also used in creating the Delaware.

How they compare

Against the Rhode Island Red, the New Hampshire is lighter in color, matures a little faster, and is often a bit calmer and broodier. Production RIRs usually lay more eggs. Heritage RIRs and New Hampshires are closer in laying.

Where to get them

New Hampshires are sold by many US hatcheries and are fairly easy to find. Show-quality birds come from breeders. The breed has appeared on the Livestock Conservancy list in the past, so heritage lines are worth supporting. Be aware that some hatchery birds sold as New Hampshire Reds may be closer to production RIRs in type, so ask about the line if it matters.

Common questions about New Hampshire Reds

What is the difference between a New Hampshire and a Rhode Island Red?

New Hampshires are lighter red, were bred to mature faster, and are often broodier. RIRs, especially production strains, usually lay more.

Are New Hampshire Reds good layers?

Yes. They are good layers of brown eggs, and they hold up fairly well through winter.

Are New Hampshire Reds friendly?

Many are friendly and curious, though some are pushy with other chickens.
1072:
What to know about Norfolk Greys

The Norfolk Grey is a British breed developed in the early 1900s by Fred Myhill of Norwich. It was first shown under the name Black Marias before being renamed. The birds are mostly black with a silver and black striped neck, and roosters also have silver on the back and saddle. They have single combs.

Day to day

Norfolk Greys are a dual-purpose breed. Keepers describe them as hardy and active, with good foraging habits. They tend to do well in mixed flocks.

Eggs

Hens lay tinted or light brown eggs at a moderate rate.

Climate

They suit cool, damp British weather. Watch single combs in hard frosts.

Rarity

The Norfolk Grey nearly vanished in the 1900s and remains rare, even in Britain. It is very hard to find in the US. Most birds come from a few specialist UK breeders. If you like the black and silver look and want something easier to find, the Birchen Standard Old English has a similar color, though it is a game bird. For an easy-to-buy dual-purpose breed, the Sussex is a solid British choice.

Common questions about Norfolk Greys

Can you buy Norfolk Greys in the US?

Very rarely. They are mostly found in the UK.

What color eggs do Norfolk Greys lay?

Tinted or light brown eggs.

Are Norfolk Greys good dual-purpose birds?

They were bred as one, but rare breeds are usually kept for conservation more than production.
1076:
What we know about the Olandsk Dwarf

The Olandsk Dwarf, or Öland dwarf hen, is a Swedish landrace from the island of Öland in the Baltic Sea. It is a naturally small bird, which makes it unusual. Most bantams are shrunk-down versions of larger breeds, but this is a small landrace that developed that way on farms.

Looks and nature

Like other landraces, Olandsk Dwarfs vary in color and pattern. There is no single look. They are generally described as active, independent birds that forage well.

Eggs and broodiness

Hens lay small eggs. Landrace hens often go broody and raise chicks well, and keepers report the same for this breed.

Rarity

The Olandsk Dwarf is very rare. Sweden has conservation programs for its old landraces, and numbers are small. Only a few birds have reached the US, mostly through specialist importers and breeders. Information from backyard keepers is limited, so we have kept this page short.

Similar breeds

For other Swedish landraces that are easier to find, see the Swedish Flower Hen or the Orust. If you just want a small, friendly bird, the small yard breeds list has many options.

Common questions about Olandsk Dwarfs

Are Olandsk Dwarfs bantams?

They are small like bantams, but they are a naturally small landrace, not a miniature of a large breed.

Can you buy Olandsk Dwarfs in the US?

Rarely. Only a few breeders have them.

Do Olandsk Dwarf hens go broody?

Many do, as is common with landrace hens.
1077:
Keeping Norwegian Jaerhons

The Norwegian Jaerhon comes from the Jæren region in southwest Norway. It was developed in the 1900s from local farm chickens, and it is one of Norway's own breeds. It is a light, small-bodied layer with a single comb. Common colors are yellow-black and brown-black, with fine barring.

Autosexing chicks

Jaerhon chicks can be sexed by color at hatch. Males hatch lighter, with a pale spot on the head, while females are darker with more defined markings. That makes it easier to plan your flock and avoid extra roosters.

Day to day

Jaerhons are active, alert and fairly flighty. They forage well and are happiest with space to roam. They are small and quick, and many keepers find them hard to catch. They fly well.

Laying

Hens lay white or cream eggs and are good layers for their size. They mature fairly early. They are not known for broodiness.

Climate

From coastal Norway, they handle cool, wet weather well. In a deep freeze, keep an eye on the roosters' combs.

Rarity and similar breeds

Jaerhons are rare in the US, mostly kept by small breeders after imports in recent years. The Cream Legbar is another autosexing breed and is easier to find. The Leghorn is a light, productive white egg layer with a similar busy nature.

Who they suit

Jaerhons suit keepers who want a light, thrifty layer, like being able to sort chicks at hatch, and have room for an active bird. They are less suited to small enclosed runs or to families who want calm birds to hold.

Common questions about Norwegian Jaerhons

Can you sex Jaerhon chicks at hatch?

Yes. Males hatch lighter and females darker.

Are Jaerhons good layers?

Yes, for their size. They lay white or cream eggs.

Are Jaerhons friendly?

They tend to be flighty, but some become tame with handling.
1078:
What keeping Old English Game is really like

Old English Game descend from the fighting cocks of England, one of the oldest bird types kept in Britain. After cockfighting was banned in England in the 1800s, breeders kept the birds for exhibition and as hardy farm fowl. The result is a tight, hard-feathered, muscular chicken with an upright stance and a proud, alert look. They come in a huge range of colors, and many hatcheries list each color as its own page, from Black Breasted Red to Wheaten, Pyle and Spangled.

Hens make great mothers

Old English Game hens lay small cream or tinted eggs at a modest rate. Where they shine is raising chicks. They go broody readily, sit tight and defend their chicks fiercely. Many keepers keep a few just to hatch eggs for the rest of the flock.

Roosters need planning

The fighting instinct is still very much there in the males. Cockerels often start fighting each other young, sometimes before they are fully feathered, and fights can cause serious injuries. Most keepers house roosters separately or keep only one per flock. They are usually not aggressive with people, but they will not tolerate rival males.

Space and climate

These are active, athletic birds. They forage well, fly well and are happiest with room to range, which is why they suit a free-range setup. Confine them with a covered run or tall fence. Their tight feathering does not hold heat like fluffy breeds, but they are tough birds that handle most climates with good shelter. Single combs can be hit by frostbite in hard cold.

Large fowl vs bantam

Both sizes exist. Old English Game bantams are one of the most popular bantam breeds at US shows. Large fowl, sometimes listed by hatcheries as Standard Old English, are less common but still sold.

How they compare

The Modern Game was developed from the same roots but bred for very long legs and a slim, tall shape, and it is far less hardy. For a specific color of the large fowl, see the Black Breasted Red Standard Old English page, the classic wild-type color.

Common questions about Old English Game

Are Old English Game hens good layers?

Not especially. They lay small eggs at a modest pace, but they are excellent broody hens.

Can you keep two Old English Game roosters together?

It is risky. Many fight hard, so most keepers house males separately.

Are Old English Game chickens friendly?

Hens can become tame with handling. They are alert and active, not lap birds.
1079:
What you are really getting with Olive Eggers

An Olive Egger is not a breed. It is a cross between a hen or rooster that lays blue eggs and one that lays dark brown eggs. Blue egg genes come from birds like the Ameraucana, Araucana, Cream Legbar and many Easter Eggers. Dark brown comes from Marans, Welsummers, Barnevelders and similar breeds. The blue shell gets a brown coating on top, and the result is green to olive. Crack one open and the inside of the shell is blue or green, which shows you where the color comes from.

Because there is no breed standard, Olive Eggers do not all look alike. One hatch might give you black birds, partridge birds, birds with muffs and beards, and birds with clean faces. Many have pea combs from their blue egg parent, which is a bonus in cold weather.

Egg color depends on the parents

The shade you get comes down to how blue the blue side is and how dark the brown side is. A first generation cross from a good Marans and a good blue layer usually gives a solid olive. Some breeders cross those offspring back to Marans to push the color darker and deeper. A cross using a light brown layer gives a paler, sage green. The brown layer on top fades through the laying season the same way it does on Marans eggs, so the same hen may lay a darker olive in spring and a lighter one by late summer.

Laying pattern

Most Olive Eggers are decent layers, often better than their Marans parent. Like other backyard birds they slow down in winter and stop during the molt. Their output depends heavily on the parent breeds, so ask the seller what was used.

Temperament and care

Temperament also varies with the cross. Many are calm and curious. Some take after a flighty parent. Care is the same as for any standard-size backyard chicken. If your birds have muffs and beards, check them for mites now and then, since parasites like to hide in thick feathering. Birds with feathered legs from Marans lines need a dry run.

Climate notes

Olive Eggers handle cold well as a rule, especially pea-combed birds. In heat they do fine with shade and water. There is nothing about the cross itself that makes them fragile.

How they compare

The closest relative is the Easter Egger, which is also a mixed bird but lays blue, green or sometimes pink-tinted eggs depending on its genes. The Easter Egger vs Olive Egger comparison lays out the difference. Hatchery hybrids like the Sapphire Gem are also sold as colorful backyard layers but lay brown eggs.

Where to get them

Many US hatcheries sell Olive Eggers, and lots of small breeders sell chicks or hatching eggs from their own crosses. You can also make your own by putting a dark-egg rooster over blue-egg hens or the other way round. If the egg shade matters, ask to see eggs from the actual parent birds.

Common questions about Olive Eggers

Do Olive Eggers breed true?

No. Breeding two Olive Eggers together gives a mix of egg colors, including blue, green and brown.

How dark green will the eggs be?

It depends on the parents. Darker brown parents give darker olive eggs. Lighter brown parents give paler green.

When do Olive Eggers start laying?

Usually at about the same age as other standard backyard breeds, around five to six months, though it varies with the cross and the season.
1082:
What keeping Orloffs is like

The Orloff is associated with Russia, and its name is usually linked to Count Orlov, who is said to have helped make it popular there. Its earlier roots are often traced to Persia. The Orloff has a short, lumpy comb, a full beard and muffs, and a sturdy, upright body. Colors include mahogany, spangled, black and white.

Built for the cold

The small comb and thick feathering around the face make the Orloff a strong pick for cold winters. There is little comb to freeze, and the beard protects the wattles. It is on our list of cold climate breeds. In heat, give shade and water.

Day to day

Orloffs are generally calm and hardy. They are not fussy and handle confinement and free range. Roosters vary, as in any breed. Check the beard and muffs for mites and food buildup now and then.

Laying

Hens lay light brown or tinted eggs at a moderate rate. They are not top layers. They mature slowly.

How they compare

The Pavlovskaya is another Russian breed with a beard, but it also has a crest and feathered feet. The Faverolles has a similar beard and muffs and is easier to find.

Rarity

Orloffs are rare in the US. A few breeders keep them. Orloffs have been on the Livestock Conservancy's watch for rare breeds.

Slow to mature

Orloffs take longer than production breeds to grow up and start laying, so be patient with pullets. Roosters fill out slowly too. That steady growth is typical of old, hardy breeds kept for cold country.

Common questions about Orloffs

Are Orloffs cold-hardy?

Yes. Their small comb and thick face feathers handle cold well.

Are Orloffs good layers?

They are moderate layers of light brown eggs.

Are Orloffs rare?

Yes, especially in the US.
1083:
What it is like to keep Orpingtons

Orpingtons were developed by William Cook in Orpington, Kent, in the late 1800s. The Black came first and the Buff a few years later, and the Buff is still the one most people picture. They were meant to be a useful dual-purpose farm bird, and in backyard flocks today they are best known for being big, soft and friendly.

Most Orpingtons are calm and easy to handle. Hens will often follow you around the yard and many tolerate being picked up. That gentle nature makes them a regular pick for families. The flip side is that they are rarely the boss in a mixed flock, and pushy breeds may bully them at the feeder.

Broodiness and laying

Expect a fair number of light brown eggs. Orpingtons are not top production layers, but they lay steadily, and many keep going reasonably well through winter. The big factor is broodiness. Lots of Orpington hens go broody, sometimes more than once a year, and a broody hen stops laying. If you want to hatch chicks, that is great. If you just want eggs, be ready to break a broody now and then. Like other heavy breeds, they lay best in their first two years.

Watching weight and fluff

All that fluff hides a lot. Orpingtons put on fat easily, so go easy on scratch and treats. Fluffy vent feathers can collect droppings, which can lead to messy rear ends and attract flies in summer. Many keepers trim around the vent. That thick feathering is also a good hiding spot for lice and mites, so part the feathers and look during your regular checks.

Climate and space

Orpingtons are very cold-hardy thanks to their size and dense feathers, though roosters' single combs can still get frostbite. Heat is harder on them. In hot summers they need deep shade, airflow and cool water, and you should watch for panting and spread wings, signs of heat stress. They are not great fliers, so normal fencing holds them. Give them a bit more room than light breeds, since they are big bodied.

English vs hatchery Orpingtons

You will see English Orpingtons and hatchery or American Orpingtons. English lines are usually bigger, broader and much fluffier, and often lay fewer eggs. Hatchery birds are smaller and leaner but tend to lay better. Neither is wrong, it depends on what you want.

Colors and how they compare

Buff, black, blue, splash and white are the common colors, with lavender, jubilee and chocolate from specialty breeders. The Lavender Orpington has its own page. Against the Australorp, which was developed from Black Orpingtons, the Orpington is fluffier and broodier while the Australorp usually lays more. The Buff Orpington vs Australorp comparison covers it. Against the Wyandotte, see Wyandotte vs Orpington.

Where to get them

Buff Orpingtons are sold by almost every hatchery and farm store in spring. Black, blue and splash are common too. For English type or rare colors, go to breeders, many of whom show their birds.

Common questions about Orpingtons

Are Orpingtons good for beginners?

Yes. They are calm, hardy and forgiving, which is why they are a common first breed.

Do Orpingtons go broody a lot?

Many do. If you do not want chicks, collect eggs daily and be ready to break broody hens.

How many eggs do Orpingtons lay?

A fair amount, usually a few eggs a week from a healthy young hen. Hatchery lines generally lay more than English show lines.
1084:
Understanding the Onagadori

The Onagadori is a long-tailed chicken from Japan, from the Kochi area on the island of Shikoku. It is famous for roosters with tails that can grow to extreme lengths, many feet long in the best birds. Japan designated the Onagadori a Special Natural Monument in the 1950s, which gives it legal protection there.

Why the tail keeps growing

Most chickens molt all their feathers once a year. In the Onagadori, some tail and saddle feathers do not molt every year, so they keep growing year after year. That is what lets the tails get so long.

Special housing

In Japan, top birds are kept in tall, narrow boxes that protect the tail, and they are let out carefully on a schedule. A bird with a long tail cannot live like a normal backyard chicken. Mud, roosts and other birds would break or soil the feathers. If you keep long-tailed birds, plan on high perches, clean dry housing and very little crowding.

Hens and eggs

Hens have much shorter tails. They lay small cream or tinted eggs and are not kept for production.

Rarity outside Japan

True Onagadori are very rare outside Japan, and export has been restricted. Many birds sold in the US as Onagadori are actually Phoenix or crosses. If someone sells you an Onagadori, ask about the source and whether the tail feathers truly skip the molt. The Phoenix and Yokohama are long-tailed breeds developed from Japanese birds, and they are much easier to find.

Common questions about Onagadori

How long can an Onagadori tail grow?

In the best birds, many feet, since some tail feathers do not molt every year.

Are Onagadori and Phoenix the same?

No. The Phoenix was developed from Japanese long-tails, but its tail molts each year.

Can you buy Onagadori in the US?

True ones are very rare. Ask the seller about the source.
1086:
Keeping Penedesencas for very dark eggs

The Penedesenca is a Spanish breed from the Penedès region of Catalonia, near Barcelona. It is known for laying some of the darkest brown eggs of any breed, a deep reddish chocolate. It also has an unusual comb, often called a carnation or king's comb, with extra points at the back. Black is the most common color in the US, with partridge, wheaten and others also kept.

Day to day

Penedesencas are light, active and flighty. Many keepers describe them as wary and fast. They are excellent foragers and like room to range. They are strong fliers, and a roof on the run saves a lot of chasing. They are not a breed for people who want lap birds.

Eggs

The dark color is strongest at the start of the laying season and can fade as the year goes on, much like Marans eggs. Eggs are medium in size. Hens lay at a fair pace and are not usually broody.

Climate

Being from the Mediterranean, they do well in heat. In cold weather, protect the comb from frostbite with a dry, ventilated coop.

How they compare

The Empordanesa is a close Catalan relative that also lays dark eggs and shares the same type of comb. Marans are calmer and heavier but their eggs are less red. See our dark egg layers for more choices.

Rarity

Penedesencas are rare in the US, mostly from small breeders. Egg color varies a lot between lines, so ask for photos of eggs from the breeding hens.

Common questions about Penedesencas

Do Penedesencas lay darker eggs than Marans?

Good lines can lay eggs just as dark, with a redder tone. It depends on the hen.

Are Penedesencas friendly?

Usually not. They are flighty and wary.

Are Penedesencas good in heat?

Yes. They are a Mediterranean breed that handles warm weather well.
1087:
What we know about the Orust

The Orust is a Swedish landrace named after Orust, an island on Sweden's west coast. Like other Swedish landraces, it developed on small farms over a long time, shaped by local conditions more than by a show standard. It was nearly lost in the 1900s, and Swedish conservation work has helped keep it going.

Living with a landrace

Landrace chickens tend to be hardy, self-reliant birds that forage well and handle local weather without much fuss. Keepers of the Orust describe it in similar terms. Hens are medium-sized and lay a moderate number of eggs. As with most Nordic breeds, it suits cooler climates, and single combs should be watched in hard freezes.

Rarity

The Orust is rare even in Sweden. Very few birds are kept outside Scandinavia, and good information from backyard keepers in North America is limited. Because of that, we are keeping this page short rather than guess at details like exact laying rates or color rules. If you find a breeder, ask about the origin of their birds and what their hens actually lay.

Similar options

If you are drawn to Swedish landraces, the Swedish Flower Hen is much easier to find in the US and well documented. The Swedish Black is another Swedish breed with a following among US keepers.

Common questions about the Orust

Can you buy Orust chickens in the US?

Very rarely. Most are kept in Sweden.

Is the Orust a landrace?

Yes. It developed on farms in western Sweden rather than to a show standard.

Are Orust chickens cold-hardy?

As a Nordic landrace, they are suited to cool weather. Protect single combs in hard freezes.
1089:
Keeping the rare Pavlovskaya

The Pavlovskaya is an old Russian breed named after the town of Pavlovo. It has a lot going on in one small bird. It has a crest, a beard and muffs, a small V-shaped comb, feathered legs and feet, and stiff feathers at the hocks. Golden spangled and silver spangled are the best known colors. The breed came close to disappearing in the 1900s and was rebuilt by Russian breeders.

Day to day

Pavlovskayas are small, light birds. Keepers often describe them as active and alert, sometimes flighty. They forage well when the ground is dry.

Crest, beard and feet

All that extra feathering means extra care. Crests can block vision and hold water. Beards collect food and water. Feathered feet pick up mud. Keep the run dry and use waterers that keep faces dry, like nipples or cups. Check crests, beards and leg feathers for mites.

Eggs

Hens lay small white or cream eggs at a modest rate.

Climate

Coming from Russia, they handle cold well, and their small comb resists frostbite. Keep them dry, since wet crests and feet are more of a risk than cold itself.

How they compare

The Sultan also has a crest, beard and feathered feet, but it is white and a calmer, more ornamental bird. The Orloff is another Russian breed with a beard but no crest.

Rarity

Pavlovskayas are very rare outside Russia. Only a few breeders keep them in the US.

Who they suit

They suit experienced keepers who enjoy rare breeds and are willing to give a crested, bearded bird extra care.

Common questions about Pavlovskayas

Are Pavlovskayas good layers?

Not especially. Expect a modest number of small white or cream eggs.

Are Pavlovskayas cold-hardy?

Yes, as long as they stay dry.

Where do Pavlovskaya chickens come from?

Russia, named after the town of Pavlovo.
1092:
Why Plymouth Rocks are such a reliable backyard bird

The Plymouth Rock was developed in New England in the 1800s and became one of the most common farm chickens in America. The Barred Rock is the classic, with its black and white striped feathers, but White, Buff, Partridge, Silver Penciled, Columbian and Blue are all recognized too. White Rocks were also a key part of the modern meat chicken.

In the backyard, Rocks are about as steady as chickens get. They are calm without being lazy, curious without being flighty, and most hens are easy to handle. They forage well if you let them out, and they cope fine in a run if you do not. Roosters are generally decent, though like any breed you can get a pushy one.

Laying through the seasons

Expect a good number of light to medium brown eggs. Rocks often start laying around five to six months and keep a solid pace through their first two years. They usually lay better in winter than the fluffier heavy breeds. The molt will stop them for a while each fall. After year three, output drops, but many Rock hens keep laying at a slower rate for years. Some go broody, though less often than Orpingtons or Cochins.

Sexing barred chicks

Barred Rock chicks are black with a white spot on the head. Males often have a bigger, more blurry spot, while females have a smaller, sharper one and darker legs. It is not perfect, but it gives you a decent guess. As adults, roosters look lighter overall because they carry two copies of the barring gene. If you are unsure, our hen or roo tool can help.

Space and climate

Standard space for a large fowl breed works well. Rocks are heavy enough that they do not fly much, so normal fencing holds them. They are cold-hardy, and their single combs are medium sized, so frostbite is a risk mainly for roosters in very hard cold. They handle summer heat well enough with shade and water. All of this makes them a regular pick for beginner flocks.

How they compare

The Rock is often compared with the Australorp. Australorps tend to lay a few more eggs and are a bit more laid back, while Rocks forage harder and come in more colors. See the Australorp vs Plymouth Rock comparison. The Dominique looks similar but has a rose comb and a slightly different barring pattern, and it is an older American breed.

Hatchery vs heritage Rocks

Hatchery Barred Rocks are lighter and lay well. Heritage or show lines are bigger, blockier and have crisper barring, but often lay a bit less. Both make good backyard birds.

Where to get them

Barred and White Rocks are sold by nearly every hatchery and farm store. Buff and Partridge are common too. For Silver Penciled, Columbian or show-quality barring, look for breeders through poultry shows and breed clubs.

Common questions about Plymouth Rocks

Are Barred Rocks and Plymouth Rocks the same?

Yes. Barred Rock is the barred color variety of the Plymouth Rock breed.

Are Plymouth Rocks loud?

They are moderately quiet. Hens make the usual egg song, but they are not as noisy as many light breeds.

How long do Plymouth Rocks lay?

Their best years are the first two or three, but many keep laying at a slower pace well after that.
1093:
What we know about the Pita Pinta Asturiana

The Pita Pinta Asturiana is a traditional breed from Asturias in northern Spain. The name roughly means painted or spotted hen of Asturias, after its speckled black and white plumage, though other colors exist. It was a common farm bird in the region and declined sharply as commercial birds took over. Local breeders and conservation programs in Spain have worked to recover it.

A farm bird

The Pita Pinta is a dual-purpose breed, kept for both eggs and meat. Asturias has a mild, wet climate, and the breed is suited to those conditions. Keepers describe it as a hardy bird that does well on free range.

Rarity

Outside Spain, the Pita Pinta is extremely rare, and very few birds have been kept in the US. Because practical information from backyard keepers here is limited, we are keeping this page short rather than give you numbers we cannot back up. If you find a breeder, ask about the origin of the stock, egg color and laying from their own hens.

Similar options

For a Spanish breed that is easier to find, look at the Penedesenca, known for very dark eggs, or the White Faced Black Spanish. If you like the spotted look, mottled breeds like the Ancona are widely available.

Common questions about Pita Pinta Asturiana

Where does the Pita Pinta come from?

Asturias, in northern Spain.

Can you buy Pita Pinta chickens in the US?

Very rarely. Most are kept in Spain.

Is the Pita Pinta a dual-purpose breed?

Yes. It was kept for both eggs and meat on farms.
1094:
What keeping Phoenix chickens is really like

The Phoenix was developed in Germany in the late 1800s from long-tailed chickens imported from Japan, including birds related to the Onagadori. Breeders crossed them with other breeds to make a long-tailed bird suited to European conditions. Roosters grow long, flowing tails and saddles. Colors include silver duckwing, golden duckwing, black breasted red, white and black. The Golden Duckwing Phoenix has its own page.

The tail molts

Unlike the true Onagadori, Phoenix tail feathers do molt each year. The tail grows long over the season, often a few feet in good birds, then drops and regrows. That is still long enough to need care.

Housing for long tails

Give roosters high perches so the tail can hang without touching the floor. Keep bedding clean and dry, since a dirty tail is easy to damage. Avoid crowding, and keep roosters away from birds that pull feathers. A run with grass or clean sand helps keep tails in good shape.

Day to day

Phoenix are active, alert and often flighty. They fly well, so a covered run is useful. They forage well. Many hens tame with handling. Hens are often good broodies and mothers.

Eggs

Hens lay small cream or tinted eggs at a modest rate. They are kept for looks, not production.

Climate

They are fairly hardy. Single combs can get frostbite in hard cold, and tails need protecting from mud and ice.
