Where to get them

Several US hatcheries sell Phoenix, in both large fowl and bantam. Show lines with longer tails come from breeders.

Common questions about Phoenix chickens

How long do Phoenix tails get?

Often a few feet in good roosters, since the tail regrows each year.

Are Phoenix chickens good layers?

Modest. They lay small cream eggs.

Do Phoenix chickens need special perches?

High perches help roosters keep their tails off the ground.
1095:
Caring for Polish chickens and their crests

Polish chickens are kept for their looks. That huge pom-pom crest is the whole point, and it also shapes almost everything about daily care. Despite the name, the breed's true origin is unclear. It was well established in Western Europe, especially the Netherlands, by the 1700s. Common varieties include White Crested Black, Golden Laced, Silver Laced, Buff Laced, White and Black, plus bearded and frizzled forms.

Living with a bird that cannot see well

The crest covers much of a Polish chicken's view. They startle easily because they often do not see you coming. Talk to them as you approach, and avoid grabbing from above. Limited vision also makes them easy targets for hawks, so a covered run is a good idea if you have aerial predators. Many keepers trim the feathers around the eyes so the birds can see better. A light trim does not hurt them and grows back.

Skull and head care

Many Polish have a bony knob on top of the skull under the crest. In some birds that area is not fully closed, so a peck or knock to the head can be more serious than in other chickens. Handle the head gently, and keep them away from aggressive flock mates.

Keeping the crest clean and dry

A wet crest is a common problem. Open waterers soak it, and in winter it can freeze into clumps. Nipple waterers or cups help a lot. Check crests for lice and mites, which love to hide there. Flock mates sometimes pick at crests too. If one bird keeps pulling feathers, separate it or add more space and distractions.

Laying and temperament

Polish lay small to medium white eggs at a fair rate. They are rarely broody. Personalities run from sweet and tame to jumpy, mostly because of how well they can see. Many become friendly with gentle handling. They are often low in the pecking order and do best with other calm breeds.

Space and climate

They are small, light birds and do not need much room, but give them shelter from rain. They handle moderate cold if the crest stays dry. The small V-shaped comb resists frostbite well. In heat they do fine with shade.

How they compare

The Houdan also has a crest but is a heavier, five-toed French bird with a muffed face. The Polish vs Houdan comparison breaks down the differences. The Swiss Spitzhauben has a smaller, forward-pointing crest and is a tougher forager.

Where to get them

Most big US hatcheries sell several Polish colors, both standard size and bantam. Show-quality birds with full, round crests come from breeders, and Polish are a common sight in show halls.

Common questions about Polish chickens

Should I trim my Polish chicken's crest?

Many keepers trim feathers around the eyes to help them see. Skip it if you plan to show the bird.

Do Polish chickens lay eggs?

Yes. They lay white eggs at a fair rate, though they are kept more for looks than production.

Are Polish chickens good with other breeds?

They mix well with calm breeds. Bossy birds may peck at their crests, so watch them closely at first.
1098:
How the Porcelain d'Uccle differs from other colors

Porcelain is a color of the Belgian d'Uccle bantam. It is the same pattern as the Mille Fleur, with each feather showing a band and a white tip, but with the lavender gene added. That softens the base to a pale straw or cream and turns the black bands into a soft lavender blue. The effect is light, delicate and very pretty, which is why it is a popular color for pet and show birds.

It breeds true for color

Lavender is recessive, so a Porcelain carries two copies. Mating two Porcelains gives Porcelain chicks. Crossing a Porcelain to a Mille Fleur gives Mille Fleur looking chicks that carry the lavender gene hidden.

Keeping a pale bird clean

Light feathers show every bit of dirt, and the heavily feathered feet stain quickly in a muddy run. Sand, dry bedding and a covered run help. Strong sun can also discolor pale and lavender feathers over time, so shade is good for both comfort and color.

Breed traits

Underneath the color it is a d'Uccle. Expect a calm, friendly bantam with a beard, muffs, a single comb and feathered feet. Hens lay small cream eggs and often go broody. They are a good fit for families who want a gentle bird. Check foot feathers for mites and mud regularly.

Related pages

See the Mille Fleur d'Uccle for the most common color of this breed, and the Booted Bantam for its beardless relative.

Common questions about Porcelain d'Uccles

Are Porcelain d'Uccles rare?

They are less common than Mille Fleurs but sold by several hatcheries and many bantam breeders.

Are Porcelain d'Uccles good for kids?

Yes. They are small, calm and usually easy to handle.

Do Porcelain d'Uccles change color as they age?

The white tips often increase with each molt, just as in Mille Fleurs.
1099:
What you get in a rainbow assortment of pullets

Rainbow Assorted Females is not a breed. It is a hatchery package of sexed pullets picked to give you a basket of different egg colors. The idea is simple. You order one listing and end up with a mix of brown, dark brown, white, blue and green egg layers, plus a flock that looks varied.

How the mix is chosen

The hatchery picks the breeds, usually from whatever is hatching that week. You might get Easter Eggers or Olive Eggers for blue and green eggs, a Leghorn or two for white, and heavier birds like Barred Rocks, Wyandottes or Marans for brown. The exact mix changes by hatchery and season, and most do not let you choose. If a specific breed matters to you, order it separately.

Sexing and labeling

Because they are sold as females, the chicks are vent sexed or feather sexed. Sexing is never perfect, so there is a small chance one turns out to be a rooster. Mixed boxes also make it harder to know which chick is which breed. Take photos as they grow and compare with breed pages to figure them out.

Raising a mixed box

Raising a mix is no harder than a single breed. Brood them together and feed them the same starter. As they grow, light breeds will feather out and move faster, while heavy breeds grow slower. Expect different laying ages, since Leghorns often start sooner than Marans. Check our best breeds for colorful eggs to see what you might end up with, or use the egg predictor to plan your basket.

Common questions about Rainbow Assorted Females

Can I choose the breeds in a rainbow assortment?

Usually not. The hatchery picks, but you can ask what breeds they typically include.

Will all of them be hens?

Most will be. Sexing is very accurate but not perfect, so a rooster can slip through.

How do I tell which breed each chick is?

Wait for feathers. Comb type, leg color and feather pattern make most breeds clear by a few months old.
1101:
What makes the Red Pyle color different

Red Pyle is a color variety of the Old English Game, sold in large fowl size by some hatcheries as Red Pyle Standard Old English. The pyle color is the black breasted red pattern with the black replaced by white. Roosters are mostly white with bright orange-red on the neck, back, saddle and shoulders. Hens are creamy white with a salmon colored breast and some gold in the neck feathers.

Pyles do not always breed true

Pyle comes from a white gene sitting on top of a red pattern, and many pyle birds carry only one copy. When you breed pyle to pyle, you can get pyle, white and red colored chicks in the same hatch. If you want only pyles, talk to a breeder about how their line is bred.

Day to day

Under the color it is an Old English Game. Hens are tough, alert and go broody easily. They are among the best mothers you can keep. Roosters are confident and will fight other males, so plan on one rooster per flock or separate pens. The light coat is a little easier for hawks to spot than darker colors.

Climate and care

They handle most climates with good shelter. Their tight feathers do not insulate like fluffy breeds, so a draft-free coop is important in winter. Watch single combs in hard cold. Shade in summer also keeps the white feathers from turning brassy.

Related colors

The Black Breasted Red is the base color the pyle is built on.

Common questions about Red Pyle Old English Game

What does pyle mean in chickens?

It means a red pattern with white in place of black.

Are Red Pyle hens good mothers?

Yes. Like all Old English Game hens, they are strong broodies.

Why did my pyle chicks hatch in different colors?

Many pyles carry one copy of the white gene, so their chicks can be pyle, white or red.
1104:
Red Shavers in a backyard flock

The Red Shaver is a commercial brown egg hybrid sold under the Shaver name. The Shaver line started in Canada and is now part of Hendrix Genetics, the same company that owns the ISA brand. Red Shaver hens are mostly red with some white in the tail and body. Like most modern brown layers, they are sex-linked, so pullets are easy to sort at hatch.

What day to day life is like

Red Shavers are known as friendly, calm and easygoing birds. They are curious and often happy to be handled, which makes them a good pick for families who also want lots of eggs. They are medium-sized and do not fly much. They are rarely broody, so they keep laying through spring and summer instead of taking weeks off.

Laying pattern

Expect a young hen to lay brown eggs nearly every day in her first year. Production stays strong in year two and then drops off. Winter and the molt slow them down like any hen, but hybrids often bounce back faster than heritage birds. Because so much goes into eggs, they need a proper layer feed and oyster shell. Soft or thin shells are a sign they need more calcium.

Health and lifespan

The same tradeoff that comes with all high-production hybrids applies. Older Red Shavers are more prone to reproductive problems, and many live shorter lives than heritage breeds. If a hen stops laying and looks hunched or swollen, see a vet.

How they compare

The ISA Brown and Red Sex Link are very similar birds. Most keepers would not notice a difference in temperament or laying. The main difference is who bred them and how they were crossed.

Common questions about Red Shavers

Are Red Shavers good layers?

Yes. They are among the best layers for a backyard flock, especially in their first two years.

Do Red Shavers go broody?

Rarely. Broodiness was bred out to keep them laying.

Are Red Shavers cold-hardy?

They handle cold fairly well with a dry, draft-free coop. Watch their combs in very cold weather.
1105:
How Red Sex Links are made

Red Sex Link is a general name for a cross, not a single breed. A red rooster, usually a Rhode Island Red or New Hampshire, is mated with a hen that carries the silver gene, such as a White Plymouth Rock, Rhode Island White, Delaware or Light Sussex type. Because of how the color genes pass on, the female chicks hatch red or buff and the males hatch white or pale yellow. That lets hatcheries sell pullets with high accuracy. Hatcheries sell these crosses under names like Red Star, Golden Comet and Cinnamon Queen, and the exact parents vary.

Why the trick only works once

The color sexing only works on this first cross. If you mate two Red Sex Links, the chicks will come in mixed colors and you cannot sex them at hatch. If you want sex-linked chicks at home, you need the original parent breeds.

Day to day

Red Sex Link hens are usually friendly, sturdy and low drama. They lay brown eggs at a very good rate, start early, and rarely go broody. Production is strongest in the first two years.

What to expect long term

Like other heavy-laying hybrids, many Red Sex Links slow down after year two, and older hens are more prone to reproductive problems. They are tough in both heat and cold, with medium single combs.

Related birds

See the Rhode Island Red page for the usual father breed. The Black Sex Link uses a red rooster over a barred hen instead. The Cinnamon Queen is one of the named commercial versions of this cross.

Common questions about Red Sex Links

Can a Red Sex Link rooster be red?

In a true first-generation cross, males hatch white or pale. They may grow into white birds with some red or gold.

Are Red Sex Links good layers?

Yes. They are some of the best brown egg layers for backyard flocks.

Are Red Stars and Red Sex Links the same?

Red Star is one of several brand names hatcheries use for a red sex link cross.
1107:
Living with Redcaps

The Redcap is an old English breed from Derbyshire. Its main feature is the comb, a very large rose comb with points around the edge that sits on top of the head like a red cap. The body is a rich red-brown with black spangles and tips. It is closely related to the Hamburg.

Day to day

Redcaps are active, hardy and very good foragers. They like to roam and do best on free range. They are often flighty and fly well, and many prefer to roost high. They are not a lap breed. Their dark spangled feathers give them some cover along hedges and woodland edges, which helps when they range.

Laying

Hens lay white eggs, and plenty of them for an old breed. Broodiness is uncommon.

The comb in winter

The big rose comb is less exposed than a tall single comb, but its size and points can still be hit by frostbite in very hard cold. A dry, ventilated coop helps. They handle heat well.

Rarity

Redcaps are rare, both in Britain and the US. Redcaps are among the breeds the Livestock Conservancy has flagged as rare. A small number of breeders keep them, and occasionally a hatchery offers them.

Who they suit

Redcaps are a good fit for keepers with room to let birds range and who want a hardy white egg layer with a lot of character. They are not ideal in small enclosed runs, where an active, flighty bird can get bored and stressed.

Common questions about Redcaps

Why are they called Redcaps?

For their very large red rose comb, which looks like a cap.

Are Redcaps good layers?

Yes, they are good layers of white eggs.

Are Redcaps friendly?

Usually not very. They are active and wary, though some settle down with regular handling.
1108:
Living with Rhode Island Reds

Rhode Island Reds were developed on farms in Rhode Island and Massachusetts in the 1800s, with Malay and other Asian blood mixed into local stock. They became one of the most important American breeds and are the state bird of Rhode Island. They are known as hardy, productive birds that rarely give trouble.

In the backyard, RIRs are confident and busy. Hens are usually friendly enough to approach you for treats, but many are not big fans of being held. They are often near the top of the pecking order and can be bossy with gentle breeds. Roosters have a reputation for being protective, sometimes aggressive with people. If you plan to keep a male, raise him with handling and pick the calmest one you can.

Production Reds vs heritage Reds

This is the big thing to know. Most hatchery RIRs are production strains. They are lighter, lighter red, and lay a lot of brown eggs. Heritage RIRs, bred to the old standard, are darker mahogany, bigger and blockier, and lay fewer eggs but are a better dual-purpose bird. Both are called Rhode Island Reds. Ask which one you are buying.

Laying pattern

Production Reds lay very well in their first two years and often keep going through much of the winter. They start around five to six months. The molt shuts things down for a few weeks. They are not very broody, so you rarely lose laying time to sitting. Heritage birds lay steadily but less, and some go broody.

Space and climate

Standard large fowl space is fine. They are good foragers and enjoy free range time, but they also handle a run without much fuss. RIRs are tough in both cold and heat, which is one reason they are kept almost everywhere. In very cold winters, watch the roosters' single combs for frostbite, or choose the rose comb variety. They are a regular on lists of the best egg-laying breeds.

How they compare

The Leghorn vs Rhode Island Red comparison shows how a white egg specialist stacks up against the RIR. The Buff Orpington vs Rhode Island Red comparison is useful if you are choosing between gentleness and production. The New Hampshire Red was developed from RIRs and is lighter in color and quicker to mature.

Rhode Island Reds in hybrids

RIR roosters are one of the main parents of red sex link hybrids. Crossed with certain silver or white hens, they produce chicks that can be sexed by color at hatch. That is why many commercial brown egg layers carry RIR genes.

Where to get them

Production Reds are sold everywhere, from big hatcheries to farm stores. Heritage Reds take more searching. Look for breeders who show at poultry shows or belong to the breed club. Bantam RIRs are also widely available.

Common questions about Rhode Island Reds

Are Rhode Island Reds aggressive?

Hens can be bossy with other chickens. Roosters are more likely than some breeds to challenge people, but plenty are fine.

How many eggs does a Rhode Island Red lay?

Production strains are excellent layers, often laying most days in their first year. Heritage strains lay less.

Can Rhode Island Reds handle hot weather?

Yes, better than many heavy breeds. Give them shade, airflow and plenty of water on hot days.
1110:
Keeping Rhode Island Red bantams

The Rhode Island Red bantam is a miniature version of the large Rhode Island Red. It has the same dark red color, blocky shape and single or rose comb, in a body only a fraction of the size. It is recognized as a bantam variety, not as a separate breed.

What changes with the smaller size

Bantam RIRs eat less, need less coop and run space, and are easier for kids to pick up. They lay small brown eggs, so it takes about two to equal one large egg. Production is decent for a bantam but nowhere near a production RIR. Hens are more likely than hatchery large fowl to go broody, and they make protective mothers.

Personality

They have the same confident attitude as the big birds. Hens can be bossy, and bantam roosters are often feisty. In a mixed flock they hold their own against larger hens. If you plan to keep a rooster, raise it with lots of handling.

Space and climate

They are a good fit for small yards and urban coops. Their small size means they lose heat faster than large birds, so keep the coop draft-free in winter and watch single combs in hard freezes. They handle heat well with shade. Bantams fly better than large RIRs, so a covered run helps.

Where to get them

Many US hatcheries sell RIR bantams. Show-quality birds with deep color and good type come from breeders, and RIR bantams are common at poultry shows.

Common questions about Rhode Island Red bantams

How big do Rhode Island Red bantams get?

They are a small fraction of the large breed's size, small enough to hold in one arm.

Do Rhode Island Red bantams lay well?

They lay a fair number of small brown eggs, less than large production Reds.

Can bantam RIRs live with large chickens?

Yes. They are confident and usually hold their own, though watch for bullying at first.
1113:
What makes the Rhodebar useful

The Rhodebar is a British autosexing breed. It was developed in the mid 1900s, during a period when British breeders created several autosexing breeds by adding the barring gene to existing breeds. In the Rhodebar's case, the base breed was the Rhode Island Red. The result looks like a golden or reddish barred bird.

Sexing chicks at hatch

The point of an autosexing breed is that you can tell males from females as day-old chicks, and the breed breeds true for it. In Rhodebars, male chicks are lighter with a blurred head marking, while females are darker with clearer stripes. Unlike sex link hybrids, this works generation after generation.

Day to day

Rhodebars are generally described as hardy, practical birds like their RIR ancestors. Hens lay brown eggs at a good rate.

Similar breeds

The Cream Legbar is the best known autosexing breed and lays blue eggs. The Brussbar is another British autosexing breed with a different base.

Rarity

Rhodebars are rare, both in the UK and especially in the US. Few breeders keep them. Because details from backyard keepers are limited, this page sticks to what is well established.

Common questions about Rhodebars

What does autosexing mean?

Male and female chicks look different at hatch, and the breed keeps that trait when bred pure.

What color eggs do Rhodebars lay?

Brown eggs.

Are Rhodebars the same as red sex links?

No. Sex links only sex by color in the first cross. Rhodebars breed true.
1114:
Keeping Rosecomb bantams

The Rosecomb is one of the oldest true bantams, meaning it has no large version. It has been kept in Britain for centuries and is mainly a show bird today. Its main features are a neat rose comb with a long spike at the back, called the leader, and large, round white earlobes. Black is the classic color, with white, blue and others also shown.

A show breed

Rosecombs are bred for type and those big white earlobes. The earlobes are delicate and judges look closely at them, so breeders protect them from damage and harsh weather. Hens lay small white or cream eggs at a modest rate. They are kept for looks and showing more than eggs.

Day to day

Rosecombs are active and can be flighty. They are good fliers for their size, so put a roof on the run. Many keepers find them quick and lively rather than cuddly, though some tame well. They need little space.

Climate

Their small size means they lose heat quickly. A dry, draft-free coop is important in winter. The rose comb resists frostbite better than a big single comb.

How they compare

The Sebright is another old British true bantam with a rose comb, known for its laced feathers. The Nankin is calmer and a better broody.

Where to get them

Some hatcheries sell Rosecombs, but show-quality birds come from breeders. They are common in bantam classes at poultry shows.

Common questions about Rosecomb bantams

Are Rosecomb bantams good layers?

Not really. Hens lay small eggs, and not many of them.

Why are Rosecomb earlobes white?

It is a breed trait. Large, round white earlobes are a key show feature.

Are Rosecombs good for beginners?

They are easy to keep, but they are flighty. Beginners who want a calm bantam may prefer a Cochin or Silkie.
1115:
What to know about Sapphire Gems

The Sapphire Gem is a hatchery hybrid sold by several US hatcheries. Its exact background is not fully published, and you will see different stories about where it came from. Most sources describe it as a Plymouth Rock based layer from European stock. What keepers agree on is the result, a soft blue-gray or lavender-gray hen that lays a lot of brown eggs.

Sex-linked chicks

Sapphire Gems are sold as sex-linked. Female chicks hatch in a solid blue-gray color, while males hatch with barring and grow into barred birds. That is why most people can order them as pullets and get what they expect.

Day to day

Owners usually describe Sapphire Gems as calm, friendly and active. They forage well, handle confinement, and fit easily into mixed flocks. They are medium-sized, a little lighter than heavy heritage breeds, and do not fly much.

Laying and climate

Expect a good number of medium to large brown eggs. They are said to lay fairly well through winter. They are rarely broody. Like other production birds, their best laying years are the first two. They cope well with cold and heat, though large single combs need watching in deep cold.

Plumage notes

The blue-gray color is not identical from bird to bird. Some are darker slate, some more silvery. Since it is a hybrid, breeding two Sapphire Gems together will not give you more Sapphire Gems.

How they compare

The Sapphire Gem vs Olive Egger comparison is useful if you are weighing pretty feathers against colorful eggs. If you want a heritage barred bird that breeds true, the Plymouth Rock is a good choice.

Common questions about Sapphire Gems

What color eggs do Sapphire Gems lay?

Brown eggs, usually medium to large.

Are Sapphire Gems the same as Blue Plymouth Rocks?

No. They are a hybrid, while the Blue Plymouth Rock is a variety of a standard breed.

Are Sapphire Gems friendly?

Most are calm and friendly and do well with families.
1118:
Living with Scots Dumpies

The Scots Dumpy is an ancient Scottish breed known for its very short legs. Old names for it include Crawlers and Creepers. The body sits so low that the bird seems to waddle rather than walk. It comes in several colors, with cuckoo being common, and there are large fowl and bantam forms.

The short leg gene

Short legs in the Dumpy come from a gene that is lethal when a chick inherits two copies. When two short-legged birds are bred, part of the eggs will not hatch, and some chicks will have normal length legs. This is a normal part of breeding Dumpies, much as in the Japanese Bantam.

Day to day

Dumpies are calm, friendly birds that tame easily. They are not fast and do not fly much. Because they sit low, they get dirty quickly in mud. Keep the run dry and well drained.

Broody hens

Dumpy hens are known as good broodies and careful mothers. They lay tinted or cream eggs at a moderate rate.

Climate

From Scotland, they suit cool, damp weather, as long as they are not sitting in wet ground. Single combs should be watched in hard frost.

Rarity

Scots Dumpies are rare, in Britain and especially in the US. A few breeders keep them. If you have a small space and want a calm bird, see our small yard breeds for easier options.

Who they suit

Dumpies suit keepers who want a calm, unusual heritage bird and enjoy hatching their own chicks with a broody hen.

Common questions about Scots Dumpies

Why do Scots Dumpies have short legs?

A gene shortens the legs. It is lethal in a double dose, which lowers hatch rates.

Are Scots Dumpies good mothers?

Yes. They are known as good broodies.

Are Scots Dumpies rare?

Yes. They are hard to find outside Britain.
1120:
What keeping Sebrights is really like

The Sebright is a true bantam created in the early 1800s by Sir John Sebright in England. It is one of the oldest British bantam breeds made to a plan. Sebrights are known for their lacing. Each feather is gold or silver with a neat black edge. They have rose combs, and the roosters are hen-feathered, meaning they lack the long, pointed neck and tail feathers most roosters have.

Day to day

Sebrights are small, quick and active. Many are flighty, and they fly well, so a covered run is a must. Some become tame with regular handling. They need little space and suit small yards.

Laying

Hens lay small white or cream eggs at a modest pace. They are kept for looks, not production. They are not known as strong broodies.

Health notes

Sebrights are often said to be more prone to Marek's disease than many breeds. Buying vaccinated chicks is a good idea. Their small size also makes them more sensitive to cold, damp and drafts.

Climate

The rose comb resists frostbite. Still, give them a dry, draft-free coop in winter, since small bodies lose heat quickly. They handle heat with shade.

How they compare

The Rosecomb Bantam is another old British true bantam with a rose comb. The Nankin is often said to be part of the Sebright's background and is a calmer bird.

Where to get them

Many US hatcheries sell gold and silver Sebrights. Show birds with crisp lacing come from breeders.

Who they suit

Sebrights suit people who want small, pretty birds for a covered pen or for showing.

Common questions about Sebrights

Why do Sebright roosters look like hens?

They are hen-feathered, meaning they lack typical long rooster feathers.

Are Sebrights good layers?

No. They lay small eggs at a modest rate.

Can Sebrights fly?

Yes, quite well. A covered run is a good idea.
1121:
Keeping Seramas, the tiny chickens with big attitude

Seramas come from Malaysia and are usually called the smallest chicken breed in the world. They were developed in the late 1900s, largely credited to breeder Wee Yan Jee, who crossed Japanese bantams with small local birds. They reached the US in the early 2000s and quickly got a following, both as show birds and as pets.

What sets them apart is not just size but posture. A good Serama stands very upright, with its chest pushed forward, wings held down and tail straight up. They are judged in a lot of countries on that stance and on attitude, and they are often shown on a table instead of in a cage.

What day to day life is like

Seramas are bold, chatty and very people-friendly when handled young. Many keepers say they act more like small pets than farm birds, and some people keep them indoors in a cage or pen. Roosters crow a lot, but the crow is high and much quieter than a large rooster. That is one reason they turn up on lists of breeds for small yards, though you should still check local rules on roosters.

Eggs and laying

The eggs are tiny, often cream to light brown, and it takes several to equal one large egg. Hens can lay fairly often for their size, but they are kept for company and show, not production. Hens may go broody, and they can only cover a few eggs, so many breeders use incubators.

Cold is the main challenge

Seramas are a tropical breed with very little body mass. They do not handle cold the way a standard chicken does. If your winters drop near freezing, plan on a well-insulated, draft-free coop or bringing them into a garage or shed. Wet and cold together is the worst combination. In heat they do well, as long as they have shade and water.

Space and safety

They need little room, but their size makes them vulnerable. Cats, rats, snakes and hawks can all take a Serama. Use fine wire like hardware cloth, not chicken wire, and close every gap. Chicks are small enough to drown in a normal waterer, so add marbles or pebbles to the tray. Keeping them with large breeds is risky, since big hens can injure them.

Breeding quirks

Serama hatch rates can be lower than other breeds, and chicks can be fragile in the first weeks. Size and type vary a lot between lines, so breeders often grade birds by weight class. Frizzled Seramas are common as well.

How they compare

The Japanese Bantam is one of the Serama's ancestors and shares the upright tail, but it has very short legs and a lower stance. The Sebright is another tiny true bantam, known for laced feathers instead of posture.

Where to get them

Some US hatcheries sell Seramas, but many come from small breeders. Serama clubs and poultry shows are good places to find quality birds. Prices are often higher than for common bantams.

Common questions about Seramas

Can Seramas live outside in winter?

Only with good protection. In places with freezing winters, most keepers give them an insulated coop or bring them indoors.

Can you keep a Serama as a house chicken?

Many people do. They need a safe cage or pen, daily cleaning, and time outside in a secure space when weather allows.

How small do Seramas get?

Many adults weigh under a pound, and the smallest show birds are much lighter. Size varies by line.
1123:
What keeping Shamo is really like

The Shamo is a Japanese game breed, developed from birds brought to Japan from Southeast Asia. It is tall, upright and heavily muscled, with hard, tight feathers, a small pea or walnut comb and a fierce expression. The Shamo is protected as a Natural Monument in Japan. Several sizes exist, from large O-Shamo to the smaller Chu-Shamo and bantam forms.

A true game bird

Shamo were bred for fighting, and the instinct is strong. Roosters will fight each other, often seriously, and should be kept apart. Hens can be aggressive with other hens too. Many Shamo are calm with their keepers if handled young, but this is not a breed to mix casually into a backyard flock.

Space and housing

They are tall birds and need high coop ceilings and pop doors. Keep roosts at a sensible height to protect their legs. Their tight feathering does not insulate as well as fluffy breeds, so a dry, draft-free coop matters in winter. They handle heat well.

Laying and growth

Hens are poor layers of light brown or tinted eggs. Shamo mature slowly and take a long time to fill out. Hens can go broody.

How they compare

The Malay is another tall game bird with a similar look. The Aseel is shorter and stockier and just as game.

Rarity

Shamo are uncommon in the US and mostly kept by game breeders.

Who they suit

Shamo suit experienced keepers who want a game breed for its history and type and who can house birds separately. They are not a beginner breed or a family flock bird.

Common questions about Shamo

Are Shamo aggressive?

With other chickens, often yes, especially roosters. With people, many are calm.

Are Shamo good layers?

No. They lay few eggs.

Can Shamo live with other chickens?

It is risky. Many keepers house them separately.
1124:
What keeping Silkies is really like

Silkies look more like stuffed toys than chickens. Their feathers lack the tiny hooks that hold normal feathers together, so they feel like fur. They also have black skin and bones, five toes on each foot, feathered legs, a walnut comb, blue earlobes and, in most birds, a fluffy crest. They have been known in Asia for centuries, and today they are one of the most popular pet breeds anywhere.

Most Silkies are calm, gentle and easy to hold, which is why kids love them. They are slow movers and rarely fly. In mixed flocks they tend to sit near the bottom of the pecking order.

Broody is the default setting

Silkies are famous for going broody, often several times a year. Many keepers use them to hatch eggs from other breeds, and they make good, careful mothers. If you want eggs, though, a broody Silkie stops laying for weeks. Collect eggs often, and if needed, break the broodiness by moving her to a wire-floored crate for a few days. When not broody, Silkies lay small cream to tinted eggs at a modest pace.

Their feathers are not waterproof

Silkie fluff soaks up water and does not shed it. A Silkie caught in cold rain can get chilled fast. Give them a covered run, dry bedding and a coop without leaks. Mud is also hard on feathered feet. Keep the run dry so their toes and leg feathers do not cake with dirt, and check legs for scaly leg mites.

Crest care and vision

Big crests can block their view, which makes them jumpy and an easy target for hawks. Trim the feathers around the eyes if they seem to bump into things. Check the crest for lice and mites during your regular checks.

Health notes

Silkies are often said to be more prone to Marek's disease than many breeds. Buying vaccinated chicks is a good idea. If a Silkie suddenly loses balance or has a paralyzed leg, talk to a vet.

Space and climate

Silkies are bantam-sized in the US, so they need less room than standard breeds. Low roosts or no roosts at all work, since many prefer to sleep in a pile on the floor. They handle cold well when dry. Heat is manageable with shade. Our Silkie vs Cochin comparison is useful if you want a fluffy bird but are not sure which.

Bearded and non-bearded

Silkies come bearded and non-bearded. Bearded birds have muffs of fluff around the face. Common colors include white, black, buff, blue, splash, partridge and gray, with lavender and others from breeders. Frizzled Silkies and Satin-type crosses are also popular.

Where to get them

Almost every hatchery sells Silkies, often straight run because they are notoriously hard to sex as chicks. Many owners do not know if they have a hen or rooster until it crows or lays. For show quality birds, look for breeders at poultry shows.

Common questions about Silkies

How can you tell a Silkie hen from a rooster?

It is hard when they are young. Roosters often have bigger combs, a swept-back crest and crow by a few months old. Laying is the only sure sign of a hen.

Do Silkies need a heated coop?

Not usually. A dry, draft-free coop is enough for most climates. Wet is the real enemy.

Can Silkies live with bigger chickens?

Yes, with calm breeds. Watch for bullying, and make sure they can reach food and water.
1126:
Living with Sicilian Buttercups

The Sicilian Buttercup comes from Sicily and reached the US in the 1800s. Its name comes from its comb, a cup or crown shape with points all around the rim, like a buttercup flower. Hens are a golden buff with rows of black spangles. Roosters are a deeper orange-red with a black tail.

Day to day

Buttercups are light, active and often flighty. They are good foragers and like space. They fly well, so plan on a covered run or tall fence. Many keepers describe them as noisy and quick, not cuddly, though some tame with handling.

Laying

Hens lay small to medium white or lightly tinted eggs. They are not usually broody. Production is fair, best in warm months.

Comb and climate

As a Mediterranean breed, Buttercups handle heat well. Their open, cupped comb can get frostbite in deep cold, so they do better in mild or warm climates. They are on our list of breeds for hot climates.

How they compare

The Leghorn is a similar light Mediterranean layer that lays more eggs and is easier to find. The Buttercup is mostly kept for its unusual comb and pretty plumage.

Rarity

Sicilian Buttercups are uncommon. A few US hatcheries sell them, and some breeders keep them. They have appeared on the Livestock Conservancy priority list.

Who they suit

Buttercups suit keepers in warm areas who want something unusual and do not mind a busy, flighty bird. If you want calm hens for kids, look at a heavier breed instead.

Common questions about Sicilian Buttercups

Why is it called a Buttercup?

For its cup-shaped comb, which looks like a buttercup flower.

Are Sicilian Buttercups good layers?

Fair. They lay white or lightly tinted eggs.

Can Sicilian Buttercups handle cold?

They can with good shelter, but their combs are prone to frostbite.
1129:
How the Silver Duckwing looks and behaves

Silver Duckwing is one of the classic colors of the Old English Game. Some hatcheries sell the large fowl version as Silver Duckwing Standard Old English. It is the wild-type pattern with silver in place of red and gold.

Roosters and hens look very different

The rooster has a silvery white neck, back and saddle, with a black breast, black tail and a steel blue bar across the wing. The white patch on the wing is where the name duckwing comes from, since it looks a bit like the wing marking on some ducks. Hens are much quieter in color, with a gray body, fine darker penciling and a salmon breast. Hens blend in well outdoors, which gives some protection from hawks.

Living with them

They have the usual Old English Game traits. Hens are hardy, active foragers and very good broodies that raise chicks well. Egg laying is modest, with small cream or tinted eggs. Roosters are bold and will fight other roosters, so most keepers keep one male per pen. Expect them to fly. A covered run keeps them where you want them.

Climate

Their hard feathering is tight against the body. They cope well in heat and handle cold if the coop is dry and draft-free. Single combs can get frostbite in deep cold.

Related colors

The Silver Duckwing Jungle Fowl listing is a related silver line. If you prefer red and gold tones, the Black Breasted Red is the same pattern without silver.

Common questions about Silver Duckwing Old English Game

Why is it called duckwing?

The white and blue wing marking on the rooster looks a bit like a duck's wing pattern.

Are Silver Duckwing hens gray?

Yes. Hens are gray with fine penciling and a salmon breast.

Are Silver Duckwing Old English Game good layers?

They are modest layers of small eggs. They are kept more for hardiness and broodiness.
1131:
What the Silver Duckwing Jungle Fowl listing means

Silver Duckwing Jungle Fowl Standard Old English is a hatchery listing for a silver duckwing strain of the Old English Game in large fowl size. The jungle fowl part of the name usually points to birds that look closer to the wild red jungle fowl, the wild ancestor of chickens, in shape and pattern. Hatcheries that list both a plain silver duckwing and a jungle fowl version often mean these birds are lighter, sleeker and more like the wild type, with hens in fine gray penciling rather than a plainer coat.

Ask the seller

The naming is not set by a breed standard, so different sellers may use it differently. If the difference matters to you, ask the hatchery what makes their jungle fowl line distinct and request photos of adult birds.

Living with them

Expect alert, quick and active birds. They are strong foragers that do best with room to range, and they fly well. Hens lay a modest number of small cream or tinted eggs and are very good broodies. Roosters will fight each other, so plan for one per flock. Their wild look comes with a wild streak, and some birds stay shy around people.

Climate

They are hardy in most climates. Tight feathers mean they need a dry, draft-free coop in cold weather. A very cold snap can still nip the comb, so check it after freezing nights.

Related pages

See the Silver Duckwing Standard Old English for the regular silver line, and the Black Breasted Red Jungle Fowl listing for the red version.

Common questions about Silver Duckwing Jungle Fowl Old English

Is this a real jungle fowl?

No. It is a domestic Old English Game strain. The name describes the look.

Are they good for beginners?

They are hardy, but flighty birds and fighting roosters make them better for keepers with some experience.

Do the hens go broody?

Yes. They are strong broodies and protective mothers.
1132:
What to expect from Silverudd Blues

The Silverudd Blue was created by Martin Silverudd, a Swedish breeder who spent decades developing productive layers in the mid 1900s. In many places it is sold under the name Isbar as well. In the US it is still a rare breed, mostly sold by small breeders.

Laying and egg color

The main draw is green eggs from a hen that lays well. Shades run from pale mint to a deeper green, and they vary by hen. For a breed with colored eggs, they are known as productive layers. Like most backyard breeds, they slow down in winter and during the molt.

Colors and breeding

Silverudd Blues come in blue, black and splash. Blue is not a true-breeding color. Two blue parents give blue, black and splash chicks. A black bird bred to a splash gives all blue chicks. That makes it easy to plan if you want a lot of blue birds.

Day to day

Owners describe them as active, curious and friendly, and good foragers. They are medium-light in size, so they do not need as much room as heavy breeds, but they appreciate space to roam. They are not usually broody.

Climate notes

Coming from Sweden, they handle cold well. Their single combs are the weak spot in hard freezes, especially on roosters. Keep the coop dry and ventilated. They do fine in moderate heat with shade.

How they compare

If you want green eggs and more choice, an Olive Egger is easy to find but varies a lot. The Silverudd Blue is a true breed, so its offspring will be Silverudd Blues and lay similar eggs. The Swedish Flower Hen is another Swedish breed that has gained a following in the US. See green egg layers for more options.

Common questions about Silverudd Blues

Are Silverudd Blues rare?

Yes, in the US. They are mostly sold by small breeders.

Do Silverudd Blues lay green eggs?

Yes, usually light to medium green, varying by hen.

Are Silverudd Blues good layers?

Yes. They are known as good layers for a breed with colored eggs.
1135:
What makes the Spangled color stand out

Spangled is one of the most eye-catching colors of the Old English Game. Some hatcheries sell large fowl birds in this color as Spangled Standard Old English. It is a tricolor pattern where feathers mix red or brown, black and white, with white tips scattered over the body. No two birds look exactly alike.

Spangles change over time

The white spots often grow with each molt, so a spangled bird can look much lighter at three years old than it did at one. Chick down also varies a lot, so a spangled hatch may look like a mix of colors at first.

Breeding is not exact

Spangled birds do not all breed true to one look. Matings can give a range of spotting, from heavily white to darker, more red birds. That suits keepers who like variety and is part of the color's appeal.

Living with them

Underneath, it is an Old English Game. Hens are hardy, forage hard and make excellent mothers, going broody often. Eggs are small and cream or tinted, laid at a modest rate. Roosters will fight other males. Keep one per flock or pen them apart. They are strong fliers, so a covered run is worth having.

Climate

Tight feathering means they need a dry, draft-free coop in cold weather. They handle heat well with shade. Watch single combs in deep cold. The broken pattern blends into leaf litter, which helps against hawks.

Related pages

For a solid color that pairs well in the same flock, see the Black Standard Old English. The Mille Fleur d'Uccle has a similar three-color look in a very different, gentle bantam breed.

Common questions about Spangled Old English Game

Do spangled chickens get whiter with age?

Often, yes. White tips tend to increase after each molt.

Do spangled Old English breed true?

Not exactly. Expect variety in the amount of spotting.

Are spangled Old English hens good mothers?

Yes. They are strong broodies, like all Old English Game hens.
1136:
Keeping Speckledy hens

The Speckledy is a hybrid laying hen popular in the UK. It is usually described as a cross involving the Marans and the Rhode Island Red, and it takes after the Marans in looks, with dark cuckoo speckled feathers. It was developed as a commercial layer for backyard and small farm keepers who wanted a productive bird with a traditional look.

What day to day life is like

Speckledy hens are generally calm, sturdy and friendly. They are not as flighty as light breeds and settle well into garden flocks. Their mottled feathers give them some natural camouflage on the ground, which can help a bit against hawks.

Laying pattern

They lay medium to large brown eggs. The color is usually a rich brown, though not as dark as a good Marans egg. Being a hybrid, they lay more steadily than a pure Marans in their first couple of years, then slow down with age. Broodiness is uncommon.

Climate and care

They are hardy birds suited to a cool, damp climate like Britain's. Standard large fowl space and housing works well. Watch single combs in very hard frosts, and provide shade in hot weather. Feed a layer ration with oyster shell.

Finding them

Speckledies are mainly sold in the UK by hybrid suppliers and poultry farms selling point of lay pullets. They are uncommon in the US, where a Cuckoo Marans or a Black Sex Link fills a similar spot. Since they are a hybrid, you cannot breed them true.

Common questions about Speckledy hens

Are Speckledy hens good layers?

Yes. They are steady brown egg layers, especially in their first two years.

Are Speckledy hens the same as Cuckoo Marans?

No. They look similar, but Speckledies are a hybrid and usually lay more eggs, while Marans are a pure breed with darker eggs.

Can I get Speckledy hens in the US?

They are rarely offered in the US. Similar birds are easier to find.
1138:
What keeping Spitzhaubens is like

The Spitzhauben, or Appenzeller Spitzhauben, is Switzerland's national chicken breed, from the Appenzell region. Its name refers to the pointed lace bonnets worn there, which matches the bird's forward-pointing crest. It has a small V-shaped comb and comes most often in silver spangled, with gold spangled, black and blue also kept.

Day to day

Spitzhaubens are light, active and alert. They are excellent foragers, quick to spot danger, and good fliers. They like to roost high. Few will sit in your lap, though most learn your routine and stop panicking when you walk in. They do best with space to range.

Laying

Hens lay white eggs at a good rate for a heritage breed. They are not usually broody.

Crest care

The crest is smaller and more upright than a Polish crest, so it blocks less of the view and stays drier. Still, check it for mites, and use waterers that keep the crest dry in winter.

Climate

Coming from the Swiss mountains, they handle cold well, and the small V comb resists frostbite. They also cope with heat with shade.

How they compare

The Appenzeller page covers the Appenzeller breeds more broadly, including the Barthuhn, a bearded, rose combed relative. Compared with the Polish, the Spitzhauben is tougher, more active and a better forager.

Rarity

Spitzhaubens are uncommon in the US. A few hatcheries and breeders sell them.

Who they suit

Spitzhaubens suit keepers who want an eye-catching crested bird that still lays well and looks after itself on range. They are not ideal for tiny runs, since they are active and like to fly up to high perches.

Common questions about Spitzhaubens

Are Spitzhaubens good layers?

Yes, good layers of white eggs.

Can Spitzhaubens fly?

Yes, quite well. A covered run is helpful.

Are Spitzhaubens cold-hardy?

Yes. Their small comb and mountain origin suit cold weather.
1141:
What you get with a Standard Old English surplus order

Standard Old English Surplus is a hatchery listing, not a color or breed. It means large fowl Old English Game chicks in a mix of colors, chosen by the hatchery from whatever is hatching. You might get Black Breasted Reds, Pyles, Duckwings, Wheatens, Spangled and other colors in one box. Surplus orders are often cheaper than ordering a single color.

Check whether they are sexed

Game chicks are hard to sex, and many surplus listings are sold straight run, meaning a mix of males and females. With Old English Game that matters a lot, because roosters fight each other hard. Read the listing carefully, and plan where extra cockerels will go before the chicks arrive. Our hen or roo tool can help you sort them as they grow.

Who it suits

A surplus order suits someone who wants hardy, self-reliant birds, good broody hens and a colorful flock, and who does not care about exact colors. It is not a good pick for small backyards or for anyone who cannot handle several roosters.

Raising them

Brood them like any chicks. Watch for early sparring between cockerels, which can start sooner than with other breeds. Once grown, hens forage well, lay small cream or tinted eggs, and go broody often. Give them a covered run, since they fly well.

Telling colors apart

Many Old English colors look similar as chicks. You will usually know what you have once adult feathers come in at a few months old. Browse the individual color pages, like the Wheaten, to match them up.

Common questions about Standard Old English surplus chicks

Can I choose colors in a surplus order?

Usually not. The hatchery picks from what is available.

How many roosters will I get?

In a straight run order, expect roughly half, though it varies by hatch.

Are surplus chicks lower quality?

Not necessarily. They are usually the same stock, just mixed colors.
1142:
What keeping Sultans is really like

The Sultan comes from Turkey, where it was kept as an ornamental bird. It reached Britain in the 1850s. The breed has a full set of fancy features. It has a crest, a beard and muffs, a small V comb, heavily feathered legs and feet, stiff feathers at the hocks and five toes on each foot. White is the main color, with black and blue also kept.

Day to day

Sultans are calm, gentle and slow moving. They are kept for looks and company, not production. They are often at the bottom of the pecking order and do best with other calm breeds. They do not forage much and suit a run better than free range.

Keeping them clean and dry

All that feathering needs care. Crests can block vision and hold water. Beards get messy at the feeder and waterer. Feathered feet pick up mud and can freeze into clumps in winter. Keep the run dry, use waterers that keep faces dry, and check feathers for mites and lice regularly. Our scaly leg mites page covers a problem that is easy to miss under foot feathers.

Eggs

Hens lay small white eggs at a modest rate. They are not known as strong broodies.

Climate

They handle mild cold if they stay dry. Wet and mud are the bigger problems. They are fine in warm weather with shade.

How they compare

The Silkie shares the five toes, crest and feathered feet, and is also calm, but has fur-like feathers and goes broody often. The Houdan has five toes and a crest, with clean legs.

Rarity

Sultans are rare. Sultans have been among the rarest breeds tracked by the Livestock Conservancy. A few hatcheries sell them occasionally.

Common questions about Sultans

Are Sultan chickens good layers?

No. They lay small white eggs at a modest rate.

Are Sultans friendly?

Yes. They are calm and gentle.

Do Sultans have five toes?

Yes. Five toes on each foot is a breed trait.
1144:
Living with Sumatras

The Sumatra comes from Indonesia and reached the US and Europe in the 1800s. It is a striking bird, glossy black with a green sheen, a long flowing tail on the roosters, a small pea comb and a dark, purplish face. Some roosters grow more than one spur on each leg. Blue and white varieties also exist.

Day to day

Sumatras are active, alert and often flighty. They are strong fliers, so a covered run or tall fence is a must. They are excellent foragers and do well on free range. Many are wary of people, though some tame with handling.

Roosters

Sumatras have game bird roots, and roosters can be aggressive with other males. Keep one per flock or give them a lot of space. They are usually not aggressive with people.

Eggs and broodiness

Hens lay white or cream eggs at a modest rate. They go broody and make good mothers.

Tail care

The long tails on roosters need clean, dry bedding and high perches to stay in good shape.

Climate

They are hardy. The small pea comb resists frostbite. In heat, give shade, since black birds soak up sun.

How they compare

The Ayam Cemani is another all-black Indonesian breed, but it has black skin and organs. The Sumatra has normal skin and is mostly kept for its looks and hardiness.

Rarity

Sumatras are uncommon. The Livestock Conservancy has counted Sumatras among its priority breeds. A few hatcheries sell them.

Who they suit

Sumatras suit keepers with space who like a wild-looking bird and want good broody hens. They are less suited to small backyards or anyone who needs birds that stay put behind a low fence.

Common questions about Sumatras

Can Sumatras fly?

Yes, very well. Plan on a covered run.

Are Sumatra hens good mothers?

Yes. They are good broodies.

Are Sumatras aggressive?

Roosters can fight other males, but they are usually not aggressive with people.
1145:
Keeping Sussex hens through the year

The Sussex is an old English breed from the county of Sussex. It was a farm and table bird for generations and is still one of the most popular backyard breeds in the UK. In the US, the Speckled Sussex is the variety most people know, with its mahogany feathers tipped in black and white. Light Sussex, white with a black neck and tail, is the classic in Britain. Red, Buff, Brown, Silver, White and Coronation also exist.

Ask Sussex keepers what they like and you hear the same thing. They are curious and friendly, and many hens follow you around the garden waiting to see what you dig up. They are confident without being bullies, which makes them easy to mix with other breeds.

Laying pattern

Good Sussex strains lay well, with cream to light brown eggs. They often keep laying through winter better than many heritage breeds. Like any hen they stop during the molt and slow with age, with the best years in the first two or three. Some Sussex hens go broody and make good mothers, though they are not as broody as Orpingtons or Silkies.

Speckles change over time

If you keep Speckled Sussex, the coat changes with each molt. Young birds often have fewer white tips, and the spotting gets bolder and more white as they age. Older hens can look much lighter than they did as pullets. It is the same bird, just a new set of feathers.

Space and climate

Sussex are medium-heavy birds and do well on standard large fowl space. They love to forage and do best with room to roam, but they cope with a run. They are cold-hardy. Their single combs are medium sized, so roosters can still get frostbite in deep cold. They are fine in moderate heat with shade. Speckled hens blend into leaf litter, which helps them hide from hawks.

Sussex in other breeds

The Light Sussex has long been used as a parent for crossbred layers because it carries the silver gene. Crossed with a red rooster, it produces chicks you can sex by color. Many modern hybrid layers trace back partly to that idea.

How they compare

The Dorking is an even older English breed from the same region, with five toes and a longer body. Sussex are generally better layers. If you are trying to understand the difference between the breed and its best-known variety, see Sussex vs Speckled Sussex. The Faverolles is another gentle, curious dual-purpose breed, but with a beard and feathered feet.

Where to get them

Speckled Sussex are sold by most US hatcheries. Light Sussex are easy to find in the UK and sold by some US hatcheries. Red, Coronation and others are mostly from breeders. In the UK there are many Sussex breeders and the breed is a regular at shows.

Common questions about Sussex chickens

Are Sussex chickens friendly?

Yes. They are one of the most people-friendly breeds and do well with kids.

What color eggs do Sussex chickens lay?

Cream to light brown, depending on the hen and the strain.

Do Speckled Sussex get more white as they age?

Yes. The white tips usually increase after each molt, so older birds look more speckled.
1147:
Keeping Swedish Black hens

The Swedish Black, known in Sweden as the Svarthöna, is a Swedish breed with fibromelanosis. That gene gives it black skin, dark flesh and dark bones, the same trait seen in the Ayam Cemani and the Silkie. The feathers are black with a green sheen. The comb and face are dark too.

How it differs from the Ayam Cemani

Many keepers choose the Swedish Black as a more cold-hardy and more affordable option with the same all-black look. It comes from a cold climate and is generally described as hardy. It also tends to be easier to find than the Ayam Cemani.

Day to day

Swedish Blacks are active foragers. Keepers often describe them as friendly and curious, and many become tame. They are medium-sized and do well on standard space.

Eggs

Hens lay cream or lightly tinted eggs. The eggs are normal colored. The black is in the bird, not the egg.

Climate

From Sweden, they handle cold well. Watch single combs in hard freezes. In summer, black birds need shade.

Rarity

They are rare in the US but have grown in popularity since imports in the 2010s. Most come from small breeders.

Who they suit

Swedish Blacks suit keepers in cold climates who want the all-black look without the price of an Ayam Cemani, and who want a hen that forages and lays steadily. Buy from a breeder who can tell you where their stock came from, since lines are still small in the US.

Common questions about Swedish Blacks

Do Swedish Blacks lay black eggs?

No. They lay cream or lightly tinted eggs.

Are Swedish Blacks the same as Ayam Cemani?

No. They share the black skin trait, but they are separate breeds from different places.

Are Swedish Blacks cold-hardy?

Yes. They come from a cold climate.
1150:
What to expect from Swedish Flower Hens

The Swedish Flower Hen is a landrace from Skåne in southern Sweden. That means it developed over centuries on farms through natural selection and farmer choice, not to a show standard. Its Swedish name means something like Skåne flower hen. By the late 1900s the breed was close to disappearing, and Swedish conservation work saved it. It was imported to the US in the early 2010s and has become popular since.

The flower pattern

The name comes from the white tips scattered across the feathers, which look like flowers in a field. Base colors vary a lot, from black and blue to red, buff and gray. Some birds have small crests and some do not. No two look quite alike, and the white spotting usually increases with each molt, so a bird can look quite different at three years than at one.

Day to day

Swedish Flower Hens are generally friendly, curious and calm. Many become very tame with handling. They are active foragers and are happiest with room to roam, where they find a lot of their own food. They are not usually aggressive, and roosters are often described as reasonable. They are medium-sized birds, lighter than heavy American breeds.

Laying pattern

Expect cream to light brown eggs at a good rate for a landrace. They are steady layers and often keep going into cooler months. Some hens go broody and make good mothers, as you would expect from a farm breed. Like most hens they slow down with age.

Climate notes

Coming from Sweden, they are cold-hardy. The single comb can still get frostbite in very cold weather, especially on roosters, so keep the coop dry and ventilated. They are fairly adaptable to warmer climates as well, with shade and water.

Crested birds

Birds with crests need a bit of extra checking. Crests can hold moisture and hide lice or mites. Most Swedish Flower Hen crests are small, so it is a lot less work than with a Polish or Silkie.

How they compare

The Icelandic chicken is another Nordic landrace with lots of color variety and strong foraging instincts, though it is smaller and lays white to light-tinted eggs. If you like the spotted look, the Speckled Sussex has a similar effect and is easier to find. Both breeds are calm and good layers. The Swedish Flower Hen has more color variety.

Where to get them

They are still not common, but supply has grown. A few US hatcheries now sell them, and many small breeders sell chicks and hatching eggs. Because it is a landrace, there is no single correct look, so focus on healthy, well-grown birds. Price is usually higher than for common breeds.

Who they suit

Swedish Flower Hens suit keepers who want something a little unusual but still easy, with good laying and friendly birds. They are a good fit for free-range setups in cooler climates. If you only want maximum eggs, a production breed will lay more. Check our list of breeds for cold climates for more options like it.

Common questions about Swedish Flower Hens

Are Swedish Flower Hens rare?

They are less rare than they were, but they are still uncommon compared with mainstream breeds.

Do Swedish Flower Hens breed true?

Their offspring look like Swedish Flower Hens, but colors and crests vary a lot, as you would expect from a landrace.

Are Swedish Flower Hens friendly?

Most are. They tend to be curious and tame, especially if handled from a young age.
1151:
What we know about the Thuringian

The Thuringian, called the Thüringer Barthuhn in Germany, comes from the Thuringia region in central Germany. The German name means bearded hen of Thuringia, and the beard is its main feature. It is a small to medium bird with a rounded body and a single comb. Several colors are kept, including chamois, gold spangled, silver spangled and black.

Day to day

Thuringians are described as active, friendly birds that forage well. They are light enough to fly, so a covered run helps.

Eggs

Hens lay white or cream eggs at a moderate rate.

Beard care

Beards catch food and water, and in winter a wet beard can freeze. Waterers that keep faces dry, like nipple waterers, help. Check beards for mites from time to time.

Climate

The beard protects the face, which helps in cold weather. Watch the single comb in hard freezes.

Rarity

Thuringians are rare outside Germany and only a few breeders keep them in the US. Because details from backyard keepers here are limited, we have kept this page short. For a bearded breed that is easier to find, the Faverolles or Easter Egger are good options.

Common questions about Thuringians

Are Thuringian chickens bearded?

Yes. The beard is the breed's main feature.

Can you buy Thuringians in the US?

Rarely. Only a few breeders keep them.

What color eggs do Thuringians lay?

White or cream eggs.
1153:
What we know about the Twentse

The Twentse comes from Twente, a region in the eastern Netherlands near the German border. In Germany, the same type of bird is known as the Kraienköppe. Malay-type birds are believed to be part of its background, which shows in its upright posture, firm feathering and small walnut-like comb. Silver and gold are the best-known colors.

Day to day

Twentse are described as alert, active birds and good foragers. Their game-like roots mean roosters may not tolerate other males well, so plan on one rooster per flock.

Eggs

Hens lay cream or tinted eggs at a moderate rate.

Climate

Their small comb resists frostbite, which suits cold winters.

Rarity

The Twentse is rare in the Netherlands and Germany and very rare in the US. Reliable information from backyard keepers is limited, so this page sticks to what is well documented. If you want a game-type bird that is easier to find, look at the Malay or Old English Game, though both are more intense birds.

Common questions about the Twentse

Is the Twentse the same as the Kraienköppe?

They are generally treated as the same type of bird, known by the Dutch and German names.

Can you buy Twentse chickens in the US?

Very rarely.

What color eggs do Twentse lay?

Cream or tinted eggs.
1154:
What keeping Welsummers is really like

Welsummers come from the village of Welsum in the Netherlands, where they were developed in the early 1900s. They are best known for their eggs, which are a rich terracotta brown, often with darker speckles. They are also known for the rooster's look. A Welsummer rooster is said to be the model for the rooster on a famous cereal box.

The common color is a red partridge, with hens in warm brown with fine penciling and roosters in red, gold and black. Silver duckwing and gold duckwing Welsummers exist too, mainly from breeders.

Day to day

Welsummers are alert, active and smart. Many keepers describe them as friendly but not clingy. Hens will usually come close for treats and tolerate handling, but they would rather be out foraging. They are good free rangers and quick to spot danger. Roosters are mostly fine but, like any breed, vary from bird to bird.

Laying and egg color

Welsummers lay a moderate number of medium to large eggs. The color is darkest at the start of the laying season and often fades a bit as the year goes on. The speckles are part of the outer coating and can rub off if you scrub the egg, so wipe gently. Egg color varies a lot between lines. Hatchery Welsummers usually lay a medium brown, while breeder lines selected for color give the darker, speckled eggs. Some hens go broody, though it is not common.

Sexing chicks

Welsummer chicks are partly autosexing. Female chicks usually have darker, sharper head markings and a clear dark line from the eye, almost like eyeliner. Males are often lighter and blurrier. It is not perfect, but it gives a good guess.

Space and climate

They are medium-sized and do well on standard space, though they prefer room to roam. They handle cold well. Roosters' single combs can get frostbite in very cold weather, so ventilation matters. They handle heat reasonably with shade.

How they compare

Welsummers are most often compared with Marans. Marans eggs are darker and more chocolate, while Welsummer eggs are more terracotta and speckled. The Marans vs Welsummer comparison covers both. The Barnevelder is another Dutch breed with dark eggs, but it is heavier and calmer, with double-laced feathers. Both breeds are popular with people building a colorful egg basket.

Olive eggers from Welsummers

Welsummer roosters are a common choice for making Olive Eggers. Crossed with blue egg hens, they give green to olive eggs, because the brown coating goes over the blue shell.

Where to get them

Most US hatcheries sell red partridge Welsummers. For darker eggs, better type or other colors, look to breeders. Many breeders sell hatching eggs from their best layers, and you can often see egg photos before you buy.

Common questions about Welsummers

Are Welsummers good layers?

They are moderate layers, laying a few eggs a week. They are kept more for egg color than numbers.

Why are my Welsummer eggs not speckled?

Speckling varies by hen and strain, and it can also fade during the laying season.

Are Welsummers friendly?

Many are. They are curious and active birds that usually tolerate handling, though they prefer foraging to sitting in your lap.
1156:
Living with Vorwerks

The Vorwerk was developed in Germany around 1900 by Oskar Vorwerk. It has a buff body with a black neck and black tail, much like the Lakenvelder pattern but on buff instead of white. It has a single comb and is a medium-sized, practical bird. Bantams also exist.

Day to day

Vorwerks are active and alert, and good foragers. They are generally calmer than Lakenvelders but not lap birds. Many get used to people over time. They do not need a large coop, but they get bored in a bare, tight run, so give them ground to scratch or scatter feed for them to find. They fly better than heavy breeds.

Laying

Hens lay cream or lightly tinted eggs at a good rate for a heritage breed. They are not known as strong broodies.

Color quality

Getting a clean buff body with a solid black neck and tail is hard to breed. Many birds show some smudging. That does not matter for a backyard bird.

Climate

They are hardy and handle cold well. Watch single combs in hard freezes. Summer is manageable as long as there is shade and cool water.

Rarity

Vorwerks are rare in the US. A few breeders and occasional hatcheries sell them. If you want a similar buff bird that is easier to find, the Buff Orpington is calmer and heavier.

Who they suit

Vorwerks suit keepers who want an uncommon German breed that still lays well and does not need special care. They are a good forager for a mixed backyard flock.

Common questions about Vorwerks

Are Vorwerks good layers?

Yes, good layers of cream or lightly tinted eggs.

What is the difference between a Vorwerk and a Lakenvelder?

Both have a black neck and tail, but the Vorwerk body is buff and the Lakenvelder body is white.

Are Vorwerks friendly?

They are calmer than many light breeds, but not usually cuddly.
1158:
What wheaten means in Old English Game

Wheaten is a color variety of the Old English Game, sold by some hatcheries in large fowl size as Wheaten Standard Old English. The name mostly describes the hens. A wheaten hen is a soft, warm wheat or cream color, with a richer gold neck and some darker color in the tail and wings. She looks very different from the penciled brown hens of the black breasted red pattern.

Wheaten roosters

Roosters from wheaten lines look a lot like black breasted red roosters, with red and gold over a black breast and tail. Most people cannot tell them apart by eye. Breeders keep track of wheaten lines by the hens and the chicks.

Chicks look different too

Wheaten chicks usually hatch in a pale cream or light buff down, without the striped chipmunk pattern you see on wild-type chicks. That makes them easy to pick out in a mixed hatch.

Living with them

Wheaten hens have all the classic Old English Game traits. They are tough foragers, modest layers of small cream or tinted eggs, and some of the best broody hens around. Roosters will fight other males, so keep one per flock or house them apart. They fly well, so a covered run helps.

Climate

They are hardy birds. Tight feathers need a dry coop without drafts in winter, and single combs can get frostbite in hard cold. The pale coat handles summer sun well with shade.

Related pages

See the Black Breasted Red for the roosters these lines resemble.

Common questions about Wheaten Old English Game

Are wheaten and black breasted red the same?

Not quite. The roosters look alike, but the hens and chicks differ in color.

What color are wheaten chicks?

Usually pale cream or light buff, without stripes.

Are Wheaten Old English hens good broodies?

Yes, they are excellent sitters and mothers.
1161:
Keeping White Faced Black Spanish

The White Faced Black Spanish is one of the oldest Mediterranean breeds. It came from Spain and was popular in Britain and the US in the 1800s. It is a glossy black bird with a single comb and a large white face. That white face is actually enlarged earlobe skin, and it is the breed's trademark.

Day to day

They are active, alert and often flighty. They take to the air easily, so a covered run is worth it. They are good foragers. They are not usually broody.

Laying

Hens lay large white eggs at a good rate, best in spring and summer.

Face and comb care

The white face and large comb are sensitive. In cold weather, both can be damaged by frost. In some birds, the face can also be affected by harsh weather. A dry, draft-free coop helps a lot in winter. White Faced Black Spanish do better in mild or warm climates.

Heat

They handle heat well, though black birds need shade.

How they compare

The Minorca is a close relative with white earlobes but not the full white face. The Leghorn lays similar white eggs and is easier to find.

Rarity

The breed is rare. It has appeared on the Livestock Conservancy priority list. A few hatcheries sell them.

Who they suit

They suit keepers in mild climates who want a historic breed with big white eggs and do not need tame birds. In cold northern areas they need more care than most breeds.

Common questions about White Faced Black Spanish

Why do White Faced Black Spanish have white faces?

It is enlarged earlobe skin, a breed trait.

Are White Faced Black Spanish good layers?

Yes. They lay large white eggs.

Are they cold-hardy?

Not very. Their face and comb are sensitive to frost.
1162:
Keeping White Japanese Bantams

The White Japanese Bantam is the all-white color of the Japanese Bantam. It has a bright red single comb, white plumage and the breed's signature look, very short legs with a tall tail that stands upright past the head. It is one of many color varieties of the breed.

How white differs from patterned colors

White shows dirt, and Japanese Bantams sit so close to the ground that they get dirty easily. A clean, dry run with sand or well drained ground makes a huge difference. Some white birds also yellow or turn brassy with strong sun or certain feeds. If you plan to show, give them shade and talk to breeders about feed.

Day to day

Expect a calm, people-friendly bantam that tames easily. They are kept for looks and company more than eggs. Hens lay small cream or tinted eggs and go broody often. They are a good choice for small yards and families with gentle kids.

Breeding note

All Japanese Bantam colors share the short leg gene, which reduces hatch rates when two short-legged birds are bred. White to white matings give white chicks. If you want a contrast, look at the Black Tailed White Japanese Bantam, which has a white body with black tail and wing feathers.

Climate

They are comfortable in heat with shade but struggle with hard cold. Protect them from wet and drafts, and watch combs for frostbite.

Common questions about White Japanese Bantams

Do White Japanese Bantams stay white?

Mostly, but sun and dirt can stain them. Shade and clean bedding help.

Are White Japanese Bantams friendly?

Yes. They are calm and easy to handle.

How many eggs do Japanese Bantams lay?

A modest number of small eggs, with breaks for broodiness.
1163:
How the White Leghorn differs from other Leghorns

The White Leghorn is the best-known color of the Leghorn breed, and it is the bird behind most commercial white eggs. The breed is the same as other Leghorn colors, but the white variety has had far more selection for laying than any other. When people say Leghorns are egg machines, they usually mean White Leghorns from production lines.

Production vs show white Leghorns

There are two quite different kinds. Production White Leghorns are small, lean and lay a huge number of white eggs, often starting early and keeping a strong pace in their first year or two. Show White Leghorns are bred for the standard, with a larger body and bigger comb, and they lay noticeably less. Hatchery birds are usually closer to the production type.

Day to day

Expect busy, alert, flighty birds that do not love being caught. They rarely go broody and eat less feed than heavy breeds for the eggs they give. Expect them to clear a low fence easily, so cover the run or clip a wing.

Climate notes

White Leghorns are one of the best breeds for heat. Their light bodies and big combs help them shed heat, and white feathers reflect sun. That is why they show up so often among hot climate breeds. In cold winters, their big single combs are prone to frostbite. A dry, well ventilated coop matters a lot.

Egg color

They lay pure white eggs. If you want a basket of other shades too, see white egg layers and pair them with brown and blue layers.

Common questions about White Leghorns

Are White Leghorns the best layers?

Production lines are among the best layers you can keep, especially for white eggs.

Are White Leghorns noisy?

They can be. They are quick to sound alarms when something startles them.

Do White Leghorns get along with other breeds?

Usually, yes. They are active but not typically bullies. Give them enough space to stay busy.
1166:
Why so many keepers love Wyandottes

The Wyandotte was developed in New York state in the 1870s and accepted by the American Poultry Association in 1883 in the silver laced color. It was named after the Wyandot people. Since then many colors have been added, including golden laced, blue laced red, silver penciled, partridge, Columbian, white, black and buff. The laced varieties, with dark borders around each feather, are the ones most people picture.

Day to day

Wyandottes are solid, medium-heavy birds with a rounded shape. Most are calm and tolerant, though many are not lap chickens. They are often confident and can be bossy in a mixed flock. Hens hold their own at the feeder. Roosters are usually decent, but like any heavy breed you should pick the calmest.

The rose comb advantage

Wyandottes have a rose comb, which sits low and flat on the head. That makes them much less prone to frostbite than single-combed breeds, which is a big reason they are a favorite in cold places. Add thick feathers and a heavy body, and you get one of the best cold-weather breeds. They do less well in heat. Give them shade, airflow and plenty of water in summer.

Laying pattern

Wyandottes lay a good number of light to medium brown eggs. They are known for laying fairly well through winter, better than many breeds. They start around five to six months. Some hens go broody. Like other heritage breeds they lay best in their first two to three years.

Space and coop

Standard large fowl space works. They are not big fliers, so ordinary fencing usually holds them. They forage well but are happy in a run. Their fluffy rear feathers can collect droppings, so check vents now and then, and look for mites, which like dense feathering.

Hatchery vs show birds
