Hatchery Wyandottes are often smaller and their lacing is less crisp. Show-quality birds are rounder, with clean, even lacing. Hatchery birds are usually better layers. If you want birds for the look, a breeder is worth it.

How they compare

Wyandottes are often compared with Orpingtons. Orpingtons are larger, softer and broodier, while Wyandottes have the cold-friendly rose comb and are often a bit more assertive. See Wyandotte vs Orpington. For specific colors, the Golden Laced Wyandotte and Black Laced Red Wyandotte have their own pages. Wyandottes also show up on our list of breeds for cold climates.

Where to get them

Silver laced, golden laced, blue laced red and Columbian Wyandottes are sold by most US hatcheries and farm stores. Bantam Wyandottes are common too. Rarer colors and show lines come from breeders.

Who they suit

Wyandottes are a great fit if you live somewhere cold, want a pretty, productive bird, and do not mind a hen with a bit of attitude. They are a decent choice for families, but gentler breeds like Orpingtons are better if kids want a bird to carry.

Common questions about Wyandottes

Are Wyandottes good layers?

Yes. They are steady layers of brown eggs and often keep laying through winter.

Are Wyandottes aggressive?

They can be bossy with other chickens, but most are not aggressive toward people.

Do Wyandottes handle cold well?

Very well. Their rose comb resists frostbite and their thick feathers keep them warm.
1167:
Keeping White Old English Game

White is one of the simplest colors of the Old English Game, and some hatcheries sell the large fowl version as White Standard Old English. The whole bird is white, with a bright red comb and face. Without a pattern to look at, you notice the breed's shape more, the tight feathers, upright stance and muscular build.

Why some keepers pick white

White Old English are easy to tell apart from patterned birds, which helps if you are tracking a breeding group. Their chicks are easy to spot in a mixed hatch too. On the downside, white birds stand out to hawks and other predators more than duckwing or wheaten hens do. A covered run or good cover in the yard helps. See our guide to aerial predators if hawks are common where you live.

Keeping them white

White feathers show mud and stains, and strong sun can turn them brassy or yellowish. Clean bedding and shade help if you care about looks or plan to show.

Living with them

Hens are alert, hardy foragers and excellent broody mothers. They lay small cream or tinted eggs at a modest rate. Roosters keep the strong fighting instinct of the breed and should not be kept with other males. Expect them to fly well.

Climate

They are tough birds in most climates. In winter, tight feathering means a dry, draft-free coop matters. Watch single combs in hard cold.

Common questions about White Old English Game

Do white Old English Game breed true?

Depends on the line. Some white lines carry other colors hidden, so ask the breeder.

Are White Old English Game easy targets for hawks?

They are easier to see. Cover in the yard or a covered run lowers the risk.

Are White Old English hens good layers?

Modest. Most keepers value them for toughness and mothering, not egg counts.
1168:
What makes the Whiting True Blue different

The Whiting True Blue is a blue egg layer developed by Dr. Tom Whiting of Whiting Farms in Colorado, a company better known for raising roosters for fly tying feathers. It is a selected strain rather than a recognized breed, and it was bred with the goal of reliable blue eggs from a productive, sturdy hen. A sister line, the Whiting True Green, lays green eggs.

Looks and temperament

Since there is no breed standard, Whiting True Blues vary in color, and many look a bit like Easter Eggers. Keepers usually describe them as active and alert, sometimes a little flighty, but not wild. They forage well.

Eggs and laying

The selling point is the shell color. They lay blue eggs, and they are said to lay well for a blue egg bird. As with all blue egg layers, the blue goes all the way through the shell, unlike brown eggs, which are colored on the surface. Expect the usual slowdown in winter and during the molt.

Climate

They are sturdy, medium-sized birds that handle normal backyard winters and summers. If your birds have larger single combs, protect them from frostbite in deep cold with a dry, well ventilated coop. Give shade in hot weather.

How they compare

An Easter Egger might lay blue, green or even tinted eggs, while the True Blue is selected to lay blue. The Ameraucana is a recognized breed that lays blue eggs and has a show standard with beards and muffs. See blue egg layers for other options.

Where to get them

They are sold through some US hatcheries under the Whiting name.

Common questions about Whiting True Blues

Is the Whiting True Blue a breed?

No. It is a selected strain without a breed standard.

Do Whiting True Blues always lay blue eggs?

They are bred for it, and most do. Shade can vary from hen to hen.

Are Whiting True Blues cold-hardy?

They handle cold well in a dry, draft-free coop. Watch any bird with a big comb in hard freezes.
1173:
What keeping Yokohamas is really like

The Yokohama was developed in Germany in the late 1800s from long-tailed chickens imported from Japan. It is named after the port they shipped from. Yokohamas are slim, elegant birds with long tails on the roosters, walnut or pea combs, and colors like white and red-saddled white. Red-saddled birds are mostly white with red on the shoulders and back. Bantams are more common than large fowl in the US.

Long tails need care

Roosters grow long, flowing tails. Like the Phoenix, the Yokohama molts its tail each year, so the length grows back over the season. Give roosters high perches so the tail hangs clear, keep bedding clean and dry, and avoid crowding.

Day to day

Yokohamas are active and alert, and some are flighty. Many tame with handling. Netting over the run keeps them in and hawks out. Hens can go broody and are good mothers.

Eggs

Eggs are small and cream colored, and you will not get many. People keep Yokohamas for the look of the roosters.

Climate

The small comb resists frostbite. They handle moderate heat with shade.

How they compare

The Phoenix is a close relative with a single comb and duckwing colors. The Onagadori is the true Japanese long-tail with feathers that skip the molt.

Rarity

Yokohamas are uncommon. A few hatcheries and breeders sell them.

Where to get them

Bantam Yokohamas are offered by a few US hatcheries. Large fowl and show-quality birds with long, unbroken tails usually come from breeders.

Common questions about Yokohamas

Do Yokohama tails molt?

Yes. The tail molts each year and regrows.

Are Yokohamas good layers?

Not especially. Hens lay a small number of little cream eggs.

What is the difference between a Yokohama and a Phoenix?

Yokohamas usually have a walnut or pea comb and different colors. Phoenix have single combs.
97:
How to use this encyclopedia when a bird looks sick

Most keepers land here with a hen that looks wrong and no clear idea why. Start with what you can see, not with a disease name. Write down the main sign, how long it has been going on, how many birds have it, and whether anything changed recently, like new birds, new feed or a heat wave. It is exactly what a vet will ask for.

If you are not sure where to begin, the Chicken Doctor lets you describe what you see and works through likely causes with you.

First moves for any sick bird

  • Move her to a quiet, warm, draft-free spot away from the flock, with her own food and water.
  • Check her crop, vent, feet, eyes and breathing. Look under the feathers for mites and wounds.
  • Look at her droppings once she is alone, so you know which ones are hers.
  • Wash your hands and change shoes before you go back to the healthy birds.

Problems you must report

Some diseases are a legal matter, not just a flock matter. If several birds die suddenly, or you see swollen purple combs, twisted necks, heavy breathing and a crash in laying all at once, call your state veterinarian or extension office before you do anything else. That covers avian influenza and Newcastle disease,.

Prevention beats treatment

Keep new birds apart from your flock for about a month before mixing, keep wild birds away from feed and water, and do not share equipment with other flocks. The small flock biosecurity guide walks through the basics.

Common questions about chicken diseases

How do I find out what killed my chicken?

Ask your state animal diagnostic lab about a necropsy. Keep the body cool in a fridge, not the freezer, and call them quickly. It is the most reliable way to protect the rest of the flock.

Can I eat eggs from a sick hen?

Play it safe and do not, until you know what she has. If she is on any medication, check the product label or ask a vet about the withdrawal period.

Do I need a vet who sees chickens?

It helps a lot. Look for an avian or poultry vet, or ask your extension office who in your area will see backyard birds. Find one before you need one.
98:
What to do when the soft shell eggs keep coming

One rubbery egg is usually nothing. A run of them from the same hen, or several hens at once, is worth a closer look. Here is a simple order to work through.

  1. Figure out who is laying them. Check the roost area and nest boxes early in the morning, since soft eggs are often dropped overnight.
  2. Check the feed. Layer feed should be most of what they eat. If treats and scratch make up a big share, calcium gets diluted.
  3. Put out oyster shell in a separate dish so each hen takes what she needs. The grit and oyster shell guide explains why it goes on the side, not mixed in.
  4. Look for stress. Heat, a predator scare, new birds and moving coops can all throw off a few eggs.
  5. Watch the hen herself. Is she eating, active, and passing normal droppings?

When it stops being a feed problem

If a hen is straining, pumping her tail, sitting fluffed up, or walking like a penguin, a soft egg may be stuck inside her. That is closer to egg binding and needs action today. If soft shells show up across the flock along with sneezing or rattly breathing, a respiratory virus like infectious bronchitis may be behind it, and a vet visit or lab test makes sense.

Eating soft shell eggs

The shell is the egg's main barrier against bacteria. A soft or broken egg that has sat in bedding or droppings should go in the compost, not the kitchen. A clean one collected right away is a judgment call, but most keepers toss them to be safe.

Common questions about soft shell eggs

Is a soft shell egg normal for a new layer?

Yes, it is common in the first weeks of laying while her system settles. If it keeps going past a few weeks, check feed and calcium.

Can too much calcium cause problems?

Yes. Layer feed is too rich in calcium for chicks and roosters. Offering oyster shell free choice lets hens take what they need without forcing it on everyone.

Why does my hen eat her soft eggs?

Soft eggs break easily, and once hens taste egg some start breaking good ones too. Collect often and fix the shell problem to stop the habit forming.
99:
How to read an odd egg before you worry

Every flock lays a strange egg now and then. Before you panic, ask three questions. Is it one egg or a pattern? Is it one hen or many? And does the hen who laid it look and act healthy? A single odd egg from a bright, busy hen is almost always a hiccup. A pattern across the flock, or an odd egg from a hen who is fluffed up and quiet, is when you look deeper.

Odd eggs that are almost always harmless

  • Double yolks and tiny fairy eggs, mostly from new layers.
  • Blood spots and meat spots, which are cosmetic.
  • Green rings on hard boiled yolks, which come from cooking, not the hen.

Odd eggs that point to feed, age or stress

Thin, soft and missing shells, wrinkles and strange shapes usually trace back to calcium, heat, age or a fright. Fixing the diet and the setup clears most of these up within a few weeks.

Odd eggs that can mean illness

If wrinkled shells, watery whites and a drop in laying show up together, especially with sneezing or coughing, a respiratory virus may be moving through the flock. Check the sneezing page and consider calling a poultry vet. Blood on the shell along with a hen who keeps straining or has tissue showing at the vent needs a look the same day.

Keep a simple egg log

Write down the date, the hen if you know her, and what was odd. It takes ten seconds and turns a vague worry into a pattern you can actually act on.

Common questions about egg problems

Are weird looking eggs safe to eat?

Most are, as long as the shell is intact and clean and the egg smells normal. Toss cracked, dirty or soft eggs, and anything from a hen on medication unless the label or a vet says it is fine.

Why are all my hens laying odd eggs at once?

Something shared is the likely cause. Think feed, heat, a stressful event or an illness moving through the flock.

Do older hens lay more odd eggs?

Yes. As hens age, eggs tend to get larger with thinner shells, and shape problems become more common.
101:
Checking the hen behind a shell-less egg

A naked egg, just the membrane with no shell at all, usually turns up under the roost in the morning. Most hens lay one now and then. What matters is how the hen looks and whether it keeps happening.

A quick hands-on check

  • Pick her up and feel her belly between the legs. It should feel soft, not hard, hot or full of fluid.
  • Look at the vent. It should be moist and clean, with no tissue poking out and no crusty discharge.
  • Watch her for an hour. Straining, tail pumping or standing upright like a penguin are warning signs.
  • Check that she is eating and drinking.

When to call a vet

A shell-less egg that breaks inside a hen can lead to infection. If she seems stuck, has a swollen belly, or goes off food, read the egg binding and egg yolk peritonitis pages and get her to an avian or poultry vet. Repeated shell-less eggs from one hen over weeks also deserve a vet's opinion.

Fixing the usual causes

Make sure layer feed is the main diet, offer oyster shell on the side, and cut back treats. Give shade and cool water in hot weather. Keep the coop calm, since a fright at night can cause a hen to drop an egg before the shell is made. Young pullets often sort themselves out within a few weeks.

What about the egg?

Throw it out. With no shell, bacteria from the droppings board get straight to the contents.

Common questions about shell-less eggs

Why are shell-less eggs found under the roost?

The egg moved through too fast or was released early, often overnight, so it drops while she sleeps.

Can stress cause naked eggs?

Yes. Predators, heat, moving and new flock mates can all disrupt shell making for a few days.

Should I give my hen calcium?

Oyster shell free choice is safe for laying hens. For anything stronger, ask a vet.
102:
Making thin shells stronger again

Thin shells crack in the nest, get eaten, and let bacteria in. The fix is usually slow and boring, which is good news. Most of it comes down to feed, age and heat.

Step by step

  1. Check what is in the feeder. A complete layer feed should be the bulk of the diet, with treats kept small.
  2. Offer oyster shell in its own dish. Hens need extra calcium on days they lay.
  3. Look at the age of the hen. Hens in their second or third year often lay bigger eggs with less shell per egg.
  4. Think about the weather. Hot weather and heavy panting are linked to thinner shells, so give shade, airflow and cool water.
  5. Give it time. Shell quality takes a few weeks to respond to diet changes.

When thin shells point to something more

If a hen also has a pale comb, poor appetite or droppings that look off, look past feed. Internal worms and mites both pull condition down, and a pale comb is covered on the pale comb page. If many birds have thin or wrinkled shells and some are sneezing, a virus like infectious bronchitis is worth ruling out with a vet.

The rest of the flock

Thin shells break, and a broken egg teaches hens to eat eggs. Collect at least twice a day while you work on it, and add a little extra bedding to the nest boxes to cushion them.

Eating thin shell eggs

An intact, clean thin shell egg is fine to eat. Use it soon and throw out any that are cracked.

Common questions about thin shell eggs

Do eggshells fed back to hens help?

They can add calcium if dried and crushed so they do not look like eggs. Oyster shell is easier and more consistent.

Can a rooster cause thin shells?

No. Roosters do not affect shell quality, though mating can stress some hens.

Is vitamin D important for shells?

Yes. Hens need it to use calcium. Complete layer feed includes it, and sunlight helps too.
103:
What to do about wrinkled eggs from your flock

A wrinkled or wavy egg means something disturbed the hen while the shell was forming. That can be as simple as a loud night or as serious as a virus. The useful thing is to find out which, and that mostly comes down to how many eggs, how many hens, and how they look.

Start with a few quick checks

  1. Count. Is this one egg this month, or several a week?
  2. Match the egg to the hen if you can. Shell color, size and nest box habits help.
  3. Listen to the flock at dusk. Sneezing, gurgling or rattly breathing on the roost is a big clue.
  4. Look at the inside. Crack one wrinkled egg and see if the white is thin and runny.
  5. Think back over the last week. Predators, a move, new birds, heat or a fight in the pecking order all count.

One hen, now and then

If one hen lays the odd wrinkled egg and is otherwise bright and eating, it is almost always stress or age. Older hens lay more odd shells. Two eggs passing through close together can also bump each other and leave ripples. Keep her calm, keep layer feed as the main diet, and offer oyster shell on the side.

Several hens, plus watery whites

Wrinkled shells across the flock, especially with watery whites and a drop in laying, fit infectious bronchitis. Hens that had it young can lay poor shells for life even after they seem fine. Compare what you see with watery egg whites, then call a poultry vet or your extension office about testing. A lab answer helps you decide about vaccinating future chicks.

When it is urgent

Wrinkled eggs on their own are not an emergency. It becomes urgent if a hen is gasping, struggling to breathe, or birds start dying. Sudden deaths with breathing trouble and a crash in laying should be reported to your state veterinarian, since bird flu and Newcastle disease can start this way.

Prevention

  • Keep new birds apart for about a month before they join the flock.
  • Buy chicks from clean, tested sources, and ask about vaccines.
  • Keep wild birds out of feeders and waterers.
  • Give enough space and nest boxes so hens are not shoving each other.

What it means for eating the eggs

A wrinkled egg with an intact shell is safe to eat if it was collected clean and smells normal. Wrinkled shells are often thinner and crack more easily, so check them carefully and use them first. Toss any that are cracked.

Common questions about wrinkled eggs

Are wrinkled eggs a sign of disease?

Sometimes. A single one usually is not. A pattern across the flock, especially with breathing signs, can point to infectious bronchitis.

Will my hen go back to normal eggs?

If stress caused it, usually within a few weeks. If a virus damaged her oviduct, the shells may stay rough for good.

Can I hatch wrinkled eggs?

It is not a good idea. Shell problems affect moisture loss in the incubator and hatch rates tend to be poor.
104:
When a misshapen egg needs a second look

Round eggs, long torpedo eggs, eggs with a flat side, eggs with a ridge around the middle. Most of these come from a hen whose shell gland was a little off that day. A few are worth paying attention to. Here is how to sort them.

What to check today

  • Is the hen acting normal? Eating, scratching, and joining the flock at the feeder.
  • Is her belly soft? Feel between the legs. Hard, hot or swollen is a warning sign.
  • Is her vent clean and moist, with nothing poking out?
  • Are other hens laying odd shapes too?

If the answer is yes, yes, yes and no, you can relax and watch.

Common, harmless causes

New layers often lay odd shapes for their first few weeks. Older hens do it more as the years go by. A scare at night can make a hen hold an egg a little too long, which flattens a side or adds a band of extra shell. Crowding in the nest box and hens fighting over one favorite box can do it too.

How to tell this apart from other problems

If odd shapes come with wrinkled shells and watery whites across several birds, read wrinkled eggs, since a virus could be the real cause. If shapes are odd and shells are also thin or rubbery, look at calcium first on the thin shell eggs page. If the hen is straining and nothing is coming out, that is a different problem, covered under egg binding.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if a hen lays deformed eggs for weeks, if she seems sore when she squats, or if she gets a swollen belly or stops eating. Repeated very large or oddly shaped eggs can strain the vent and sometimes lead to prolapse.

Prevention

  • Plenty of nest boxes, kept dark and clean.
  • Layer feed as the main diet with oyster shell on the side.
  • Keep the coop secure so predators are not rattling the walls at night.
  • Avoid big changes when you can, like moving coops in the middle of laying season.

Rest of the flock and the eggs

One hen laying odd shapes says nothing about the others. Misshapen eggs are safe to eat when the shell is whole and clean. They do not fit cartons well and the shell is sometimes weaker at the odd spot, so check for hairline cracks.

Common questions about misshapen eggs

Why is my chicken laying long pointy eggs?

Usually the shell gland or the timing of the egg's trip was a little off. It is common in new layers and older hens.

Are misshapen eggs good for hatching?

Not really. Odd shapes tend to hatch poorly, so pick normal eggs for the incubator.

Can stress really change egg shape?

Yes. A fright can make a hen hold an egg longer, which leaves flat sides or extra bands of shell.
105:
Meat spots and what they mean in your kitchen

A meat spot is a small brown or reddish speck in the white or on the yolk. It is usually a bit of tissue that came loose inside the hen as the egg formed, or an old blood spot that has turned brown. It looks odd, but it is not a sign that the egg is bad or that the hen is sick.

What to do with the egg

  1. Crack eggs into a small bowl first, not straight into the pan or batter.
  2. If you see a spot, lift it out with the tip of a spoon or a piece of shell.
  3. Check the egg smells normal and the yolk and white look fresh.
  4. Cook it as usual.

If the idea bothers you, toss it or feed it cooked to your dog. There is no food safety reason you have to.

How to tell a meat spot from something else

A bright red spot is more likely a fresh blood spot, covered on the blood spots in eggs page. A green, black or fuzzy patch is not a meat spot at all. That is spoilage or mold, and the egg should go straight in the trash. A pink or iridescent white can mean bacterial spoilage too. A green ring on a hard boiled yolk is just cooking, and has nothing to do with the hen.

Are some hens more likely to have them?

Meat spots seem to show up more often in brown eggs, partly because they are harder to spot when commercial eggs are candled. Some individual hens lay them more often than others. Stress and age can play a part. Commercial eggs are candled to catch most of these before they reach the store, which is why many people never see one until they keep chickens.

When it might matter

A meat spot by itself is not a reason to call a vet. Pay more attention if the same hen also has blood on her shells, a hard or swollen belly, keeps straining, or seems quiet and off her food. Those signs point to a reproductive problem, and the egg yolk peritonitis page explains what to watch for.

Prevention, as far as it goes

  • Keep stress low with a secure coop and enough space.
  • Feed a complete layer feed rather than mostly scratch and scraps.
  • Avoid handling hens roughly when they are about to lay.

You cannot prevent every spot, and you do not need to.

The rest of the flock

Meat spots are not contagious and do not point to a flock-wide problem. If you start seeing lots of them along with other changes in eggs, like thin shells or watery whites, look at the whole picture on the egg problems overview.

Common questions about meat spots in eggs

Is it safe to eat an egg with a meat spot?

Yes. Remove the spot if you like and cook the egg normally.

Does a meat spot mean the egg was fertilized?

No. A fertile egg shows a small white bullseye on the yolk, not a brown speck.

Why do I see more meat spots in brown eggs?

They tend to be more common in brown eggs and are harder to see when candling a dark shell, so more slip through.
106:
Blood spots and when to look closer at your hen

A blood spot is a small red dot on the yolk or in the white. It happens when a tiny blood vessel breaks as the yolk is released. It is cosmetic, it is common, and on its own it does not mean your hen is sick. Still, there are a few things worth checking if you start seeing a lot of them.

What to do with the egg

Crack eggs into a separate bowl. If you see a spot, scoop it out with a spoon and cook the egg as usual. The egg is fine to eat. If the spot is large and the white is pink throughout, or the egg smells off, throw it out instead.

If one hen keeps doing it

  1. Figure out which hen it is by shell color or by checking nests through the day.
  2. Look at her stress level. Is she low in the pecking order, being chased, or startled at night?
  3. Check the feed. Hens on a mostly scratch or kitchen scrap diet may miss vitamins they get from complete layer feed, and vitamin A is often mentioned in connection with blood spots.
  4. Look her over for mites. Check around the vent and under the wings, especially at night with a flashlight.
  5. Watch how she acts. Bright and eating is reassuring.

How to tell this apart from other problems

Blood inside the egg is not the same as blood on the outside of the shell. Streaks of blood on the shell come from the vent and have their own causes, covered on blood on egg shells. A brown speck is usually a meat spot, which is just as harmless. Blood in the droppings is a separate health issue altogether, and it is worth reading the bloody droppings page if you see that.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if a hen has blood spots along with a pale comb, weight loss, lethargy, or bleeding anywhere else. Those point to something more than a broken vessel. A one-off spot in an otherwise healthy flock needs no vet visit.

Prevention

  • Feed a complete layer ration as the main diet.
  • Keep the coop secure so night predators do not panic the flock.
  • Give enough room so lower hens are not constantly chased.
  • Handle laying hens gently.

Selling or giving away eggs

If you share eggs, candling with a bright flashlight in a dark room catches most spots. Some people are put off by them even though they are safe, so it is worth checking before eggs leave your kitchen.

Common questions about blood spots in eggs

Does a blood spot mean the egg is fertilized?

No. A blood spot is from a burst vessel. Fertile eggs look the same as infertile ones unless they have been incubated.

Are blood spots more common in young hens?

They can show up in new layers and in older hens. Stress at any age makes them more likely.

Can I stop my hens from laying blood spots?

You can reduce them with good feed and low stress, but some hens will still lay the occasional one.
107:
What double yolks mean for your hen and your eggs

A double yolk happens when a hen releases two yolks close together and they end up wrapped in one shell. It is mostly a sign of a young hen whose cycle has not settled yet, or a heavy breed that lays big eggs. For most flocks it is a fun surprise, not a problem. There are a few things to keep an eye on, though.

Check the hen if the eggs are huge

Double yolk eggs are big, and big eggs are harder to pass. After a hen lays a very large egg, take a minute to look at her.

  • Look at the vent. A little blood on the shell is common with big eggs. Tissue sticking out of the vent is not.
  • Watch her for straining, tail pumping or sitting in the nest for hours without laying.
  • Make sure she is eating, drinking and moving normally afterwards.

How to tell this apart from a problem

If a hen lays one huge egg and then acts normal, she is fine. If she strains for a long time and nothing comes out, read egg bound right away. If pink or red tissue is showing at the vent after a big egg, that is a vent prolapse and she needs to be separated from the flock so others do not peck at it. Blood smears on the shell without any other signs are covered on blood on egg shells.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet the same day if a hen has a prolapse that does not go back in or looks dark or dry, if she is straining and cannot pass an egg, or if she becomes weak and fluffed up. These can turn serious fast.

Why it happens more in some flocks

Pullets in their first months of laying are the most common source. Some heavier, high-production breeds lay more double yolks than lighter breeds. Things that push a hen to ovulate fast, like adding bright light suddenly, can make them more likely too. Hens tend to lay fewer as they settle into a steady rhythm.

Prevention, if you want fewer

  • Let pullets start laying on their own schedule, not with sudden extra lighting.
  • Feed a complete layer ration rather than a high-energy treat-heavy diet.
  • Keep hens at a healthy weight. Overweight hens have more laying problems in general.

Eating and hatching double yolks

Double yolk eggs are perfectly safe to eat. Count them as about one and a half eggs in baking. They are not good for hatching. Two chicks rarely develop in one shell, and there is usually not enough room or air for either to survive.

Common questions about double yolk eggs

Is a double yolk egg a sign of twins?

It could hold two embryos if fertile, but twin chicks almost never hatch from one egg.

Do double yolk eggs hurt the hen?

They can strain the vent because they are large. Most hens pass them fine, but watch for straining or prolapse.

Will my hen keep laying double yolks?

Usually not for long. They tend to fade as a young hen's cycle settles down.
108:
When a fairy egg is fine and when it is not

A fairy egg is a tiny egg, sometimes no bigger than a grape, and it often has no yolk inside. Keepers also call them wind eggs or fart eggs. They happen when a small bit of tissue or white sets off the egg making process without a yolk. In most flocks they are a one-off and nothing to worry about.

Who usually lays them

  • Pullets just starting to lay, while their system finds its rhythm.
  • Hens coming back into lay after a molt or a winter break.
  • Hens near the end of their laying season.
  • Bantams, whose normal eggs are small anyway. Do not mistake a normal bantam egg for a fairy egg.

What to check if they keep coming

  1. Work out which hen is laying them. Watch the nest boxes or note the shell color.
  2. Look at her overall condition. Feel the keel bone for weight loss and check the comb color.
  3. Check for mites and lice around the vent and under the wings.
  4. Look at her droppings and appetite.
  5. Review the feed. A complete layer ration should be most of the diet.

How to tell this apart from other problems

A small egg with a thin or rubbery shell points more to calcium or stress, covered on soft shell eggs. A hen who lays tiny eggs and then stops laying altogether, while looking quiet and losing weight, may have a reproductive or internal problem. The not laying eggs page walks through that side. If a hen's belly is swollen or feels like it holds fluid, that is a vet visit, not a wait-and-see.

When to call a vet

One or two fairy eggs from a healthy hen need no vet. Call an avian or poultry vet if a hen lays only tiny eggs for weeks, if she seems sick, or if she is straining often. Older hens with ongoing laying trouble sometimes have tumors or infections of the reproductive tract that only a vet can sort out.

Prevention

You cannot prevent the odd fairy egg, especially from new layers. You can make them less likely by keeping stress low, feeding a balanced layer ration, controlling mites, and letting pullets start laying at their natural age rather than pushing them with sudden extra light.

The flock and the egg itself

Fairy eggs are not contagious and do not mean the rest of the flock is unwell. A clean, intact fairy egg is safe to eat, though there is not much in it. Many keepers save them as a keepsake. They will not hatch, since there is no yolk to feed a chick.

Common questions about fairy eggs

Why is there no yolk in my tiny egg?

The egg making process started without a yolk being released, so the hen built a small egg around a bit of white or tissue.

Are fairy eggs a sign my hen is about to start laying?

Often, yes. Many pullets lay one or two before regular eggs begin.

Is it bad luck to get a fairy egg?

Old folklore said so, but it is just a normal hiccup in egg production.
109:
Sorting out watery whites at home

A runny white that spreads across the pan can come from the egg, the hen, or how the egg was stored. Most of the time it is about age, of either the egg or the hen. Sometimes it points to an illness in the flock. Here is how to tell which.

Check the egg first

  1. How old is it? Whites thin out as eggs age, faster at room temperature than in the fridge.
  2. Where was it stored? A warm counter in summer ages eggs quickly.
  3. Crack a fresh one. Collect an egg straight from the nest and crack it within the hour. If that white stands up nicely, storage was the issue.
  4. Do a float test. A fresh egg sinks and lies flat. One that stands on end is older. One that floats should be thrown out.

Then check the hen

If even fresh eggs have watery whites, look at who is laying them. Hens in their second or third year and beyond tend to lay eggs with thinner whites. That is normal aging and not a health problem.

How to tell this apart from illness

Watery whites across several hens, together with wrinkled or thin shells and a drop in laying, fit infectious bronchitis. You may also hear sneezing or rattly breathing on the roost at night. Compare with wrinkled eggs, and if both are showing up, talk to a poultry vet or your extension office about testing. Hens infected young can lay poor quality eggs for life, so knowing for sure helps you plan.

When it is urgent

Watery whites are never an emergency on their own. It is urgent if birds are gasping, have swollen faces, or start dying. Sudden deaths with breathing signs should be reported to your state veterinarian.

Prevention

  • Collect eggs at least once a day, more often in hot weather.
  • Store eggs in the fridge if you want them to keep their quality longest.
  • Keep new birds apart for about a month before adding them.
  • Feed a complete layer ration. Poor nutrition affects egg quality overall.

Eating eggs with watery whites

A watery white on its own does not make an egg unsafe. If the egg sank in water, smells normal and the shell was clean and uncracked, it is fine to eat. Runny whites are harder to poach and fry neatly, so use those eggs for scrambling or baking.

Common questions about watery egg whites

Why are my farm fresh eggs runny?

Check how long they sat before you cracked them and where. If even fresh eggs are runny, the hen's age or a past illness is likely.

Do older hens lay runnier eggs?

Yes. White quality tends to drop as hens get older.

Does the fridge keep whites firm?

It slows the thinning a lot compared with leaving eggs on the counter.
110:
Why the green ring is a kitchen issue, not a chicken issue

The gray-green ring around a hard boiled yolk comes from cooking. When an egg is heated for a long time, sulfur from the white reacts with iron in the yolk and leaves a thin dark layer where they meet. It has nothing to do with your hen's health, her feed or the freshness of the egg in the way most people think. That is good news for worried keepers.

How to stop it next time

  1. Do not boil eggs hard for a long time. Bring the water to a boil, then lower the heat or turn it off and let the eggs sit covered.
  2. Time it. Overcooking is the main cause.
  3. Cool them fast. Move eggs straight into cold or ice water when they are done.
  4. Peel and eat or chill them soon after cooling.

Very fresh eggs can be harder to peel, so many keepers set aside eggs that are a week or two old for boiling.

How to tell this apart from a real problem

A green ring only shows up after cooking. If a raw egg has green, black or fuzzy patches, that is spoilage or mold, and the egg should be thrown out. A green tinted raw yolk is usually from diet, since some plants and feeds can shift yolk color. If your hens lay eggs with odd insides, like blood spots or watery whites, those have their own causes.

Yolk color in general

Yolk color comes mostly from what the hen eats. Free-range hens eating greens and bugs often lay darker orange yolks. Hens on mostly grain feed lay paler yellow ones. Neither color means the egg is more or less healthy to eat, and a pale yolk is not a sign of disease on its own. A sudden change across the flock usually tracks a change in feed or season.

Is there ever a reason to call a vet?

Not for a green ring. If you are seeing problems with the hen herself, like poor appetite, a pale comb or odd droppings, look at those signs separately. The Chicken Doctor can help you work through symptoms.

What it means for eating the egg

A green ring is safe to eat. Some people notice a slightly sulfur taste or a chalky texture in overcooked yolks, but there is no harm in it. If the egg was stored properly and smelled normal when you peeled it, go ahead.

A note on storing boiled eggs

Once boiled, eggs lose their natural protective coating, so keep them in the fridge and use them within about a week. Do not leave boiled eggs sitting out at room temperature for hours.

Common questions about green rings around yolks

Is a green yolk ring safe to eat?

Yes. It is a harmless reaction between sulfur and iron caused by long cooking.

Do fresh eggs get green rings too?

Yes, any egg can if it is overcooked. Freshness is not the main factor.

Can feed make the yolk green?

Some feeds and plants can tint a raw yolk, which is different from the cooked ring. If you are unsure about a raw yolk, toss it.
111:
Checking your hen after you find blood on a shell

A smear or streak of blood on the outside of an egg comes from the hen's vent, not from inside the egg. The most common reason is simple. A young hen or a hen laying a big egg stretched a little too much and a tiny vessel tore. It heals on its own. Still, blood on the shell is a cue to look at the hen, because a few causes need quick action.

What to do right now

  1. Find the hen. Check who was in the nest, or look for a hen with a damp or reddish vent area.
  2. Look at the vent in good light. It should be moist and pink, with no tissue hanging out and no open wound.
  3. Check for pecking. Other hens are drawn to red, and a small spot can turn into a wound fast.
  4. Look for mites around the vent. Heavy mite loads can leave the skin scabby and sore.
  5. Watch her over the next few eggs.

How to tell this apart from more serious problems

If tissue is pushing out of the vent and not going back in, that is a vent prolapse. Separate her right away so the others cannot peck at it. If the blood is on the shell along with fresh blood in her droppings, that is a different issue, often coccidiosis in younger birds. If hens are pecking each other's vents, read cannibalism and feather pecking, since this can spiral quickly.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if there is a prolapse that will not stay in, if tissue looks dark, dry or damaged, if there is a deep wound, or if the hen keeps bleeding egg after egg. Ongoing bleeding with a pale comb and weakness also needs a vet.

Supportive care

  • Keep the hen apart in a quiet, clean space if she has any open wound.
  • Clean the area gently with plain saline or clean warm water.
  • Keep her calm and dim. Less light means less laying pressure and less pecking.
  • Offer layer feed and fresh water, with oyster shell on the side.

Prevention

Let pullets come into lay naturally rather than pushing them with sudden extra light. Keep hens at a healthy weight. Control mites. Give enough space so bored hens are not picking at each other.

The eggs and your own hygiene

An egg with a little blood on the shell is safe once cleaned, as long as the shell is intact. Wipe it off or wash it in water warmer than the egg, then refrigerate it. Wash your hands after handling eggs and hens, since chickens can carry salmonella on their feathers and skin even when they look healthy.

Common questions about blood on egg shells

Is blood on the eggshell normal?

A small streak now and then is common, especially from new layers. Repeated or heavy bleeding is not.

Can I eat an egg with blood on the shell?

Yes, if the shell is intact. Clean it, refrigerate it and wash your hands.

Why do my hens peck at a bleeding hen?

Chickens are drawn to red and to wounds. Separate her until she heals.
112:
Keeping eggs clean and safe in a backyard coop

Dirty eggs are mostly a coop setup problem, not a hen problem. Mud from the run, droppings in the nest, and broken eggs smearing the others are the usual causes. Fixing those is easier than washing every egg. But if the dirt is mostly runny droppings, it is worth checking the hens too.

Fixing the nest boxes and coop

  1. Keep nest boxes lower than the roost bars, so hens sleep on the roost and not in the nests.
  2. Block nest boxes at night if hens keep sleeping in them.
  3. Add fresh, dry bedding often. Straw, shavings or pads all work if they are kept clean.
  4. Collect eggs at least once a day, twice in muddy or hot weather.
  5. Add gravel, sand or a mat at the coop door so muddy feet get wiped before the nest.
  6. Remove any broken egg right away and replace the bedding under it.

The roosts and nest boxes guide covers spacing and heights.

When dirty eggs point to a health problem

If eggs are coated in watery or stained droppings, look at the hens. Runny droppings stuck to the vent feathers can mean diarrhea or an infection. Read watery droppings if you see loose stool, and vent gleet if a hen has a crusty, smelly vent. Heat can also cause watery droppings because hens drink more.

To wash or not to wash

Eggs come out with a natural coating called the bloom that helps keep bacteria out. Many keepers leave clean eggs unwashed and store them that way. For lightly soiled eggs, dry brush or gently wipe the spot. If you need to wash, use running water that is warmer than the egg, never cold, and never soak them, since that can pull bacteria through the shell. Dry them and refrigerate them after washing. Once washed, keep them in the fridge.

Which eggs to throw out

  • Cracked eggs, especially if they sat in dirty bedding.
  • Eggs that are heavily coated in droppings.
  • Eggs of unknown age found in a hidden nest. Float test them and toss any that float.

Protecting yourself and your family

Healthy chickens can carry salmonella on their feathers, feet and eggshells. Wash your hands with soap after collecting eggs or handling birds. Keep egg collection baskets and coop boots out of the kitchen. Cook eggs fully for young children, older adults and anyone with a weak immune system.

Common questions about dirty eggs

Should I wash fresh eggs before storing them?

Many keepers do not, if eggs are clean. If you do wash them, use warm water and refrigerate them afterwards.

Can I eat eggs with poop on them?

Lightly soiled eggs with intact shells can be cleaned and eaten. Heavily soiled or cracked eggs should be thrown out.

Why are my eggs suddenly dirty?

Check for hens sleeping in nests, wet bedding, a muddy run, or a hen with runny droppings.
113:
Working out why your hen stopped laying

Most hens that stop laying are not sick. They are molting, broody, short on daylight, or simply getting older. The trick is ruling out the few causes that do need help. Work through this in order.

Rule out the normal reasons first

  • Daylight. Laying slows hard in fall and winter as days get shorter.
  • Molt. Feathers on the floor and a scruffy hen usually mean a laying break of several weeks. See the annual molt for what to expect.
  • Broodiness. A hen who sits flat in the nest, growls and puffs up is focused on hatching, not laying.
  • Age. Hens lay less each year after their first couple of seasons.
  • Hidden nest. Free-range hens are good at laying in a bush you have never checked.

Then look at the hen

Pick her up. Check her weight by feeling the keel bone, look under feathers near the vent for mites and lice, and look at the comb. A pale shrunken comb in spring, a swollen belly, or a hen standing upright and still all suggest a health problem. The not laying symptom page covers the health side in more detail.

When to call a vet

Call if she stops eating, has a swollen or squishy belly, keeps straining, or the whole flock stops laying at once with sneezing or odd droppings. A sudden flock-wide drop with deaths is something to report to your state veterinarian.

Helping her get back on track

Keep layer feed as the main diet, cut back treats, and add protein during molt. If you add light in winter, add it in the morning and keep it consistent.

Common questions about a hen that stopped laying

How long does a laying break from molting last?

Usually several weeks, sometimes a couple of months. Laying returns once feathers grow back.

Will she ever lay again?

If the cause is daylight, molt or broodiness, yes. Older hens may lay only a few each season.

Does stress stop laying?

Yes. Moving, predators and new birds can pause laying for a week or two.
116:
What to do when a chicken starts sneezing

One sneeze after a dust bath is nothing. A bird who keeps sneezing for a day or two, or several birds sneezing at once, deserves attention. Respiratory infections spread fast and some leave birds as lifelong carriers.

Today, in this order

  1. Separate the sneezing bird into a clean, draft-free pen.
  2. Look at her face. Clear or cloudy discharge from the nostrils, bubbles in the eye or a swollen face all matter.
  3. Smell near the nostrils. A foul smell is a strong clue.
  4. Check the coop air. Strong ammonia, dusty bedding and poor airflow cause sneezing on their own.
  5. Listen to the whole flock on the roost at dusk.

How to tell causes apart

Dust or ammonia sneezing usually clears once you change the bedding and open up vents, and the birds stay bright. Bubbly eyes with sneezing point to mycoplasma. A smelly swollen face suggests infectious coryza. Sneezing that turns into gasping or rattling is covered under wheezing.

When to call for help

Call a poultry vet if breathing becomes noisy, the face swells, or birds stop eating. If several birds get sick quickly and some die, call your state veterinarian or extension office right away, because avian influenza and Newcastle disease must be reported.

Supportive care

Keep her warm but in fresh air, with clean water and feed she will eat. Wipe discharge with a damp cloth. Do not use human cold products.

Flock and eggs

Hold off adding or selling birds until you know the cause. If a vet prescribes treatment, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal.

Common questions about chicken sneezing

Is it normal for chickens to sneeze sometimes?

Yes, an occasional sneeze from dust is normal. Constant sneezing is not.

Can a sneezing chicken infect people?

Most common chicken colds do not infect people. Still wash your hands after handling sick birds, and report sudden flock deaths.

Will my chicken get better on its own?

Dust-related sneezing usually does. Infections may linger or come back, so ask a vet.
117:
A coughing chicken, what to check first

A chicken cough sounds like a short hack, sometimes with a head shake. It almost always means something is irritating the airway, from dust and ammonia to a virus. Coughing that comes with blood or gasping is serious.

Step by step

  • Move the bird to a quiet, clean, well-ventilated pen.
  • Look inside the beak with a flashlight. Yellow patches in the mouth or throat can be wet fowl pox or a fungal problem.
  • Check for bloody mucus on her beak, feathers or the walls. That points strongly to laryngotracheitis (ILT).
  • Check the coop for dust, mold and ammonia smell.
  • Count how many birds are coughing.

When it is an emergency

Stretching the neck to breathe, gasping with the beak open, or coughing up blood needs a vet the same day. Many states treat ILT as a reportable disease, and avian influenza and Newcastle disease must be reported. If birds are dying, call your state veterinarian or extension office. A necropsy at a state lab is the surest way to know.

Look-alikes

Gurgling and rattling are covered under wheezing. Head shaking without coughing can be mites in the ears or something stuck in the mouth.

Helping her through

Keep her calm and in fresh air. Offer water and soft feed. Do not try to clear her throat with your fingers, as you can push things deeper.

Flock and eggs

Do not bring in new birds or take birds to shows while anyone is coughing. If you use any medication, check the product label or ask a vet about eating eggs.

Common questions about chicken coughing

Why does my chicken cough at night?

Dust and ammonia build up in a closed coop at night. Improve ventilation. If it continues, look for infection.

Can chickens cough from a cold?

Chickens do not get the human cold, but they get several respiratory infections that cause coughing.

Is a coughing chicken contagious?

Often, yes. Separate her until you know the cause.
119:
Helping a chicken with rattly or wheezing breath

Rattling, gurgling or a whistle when a chicken breathes means fluid or mucus in the airway. It is louder at night on the roost. This is more serious than a sneeze and needs quick action.

Do these things now

  1. Separate the bird into a warm, dry, well-ventilated space. Fresh air matters more than warmth.
  2. Watch her breathe. Tail bobbing and open-beak breathing mean she is working hard.
  3. Look for bubbly eyes, nasal discharge or a swollen face.
  4. Check the bedding and feed for mold. Moldy material can cause aspergillosis, especially in chicks.
  5. Listen to every bird on the roost tonight.

Telling it apart

Wheezing with foamy eyes often fits mycoplasma. Rattles with watery whites and wrinkled eggs fit infectious bronchitis. Gasping with bloody mucus points to ILT. Heat stress causes heavy panting, but panting is fast and silent, not rattly. See coughing for more.

When to call

Call a poultry vet the same day for open-beak breathing at rest. If several birds get sick fast or start dying, contact your state veterinarian or extension office. Avian influenza and Newcastle disease are reportable, and fast reporting protects your neighbors' flocks too.

Supportive care

Offer water she can reach easily and feed she likes. Keep stress low. Do not use human vapor rubs or oils near her face.

The flock and the eggs

Some birds that recover stay carriers. Talk to a vet about testing before you add new birds. Check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal for any treatment.

Protect yourself

Wash your hands and change your shoes after caring for sick birds, especially before visiting other flocks.

Common questions about chicken wheezing

Why does my chicken sound gurgly?

Fluid in the airway, usually from infection. It is worth a vet visit.

Is wheezing in chickens always disease?

Not always. Dust and ammonia can cause it, but infection is common.

Can I give my wheezing chicken antibiotics from the feed store?

Ask a vet first. Many respiratory problems are viral, and the wrong product can harm her or affect the eggs.
122:
What to do when a chicken stands still and fluffed up

A chicken that stands hunched with fluffed feathers, eyes half shut and no interest in food is telling you she feels bad. Chickens hide illness well, so by the time you see this, she may be fairly sick. Lethargy is not a diagnosis. It is a cue to look closely.

A quick head to tail check

  • Crop. Feel it in the morning. It should be empty. Hard, squishy or swollen is a lead.
  • Belly. Feel between the legs. Swollen or fluid-filled can mean an egg problem.
  • Vent. Look for a stuck egg, a prolapse or crusty discharge.
  • Comb. Pale suggests blood loss or anemia. Purple can mean poor circulation.
  • Feathers. Part them for mites and lice, and check for hidden wounds.
  • Droppings. Note color and consistency once she is alone.

Look-alikes

Standing upright like a penguin with tail down points toward egg binding or peritonitis. Fluffed up with bloody droppings in a young bird often means coccidiosis. Panting with wings held out is heat stress.

When it is urgent

Lethargy with no eating or drinking for a day, labored breathing or collapse means call a vet now. Several lethargic birds at once, or sudden deaths, should be reported to your state veterinarian.

Supportive care

Keep her warm, quiet and dim, with water close by. Offer layer feed mixed with a little water. Electrolytes made for poultry can help. See the first aid kit list.

Flock and eggs

Hold off on eating her eggs until you know what is wrong, and check the product label or ask a vet if she is treated.

Common questions about a lethargic chicken

Why is my chicken just standing in one spot?

She is likely ill or in pain. Do a full check and isolate her.

Can heat make chickens lethargic?

Yes. Look for panting and spread wings, and cool her gently.

How long can a chicken go without eating?

Not long. A day without food or water is a reason to call a vet.
124:
Is it a health problem or just a laying break?

Most hens that stop laying are healthy. The common reasons are short days, molt, broodiness, age and stress. The health side is what this section is about, because a few causes need a vet and some need reporting.

Signs that point to illness

  • She is fluffed up, quiet or off her food.
  • Her belly is swollen, hard or feels like a water balloon.
  • She stands upright like a penguin or keeps straining.
  • Her comb is pale in a season when it should be red.
  • Her droppings look wrong for more than a day or two.

What to do

  1. Separate her for a closer look.
  2. Check for mites and lice around the vent at night.
  3. Feel the keel bone. A sharp keel means she has lost weight.
  4. Check feed. Too many treats or scratch can stop laying.
  5. Look for a hidden nest before you assume anything.

Look-alike problems

A swollen belly with lethargy can mean egg yolk peritonitis. Straining with no egg is egg binding. A pale comb with weight loss can be worms or mites, covered under anemia.

When the whole flock stops

A sudden drop across the flock, with sneezing, odd eggs or deaths, is a different matter. Respiratory viruses can do this, and so can avian influenza and Newcastle disease. If birds are dying, call your state veterinarian or extension office before moving any birds.

When to call a vet

Call if she stops eating, has a swollen belly, keeps straining, or does not improve in a few days of rest and good feed.

About the eggs

When she starts laying again, eggs are fine to eat unless she was given medication. In that case, check the product label or ask a vet.

Common questions about chickens not laying eggs

Can worms stop a hen from laying?

A heavy worm load can pull her condition down enough to slow or stop laying. A vet can run a fecal test.

Why did all my hens stop laying at once?

Look for a shared cause like short days, molt season, a feed change, a predator scare or an illness.

Is my old hen sick or just done laying?

If she is bright, eating and active, she is probably just older. Lethargy or a swollen belly means a vet visit.
125:
Working out why a comb has gone pale

A comb that fades from red to pink or white, or shrinks and looks dull, reflects what is happening with blood flow and hormones. It can be completely normal during molt or a winter laying break. It can also mean blood loss from parasites or a hidden illness.

Normal reasons first

Hens that are not laying often have smaller, paler combs. That includes molting hens, broody hens, young pullets and hens on a winter break. If she is eating and active, this is likely it. See the annual molt for that pattern.

Checks to do today

  1. Go out at night with a flashlight and look for red mites on the roost ends and in cracks. They hide by day and feed at night.
  2. Part the feathers around the vent and under the wings for northern fowl mites and lice.
  3. Look at the droppings for worms or blood.
  4. Feel her keel bone for weight loss.
  5. Look at her eyelids and face skin. If they are pale too, she may be anemic.

Look-alikes

Pale comb with bloody droppings in a young bird points to coccidiosis. Pale comb with a swollen belly suggests a reproductive problem. Blue or purple comb is different, and with sudden deaths it can be a sign of avian influenza, which must be reported to your state veterinarian. More on pale combs from parasites is on the anemia page.

When to call a vet

Call if she is pale and lethargic, not eating, or losing weight. A vet can check for worms and blood problems. Do not wait if the pale comb comes with breathing trouble or collapse.

Treating parasites

If you find mites, treat every bird and the coop, using products labeled for poultry. See mites and lice. Check the product label or ask a vet about eating eggs during treatment.

Common questions about a pale chicken comb

Why is my hen's comb pale but she seems fine?

She is most likely not laying right now. Molt, broodiness and winter breaks all do this.

Can mites cause a pale comb?

Yes. Heavy mite loads feed on blood and can make a bird anemic.

Will her comb go red again?

Usually, once she comes back into lay or the underlying cause is fixed.
129:
Handling watery droppings without panic

Watery droppings are not always diarrhea. In hot weather, chickens drink more and pass more water. Stress and treats like watermelon do it too. True diarrhea comes with a dirty vent, a dull bird and droppings that stay loose for days.

What to do first

  1. Separate the bird so you can see her own droppings.
  2. Note color. Watery and clear, green, yellow, foamy or bloody all mean different things.
  3. Check the vent. Crusted or pasted feathers need gentle cleaning with warm water.
  4. Think about the last few days. Heat, new treats, moldy feed or a feed change?
  5. Make sure she is drinking. Diarrhea dehydrates birds fast.

Look-alikes

Blood or red mucus in young birds points to coccidiosis. Bright green watery droppings with a sick bird are covered under green droppings. A smelly, crusty vent with white discharge can be vent gleet. Normal cecal droppings are pasty and brown and show up once or twice a day.

When to call a vet

Call if diarrhea lasts more than two or three days, if the bird stops eating, if you see blood, or if several birds are affected. Sudden diarrhea in many birds with deaths should be reported to your state veterinarian or extension office.

Supportive care

Offer clean water and poultry electrolytes. Cut out treats and feed plain layer or starter feed. Keep her clean and dry.

People, eggs and hygiene

Chickens can carry salmonella and other germs in their droppings even when they look fine. Wash hands after handling birds, eggs or bedding. Keep birds out of the kitchen. Toss eggs that are soiled with diarrhea. If she is medicated, check the product label or ask a vet about eating eggs.

Common questions about watery chicken droppings

Is watery poop normal in summer?

Yes, a bit. Chickens drink more in heat and droppings get wetter.

What is a cecal dropping?

A pasty, smelly, brown dropping that comes from the ceca a couple of times a day. It is normal.

Can I give my chicken yogurt for diarrhea?

A little will not hurt, but it does not cure disease. Too much dairy can make diarrhea worse.
130:
Figuring out what green droppings mean

Dark green droppings are often normal for chickens that eat a lot of grass and greens. Bright green, watery droppings are different. They usually mean the bird has stopped eating and is passing bile, which is why they are a warning sign.

Quick checks

  • Is she eating? Watch her at the feeder and feel her crop at night. An empty crop at bedtime is a bad sign.
  • Is she acting normal, or fluffed up and quiet?
  • Have the birds been out on fresh grass?
  • Are several birds affected?

Look-alikes and causes

A bird that has not eaten for a day from any cause, like a crop problem or an egg stuck inside, can pass green droppings. Check the not eating page. Internal worms, Marek's and serious infections can all cause it too. Green watery droppings in several birds, with sudden deaths, swollen heads or breathing trouble, can be a sign of avian influenza or Newcastle disease.

When to report and when to call a vet

If several birds are sick or dying suddenly, call your state veterinarian or extension office right away and do not move birds off your property. For a single bird that is off her food, call a poultry vet if she does not start eating within a day.

Supportive care

  1. Isolate her somewhere warm and quiet.
  2. Offer water with poultry electrolytes.
  3. Tempt her with wet layer feed or scrambled egg.
  4. Check her crop and vent for the reason she stopped eating.

The first aid kit list covers what to keep on hand.

Hygiene and eggs

Wash your hands after handling sick birds and their droppings. Use separate boots for the coop. Hold off on eating eggs from a sick hen, and check the product label or ask a vet if she gets any treatment.

Common questions about green chicken droppings

Are green droppings normal in chickens?

Dark green droppings from birds on pasture can be normal. Bright green and watery is a warning sign.

Can green poop mean bird flu?

It can be one sign, along with sudden deaths and swelling. Report suspected cases to your state veterinarian.

Why does not eating cause green droppings?

With no food passing through, bile colors the droppings green.
131:
What to do when you see blood in the droppings

Blood in chicken droppings, especially in birds under a few months old, often means coccidiosis, and it can move fast. Act the same day. Not every red dropping is blood though, so look carefully first.

Is it really blood?

Chickens sometimes shed bits of intestinal lining that look orange, red and stringy. One of those in a healthy bird is normal. Red from beets or berries is also harmless. Real trouble looks like fresh red blood or dark tarry droppings, along with a dull, hunched bird.

Step by step

  1. Separate any bird that is fluffed up, hunched or not eating.
  2. Look at the rest of the flock, especially young birds.
  3. Check the brooder or coop for wet, dirty bedding around the waterer.
  4. Replace wet bedding and clean waterers.
  5. Call a vet or feed store about a coccidiosis treatment and follow the label exactly.

The coccidiosis page covers prevention and treatment in more depth.

Look-alikes

Blood on the eggshell is from the vent, not the gut, and is covered on blood on egg shells. A wound near the vent can also leave blood on droppings. Severe worm loads can cause blood too, and a fecal test sorts this out.

When it is an emergency

Chicks with bloody droppings can die within days. Call right away if a bird is collapsing, if several are sick, or if you are not seeing improvement soon after starting treatment. Unexplained deaths are worth a necropsy at your state lab.

Eggs and hygiene

Coccidia do not infect people, but other germs in droppings can. Wash hands after handling birds and bedding. If you treat laying hens, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal.

Common questions about bloody chicken droppings

Can adult chickens get coccidiosis?

Yes, though it is more common in young birds. Stress, wet bedding and new birds raise the risk.

Is intestinal lining in poop normal?

Occasional orange or red stringy tissue in a healthy bird is normal shedding.

Does medicated feed stop all coccidiosis?

It helps chicks build immunity but does not guarantee it. Keep bedding dry too.
135:
Emergency care for an egg bound hen

An egg bound hen has an egg stuck in her oviduct or vent. She may strain, pump her tail, stand like a penguin, sit in the nest for hours, or go quiet and fluffed. This can turn deadly within a day or two, so act now.

Right now

  1. Bring her inside to a warm, quiet, dim crate.
  2. Gently feel her lower abdomen and around the vent. You may feel a hard egg.
  3. Give her a warm, shallow bath for about 15 to 20 minutes. Warm water helps her relax.
  4. Dry her well and keep her warm.
  5. Offer water and let her rest in the dark.

Some keepers apply a water-based lubricant around the vent. Calcium can help muscles contract, but ask a vet before giving more than oyster shell, since the right product and amount matter.

What not to do

Never pull the egg. Never break it inside her unless a vet guides you, because sharp shell can cut her and broken contents can cause infection.

Look-alikes

Straining with tissue showing is prolapse. A swollen, squishy belly with a penguin stance can be egg yolk peritonitis. A hen sitting flat and growling is likely broody.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if she has not passed the egg within a few hours of care, if she is weak or breathing hard, or if you can see the egg but it will not move.

Prevention

Layer feed as the main diet, oyster shell on the side, healthy weight, and not too many treats. See the egg binding guide for more.

Common questions about egg bound chickens

How long can a chicken be egg bound?

Not long. Without help, many hens become critical within a day or two.

Can an egg bound chicken still poop?

Sometimes not, because the egg can block the vent. That makes it more urgent.

Why do hens get egg bound?

Large eggs, low calcium, obesity, cold, and very young or older hens all play a part.
136:
Caring for a chicken with a swollen or closed eye

A swollen eye can come from something as small as a scratch or a bit of dust, or it can be the first sign of a respiratory infection that will move through the flock. The way to tell is to look closely, separate the bird, and watch what develops over the next day or two.

What to do right now

  1. Separate her. Put her in a clean crate or pen away from the flock, with her own food and water. If it is contagious, this buys time for the others.
  2. Look closely in good light. Is it one eye or both? Is there clear fluid, foamy bubbles, or thick yellow or cheese-like material?
  3. Smell her face. A foul smell from the eye or nostrils points toward infectious coryza.
  4. Check the nostrils for discharge, and listen to her breathing.
  5. Gently flush the eye with sterile saline to remove dust or debris.
  6. Look the rest of the flock over the same day.

How to tell this apart from look-alike problems

  • One eye, no other signs, recent fight or dusty bedding. Likely injury or irritation.
  • Foamy bubbles in the corner of the eye with sneezing. Often mycoplasma (MG).
  • Swollen face and wattles with a bad smell. Think infectious coryza.
  • Scabs on the comb plus sores near the eye. Could be fowl pox.
  • Hard, cheesy lump under the eyelid. Often a pocket of pus that a vet may need to remove.

When it is an emergency

Get help quickly if she cannot see well enough to find food and water, if breathing is noisy or labored, if her whole face is swelling, or if several birds are affected at once. Sudden swelling of the face and head along with deaths in the flock is something to report to your state veterinarian or extension office, since avian influenza can cause swelling around the head.

Supportive care while you wait

Keep her warm and out of drafts. Put food and water where she can find them easily, and dip her beak in the water so she knows where it is. Keep the eye clean with saline. Do not put human eye drops or creams in her eye unless a vet says to.

The rest of the flock and the eggs

If this turns out to be MG or coryza, birds that recover can stay carriers for life and infect new birds. A vet or lab test helps you decide how to manage the flock going forward. If a vet prescribes medication, check the product label or ask the vet about the egg withdrawal period before eating eggs again.

Common questions about a chicken's swollen eye

Can a chicken's swollen eye heal on its own?

If it is a small scratch or irritation, often yes within a few days. If it gets worse or spreads, it is likely an infection.

Is a swollen eye contagious?

It can be. Respiratory infections often show up in the eyes first, so separate the bird until you know.

What does a bubbly eye mean in chickens?

Foamy bubbles in the eye corner are a classic sign of mycoplasma. Ask a vet about testing.
137:
Getting a chicken that will not eat back on track

A chicken that stops eating is a chicken that is sick, stressed or in pain. Most common causes can be found with a hands-on check. The main thing is not to wait days.

Check these in order

  1. Crop. Feel it first thing in the morning. It should be empty. Hard means impacted crop. Squishy and sour-smelling means sour crop.
  2. Mouth. Look for sores, yellow patches or something stuck.
  3. Vent and belly. A stuck egg or swollen belly stops appetite fast.
  4. Feathers and skin. Hidden wounds and heavy mites both cause it.
  5. Water. Is the waterer working, clean and not frozen?
  6. Recent change. New feed, a heat wave, a molt or bullying at the feeder?

Look-alikes

Molting hens often eat less and seem grumpy but stay alert. Broody hens barely eat and leave the nest only once a day. Bullied hens look hungry but cannot get to the feeder. A sick bird is dull, fluffed and not interested even in treats.

When to call a vet

Call if she has not eaten or drunk for a day, if she is losing weight, or if you find something you cannot fix. If several birds stop eating at once and some die, report it to your state veterinarian.

Supportive care

Isolate her somewhere warm. Offer wet feed, scrambled egg or a little mash. Add poultry electrolytes to her water. See first aid kit for supplies.

Eggs

Hold off on her eggs until she is well. If she is treated, check the product label or ask a vet.

Common questions about a chicken not eating

How long can a chicken go without food?

Only a short time before it becomes dangerous. Act within a day.

Why is my chicken drinking but not eating?

Crop problems, a stuck egg and pain are common. Do the full check.

Do chickens eat less in summer?

Yes, a bit, but a bird that refuses food completely is not just hot.
141:
Treating bumblefoot at home and knowing when to stop

Bumblefoot is an infection in the foot, usually from staph bacteria that get in through a small cut. You see a round swelling on the footpad, often with a black scab. Caught early it is easy to manage. Left alone it can spread into the bone.

Early care

  1. Separate her on soft, clean bedding.
  2. Soak the foot in warm water with Epsom salt for 10 to 15 minutes to soften the scab and clean the area.
  3. Dry it well.
  4. Apply a wound spray or ointment made for animals and wrap with a light, padded bandage.
  5. Change the dressing daily and watch the swelling.

Soaking helps clean and soften, but it does not cure the infection on its own.

Should you cut it?

Many keepers try to remove the core. It can work, but it is painful and messy, and it is easy to make things worse. A vet can do it properly and prescribe antibiotics if needed.

Look-alikes

Rough raised scales are scaly leg mites. A limp with a normal foot may be a sprain or Marek's, covered on limping.

When to call a vet

Call if the swelling is large, hot or spreading up the leg, if she cannot walk, or if it keeps coming back.

Prevention

  • Lower roosts so birds do not land hard.
  • Use smooth, wide perches.
  • Keep bedding dry and clear of sharp debris.

Eggs and hygiene

Eggs are fine to eat unless she gets medication, in which case check the product label or ask a vet. Wear gloves, since staph can infect cuts on your hands.

Common questions about bumblefoot in chickens

Is bumblefoot contagious?

Not directly, but the same coop conditions can cause it in other birds.

Can bumblefoot heal without surgery?

Mild cases sometimes improve with soaks and dressings. Deep ones usually need a vet.

What does bumblefoot look like?

A round swelling on the bottom of the foot, often with a black scab.
142:
Dealing with scaly leg mites step by step

Scaly leg mites are tiny mites that burrow under the scales on a chicken's legs and feet. The scales lift, thicken and crust over, and the legs can look rough, chalky or swollen. It is slow, it is uncomfortable for the bird, and left alone it can cause lameness. The good news is that it is very manageable once you spot it.

What to do right now

  1. Check every bird. Scaly leg mites spread on roosts and by contact, so if one bird has them, others may too.
  2. Compare legs side by side. Healthy scales lie flat and smooth. Affected scales stick up and may have white crusty material under them.
  3. Separate badly affected birds if they are limping or have open sores.
  4. Do not pick or pull off scales. That can make the legs bleed and invite infection.
  5. Start treatment for the whole flock, not just the worst bird.

Treatment options

Many keepers coat the legs with petroleum jelly or a plant oil to smother the mites, repeating every few days for several weeks. This can help, but it is slow and has to be kept up. There are also products labeled for mites on poultry. Use only products whose label covers chickens, follow the directions exactly, and ask a vet if you are unsure. The old scales will not smooth out right away. They usually look better after the bird molts or grows new scales.

How to tell this apart from other leg problems

Older birds naturally have rougher, thicker scales, but they still lie flat. A swelling on the bottom of the foot with a dark scab is more likely bumblefoot. A bird that is limping with normal looking scales may have an injury or a joint problem, covered on the limping page. Mites and lice on the body are a different problem with different treatment, though it is smart to check for them at the same time.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if the legs are bleeding, swollen and hot, if toes look like they are losing circulation, or if a bird cannot walk or stand. Severe cases can damage joints and toes.

Clean the coop too

  • Strip out old bedding and nest material.
  • Scrub roost bars, and treat or replace old rough wood that is hard to clean.
  • Check new birds' legs before they join the flock, and keep them apart for about a month.

The coop cleaning kit page lists simple tools that make this easier.

Eggs and the rest of the flock

Scaly leg mites do not affect eggs directly, and eggs from birds treated with petroleum jelly on their legs are fine to eat. If you use any insecticide or medicated product, check the product label or ask a vet about whether there is an egg withdrawal period. Scaly leg mites do not live on people.

Common questions about scaly leg mites

How do chickens get scaly leg mites?

From other infected birds, shared roosts and bedding. Wild birds and new flock members are common sources.

How long does it take for scales to look normal?

Weeks to months. The mites can be gone well before the scales smooth out.

Can scaly leg mites kill a chicken?

Rarely on their own, but bad cases can cause lameness, infection and loss of toes.
143:
What to do about a squishy, sour crop

A healthy crop is full at night and empty by morning. A sour crop stays full, feels soft and squishy like a water balloon, and the bird's breath smells sour or yeasty. It is usually a yeast overgrowth after food sat too long in the crop.

Today

  1. Check her crop first thing in the morning, before she eats. Full and squishy confirms it.
  2. Separate her and take away food for a short time, but leave water.
  3. Gently massage the crop downward to help it move. Stop if she struggles.
  4. Offer small amounts of soft food once the crop starts to empty.
  5. Check the coop for moldy feed, long grass or stale water.

About making her vomit

You will see advice online to tip a hen forward and empty the crop. It carries a real risk of her inhaling the fluid, which can kill her. Only do it if a vet shows you how.

Look-alikes

A hard, doughy crop is impacted crop, and the fix is different. A full crop in a bird that is not eating can also be a sign of a blockage further down, including a stuck egg or Marek's in young birds. See sour crop for more on the yeast side.

When to call a vet

Call if the crop is still full after a day of care, if she is weak or losing weight, or if it keeps coming back. A vet can prescribe an antifungal and look for an underlying cause.

Prevention

Fresh feed, clean water, no moldy scraps, and short grass in the run. Avoid long stringy grass clippings.

Eggs

If she gets medication, check the product label or ask a vet before eating her eggs.

Common questions about sour crop in chickens

How do I know if my chicken has sour crop?

A soft, squishy crop in the morning and sour breath are the main signs.

Can sour crop go away on its own?

Mild cases sometimes clear with care. Ongoing ones need a vet.

Does apple cider vinegar cure sour crop?

No. It will not cure a yeast infection. Ask a vet about a proper treatment.
147:
Sorting molt from mites, pecking and stress

Feather loss has a handful of common causes, and where the feathers are missing tells you a lot. Molt is normal. Parasites, bullying and over-mating are fixable once you know which one you are dealing with.

Look at the pattern

  • Feathers everywhere on the coop floor, new pin feathers coming in, laying stopped. That is molt.
  • Bare back and back of the head in hens with a rooster. That is mating damage.
  • Bare vent area, scabby skin, crawling specks. Check for mites and lice.
  • Broken feathers, bare spots on the back or tail, one bird always picking. That is feather pecking.
  • Bare breast on a broody hen. She pulled them to warm the eggs.

What to do

  1. Check each bird at night with a flashlight. Part feathers at the vent and under the wings.
  2. Look at the roost for red mites in cracks.
  3. Watch the flock for a bully.
  4. Check the feed protein. Layer feed with treats kept low is the base.
  5. Look for open skin. Separate any bird with a wound, since red skin draws pecking.

When to call a vet

Call if bare skin is red, swollen or weeping, if a bird has deep wounds, or if she is losing weight and the cause is not clear.

Helping regrowth
