Extra protein helps during molt. A hen saddle can protect a hen's back from a rooster. Handle molting birds gently, as new pin feathers bleed easily if bumped.

Eggs and hygiene

Feather loss alone does not affect eggs. If you treat for mites, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal.

Common questions about chickens losing feathers

Why is my chicken losing feathers in fall?

Most likely the annual molt. It is normal and usually lasts several weeks.

Can stress cause feather loss?

Yes. A big scare can cause a partial molt.

Will feathers grow back?

Yes, usually after the next molt or once the cause is fixed.
148:
Finding out why your chicken is limping

A limp can come from a splinter, a sprain from jumping off a high roost, an infection in the foot, or something deeper like a nerve problem. Most limps are physical injuries that heal with rest. A few are early signs of a disease you need to know about. A careful look tells you a lot.

What to do right now

  1. Catch her calmly, ideally at night from the roost when chickens are sleepy.
  2. Look at the bottom of both feet. A round swelling with a dark scab is a classic sign of bumblefoot.
  3. Check between the toes for splinters, wire, string or hair wrapped around a toe.
  4. Feel each leg and joint gently and compare sides. Heat, swelling or a grinding feel are important.
  5. Look at the scales for crusting or lifting.
  6. Watch her walk on a flat surface. Does she favor one leg, or drag both?

How to tell common causes apart

  • Swelling on the footpad with a black scab. Bumblefoot.
  • Rough, raised, crusty scales. Scaly leg mites.
  • One leg forward and one back, or a young bird losing use of a leg or wing over days. This can be Marek's disease, especially in unvaccinated birds a few months old.
  • Sudden limp after a fall or a fight, with normal looking feet. Likely a sprain or bruise.
  • Weak legs in a heavy, fast-growing meat bird. Often weight and growth related.

Supportive care

Put her in a small, quiet pen with soft bedding so she does not have to move much. Put food and water within easy reach. Remove anything wrapped around a toe carefully with small scissors. Clean small cuts with saline. Give a sprain a week or two of rest before deciding it is something worse.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if a leg looks broken or bent at an odd angle, if a joint is hot and swollen, if there is a deep wound, or if she stops eating. Paralysis spreading to the wings or neck, or several birds going lame, also needs a vet or lab diagnosis. Sudden weakness that climbs from the legs to the neck can be botulism.

Prevention

  • Keep roosts at a height birds can jump down from without a hard landing.
  • Use smooth, splinter-free perches.
  • Clear sharp wire, nails and string from the run.
  • Vaccinate chicks against Marek's when you buy them.

The flock and the eggs

A limp from injury is not contagious. If you suspect Marek's, a lab test helps you understand the risk to the rest of the flock. Eggs from a limping hen are fine to eat unless she is on medication, in which case check the product label or ask a vet.

Common questions about a chicken limping

Can a limping chicken heal on its own?

Mild sprains and bruises often heal with a week or two of rest. Infections and nerve problems usually do not.

Why is my young chicken suddenly lame?

Injury is common, but Marek's disease is a concern in young birds, especially unvaccinated ones.

How do I check for bumblefoot?

Look for a round swelling on the footpad, often with a dark scab in the middle.
149:
Clearing mites from birds and the coop

Mites are tiny parasites that feed on blood or skin. The two most common are northern fowl mites, which live on the bird, and red mites, which hide in the coop by day and feed at night. Treating only the birds or only the coop is the most common reason mites come back.

Confirm what you have

  1. Check birds at night. Part feathers around the vent and under the wings.
  2. Wipe a white paper towel along the underside of the roost after dark. Red or gray smears mean red mites.
  3. Look for dirty-looking feathers near the vent, scabs and pale combs.
  4. Check nest boxes and cracks in wood.

Treatment plan

  • Treat every bird, not just the worst.
  • Use only products labeled for poultry, and follow the label for how much and how often.
  • Repeat treatment as the label says. Mite eggs hatch after the first round.
  • Strip out bedding and nest material and bag it.
  • Scrub roosts and cracks, and treat the coop with a labeled product.

Many keepers add wood ash or a dust bath area. That helps birds keep mites down, but it does not clear an infestation on its own.

Look-alikes

Lice are larger, move fast and leave egg clusters at the feather base. Scaly leg mites live under leg scales and need different care. Feather loss from molt or pecking has no crawling pests.

When to call a vet

Call if birds are pale, weak or losing weight, since heavy mites can cause anemia and death, especially in chicks and broody hens.

Eggs and people

Check the product label or ask a vet about eating eggs during treatment. Bird mites can bite people but do not live on us. Wash and change clothes after coop work. The mites and lice page has more.

Common questions about chicken mites

Can chicken mites live in my house?

They may bite briefly but need birds to survive and reproduce.

How often should I check for mites?

Once every week or two, and always before adding new birds.

Does diatomaceous earth kill mites?

Results are mixed and dust can irritate lungs. Use labeled products for a real infestation.
152:
Getting shell quality back on track

Soft, thin or rubbery shells usually come down to calcium, age, heat or stress. A few hens lay them for health reasons. This section is about checking the hen, not just the egg.

Quick checklist

  1. Feed. Layer feed should be most of the diet. Scratch and kitchen scraps dilute calcium.
  2. Oyster shell. Offer it in a separate dish, all the time.
  3. Age. New layers and older hens lay more poor shells.
  4. Heat. Shade, airflow and cool water during heat waves.
  5. Stress. Predators, moving and new flock mates can all disrupt shells for a few days.

When it is the hen, not the feed

If a hen is lethargic, straining, or standing like a penguin, she may have a soft egg stuck inside. Read egg bound now. If several birds have poor shells with sneezing, watery whites or wrinkled eggs, a virus like infectious bronchitis may be behind it. A vet or extension office can arrange testing.

When to call a vet

Call if she stops eating, has a swollen belly, or poor shells continue for weeks despite good feed and oyster shell.

Prevention

Keep treats to a small share of the diet. Do not feed layer feed to chicks or roosters, since too much calcium harms them. The grit vs oyster shell guide explains why both matter.

Eggs

Toss soft or cracked eggs, since the shell is the main barrier against bacteria. Collect often to stop hens learning to eat broken eggs.

Common questions about soft shell eggs from chickens

Can stress make a hen lay soft eggs?

Yes. A fright or a heat wave can cause a few soft eggs.

How long until shells improve?

Often a couple of weeks after fixing feed and calcium.

Should I add calcium to the water?

Ask a vet first. Oyster shell free choice is the safe default for laying hens.
1172:
What to do when you suspect anemia

Anemia means a chicken does not have enough red blood cells. You see it as a pale comb and wattles, pale skin around the eyes, weakness, and sometimes a bird that tires easily or breathes faster after moving. Anemia is a sign, not a disease on its own, so the real job is finding the cause.

Step by step

  1. Separate the bird somewhere quiet and warm. Anemic birds handle stress poorly.
  2. Go out at night with a flashlight. Check the ends and undersides of roost bars and cracks in the wood for red mites. They hide by day and feed at night.
  3. Part the feathers around the vent and under the wings. Look for northern fowl mites and lice, and for gray, crusty patches of mite debris.
  4. Look at fresh droppings. Blood, or worms you can see, are important clues.
  5. Check for wounds you might have missed, including under the wings and around the vent.
  6. Feel the keel bone. A sharp keel means weight loss.

Common causes

  • Blood-feeding mites, especially red mites and northern fowl mites. See external mites and lice.
  • Coccidiosis, which damages the gut and causes blood loss, mostly in younger birds.
  • Heavy worm loads, covered under internal worms.
  • Bleeding from a wound, a peck injury or a broken blood feather.
  • Chronic disease, including tumors from Marek's or leukosis in older birds.

How to tell this apart from a normal pale comb

Hens that are not laying, including molting, broody and winter-break hens, often have paler, smaller combs. If she is bright, eating well and has a normal weight, that is probably what you are seeing. The pale comb page covers that difference. Anemia comes with other signs like weakness, pale eyelids, weight loss or parasites.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if she is weak, will not eat, collapses, or does not improve after you treat for parasites. A vet can check a blood sample and do a fecal test for worms and coccidia. If several birds are losing condition or dying, a necropsy at your state diagnostic lab is the best way to find the cause.

Supportive care

Keep her warm, quiet and away from flock mates who might bully her. Offer good layer feed, a little extra protein and clean water. Poultry vitamins and electrolytes can support her while you deal with the cause, but they do not fix anemia on their own.

Prevention

Check birds and roosts for mites every week or two. Keep bedding dry. Quarantine new birds for about a month and check them for parasites before they join the flock.

The flock and the eggs

If mites or worms are the cause, treat the whole flock and the coop, not just one bird. If you use any dewormer or mite product, check the product label or ask a vet about the egg withdrawal period.

Common questions about anemia in chickens

What does an anemic chicken look like?

Pale comb, wattles and face skin, weakness and often weight loss.

Can mites really cause anemia?

Yes. Heavy infestations of blood-feeding mites can make birds seriously anemic, especially chicks and broody hens.

Will iron supplements help my chicken?

Do not give supplements without a vet's advice. Fixing the cause, like parasites, matters most.
1174:
Helping your flock through the annual molt

Molt is when chickens drop old feathers and grow new ones. It usually happens once a year, often in late summer or fall as days get shorter. It is normal, but it is hard on their bodies. Feathers are mostly protein, so a molting hen puts her energy into regrowth and usually stops laying.

What a normal molt looks like

  • Feathers all over the coop floor, often starting at the head and neck and moving down the body.
  • Pin feathers, which look like little quills, poking through the skin.
  • Less laying, or none at all.
  • A grumpy hen who does not want to be touched.
  • Some hens molt quickly and look bald for a short while. Others molt slowly over months.

What to do during molt

  1. Boost protein. Switch to or mix in a higher protein feed, or add protein treats in moderation. The protein during molt guide covers the details.
  2. Cut back on scratch and low protein treats.
  3. Handle gently, if at all. Pin feathers carry a blood supply and are sore when touched.
  4. Keep them out of drafts and wet weather, since they lose some insulation.
  5. Do not add new birds or make big changes. Molt is stressful enough.

How to tell molt apart from a problem

Molt is even and follows a pattern, with new feathers coming in behind the old ones. Missing feathers in one spot, broken feathers, or scabby skin point elsewhere. Bare backs in hens with a rooster are mating damage. Crawling specks and dirty-looking vent feathers mean mites or lice. One bird picking at another is feather pecking. The feather loss page sorts through these.

When to call a vet

Molt itself does not need a vet. Call if a molting bird is lethargic, stops eating, loses a lot of weight, or has red or swollen skin. A broken blood feather that keeps bleeding also needs attention. Apply gentle pressure, and if it does not stop, call a vet.

Molt and eggs

Expect laying to pause for several weeks to a couple of months. Most hens come back into lay once new feathers are in, and many lay better shells afterwards. There is no reason to worry about eating eggs from a molting hen. Some keepers add extra light during molt to keep laying going, but it is often better to let hens rest.

Why some birds molt harder

Older hens and high-production breeds often have more dramatic molts. Stress, a hard broody spell, or a sudden change in light can trigger an out of season or partial molt.

Rest of the flock

Molt is not contagious, though hens often molt around the same time because they share the same daylight. Keep an eye on bullying, since molting hens slip down the pecking order.

Common questions about chicken molting

How long does a chicken molt last?

Often several weeks, sometimes two or three months depending on the hen.

Do chickens stop laying when they molt?

Usually, yes. Laying returns once feathers grow back.

Why is my young chicken molting?

Chicks and pullets go through juvenile molts as they grow. That is normal.
1177:
What to do if you suspect aspergillosis

Aspergillosis is a fungal infection of the lungs and air sacs. It comes from breathing in spores of Aspergillus mold, which grows in damp bedding, moldy feed and wet litter. It is most common in young chicks, which is why it is called brooder pneumonia, but older birds can get it too, especially if they are stressed or living in damp, dusty conditions.

Signs to watch for

  • Gasping, open-beak breathing or rapid breathing.
  • Lethargy, sitting fluffed up, or chicks huddling and not eating.
  • Drinking more than usual.
  • In older birds, a slow decline with breathing trouble and weight loss.
  • Sometimes twisted necks or wobbliness if the infection reaches the brain.

Step by step

  1. Remove every bit of damp or moldy bedding and feed right away.
  2. Clean and dry the brooder or coop thoroughly before adding fresh, dry bedding.
  3. Check feed bags and feeders for clumps, musty smells or visible mold, and throw out anything suspect.
  4. Move sick birds to a clean, dry, well-ventilated space.
  5. Call a vet to confirm what you are dealing with.

How to tell this apart from other breathing problems

Aspergillosis does not spread from bird to bird the way viral or bacterial respiratory diseases do. Birds get it from the environment. So if several birds sharing the same moldy bedding get sick, but there is no sneezing, nasal discharge or bubbly eyes, mold is a likely culprit. Sneezing, discharge and foamy eyes fit other infections more, covered on the wheezing and sneezing pages. Heavy panting in hot weather is heat stress.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet as soon as you see gasping, especially in chicks. Aspergillosis is hard to treat once it is established, and a vet or state lab can confirm it, often by necropsy of a bird that has died. Knowing the cause stops you from treating for the wrong thing.

Supportive care

Keep the bird warm, calm and in clean, fresh air. Offer water and easy feed. Home remedies do not clear a fungal lung infection, and treatment, if any, has to come from a vet.

Prevention

  • Keep bedding dry. Change wet spots under waterers daily.
  • Store feed in a sealed, dry container and buy only what you will use in a few weeks.
  • Never use moldy hay or straw for bedding.
  • Ventilate well. The ventilation guide explains how much airflow a coop needs.

People, eggs and the rest of the flock

The same mold can affect people, especially those with weak immune systems or lung conditions. Wear a dust mask when cleaning out moldy bedding, and wash up afterwards. Healthy birds in the flock are not at risk from the sick bird itself, only from the moldy environment. If a vet prescribes treatment, check the product label or ask the vet about eggs.

Common questions about aspergillosis in chickens

Is aspergillosis contagious between chickens?

No. Birds catch it from mold in the environment, not from each other.

Can chickens recover from aspergillosis?

Some mild cases do, but established infections are hard to treat. Prevention matters most.

What bedding causes aspergillosis?

Any bedding that stays damp and grows mold, including wet straw, hay and shavings.
1179:
If you think your flock has bird flu

Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) is a fast-moving, often deadly virus in poultry. It spreads through wild birds, especially waterfowl, and on shoes, equipment and clothing. It is a reportable disease. If you suspect it, you are required to report it, and reporting fast helps protect every flock around you.

Signs that should make you call right away

  • Several birds dying suddenly, sometimes with no warning signs.
  • Swelling around the head, eyes, comb or wattles.
  • Purple or blue discoloration of the comb, wattles or legs.
  • Severe drop in laying, soft or misshapen eggs.
  • Coughing, sneezing, gasping, nasal discharge.
  • Lack of energy, poor appetite, twisted necks or stumbling.
  • Diarrhea.

What to do right now

  1. Call your state veterinarian or your local extension office. They will tell you how to proceed and can arrange testing.
  2. Do not move any birds, eggs, manure or equipment off your property.
  3. Do not take dead birds to a lab or vet unless officials tell you to. Bag them and keep them cold, away from other animals.
  4. Keep people and pets away from the flock.
  5. Keep your other birds confined and away from wild birds.

How to tell this apart from other problems

Many diseases cause coughing or a drop in laying. What sets HPAI apart is the speed and the death rate, often several birds lost in a day or two. Newcastle disease can look very similar and is also reportable. Single birds that slowly get sick are more likely to have something else, like infectious coryza or mycoplasma. Only lab testing can confirm HPAI, which is why calling officials is the right first step.

Protecting yourself and your family

Bird flu can infect people, though it is uncommon. Avoid touching sick or dead birds with bare hands. Wear gloves, a mask and eye protection if you must handle them, and wash your hands with soap afterwards. Change clothes and shoes after coop work and wash them. Keep children away. Tell your doctor if you get eye redness, fever or flu-like symptoms after contact with sick birds.

Prevention

  • Keep wild birds away from feed, water and the run. Cover runs if waterfowl are nearby.
  • Use dedicated coop shoes or boot covers.
  • Do not share equipment with other flocks.
  • Quarantine new birds and be cautious at swaps and shows during outbreaks.

The Defend the Flock biosecurity page goes deeper.

Eggs and the rest of the flock

Do not eat, sell or give away eggs from a flock suspected of HPAI. Follow the instructions officials give you. There is no home treatment, and home remedies do not cure it.

Common questions about avian influenza in chickens

Do I have to report bird flu in backyard chickens?

Yes. Contact your state veterinarian or extension office if you suspect it.

Can I eat eggs during a bird flu outbreak nearby?

If your own flock is healthy, properly cooked eggs are generally considered safe. If your birds are sick, do not eat or share their eggs.

How does bird flu get into backyard flocks?

Mostly from wild birds and their droppings, and on shoes, equipment and visitors.
1180:
What to do if a chicken shows signs of botulism

Botulism is not an infection that spreads from bird to bird. It is poisoning from a toxin made by bacteria that grow in rotting material, like a dead animal, spoiled food or stagnant water. Chickens get it by eating that material, or the maggots that feed on it. The toxin causes paralysis that usually starts in the legs and works its way up to the wings and neck. That limp, floppy neck is where the name limberneck comes from.

Signs to look for

  • Weak legs, sitting down and unwilling to stand.
  • Drooping wings.
  • Neck lying flat on the ground, unable to hold the head up.
  • Eyelids drooping or half closed.
  • In bad cases, breathing trouble.

Step by step, right now

  1. Search the run, coop and nearby area for the source. Look for a dead rodent, bird or other animal, rotting kitchen scraps, spoiled feed or a puddle of stagnant water.
  2. Remove it, wearing gloves, and double bag it.
  3. Move the sick bird to a quiet, shaded, cool pen.
  4. Get water into her. A bird that cannot lift its head cannot drink. Offer water often by dribbling small amounts on the side of the beak, carefully, so she does not inhale it.
  5. Check the rest of the flock for early leg weakness.
  6. Call an avian or poultry vet.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Botulism paralysis is floppy and climbs upward, and the bird is usually alert in the eyes. Marek's disease also causes leg paralysis, but often one leg forward and one back, and usually in younger birds over a longer time. A twisted neck that turns or tilts the head, rather than letting it hang, is more like wry neck. Sudden paralysis in several birds with deaths and other signs should also be reported to your state veterinarian, since Newcastle disease can cause nerve signs.

When to call a vet

Call a vet right away. Mild cases sometimes recover with good supportive care over days. Severe cases, especially birds with breathing trouble or a neck that is fully limp, are often fatal. A vet can advise on care and on whether any treatment is worth trying.

Supportive care

Keep her cool, quiet and comfortable on soft bedding. Prop her upright with a rolled towel so she can breathe more easily. Keep up with water. Home remedies do not cure botulism. Supportive care just gives her body time to clear the toxin.

Prevention

  • Remove dead animals from the run and coop area promptly.
  • Do not feed spoiled food or rotting scraps.
  • Drain or fill low spots where water sits stagnant in summer.
  • Control flies and maggots around compost and manure.

Eggs and your own safety

Do not eat eggs from a hen sick with botulism. Wear gloves when handling carcasses and rotting material, and wash your hands well afterwards.

Common questions about botulism in chickens

Is botulism contagious between chickens?

No, but birds sharing the same source can all get sick. Find and remove it.

Can chickens survive botulism?

Some recover with supportive care, especially mild cases. Severe paralysis is often fatal.

What causes limberneck?

Eating toxin from rotting material, dead animals or maggots that fed on them.
1184:
A practical bumblefoot plan from first scab to full recovery

Bumblefoot is a bacterial infection of the foot, most often caused by staph. It starts when bacteria get into a small cut or a pressure sore on the footpad. The body walls off the infection, which creates a hard core of pus under the skin. That core is why it does not just go away on its own once it is established.

How to check your birds

Pick up each bird and look at the bottom of both feet. Healthy footpads are smooth, even and cool. Early bumblefoot looks like a slightly shiny, red or swollen pad. Later it shows a round, hard swelling with a dark brown or black scab in the center. You may also see a limp, swelling between the toes, or a bird that sits more than usual.

Caring for a mild case

  1. Bring her in and put her on clean, soft bedding.
  2. Soak the foot in warm water with Epsom salt to soften the scab and clean it.
  3. Dry well and apply an animal wound spray or ointment.
  4. Pad and wrap the foot so pressure is taken off the pad.
  5. Change the wrap every day or two and watch for change.

Soaks and wraps support healing. They do not kill a deep infection by themselves.

When home care is not enough

If the swelling is large, the core is deep, it is hot or spreading up the leg, or you have tried care for a week or two without improvement, take her to an avian or poultry vet. A vet can remove the core cleanly with pain control and give the right antibiotic if needed. Infection that reaches the bone or tendons is very hard to fix.

How to tell this apart from other foot and leg problems

Crusty, lifted scales along the leg are scaly leg mites, not bumblefoot. A swollen hock or joint without a footpad lesion may be an injury or a joint infection. A limp with healthy-looking feet needs other checks, covered on chicken limping. Frostbitten toes look dark and dry, and show up after cold snaps.

Prevention

  • Keep roosts low enough that birds do not land hard. Heavy breeds are most at risk.
  • Use wide, smooth roosts with no splinters.
  • Keep the run free of wire scraps, sharp stones and glass.
  • Keep bedding dry. Wet, dirty floors soften the skin.
  • Keep birds at a healthy weight.

The roosts and nests guide has setup tips.

The flock, the eggs and your hands

Bumblefoot does not jump from bird to bird, but if the coop setup caused one case it may cause more. Check everyone's feet. Eggs from a bird with bumblefoot are fine unless she is on medication, in which case check the product label or ask a vet. Wear gloves when you handle the wound, since staph can infect cuts on your hands.

Common questions about bumblefoot

What causes bumblefoot in chickens?

Bacteria getting into a small cut or pressure sore on the footpad, often from hard landings or rough perches.

How long does bumblefoot take to heal?

Mild cases can improve in a couple of weeks. Cases that need surgery take longer.

Can bumblefoot kill a chicken?

It can if the infection spreads deep into the foot or the body. Treat it early.
1185:
Stopping feather pecking before it turns bloody

Chickens peck. It is how they explore and sort out who is in charge. The problem starts when pecking turns into pulling feathers, picking at skin, or attacking a wound. Chickens are drawn to red, so once there is blood, it can become cannibalism quickly. Acting early is the whole game.

What to do the moment you see blood

  1. Remove the injured bird right away. Do not wait to see if it settles down.
  2. Rinse the wound with saline or clean water and look at how deep it is.
  3. Apply an animal wound spray. Colored sprays help hide the red that draws pecking.
  4. Keep her apart until the wound is fully healed and covered with feathers or a dry scab.
  5. Watch the flock for the bird or birds doing the pecking.

Common causes

  • Crowding. Too many birds in too little space is the number one driver.
  • Boredom. Nothing to scratch, forage or dust bathe in.
  • Low protein. Birds may pull and eat feathers when protein is short.
  • Heat and bright light. Hot, brightly lit coops make birds more irritable.
  • A visible wound or prolapse that draws attention.
  • Mixing birds of different sizes or adding new birds too fast.

How to tell this apart from other feather loss

Pecking damage looks like broken feathers and bare patches on the back, tail or vent, often on lower ranking birds. Even feather loss with pin feathers coming in is molt. Bare backs in hens kept with a rooster are mating wear. Dirty-looking vent feathers with crawling specks are mites. The feather loss page helps sort these out. If the pecking is aimed at a red, swollen vent, check for vent prolapse.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet for deep wounds, wounds near the vent or eyes, bleeding that will not stop, or a bird in shock who is limp and cold. Pecking injuries can get infected even when they look small.

Fixing the flock

  • Give more space, or reduce bird numbers. The coop size per bird guide gives rough targets.
  • Add things to do, like a dust bath area, hanging greens, piles of leaves or scattered scratch.
  • Feed a complete feed with enough protein, and keep treats low.
  • Use dimmer light inside the coop if birds spend time there during the day.
  • If one bird is the ringleader, separating her for a few days can reset her place in the pecking order.

Eggs

Egg eating often travels with pecking problems. Collect eggs often, keep nests dark, and fix soft shells. If a bird needs medication for a wound, check the product label or ask a vet about eggs.

Common questions about feather pecking and cannibalism

Why are my chickens pecking each other bloody?

Crowding, boredom, low protein and the sight of blood are the most common reasons.

When can an injured hen go back to the flock?

Once the wound is fully healed and no longer red. Reintroduce her slowly.

Does a red light stop pecking?

Red light makes blood less visible and can reduce pecking indoors, but it does not fix the underlying cause.
1186:
Acting fast when coccidiosis hits

Coccidiosis is caused by tiny parasites called coccidia that damage the lining of the gut. Almost every flock has some coccidia around, and birds slowly build immunity to them. Trouble starts when young birds pick up a big dose, usually from wet, dirty bedding. It can kill chicks in days, so speed matters.

Signs to watch for

  • Bloody or mucus-filled droppings, though not every case shows blood.
  • Chicks or young birds hunched, fluffed up and sleepy.
  • Not eating, but sometimes still drinking.
  • Pale comb and skin in older birds.
  • Slow growth or weight loss.

What to do right now

  1. Get a treatment that is labeled for coccidiosis in poultry from a feed store or vet. Follow the label exactly for how much and how long. Treat the whole group, not just the sick ones.
  2. Pull out all wet and dirty bedding and replace with clean, dry bedding.
  3. Clean and refill waterers, and raise them so droppings do not get in.
  4. Separate very weak birds so they can be watched and kept warm.
  5. Check on the flock several times a day for the next few days.

How to tell this apart from other gut problems

A bit of orange or red stringy tissue in a healthy bird's droppings is normal gut shedding, not coccidiosis. Pasty brown cecal droppings once or twice a day are normal too. Worms can cause weight loss and diarrhea, and a fecal test can tell the difference. Watery green droppings in a bird that is not eating point to other causes, covered on green droppings. The bloody droppings page walks through what red in the droppings can mean.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if birds are dying, if you do not see improvement within a couple of days of starting treatment, or if older birds are getting sick. A vet or state lab can do a fecal test or necropsy to confirm it, since other diseases can look similar.

Prevention

  • Keep brooder and coop bedding dry. Wet spots under waterers are the main hot spot.
  • Do not overcrowd chicks.
  • Medicated chick starter can help chicks build immunity. If your chicks were vaccinated for coccidiosis, ask the hatchery whether to use medicated feed, since some products can work against the vaccine.
  • Expose chicks to small amounts of soil from your yard gradually as they grow, rather than all at once.
  • Keep new birds apart for about a month before mixing.

The coccidiosis guide has more on prevention.

Eggs, people and the rest of the flock

Chicken coccidia do not infect people, but droppings carry other germs, so wash your hands after cleaning. If you treat laying hens, check the product label or ask a vet about the egg withdrawal period. Older birds that survived often carry some immunity, but new chicks will not.

Common questions about coccidiosis

Can coccidiosis be cured?

Yes, birds often recover with fast treatment from a labeled product and clean, dry bedding.

Can older chickens get coccidiosis?

Yes, especially when stressed, newly moved or exposed to a strain they have not met.

Does apple cider vinegar prevent coccidiosis?

There is no good evidence that it does. Dry bedding and proper treatment are what work.
1190:
Getting an egg bound hen through the next few hours

Egg binding means an egg is stuck somewhere in the hen's oviduct or near the vent. She cannot pass it, and the pressure can block her droppings and press on her organs. Some hens pass the egg with a little help. Others need a vet. The longer it goes, the worse the odds.

Signs that point to egg binding

  • Straining or pumping the tail with nothing coming out.
  • Standing upright like a penguin, or walking with a wide waddle.
  • Sitting in the nest box for hours, coming out and going back in.
  • Fluffed up, quiet, eyes half closed.
  • No droppings, or small wet ones.
  • A hard lump you can feel low in the abdomen.

What to do, in order

  1. Bring her inside to a warm, quiet, dim spot. Stress and cold make it worse.
  2. Give her a warm, shallow soak, enough to cover the vent, for a while. Hold her gently and keep the water warm, not hot.
  3. Dry her well and put her in a dark crate with a towel.
  4. Offer water. If she will drink, that is a good sign.
  5. Give her a few hours of quiet and check back.

Ask a vet before giving anything beyond oyster shell. Calcium can help muscles contract, but the type and amount matter.

Things to avoid

Do not try to pull the egg or reach inside her. Do not break the egg yourself unless a vet is talking you through it, since sharp shell and egg contents left inside can cause injury and infection.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

A broody hen also sits in the nest for hours, but she flattens out, growls and puffs up rather than straining. Tissue sticking out of the vent is a prolapse, which can happen during or after binding. A swollen, squishy belly that feels like fluid rather than a hard egg points more to egg yolk peritonitis.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if the egg has not passed within a few hours of care, if she is getting weaker, breathing hard, or cannot stand. A vet can use medication, help pass the egg, or remove it safely.

Prevention

  • Feed a complete layer ration, with oyster shell on the side.
  • Keep treats and scratch to a small share of the diet.
  • Keep hens at a healthy weight and active.
  • Let pullets start laying at their natural age.

More detail is in the egg binding guide.

The flock and the eggs

Egg binding is not contagious. If one hen keeps getting bound, ask a vet about why, since some hens have an underlying problem. If she gets medication, check the product label or ask a vet before eating her eggs.

Common questions about egg binding

How do I know if my chicken is egg bound or broody?

Broody hens flatten and growl. Egg bound hens strain, pump their tails and seem unwell.

Can a hen die from being egg bound?

Yes, if the egg is not passed. Act quickly and call a vet if care does not work.

Will a warm bath help an egg bound hen?

It often helps her relax and can help the egg pass, but it is not a guarantee.
1191:
What to do if you suspect egg yolk peritonitis

Egg yolk peritonitis happens when yolk ends up in the abdomen instead of moving down the oviduct. The yolk can trigger inflammation and, often, a bacterial infection. It is one of the more common serious problems in laying hens, especially high-production breeds and older layers. It is not something to treat at home on your own.

Signs to watch for

  • A swollen lower belly that may feel soft, squishy or like a water balloon.
  • Standing upright like a penguin, or walking with a waddle.
  • Stopped laying, or laying odd eggs before stopping.
  • Lethargy, sitting fluffed up, and poor appetite.
  • Yellow-stained or watery droppings, and a dirty vent.
  • Breathing harder than usual if fluid presses on the air sacs.

What to do right now

  1. Separate her somewhere warm, quiet and clean.
  2. Feel her abdomen gently. Note if it feels hard, soft, hot or fluid-filled.
  3. Check the vent for a stuck egg or prolapse.
  4. Offer water and easy food, and watch whether she eats.
  5. Call an avian or poultry vet. This is a vet problem.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

A hard egg-shaped lump near the vent with straining is more likely egg binding. A hen that sits in the nest, flattens and growls is broody, not sick. Fluid in the belly can also come from heart or liver problems and tumors, which only a vet can sort out. A crusty, smelly vent without belly swelling points more to vent gleet.

When it is an emergency

Call the vet the same day if she is breathing hard, will not eat, or is going downhill. A vet may drain fluid, prescribe antibiotics, or talk to you about a hormone implant to stop her laying for a while. Some hens recover, but it often comes back.

Supportive care while you wait

Keep her warm and calm. Offer water, layer feed mixed with a little water, and something she likes. Do not squeeze or press on her belly. Home remedies do not cure peritonitis.

Prevention

You cannot prevent every case. Things that may help include keeping hens at a healthy weight, feeding a complete layer ration, keeping stress low, and not pushing extra laying with artificial light. Some keepers with high-production hens talk to their vet about laying control for hens that keep having problems.

The flock and the eggs

Egg yolk peritonitis is not contagious, though other hens of the same breed and age may be at similar risk. Do not eat eggs from a hen who is sick, and if she is treated, check the product label or ask a vet about the egg withdrawal period.

Common questions about egg yolk peritonitis

Can a chicken survive egg yolk peritonitis?

Some do with vet treatment, but it can be serious and often recurs.

What does a hen with peritonitis look like?

Swollen, soft belly, penguin stance, lethargy and no laying.

Is egg yolk peritonitis contagious?

No. It is a problem inside one hen, not an infection that spreads.
1192:
A full plan for mites and lice in your flock

Almost every keeper deals with mites or lice at some point. They come in on wild birds, new flock members, used equipment and even on your clothes. A light load just makes birds itchy and scruffy. A heavy load can cause anemia, stop laying and kill chicks and broody hens. The key is to find them early and treat the birds and the coop together.

Know which pest you have

  • Lice are straw colored, flat and fast. They live on the bird and eat skin and feather debris. Their eggs stick in white clusters at the base of feathers, often around the vent.
  • Northern fowl mites are tiny dark specks that live on the bird. Look for dirty-looking, crusty feathers around the vent.
  • Red mites hide in cracks in the coop by day and crawl onto birds at night to feed on blood. You often will not find them on birds in daylight.

Step by step

  1. Check every bird, ideally at night with a flashlight, around the vent, under the wings and on the head.
  2. Run a white paper towel along the underside of roosts after dark. Red smears mean red mites.
  3. Strip out all bedding and nest material and bag it.
  4. Scrub roosts, nest boxes and cracks. Pay attention to roost ends where red mites gather.
  5. Treat all birds with a product labeled for poultry, following the label for amount and timing.
  6. Treat the coop with a labeled product if you have red mites.
  7. Repeat as the label directs. Eggs hatch after the first round, so one treatment is rarely enough.

How to tell this apart from other problems

Feather loss with no pests is often molt or pecking, covered on feather loss. Crusty, raised leg scales are scaly leg mites, a different mite with different care. A pale comb can come from mites, worms or other causes. See anemia if birds look washed out.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if birds are weak, pale, losing weight or dying, if chicks are infested, or if pests keep coming back after proper treatment.

Prevention

  • Check a few birds every week or two.
  • Give birds a dry dust bath area. It helps them keep pests down, though it will not clear an infestation.
  • Quarantine new birds for about a month and check them before they join the flock.
  • Keep wild birds out of the coop.
  • Use smooth, sealed roosts with fewer cracks for red mites to hide in.

Eggs and people

Many mite and lice products have rules about eggs. Check the product label or ask a vet about the egg withdrawal period. Poultry mites may bite people, but they do not live or breed on humans. Change and wash your clothes after a coop clean-out, and wash your hands.

Common questions about mites and lice on chickens

How do I know if my chickens have lice or mites?

Look at the vent and under the wings. Lice move fast and leave egg clusters. Mites are tiny specks and leave crusty feathers.

Can chickens get rid of mites on their own?

Dust bathing helps with light loads, but an infestation usually needs treatment.

Do I need to treat the coop for lice?

Lice live mostly on birds, but cleaning the coop and nests helps stop reinfestation.
1196:
Caring for a flock with fowl pox

Fowl pox is a slow-spreading virus. It mostly travels by mosquitoes, so cases tend to show up in warm, wet months. It can also spread through cuts and contact with scabs. There are two forms. Dry pox causes wart-like scabs on the comb, wattles and face. Wet pox causes yellowish patches in the mouth, throat and windpipe. Dry pox is more common and usually milder. Wet pox is more dangerous because it can block breathing and eating.

What to do right now

  1. Separate birds with obvious scabs or mouth sores if you can, especially from unaffected birds.
  2. Look inside the mouth of any affected bird with a flashlight. Yellow, cheesy patches mean wet pox.
  3. Make sure every sick bird is eating and drinking. Soft, wet feed is easier for birds with mouth lesions.
  4. Leave the scabs alone. Picking them invites infection.
  5. Cut down mosquito breeding areas around the coop.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Dry pox scabs look like dark, warty bumps, often on the comb. Peck wounds and frostbite can look similar, but frostbite shows up after cold snaps and turns tips black, while peck wounds are fresh and linear. Yellow patches in the throat can look like a fungal infection, and gasping with bloody mucus is more like ILT. Sores near the eye with swelling can also fit respiratory infections covered on the swollen eye page.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if a bird is struggling to breathe, cannot eat because of mouth lesions, or if many birds are affected. A vet can confirm it and sometimes gently remove lesions blocking the airway. Do not try to scrape lesions out of a bird's throat yourself.

Supportive care

There is no cure that kills the virus once a bird has it. Most birds with dry pox recover in a few weeks. Supportive care helps them through it. Keep them in a clean, calm space with easy access to water and soft food. A gentle antiseptic on scabs can help prevent secondary infection, but it does not cure pox.

Prevention

  • Vaccines are available for fowl pox. Ask a vet or hatchery whether it makes sense for your area.
  • Reduce mosquitoes by draining standing water and keeping grass trimmed around the run.
  • Quarantine new birds and check them for scabs before mixing.

The flock, eggs and people

Birds that recover are usually immune to that virus. Fowl pox does not infect people. It can slow down laying while birds are sick. Eggs from a recovering hen are fine to eat if she is eating and acting normal, and if she has been treated with anything, check the product label or ask a vet. See the disease encyclopedia for other conditions that cause scabs or lesions.

Common questions about fowl pox

Is fowl pox contagious to humans?

No. It only affects birds.

How long does fowl pox last in chickens?

Dry pox usually runs its course in a few weeks. Wet pox can take longer and is more serious.

Can chickens recover from fowl pox?

Most birds with dry pox recover and become immune. Wet pox has a higher death rate.
1197:
Treating frostbite and stopping it next winter

Frostbite happens when tissue freezes. In chickens it shows up most on large single combs, wattles and toes. Cold alone is only part of the story. Damp air inside the coop is often the bigger cause, because wet tissue freezes faster. A bird with frostbite needs gentle care, and the coop usually needs a change.

Signs of frostbite

  • Pale, gray or white tips on the comb or wattles at first.
  • Swelling and blisters over the next day or two.
  • Tips that turn dark or black over days to weeks.
  • Limping or reluctance to walk if toes are affected.

What to do right now

  1. Bring the bird somewhere cool but above freezing. Do not take her straight into a hot house.
  2. Warm the area slowly. Lukewarm water on the feet, or a lukewarm damp cloth on the comb, works. Never use hot water, a hair dryer or direct heat.
  3. Do not rub or massage frostbitten tissue. It damages it further.
  4. Pat dry and keep her in a calm, dry space.
  5. Leave blisters and dark tissue alone. Do not cut them off.

Over the next few weeks

Dead tissue usually dries up and falls away on its own. The comb or toes may end up shorter. Watch for signs of infection like swelling, heat, a bad smell or pus. Keep her separate if others are pecking the dark tissue.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Black spots on a comb in summer are more likely dry fowl pox. A purple or blue comb across many birds, especially with deaths, is not frostbite. That can be a sign of avian influenza and should be reported to your state veterinarian.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if toes or feet are badly affected, if there are signs of infection, or if she stops eating. Severe foot frostbite can affect her ability to walk and may need more than home care.

Prevention

  • Ventilation is the big one. Moist air from breath and droppings needs to escape. Vents up high, out of drafts at roost level, help. The coop ventilation guide explains it.
  • Remove wet bedding and keep waterers out of the coop at night if you can.
  • Use wide, flat roosts so birds cover their toes with their feathers while sleeping.
  • Pick breeds with small combs if you live somewhere very cold.
  • Do not seal the coop airtight to keep it warm. That traps moisture.

The cold weather care page has more winter tips.

The flock and the eggs

Frostbite is not contagious. If one bird got it, others with big combs may be at risk too, so check the flock. Eggs from a frostbitten hen are fine to eat. Laying may drop for a while from the stress.

Common questions about frostbite in chickens

At what temperature do chickens get frostbite?

There is no single number. Damp air and wind make frostbite more likely even on mildly freezing nights.

Should I put petroleum jelly on combs?

Some keepers do, but evidence that it prevents frostbite is weak. Dry air and good ventilation matter more.

Will a frostbitten comb grow back?

No. Lost tissue does not regrow, but the bird usually heals well.
1198:
Cooling a chicken in heat stress, step by step

Chickens do not sweat. They cool off by panting and holding their wings away from their bodies. When it gets too hot, especially with high humidity, they cannot shed heat fast enough. Heat stress can kill birds within hours, and heavy breeds and older birds are most at risk.

Signs to watch for

  • Panting with the beak open.
  • Wings held out from the body.
  • Pale comb and wattles.
  • Lethargy, standing still, eyes closing.
  • Not eating, and fewer or thin-shelled eggs.
  • Stumbling, collapse or seizures in severe cases.

What to do right now

  1. Move the bird to shade or a cool, airy place indoors.
  2. Offer cool, clean water. Not ice cold.
  3. Stand her feet and legs in cool water, or wet her legs, comb and under the wings. Do not dunk her whole body in cold water, as that can cause shock.
  4. Run a fan nearby for airflow.
  5. Add poultry electrolytes to the water if you have them.
  6. Check the rest of the flock. If one bird is in trouble, others may be close.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Heat panting is fast and quiet. Gurgling, rattling or sneezing points to a respiratory problem covered on wheezing. A lethargic bird in cool weather is not heat stressed, so look at other causes on lethargy. Several birds dying suddenly in hot weather with no panting, or with swelling and purple combs, should be reported to your state veterinarian.

When it is an emergency

A bird that has collapsed, is having seizures, or does not respond needs cooling right away and a vet if one is reachable. Birds that recover may stay weak for a day or two, so keep them quiet.

Prevention

  • Plenty of shade in the run, through the hottest part of the day.
  • More waterers in summer, kept in the shade and refilled with cool water.
  • Good coop ventilation, so heat escapes at night.
  • Frozen treats like chilled fruit help a little.
  • Avoid scratch grains in the afternoon, since digesting them adds body heat.
  • Do not handle or move birds in the heat of the day.

The water and hot weather guide covers how much they drink.

The flock and the eggs

Heat stress is not contagious, but it affects the whole flock at once. Expect laying to drop and shells to thin during heat waves. Collect eggs more often in hot weather and refrigerate them quickly. Eggs from heat-stressed hens are safe if they are collected fresh and clean.

Common questions about heat stress in chickens

How hot is too hot for chickens?

It depends on humidity, breed and shade. Watch the birds. Open-beak panting and spread wings mean they are struggling.

Should I give my chickens ice water?

Cool water is best. Very cold water or ice baths can shock an overheated bird.

Do chickens stop laying in the heat?

Many lay less and lay thinner shells during hot spells.
1202:
Clearing an impacted crop safely

An impacted crop is a blockage. Food, long grass, straw, string or other material packs into the crop and cannot move on. The crop feels hard or doughy and stays full even after a night without eating. Left alone, the bird slowly starves.

Signs to watch for

  • A crop that is still full and firm first thing in the morning.
  • Bird eating less, or not at all.
  • Fluffed up, quiet and losing weight.
  • Stretching the neck or seeming uncomfortable.
  • Bad breath if it has started to ferment.

Step by step at home

  1. Confirm it. Check the crop in the morning before she eats. Healthy crops are empty by then.
  2. Remove food for a short time, but always leave water.
  3. Offer a little water and gently massage the crop with your fingers, working the mass apart and down. Do this a few times a day.
  4. Once it softens and begins to empty, offer small amounts of soft, wet food.
  5. Check each morning for progress.

What not to do

Avoid holding her upside down to empty the crop. She can inhale fluid and die. Do not try to pull material out through her mouth. Only a vet should do anything more invasive.

How to tell this apart from sour crop

Impacted crop is hard or doughy. Sour crop is soft and squishy and smells sour. They can overlap, since a blockage can turn sour. A crop that stays full with a normal feel can also mean a problem further down, such as an egg stuck inside or a tumor. The not eating page covers other causes.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if the crop is still hard after a day or two of care, if she is weak or losing weight, or if you suspect she swallowed string, plastic or something sharp. A vet can do a small surgery to remove the blockage, and birds often do well after it.

Prevention

  • Keep grass in the run short. Long, tough grass is a common cause.
  • Do not give long grass clippings or straw that birds may swallow.
  • Make sure birds always have grit if they eat anything besides complete feed. See the grit guide.
  • Pick up string, twine and plastic from the run.

The flock and the eggs

Impacted crop is not contagious, but if one bird got it from long grass or string, others may be at risk. Eggs are fine to eat unless she gets medication, in which case check the product label or ask a vet.

Common questions about impacted crop

How do I know if my chicken has an impacted crop?

A firm, full crop first thing in the morning is the main sign.

Can a chicken live with an impacted crop?

Not for long. If it does not clear, she will slowly starve. Get help if it does not improve.

Does olive oil help an impacted crop?

Some keepers use a little, but it can be inhaled and is not a cure. Massage and a vet are safer.
1203:
What to do if coryza shows up in your flock

Infectious coryza is a bacterial respiratory disease that spreads quickly between chickens. It comes on fast, often within days of exposure, and the bad smell is the giveaway. Birds that recover usually stay carriers for life, which changes how you manage the whole flock going forward.

Signs to watch for

  • A swollen face and wattles, sometimes one side more than the other.
  • Eyes swollen or closed, with sticky discharge.
  • Thick, smelly nasal discharge.
  • A foul smell around the head, often noticed before anything else.
  • Sneezing, drop in laying and poor appetite.

Step by step

  1. Separate sick birds right away into a clean, well-ventilated space.
  2. Check every other bird. Smell around their heads, and look at eyes and nostrils.
  3. Clean the eyes and nostrils gently with saline.
  4. Call an avian or poultry vet. Testing confirms it, and a vet can decide whether treatment makes sense.
  5. Stop adding, selling or showing birds until you know what you have.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Bubbly eyes and slower onset point more to mycoplasma. Coughing up bloody mucus suggests ILT. A swollen eye with no smell and no other signs may just be an injury, covered on the swollen eye page. Sudden swelling of the head with purple combs and fast deaths can be avian influenza, which must be reported to your state veterinarian.

When to call

Call a vet as soon as you suspect it. Some states track coryza, so ask your vet or extension office whether it needs reporting where you live. Treatment from a vet can ease signs, but it does not clear the carrier state.

Supportive care

Keep birds warm, dry and out of drafts. Make water and food easy to find, since swollen eyes can make that hard. Wipe discharge away. Home remedies may comfort, but they do not cure coryza.

Long-term flock decisions

Because recovered birds carry the bacteria, many vets recommend a closed flock, meaning no new birds in and no birds out, or starting fresh after a full clean-out. Talk this through with a vet. Do not sell or give away birds from an infected flock.

Prevention

  • Buy from clean, tested sources.
  • Quarantine new birds for about a month.
  • Avoid mixing ages and sources.
  • Do not share equipment with other flocks.

See small flock biosecurity for more.

Eggs and people

Coryza is not known to infect people. Wash hands after handling sick birds anyway. If birds are treated, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal.

Common questions about infectious coryza

What does coryza smell like?

A strong, foul, rotten smell around the face and nostrils.

Can chickens recover from coryza?

Many recover from the signs, but they usually stay carriers.

Can I add new chickens after coryza?

New birds will likely catch it from carriers. Talk to a vet before adding any.
1204:
Managing infectious bronchitis in a backyard flock

Infectious bronchitis (IB) is a coronavirus of chickens. It is not the same as human coronaviruses and does not infect people. It spreads fast through the air and on equipment, and it can damage both the airway and the reproductive tract. In chicks it can be deadly. In laying hens it often shows up as a sudden drop in laying and poor quality eggs.

Signs to watch for

  • Sneezing, coughing and rattly breathing, especially in young birds.
  • Watery eyes and nasal discharge.
  • A sudden drop in laying.
  • Thin, wrinkled, misshapen or soft shells.
  • Watery whites inside the eggs.
  • Some strains affect the kidneys and cause wet droppings.

What to do

  1. Separate birds with breathing signs into a warm, clean, well-ventilated space.
  2. Check chicks closely. Keep them warm, since they get sick faster.
  3. Make sure every bird has easy access to water and food.
  4. Stop moving birds in or out.
  5. Call an avian or poultry vet or your extension office about testing.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

IB, mycoplasma, coryza and ILT can all cause breathing signs. The egg changes are a strong pointer to IB. If you see wrinkled shells or runny whites across the flock, compare with wrinkled eggs and watery egg whites. A foul smell is more like coryza. Bloody mucus points to ILT. Sudden heavy deaths with breathing signs need reporting to your state veterinarian, since avian influenza and Newcastle disease can look like this at first.

When to call a vet

Call if chicks are sick, if birds are dying, or if you want a firm diagnosis. Testing is the only way to know for sure, and it helps you decide about vaccines.

Supportive care

There is no treatment that kills the virus. Antibiotics do not treat viruses, though a vet may use them for secondary infections. Keep birds warm, dry, and well ventilated with clean air. Offer water with poultry electrolytes. Reduce stress.

Prevention

  • Vaccines for IB exist. Ask your hatchery or vet which ones fit your area, since there are many strains.
  • Hold new birds apart for a month or so before they meet the flock.
  • Keep wild birds away from feed and water.
  • Use dedicated coop shoes. See the respiratory disease guide for more.

Eggs and the rest of the flock

Hens that had IB as chicks may lay poor shells for life even when healthy. Eggs from recovered hens are safe to eat if intact and clean. If a vet prescribes anything, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal. Wash hands after handling sick birds.

Common questions about infectious bronchitis

Is chicken infectious bronchitis contagious to humans?

No. It is a chicken virus and does not infect people.

How long does infectious bronchitis last?

Breathing signs often clear in a couple of weeks. Egg quality damage can last much longer.

Can vaccinated chickens get bronchitis?

Yes, if a strain differs from the vaccine, but vaccinated birds often get milder disease.
1208:
What to do if you suspect ILT

Infectious laryngotracheitis (ILT) is a herpesvirus that attacks the windpipe. In bad outbreaks, birds gasp, stretch their necks to breathe and cough up bloody mucus. Milder strains look more like a lingering cold. Birds that recover, and birds given some types of vaccine, can carry the virus for life and shed it when stressed. Many states treat ILT as a reportable disease.

Signs to watch for

  • Gasping, with the neck stretched up and the beak open.
  • Coughing, sometimes with a honking or gurgling sound.
  • Bloody mucus on the beak, face, feathers or coop walls.
  • Watery eyes and swollen eyelids in milder cases.
  • Drop in laying, lethargy, and deaths in severe outbreaks.

Step by step

  1. Call your state veterinarian, a poultry vet or your extension office. Testing confirms ILT and tells you what rules apply in your state.
  2. Separate sick birds into a calm, well-ventilated space.
  3. Stop all movement of birds, eggs and equipment off the property until you have advice.
  4. Keep visitors away, and do not visit other flocks.
  5. Keep any dead birds cold, not frozen, in case a lab wants to test them.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Bloody mucus is the strongest clue for ILT. Yellow cheesy patches in the throat can be wet fowl pox. Wrinkled eggs and watery whites with breathing signs point more to infectious bronchitis. A foul smell with a swollen face fits coryza. Sudden heavy losses can also be avian influenza or Newcastle disease, which is why a lab test and a call to officials come first. The coughing page compares these.

When it is an emergency

Gasping birds are in real distress. Call right away if birds are struggling to breathe or dying. Do not try to clear the throat with your fingers or a swab. You can cause bleeding or push mucus further in.

Supportive care

There is no cure for the virus. Keep birds calm, warm and in clean, moving air. Offer water and soft food. A vet may suggest treatment for secondary infections. Home remedies do not cure ILT.

Prevention and long-term choices

Vaccines exist, but vaccinated birds can become carriers, so they are usually used where ILT is already a problem. Talk to your vet or state officials before vaccinating. Quarantine new birds for about a month and buy from tested sources. If your flock had ILT, a closed flock is often recommended. See the Defend the Flock page for biosecurity basics.

Eggs, people and the flock

ILT does not infect people. Still wash hands and change clothes after handling sick birds so you do not carry the virus to other flocks. Ask officials about selling or sharing eggs during an outbreak. If a vet treats your birds, check the product label or ask the vet about egg withdrawal.

Common questions about laryngotracheitis

Is ILT reportable?

In many states, yes. Contact your state veterinarian or extension office to find out.

Can chickens recover from ILT?

Many do, but survivors usually become carriers.

How does ILT spread?

Through the air, on people, shoes and equipment, and from carrier birds.
1209:
Checking for worms and treating them the right way

Most chickens that go outside carry some worms. Light loads often cause no obvious harm. Heavy loads steal nutrients, cause weight loss and diarrhea, and can stop laying. Roundworms are the ones you might see in droppings. Capillary worms are tiny and can do a lot of damage without you ever seeing them. Cecal worms are mostly harmless to chickens but can carry blackhead disease, which is deadly to turkeys.

Signs of a heavy worm load

  • Weight loss despite eating, and a sharp keel bone.
  • Pale comb and wattles.
  • Diarrhea, or droppings with visible worms.
  • Drop in laying.
  • Lethargy and a scruffy look.

What to do

  1. Get a fecal test. Bring a fresh dropping sample to a vet. It tells you which worms you have and how heavy the load is, which decides what treatment is needed.
  2. Choose a dewormer that is labeled for poultry and for the worms found. Not every product covers every type.
  3. Follow the label exactly for how much, how often, and whether to repeat.
  4. Treat the whole flock at the same time.
  5. Clean out bedding and rest or rotate run areas if you can.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Weight loss and pale combs can also come from mites, coccidiosis or tumors. Check for mites at night and read anemia for more. Bloody droppings in young birds are more likely coccidiosis. Stringy orange tissue in droppings is normal gut lining, not worms. Long white or tan worms in droppings are most likely roundworms.

When to call a vet

Call if birds are losing weight, weak, or dying, or if you are not sure what to use. A vet can recommend the right product and tell you whether it can be used on laying hens.

Herbal and natural dewormers

Garlic, pumpkin seeds and herbal blends are popular, but there is no good evidence they clear a real worm burden. They will not cure an infestation. If you use them, keep doing fecal tests to see what is actually happening.

Prevention

  • Keep bedding and runs as dry as you can. Worm eggs survive well in damp soil.
  • Rotate runs or give ground a rest if you have the space.
  • Raise feeders and waterers so droppings do not get in.
  • Run a fecal test a couple of times a year rather than deworming blindly.
  • Keep chickens away from turkeys if cecal worms are present.

Eggs and the flock

Many dewormers have egg withdrawal periods, and some are not approved for laying hens at all. Check the product label or ask a vet before eating eggs. Wash your hands after handling droppings. See the common poultry diseases guide for more.

Common questions about worms in chickens

How do I know if my chickens have worms?

A fecal test at a vet is the reliable way. Visible worms in droppings mean a heavy load.

How often should I deworm chickens?

Base it on fecal tests rather than a fixed schedule. Ask a vet for your setup.

Can people get worms from chickens?

The common chicken worms are not considered a risk to people, but wash your hands after handling droppings.
1210:
Living with Marek's disease in a backyard flock

Marek's disease is caused by a herpesvirus that is extremely common wherever chickens are kept. It spreads in feather dander, and the virus can survive in coop dust for months. Most flocks have been exposed. The disease shows up mostly in young birds, often between a few weeks and several months old, and it can cause paralysis, tumors, weight loss and death. There is no cure, but vaccination works well.

Signs to watch for

  • Paralysis of one or both legs, often one leg forward and one back.
  • A drooping wing or twisted neck.
  • Gray or irregular pupils, sometimes called gray eye, and vision loss.
  • Weight loss despite eating.
  • Sudden death in birds that seemed only slightly off.

What to do if you suspect it

  1. Separate the affected bird into a quiet pen with food and water within reach.
  2. Rule out other causes like injury, bumblefoot or a stuck toe.
  3. Keep her clean and comfortable. Some birds with mild signs recover for a while.
  4. If a bird dies, keep the body cool and contact your state diagnostic lab about a necropsy. It is the only reliable way to confirm Marek's.
  5. Think about the rest of the flock and future chicks.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Leg paralysis can also come from injury, botulism or vitamin problems. Botulism paralysis climbs from the legs up to the neck and usually affects birds that ate rotting material. A twisted neck alone is often wry neck. A swollen foot or footpad scab is bumblefoot. The limping page walks through these checks.

When to call a vet

Call a vet or lab if several young birds go lame, if birds are wasting away, or if you are losing birds without a clear cause. Knowing it is Marek's changes how you plan the next batch of chicks.

Prevention

  • Buy vaccinated chicks. The vaccine needs to be given at hatch or in the egg to work best.
  • Keep new chicks away from older birds and their dust for the first weeks so the vaccine has time to work.
  • Keep the brooder clean and low in dust.
  • Some breeds have more natural resistance than others. Ask your hatchery.

The vaccine reduces tumors and deaths but does not stop birds from carrying or spreading the virus. The Marek's guide explains more.

The flock, eggs and people

Marek's does not infect people, and eggs from a flock with Marek's are considered safe to eat. Survivors can shed the virus for life, so assume a flock that has had it will expose any new birds. Do not sell or give away birds as healthy if Marek's has been confirmed in your flock.

Common questions about Marek's disease

Can a chicken recover from Marek's?

Some birds with mild signs seem to recover, but they remain carriers and can relapse.

Can I eat eggs from hens with Marek's?

Marek's is not a risk to people, and eggs are generally considered safe.

Should I vaccinate my chicks for Marek's?

Yes, it is one of the most useful vaccines for backyard flocks.
1212:
What an MG diagnosis means for your flock

Mycoplasma gallisepticum (MG) is a bacterial infection that causes chronic respiratory disease. It moves slowly compared with viruses, but it sticks around. Birds that recover usually stay carriers for life, and it can pass from hen to chick through the egg. That is why MG is a long-term flock decision, not just a sick bird.

Signs to watch for

  • Foamy bubbles in the corner of the eye.
  • Sneezing, nasal discharge and a swollen face around the eyes.
  • Rattling or gurgling breath, especially on the roost at night.
  • Drop in laying and weight loss over time.
  • Signs that flare up with stress, cold or moving birds.

Step by step

  1. Separate birds with signs into a clean, well-ventilated space.
  2. Check the rest of the flock, especially eyes and breathing at dusk.
  3. Improve ventilation and reduce dust and ammonia. These make MG worse.
  4. Call an avian or poultry vet, or your extension office, about testing. A blood or swab test confirms MG.
  5. Stop adding, selling, hatching from or showing birds until you know.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Foamy eyes are a strong pointer to MG. A foul smell with a swollen face fits infectious coryza. Wrinkled eggs and watery whites alongside breathing signs fit infectious bronchitis. Bloody mucus suggests ILT. Many flocks have more than one infection at once, which is why testing helps.

Reporting and testing

MG is part of the National Poultry Improvement Plan testing that many hatcheries use, and some states track it. Ask your extension office or state veterinarian what applies where you live. If you buy chicks, look for sources that test for MG.

When to call a vet

Call if birds have trouble breathing, stop eating or lose weight, or when you first suspect MG. A vet can prescribe treatment that eases signs, but it does not clear the carrier state.

Supportive care

Fresh air without drafts, clean bedding, clean water and low stress. Wipe discharge from eyes and nostrils. Home remedies may make birds feel better but they do not cure MG.

Long-term decisions

Many vets suggest running a closed flock after MG. That means no new birds in and no birds out, and no hatching eggs to share. Some keepers choose to start over after a full clean-out. Talk options through with a vet.

Eggs and people

MG is not a known risk to people, and eggs are generally fine to eat. Do not hatch or share hatching eggs from infected hens, since MG passes through the egg. If birds are treated, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal. See the respiratory disease guide for more.

Common questions about mycoplasma in chickens

Can chickens recover from mycoplasma?

Signs often ease, but birds usually stay carriers for life.

How do chickens get MG?

From carrier birds, wild birds, contaminated equipment and through the egg from infected hens.

Can I add new birds to a flock with MG?

They will likely get infected. Talk to a vet before adding any.
1215:
What to do if you suspect Newcastle disease

Newcastle disease is a viral disease of birds. Mild strains are fairly common and cause light breathing signs. Virulent Newcastle disease is very different. It spreads fast, kills large numbers of birds, and is a reportable disease. If you suspect it, you must contact your state veterinarian or extension office. Fast reporting is the best protection for your flock and every flock near you.

Signs that should make you call right away

  • Sudden deaths, sometimes several birds in a day.
  • Gasping, coughing and sneezing.
  • Nerve signs like trembling, twisted necks, circling, paralysis of legs or wings.
  • Swelling around the eyes and neck.
  • Green, watery diarrhea.
  • Sudden drop in laying and thin or misshapen eggs.

Step by step

  1. Call your state veterinarian or extension office. Describe what you see and follow their instructions.
  2. Do not move birds, eggs, manure or equipment off your property.
  3. Keep dead birds bagged and cool, away from pets and wildlife, until officials tell you what to do with them.
  4. Keep all visitors away from your birds.
  5. Keep the flock confined and away from wild birds.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Newcastle disease and avian influenza look very alike, and only a lab test can tell them apart. Both are reportable. A single twisted neck in an otherwise healthy flock is more often wry neck from injury or vitamin issues. Paralysis that climbs from the legs up after birds ate rotting material is more like botulism. Slow, mild breathing signs without deaths are more typical of mycoplasma or bronchitis. When in doubt, report.

Protecting yourself

Newcastle disease can cause mild eye irritation in people who handle infected birds, usually red, watery eyes. Wear gloves and eye protection if you must handle sick or dead birds. Wash your hands, change clothes and shoes, and keep children away from sick birds.

Prevention

  • Buy birds from reputable, tested sources.
  • Quarantine new birds for about a month.
  • Keep wild birds away from feed and water.
  • Do not share equipment, and clean your shoes after visiting other flocks or feed stores.
  • Be careful with birds that come from outside legal channels. Illegally imported birds have spread virulent Newcastle in the past.

The Defend the Flock page has more.

Eggs and the rest of the flock

Do not eat, sell or share eggs from a flock suspected of Newcastle disease. Follow officials' instructions. There is no home treatment, and home remedies do not cure it.

Common questions about Newcastle disease

Is Newcastle disease reportable?

Yes. Contact your state veterinarian or extension office if you suspect it.

Can humans catch Newcastle disease?

It can cause mild eye irritation in people, but it is not a serious human illness.

Is there a vaccine for Newcastle disease?

Yes. Ask a vet whether it makes sense for your flock and area.
1216:
First aid for a chicken after a predator attack

A predator attack leaves more damage than you can see. Bite wounds can be tiny on the outside and deep underneath, and bacteria from teeth and claws cause serious infection. Shock is a real risk too. The first hour matters.

Step by step, right now

  1. Secure the rest of the flock. The predator may come back, so lock birds in and check the coop for gaps.
  2. Bring the injured bird somewhere warm, quiet and dim. A box with a towel works.
  3. Let her calm down for a few minutes before you examine her. Birds in shock can die from extra stress.
  4. Stop bleeding with gentle, steady pressure using clean gauze.
  5. Look her over carefully. Part feathers on the back, under the wings, around the neck and near the vent. Wet the feathers to see the skin.
  6. Flush wounds with saline or clean warm water.
  7. Apply a wound spray or ointment made for animals. Avoid products with painkillers in them, since some human products can be harmful to birds.
  8. Keep her separate from the flock while she heals.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet for deep punctures, wounds you can see muscle or bone through, large flaps of skin, bleeding you cannot stop, or a bird who is limp, cold or breathing hard. Bites from mammals often need antibiotics, and a vet may need to close large wounds. Check the product label or ask the vet about eggs while she is treated.

Watching for infection

Check wounds every day. Redness, swelling, heat, a bad smell, or green or yellow pus mean infection. Also watch for fly eggs and maggots in warm weather. Keep her indoors or screened until wounds close.

How to tell this apart from other wounds

Peck wounds from flock mates are often on the back, tail or vent and keep getting worse if the bird stays in the flock. Those are covered under feather pecking. Bare backs from a rooster are mating wear. If you are not sure what attacked, the predator identification page can help you read the signs.

Prevention

  • Use hardware cloth, not chicken wire, for coop windows and runs.
  • Bury or apron wire around the run to stop diggers.
  • Lock birds in every night.
  • Cover runs if hawks are a problem.

See predator-proofing basics for a fuller setup.

Rest of the flock

Check every bird after an attack, since others may have hidden injuries. Stress can stop laying for a while. Eggs from uninjured birds are fine to eat. Wear gloves when handling wounds and wash your hands well.

Common questions about predator wounds in chickens

Can a chicken survive a predator attack?

Many do with quick first aid and good wound care. Deep bites and shock are the biggest risks.

Should I give my chicken antibiotics after an attack?

Ask a vet. Mammal bites often need them, but the right product depends on the wound.

When can an injured hen rejoin the flock?

Once wounds are fully healed. Reintroduce her slowly to avoid pecking.
1218:
Getting rid of scaly leg mites for good

Scaly leg mites burrow under the scales of the legs and feet and live their whole lives there. As they feed, they push the scales up and leave crusty debris behind. The legs end up looking thick, rough and lumpy. It does not happen overnight, which is why it is easy to miss until it is fairly advanced. Older birds are often worse simply because they have had longer to build up a load.

How to spot it

  • Scales that stand up instead of lying flat and smooth.
  • White or gray crusty material under and between scales.
  • Legs that look thicker than normal.
  • In bad cases, limping, swollen toes, or bleeding where scales have come loose.

A plan that works

  1. Check the legs of every bird, not just the one you noticed. Mites spread along shared roosts.
  2. Gently clean the legs with warm, soapy water and a soft brush. Do not pry off scales.
  3. Dry the legs well.
  4. Coat legs and feet with petroleum jelly or a plant-based oil to smother the mites. Repeat every few days for several weeks. This is slow, and stopping early is why it comes back.
  5. If the infestation is bad, ask a vet about a treatment labeled for poultry, and follow the label exactly.
  6. Clean the coop. Strip bedding, scrub roosts, and treat or replace rough, cracked wood.

Patience with the scales

Killing the mites does not make the legs look normal right away. The damaged scales stay rough until they shed and new ones grow, which can take months and often happens with a molt. Judge progress by whether the crusting stops getting worse, not by how pretty the legs look.

How to tell this apart from look-alikes

Older birds get naturally thicker scales, but they still lie flat. A swelling on the bottom of the foot with a dark scab is bumblefoot. Dark, dry toe tips after a cold snap point to frostbite. Mites and lice on the body are a separate issue, covered on external mites and lice, though it is a good idea to check for them at the same time.

When to call a vet

Call an avian or poultry vet if legs are bleeding, very swollen or hot, if toes look like they are losing circulation, or if a bird cannot walk. Severe cases can lead to infection and the loss of toes.

Prevention

  • Check legs when you do your regular health checks.
  • Look at new birds' legs closely before you buy, and quarantine them for about a month.
  • Use smooth, sealed roosts that are easy to clean.
  • Replace bedding regularly.

Eggs and the rest of the flock

Scaly leg mites do not affect egg safety, and petroleum jelly on the legs is not a problem for eating eggs. If you use any insecticide or medicated product, check the product label or ask a vet about egg withdrawal. These mites do not live on people.

Common questions about scaly leg mites

Does petroleum jelly kill scaly leg mites?

It can smother them if applied often for several weeks. It is slow, and heavy cases may need a labeled product.

Are scaly leg mites contagious?

Yes, between birds, mostly through shared roosts and bedding.

Why do my old hen's legs look rough?

Aging thickens scales, but if they lift or crust, check for mites.
1221:
