The Plymouth Rock is an American classic, best known in its barred black and white pattern.

By goal

  • Eggs. The Australorp has a strong reputation as a layer and often has a slight edge. Plymouth Rocks are also good, steady layers.
  • Temperament. Australorps tend to be quiet and calm. Plymouth Rocks are curious, friendly and a bit more chatty.
  • Kids. Both are good. Rocks often follow people around, which kids love.
  • Cold. Both are cold-hardy. Each has a single comb, so keep the coop dry to prevent frostbite.
  • Heat. Both can do it with shade. The Australorp's black feathers soak up more sun.
  • Meat. Both are dual-purpose. Plymouth Rocks have a long history as table birds.
  • Noise. Australorps are usually quieter.

Together in one flock

These two get along well. They are similar in size and both fairly easygoing. The Rocks may be a little more forward at treat time. A mixed flock of black Australorps and barred Rocks is easy to tell apart at a glance, which helps when you are tracking who is laying and who is not. Both are good foragers if you let them free-range, and the barred pattern gives Rocks a bit of camouflage.

What tips the decision

Personality. If you want a quiet, low-drama bird, go Australorp. If you want a bird with more chatter and curiosity, go Plymouth Rock.

Broodiness. Australorps go broody now and then. Plymouth Rocks can too, but many lines are less inclined. If you want eggs only, ask your source about their line.

Heat. In a very hot, sunny yard with little shade, the lighter barred pattern of the Rock is a slight advantage.

Still undecided? The breed matcher can weigh your climate and goals.

Common questions about Australorps vs Plymouth Rocks

Are Australorps good for beginners?

Yes. They are calm, hardy and lay well, which makes them a common first breed.

Is a Barred Rock the same as a Plymouth Rock?

Yes. Barred is the best known color variety of the Plymouth Rock. Other colors exist too.

Do Australorps lay in winter?

Many keep laying better than most breeds through winter, though all hens slow down with short days.
257:
Easter Egger or Ameraucana, what is the real difference?

This is one of the most confusing comparisons in chicken keeping, because the two often get sold under the same name. The Ameraucana is a recognized breed with a written standard. It has a beard and muffs, a pea comb, slate legs and lays blue eggs. The Easter Egger is not a breed at all. It is a mixed bird that carries the blue egg gene, and it can lay blue, green, olive or sometimes tinted eggs.

Choose by what you want

  • Eggs. Easter Eggers are often the better layers and come with a surprise color. Ameraucanas give you true blue eggs.
  • Temperament. Easter Eggers are usually friendly and curious. Ameraucanas tend to be a bit more reserved, though many are sweet.
  • Kids. Easter Eggers. They are easygoing, and the colorful eggs are a big hit with kids.
  • Climate. Both often have pea combs, which hold up well in cold. Both handle heat reasonably with shade.
  • Meat. Neither is a meat bird. Both are light to medium in size.
  • Noise. Both are moderate.

Raising them in one flock

They get along fine. In fact, many keepers have both without knowing it. Since Easter Eggers vary in look, a mixed group can include birds with muffs, beards, pea combs and many feather colors. Ameraucanas look much more uniform. Neither tends to be a bully, so they also mix well with most other backyard breeds.

The deciding factors

Do you plan to show or breed? If you want to show birds or breed to a standard, you need a true Ameraucana from a breeder. Easter Eggers cannot be shown as a breed.

Do you need blue, or just colorful? If you want a guaranteed blue egg, get an Ameraucana or another true blue layer. If any shade of blue or green makes you happy, Easter Eggers are cheaper and easier to find.

What does the seller call it? Many hatchery chicks labeled "Ameraucana" or "Americana" are Easter Eggers. If the seller cannot tell you the variety and line, assume Easter Egger.

For more on how the blue egg gene works, see the blue egg guide.

Common questions about Easter Eggers vs Ameraucanas

How can I tell if my bird is a real Ameraucana?

Check for slate or blue legs, a pea comb, a beard and muffs, a recognized color, and blue eggs. Missing any of these usually means Easter Egger.

Do Easter Eggers lay blue eggs?

Some do. Others lay green, olive or tinted eggs. Each hen lays her own color for life.

Are Ameraucanas and Araucanas the same?

No. They are separate breeds. Araucanas are often rumpless and have ear tufts.
259:
Leghorn or Rhode Island Red, which should you keep?

These are two of the hardest-working layers you can get, but they work in very different ways. The Leghorn is a light, quick Mediterranean bird that lays large white eggs and burns little feed doing it. The Rhode Island Red is a sturdy American dual-purpose bird that lays brown eggs and shrugs off rough weather.

Pick by goal

  • Eggs. Both are excellent. Leghorns are among the most efficient layers of any breed. Reds are close behind, with brown shells.
  • Temperament. Reds are calmer and easier to handle. Leghorns are flighty, alert and rarely want to be held.
  • Kids. Rhode Island Red hens are the better choice for kids who want to pet their birds.
  • Cold. Reds handle cold better. The Leghorn's big single comb is prone to frostbite.
  • Heat. Leghorns are built for heat, with a light body and big comb that sheds warmth.
  • Meat. Reds are heavier and useful as a table bird. Leghorns are too light to be worth it.
  • Noise. Leghorns tend to be louder and more excitable. Reds are moderate.

Keeping them in one flock

They can share a coop, but expect some tension. Both are confident birds. Leghorns are quick and tend to avoid fights by running, while Reds hold their ground. Give them plenty of space, a covered run or tall fence for the Leghorns, which fly well, and more than one feeder. The upside is a carton of white and brown eggs that makes it easy to see who is laying.

What usually decides it

Your winters. In a cold climate, the Leghorn's comb needs extra care and a very dry coop. The Red is the easier keep.

Your fence height. Leghorns fly. If you free-range near a garden or neighbors, they may go where you do not want them. Reds stay put more.

How you feel about handling. If you want birds that tolerate being picked up, go Red. If you are happy watching from a distance and collecting eggs, Leghorns are rewarding and low-cost to feed.

See how each fits your yard with the egg predictor.

Common questions about Leghorns vs Rhode Island Reds

Do Leghorns lay more eggs than Rhode Island Reds?

Leghorns often lay slightly more, and eat a bit less to do it. Both are strong layers.

Are Leghorns good for beginners?

They are hardy and easy to feed, but their flighty nature can frustrate new keepers who want friendly birds.

Can Leghorns live in cold climates?

Yes, with a dry, well-ventilated coop. Watch their combs closely in very cold weather.
262:
Marans or Welsummer for dark eggs?

If you are shopping for dark brown eggs, these two are the names you keep hearing. The Marans, from France, is known for the darkest chocolate eggs of any common breed. The Welsummer, from the Netherlands, lays a warm terracotta egg, often with darker speckles. Both are beautiful. Here is how to choose.

By goal

  • Egg color. Good Marans lines lay the darkest eggs. Welsummer eggs are a rich reddish brown, and the speckling is their signature.
  • Egg numbers. Both are moderate layers. Neither matches a production hybrid.
  • Temperament. Marans are usually calm and quiet. Welsummers are friendly but busy and active.
  • Kids. Both can be good. Calm Marans may be easier to pick up.
  • Climate. Both are fairly cold-hardy. Both have single combs, so keep the coop dry in winter.
  • Meat. Marans are often kept as a dual-purpose bird and dress out well. Welsummers are lighter.
  • Noise. Both are moderate. Welsummers can be a bit chattier when foraging.

Raising them side by side

They get along well and make a lovely pair in the yard. The bigger difference is in daily habits. Welsummers love to forage and range widely if allowed, while Marans are happy to stay closer. Both generally fit into a mixed flock without much drama. If you mix them with blue egg layers, you have the start of a great colorful carton, and you can even breed Olive Eggers.

The real deciding factors

Line matters more than breed. Many hatchery Marans lay medium brown eggs, not the dark chocolate seen in photos. If deep color is the goal, buy from a breeder who selects for it and ask to see eggs from the parent flock.

Do you free-range? Welsummers are better foragers and more predator aware, with coloring that blends into the ground.

Do you want speckles? If you love a speckled, painted look, Welsummers are hard to beat.

Both breeds' eggs fade through the laying season and darken again after a rest. The dark egg guide explains why.

Common questions about Marans vs Welsummers

Which lays darker eggs, Marans or Welsummer?

Well-bred Marans usually lay darker eggs. Welsummers lay a reddish brown with speckles.

Can I cross Marans and Welsummers?

Yes. The chicks will usually lay brown eggs, with shade depending on the parents.

Why are my Marans eggs not very dark?

The line may not be selected for color, or the hen is in the later part of her laying cycle.
264:
Wyandotte or Orpington, which one suits your yard?

Both breeds are heavy, cold-hardy, brown egg layers with a lot of fans. They also come in many striking colors. The big differences are personality, comb type and how they handle the pecking order. The Wyandotte has a low rose comb and is famous for laced feather patterns. The Orpington is the large, fluffy, gentle bird most people picture when they think of a friendly hen.

Goal by goal

  • Eggs. Both are good, steady layers. Many keepers find Wyandottes slightly more consistent, partly because Orpingtons go broody more.
  • Temperament. Orpingtons are very docile. Wyandottes are usually calm but more independent, and some can be bossy.
  • Kids. Orpingtons are the safer bet for small kids who want to cuddle.
  • Cold. Wyandottes have the edge. The rose comb is far less likely to get frostbite than the Orpington's single comb.
  • Heat. Both are heavy and fluffy, so give both shade and airflow.
  • Meat. Both are dual-purpose. Orpingtons tend to be heavier.
  • Noise. Both are fairly quiet hens.

Together in one flock

They usually mix well. A Wyandotte may take a higher spot in the pecking order, but Orpingtons rarely contest it. Watch new introductions, since a confident Wyandotte can be pushy with new birds. With enough space and two feeders, a mix of laced Wyandottes and solid Orpingtons is a good-looking and low-stress flock.

What decides it

Winter severity. In a very cold area, the Wyandotte's rose comb is a real advantage. A single comb Orpington can still do fine, but you will want to watch the comb on the coldest nights and make sure the coop vents moisture well.

Color choice. Both come in many colors. Wyandottes are known for laced patterns like silver and gold laced. Orpingtons are best known in buff, with black, blue and lavender also common. If you love a particular look, that can settle it on its own.

Broodiness. Orpingtons go broody often. Some keepers want that for hatching. Others find it frustrating.

How hands-on you are. If you want a bird to sit on your lap, Orpington. If you want a sturdy, good-looking bird that is a bit more self-sufficient, Wyandotte.

For more breeds that do well in harsh winters, see the cold climate breeds guide.

Common questions about Wyandottes vs Orpingtons

Are Wyandottes aggressive?

Most are calm with people. Some hens can be bossy with flock mates, especially newcomers.

Which is bigger, Wyandotte or Orpington?

Orpingtons are usually larger and heavier, and their fluffy feathers make them look even bigger.

Do Wyandottes go broody?

Some do, but usually less often than Orpingtons.
266:
Brahma or Jersey Giant, which big chicken should you get?

These are two of the largest chicken breeds you can keep. Both are calm, cold-hardy and lay brown eggs. But they grow differently, look very different and suit different keepers. The Brahma has feathered feet, a pea comb and a gentle, almost stately way about it. The Jersey Giant, an American breed, is usually black or white, with clean legs and a single comb, and is often called the largest American breed.

By goal

  • Eggs. Both are moderate layers. Brahmas are known for laying well through cold months.
  • Temperament. Both are calm and gentle. Brahmas are often described as especially docile.
  • Kids. Both are good, but they are heavy. Teach kids to support the whole body.
  • Cold. Brahmas edge it with their pea comb and feathered feet. Jersey Giants handle cold well but watch the comb.
  • Heat. Both struggle more than lighter breeds. Shade and water are a must.
  • Meat. Both are big, but slow to mature. Jersey Giants take a long time to fill out, which makes them costly to raise for meat.
  • Noise. Both hens are fairly quiet.

In one flock

They get along very well. Both are laid back and tend to avoid fights. The issue is more about how they fit with smaller breeds. Their size alone can push lighter birds away from food, even without aggression. Use several feeders and waterers, and make sure smaller birds have a place to eat in peace.

Deciding factors

Coop setup. Big birds need bigger pop doors, sturdy roosts placed low enough to hop down from without injury, and more floor space than standard breeds. Go above the usual 4 square feet per bird.

Mud. Brahma foot feathers pick up mud and can ball up with ice. In wet climates, that means more foot care. Jersey Giants avoid that.

Patience. Both grow slowly, and Jersey Giants are especially slow. If you want a fast meat bird, neither is the answer.

Use the feed calculator to plan for their bigger appetites.

Common questions about Brahmas vs Jersey Giants

Which chicken is bigger, Brahma or Jersey Giant?

Both are very large. Jersey Giants are often a little heavier, but individual birds and lines vary.

Are Brahmas good layers?

They are moderate layers and are valued for laying through winter.

Do giant breeds need special roosts?

Lower, wider roosts help prevent leg and foot injuries when heavy birds jump down.
268:
Barred Rock or Barnevelder, which hen is for you?

These two make a tempting pair. Both are calm, cold-hardy brown egg layers with eye-catching feathers. The Barred Plymouth Rock is the classic American black and white barred hen. The Barnevelder is a Dutch breed best known for its double-laced feathers and very dark brown eggs.

Choosing by goal

  • Eggs. Barred Rocks usually lay more eggs. Barnevelders lay fewer, but the eggs are a deeper brown, sometimes with a matte finish.
  • Temperament. Both are calm. Barred Rocks are curious and chatty. Barnevelders are quiet and gentle.
  • Kids. Both are good family birds. Barred Rocks are often the friendlier of the two, while Barnevelders are easy to handle but less likely to seek attention.
  • Cold. Both handle cold well. Both have single combs, so a dry coop is key.
  • Heat. Both manage with shade. Neither is built specifically for heat.
  • Meat. Barred Rocks are the better table bird of the two.
  • Noise. Barnevelders tend to be quieter.

How they do together

They are a good match. They are similar in size and both easygoing, so fights are rare. Barred Rocks may be more forward at feeding time. The mix also gives you two egg shades, which makes it easy to see who is laying. Both forage well if you free-range, and the barring and lacing patterns both help them blend in.

What tips it one way or the other

Egg count or egg color? This is the main question. If you want the most eggs, choose the Barred Rock. If you want darker eggs in your basket, the Barnevelder brings that, even if the numbers are lower.

Availability. Barred Rocks are easy to find at almost any hatchery or feed store. Barnevelders are less common, and good lines with strong lacing and dark eggs may need a breeder.

Noise. If you live close to neighbors, the quieter Barnevelder can be a small advantage.

See more dark egg layers in the dark brown egg guide.

Common questions about Barred Rocks vs Barnevelders

Are Barnevelders good layers?

They are moderate layers. They are valued more for their egg color and looks than for numbers.

Can you sex Barred Rock chicks?

Often, yes, with some practice. Female chicks tend to have darker legs and a smaller, sharper head spot than males.

Do Barnevelder eggs get lighter?

Like other brown egg layers, their eggs often fade over the laying season and darken again after a break.
271:
Sussex or Speckled Sussex, what is the difference?

This one surprises a lot of people. The Speckled Sussex is not a separate breed. It is one color variety of the Sussex, a heritage English breed. Other varieties include the Light Sussex, which is white with a black neck and tail, along with Red and others. So the choice here is mostly about color and line, not breed traits.

What stays the same

All Sussex share the same basic nature. They are calm, curious and friendly, good foragers, cold-hardy and solid layers of light brown to tinted eggs. They are also useful as a dual-purpose bird. Many go broody from time to time.

Which variety by goal

  • Eggs. Laying depends more on the line than the color. Some keepers find Light Sussex lines lay a bit better, but that varies by source.
  • Temperament. The same across varieties. Speckled birds have a reputation for being especially curious and people-friendly, though that is more anecdote than rule.
  • Kids. Any Sussex is a good family bird.
  • Climate. All varieties handle cold well. Give shade in heat.
  • Meat. Utility lines of Light Sussex have a long history as table birds.
  • Noise. Moderate, the same across varieties.
  • Free-ranging. The speckled pattern gives better camouflage from hawks than the white Light Sussex.

Mixing varieties in one flock

Mixing Sussex varieties is easy, since they share the same temperament. It also helps you tell birds apart. If you plan to breed, keep in mind that crossing varieties will not give you clean show colors in the chicks.

The deciding factors

Looks over time. Speckled Sussex often get more white spots after each molt, so a hen can look more speckled every year. Many keepers love that.

Predator pressure. If hawks are a problem and you free-range, the speckled variety blends in better.

Purpose. If you want a utility bird for eggs and meat, ask breeders about their line's production. That matters more than the color.

See how Sussex fit into a homestead flock in the dual-purpose breeds guide.

Common questions about Sussex and Speckled Sussex

Is Speckled Sussex a different breed from Sussex?

No. It is a color variety of the Sussex breed.

Why does my Speckled Sussex have more white spots now?

The white tips on their feathers often increase after each molt. It is normal.

What color eggs do Sussex lay?

Light brown to tinted or cream, and some keepers say their eggs look slightly pink.
273:
Sapphire Gem or Olive Egger, which one should you add?

These two get compared because both are popular newer additions to backyard flocks, but they are very different birds. The Sapphire Gem is a hybrid known for soft blue-gray feathers and good laying of brown eggs. The Olive Egger is a cross bred for its olive green eggs, and its looks vary a lot.

By goal

  • Eggs. If you want lots of eggs, Sapphire Gems are known as strong layers. If you want unusual egg color, Olive Eggers win.
  • Egg color. Sapphire Gems lay light to medium brown eggs. Olive Eggers lay olive or green.
  • Temperament. Sapphire Gems are often described as calm and friendly. Olive Eggers depend on their parents and can range from mellow to flighty.
  • Kids. Sapphire Gems are a safer bet for a predictable, calm bird.
  • Climate. Both are generally hardy. Olive Eggers from a pea comb parent may hold up better in cold.
  • Meat. Neither is a meat bird.
  • Noise. Both are moderate.

Living together

They mix easily. Neither is known for bullying, and they look nothing alike, so telling them apart is simple. Together they give you a carton with brown and olive eggs. Add a blue and a white layer and you have a full rainbow.

What usually decides it

Numbers or novelty. This is the main question. If your goal is a full egg basket, Sapphire Gems are the practical pick. If you want a conversation piece in the carton, go Olive Egger.

Space and feed. Both are medium-size birds that fit a normal backyard coop. Plan the usual 4 square feet inside per hen and give each a balanced layer feed with oyster shell on the side.

Predictability. Sapphire Gems are fairly uniform in looks and behavior. Olive Eggers are a mix, and you may not know the exact egg shade until they start laying.

Hatching plans. Neither breeds true. Hatching eggs from either will not give you the same bird again. To get more Olive Eggers, you cross a blue egg layer with a dark brown layer. The olive egg guide explains how.

Common questions about Sapphire Gems vs Olive Eggers

What color eggs does a Sapphire Gem lay?

Brown eggs, usually light to medium. The blue in the name refers to the feathers, not the eggs.

Do Olive Eggers lay every day?

Many lay well, but output depends on the parent breeds. Expect a good but not exceptional layer.

Are Sapphire Gems good for beginners?

Yes. They are generally calm, hardy and good layers, which suits a first flock.
276:
Buff Orpington or Australorp, which is better for you?

These two are closely related. The Australorp was developed in Australia from Orpington stock, with a focus on egg laying. The Buff Orpington stayed closer to the original English type, heavy and very fluffy. So the comparison is really about which direction you want, more eggs and a sleeker bird, or more fluff and a softer, broodier hen.

Goal by goal

  • Eggs. The Australorp usually lays more. It is known as one of the better heritage layers.
  • Temperament. Both are calm. Buff Orpingtons are famously cuddly. Australorps are gentle but a little more reserved.
  • Kids. Both are great. The Buff Orpington's patience makes it a classic kids' chicken.
  • Cold. Both handle cold well. Both have single combs, so keep the coop dry.
  • Heat. Both need shade. Black Australorps absorb more sun, and fluffy Orpingtons hold more heat, so neither is ideal in extreme heat.
  • Meat. Buff Orpingtons are heavier and a better table bird.
  • Noise. Both are fairly quiet.

Keeping both in one flock

This is one of the easiest pairings there is. They share a similar size and mellow nature, so fights are rare. The golden and black feathers make it easy to tell them apart. Both may go broody, Orpingtons more often, so have an extra nest box ready in spring. They also mix well with most other calm breeds.

Deciding factors

Egg priority. If eggs are your main reason for keeping chickens, the Australorp is the better choice.

Broodiness. Buff Orpingtons go broody more often. That is good news if you want hens to hatch chicks and bad news if you want steady eggs.

Climate. In a hot, sunny yard, the difference is small but real. Give either breed shade, but watch the black Australorp more closely on the hottest days.

Feather care. Buff feathers fade in strong sun and can look a little washed out by late summer. Black Australorp feathers hold their shine. It does not affect health, only looks.

Looks. Some people simply love the golden fluff of a Buff. Others prefer the beetle green shine of an Australorp in the sun.

Still deciding? The beginner breeds guide covers both in more detail.

Common questions about Buff Orpingtons vs Australorps

Are Australorps and Orpingtons related?

Yes. Australorps were developed from Orpingtons in Australia, bred for laying.

Which is friendlier, Buff Orpington or Australorp?

Both are friendly. Buff Orpingtons are often seen as the more cuddly of the two.

Do Australorps go broody?

Some do, but usually less often than Buff Orpingtons.
279:
Polish or Houdan, which crested chicken should you choose?

Both of these breeds wear a big crest of feathers on their heads, and both lay white eggs. That is where most of the similarity ends. The Polish is a small, light ornamental bird with a crest so large it can block its vision. The Houdan, a French breed, has a crest plus a beard and muffs, a mottled pattern and an unusual trait, five toes on each foot instead of four.

By goal

  • Eggs. Both lay white eggs at a moderate rate. Neither is a top layer.
  • Temperament. Polish can be flighty and easily startled, often because they cannot see well. Houdans are usually calmer and gentle.
  • Kids. Houdans are the better choice. Polish can be sweet, but sudden movements startle them.
  • Cold. Both have small combs, which helps. Wet crests can freeze, though, so keep them dry.
  • Heat. Both manage with shade. Neither is heavy.
  • Meat. Houdans were historically used as table birds in France. Polish are too small.
  • Noise. Both are moderate. Startled Polish can be loud.

Raising them together

They work well together because both are gentle, crested birds. Crested breeds are often picked on by others, since flock mates like to peck at the crest. Keeping crested birds together, or with very calm breeds, reduces that. Raise them alongside each other from chicks if you can.

Crest care for both

  • Check crests often for mites and lice, which like to hide there.
  • Use waterers that keep crests and beards dry, such as nipple waterers or cups.
  • Talk softly when you approach, so a bird that cannot see you is not startled.
  • Some keepers trim the crest a little around the eyes to help vision.

What decides it

Hawks. Crested birds have poor upward vision. If you free-range in hawk country, a covered run is wise for either. Read more on aerial predator protection.

Calmness. If you want a quieter, steadier bird, choose the Houdan.

Show or just for fun. Polish come in many colors and are a favorite at poultry shows. Houdans are rarer, so good stock can take more effort to find. Check with breeders before you set your heart on one.

Common questions about Polish vs Houdan chickens

Can Polish chickens see?

Yes, but their crest can block a lot of their vision, which makes them jumpy.

Do Houdans really have five toes?

Yes. Five toes is part of the breed.

Are crested chickens hard to keep?

Not hard, but they need a bit more care, mainly keeping crests clean, dry and free of pests.
280:
Easter Egger or Olive Egger, which should you hatch or buy?

Both of these are mixed birds bred for colorful eggs, and both come with a bit of mystery. The Easter Egger carries the blue egg gene and lays blue, green or sometimes tinted eggs. The Olive Egger is usually a cross between a blue egg layer and a dark brown egg layer, so its eggs come out olive.

Pick by goal

  • Egg color. Want blue to light green? Easter Egger. Want olive or deep green? Olive Egger.
  • Egg numbers. Both are usually good layers. Easter Eggers have a reputation for being steady and reliable.
  • Temperament. Easter Eggers are typically friendly and curious. Olive Eggers vary based on their parents.
  • Kids. Both can be good. Easter Eggers are the more predictable pick.
  • Climate. Many Easter Eggers have pea combs that hold up well in cold. Olive Eggers may have a single or pea comb depending on parents.
  • Meat. Neither is a meat bird. Olive Eggers with Marans in them may be a bit larger.
  • Noise. Both are moderate.

Together in one flock

They get along well, since both are usually easygoing. Together they give you a wide spread of blues, greens and olives. Because both vary in looks, you may need leg bands to keep track of who lays what.

The genetics that decide it

Blue eggs come from a dominant gene that puts color through the whole shell. Brown is a coating added at the end. An Easter Egger with a little brown in its background lays green. An Olive Egger has a heavier brown parent, so the coat is thicker and the egg is darker. If you want to hatch your own Olive Eggers, cross a blue layer with a dark brown layer such as a Marans. Using a blue parent with two copies of the blue gene means every daughter lays a blue-based egg. The green egg guide explains the shade range.

Other deciding factors

Availability. Easter Eggers are easy to find at most hatcheries. Olive Eggers are increasingly available, or you can make your own.

Predictability. Neither breeds true. Each hen's egg color is a surprise until she starts laying.

Common questions about Easter Eggers vs Olive Eggers

Is an Olive Egger a type of Easter Egger?

They overlap. Both carry the blue egg gene. Olive Eggers usually have a dark brown egg parent, which gives olive shells.

Can an Easter Egger lay olive eggs?

Some do, if they inherited enough brown egg genes.

What rooster makes Olive Eggers?

Either parent can carry the genes. A common route is a dark egg Marans rooster over blue egg hens, or the reverse.
292:
Why brown eggs are brown

Every chicken egg starts out white. The shell is made of calcium carbonate, which is naturally white. A brown egg gets its color near the very end of the process, when the hen's shell gland lays down a brown pigment over the outside of the shell. That is why brown is often called a coating. Crack a brown egg and look at the inside of the shell. It is white or close to it.

How much brown a hen adds

The shade depends on how much pigment a hen puts down, and that is mostly genetic. Some breeds lay a light tan egg. Others lay a deep reddish or chocolate brown. Within one breed, individual hens still vary, which is why a carton from one flock can hold several shades. Popular brown layers include the Rhode Island Red, the Australorp, the Plymouth Rock and the Orpington, along with high-output sex link hybrids.

Why brown eggs get lighter over the season

Many keepers notice that the first eggs of spring are the darkest, and the color fades as the laying season goes on. A hen has a limited amount of pigment to give each egg. When she lays often, the coating can get thinner. Color also tends to lighten as a hen gets older. Stress, heat, illness and some medications can make eggs come out paler for a while. After the molt and a rest, many hens come back with darker eggs again.

If one hen's eggs suddenly turn much paler or develop odd texture, it is worth watching her. The guide to thin shell eggs covers what to check.

Brown egg myths

  • Brown eggs are healthier. Shell color does not change the nutrition inside. Diet and freshness matter far more.
  • Brown eggs taste better. In blind tests, most people cannot tell them apart. A backyard egg tastes better because it is fresher and the hen eats a varied diet, not because of the shell.
  • Brown eggs have thicker shells. Shell strength comes from the hen's age, health and calcium, not the color.
  • You can tell egg color by feather color. No. A white-feathered bird can lay brown eggs. Earlobe color is a loose hint at best, with many exceptions.

Can you make brown eggs darker?

Not much. You cannot feed a hen into laying a darker egg than her genetics allow. What you can do is keep her healthy, cool in summer and free of stress, so she lays as close to her natural color as possible. If you want deep brown eggs, pick a breed known for them.

Common questions about brown eggs

Why are some brown eggs spotted?

Speckles happen when pigment goes on unevenly. It is common and harmless.

Does the bloom affect color?

The bloom is a thin protective layer over the shell. It can give eggs a soft, slightly matte look. Washing removes it, which can make some eggs look a touch lighter or shinier.

Why does my brown egg rub off?

Freshly laid eggs sometimes have a coating that smudges before it dries. It is the same pigment that gives the egg its color.
293:
What makes an egg white

A white egg is simply a shell with no pigment added. All chicken eggshells are built from calcium carbonate, which is white. Hens that lay brown eggs add a brown coat on top at the end. Hens that lay blue eggs put blue pigment through the whole shell. White egg layers do neither. That makes white the starting point for every egg color.

Which breeds lay white eggs

Many white egg layers come from the Mediterranean region. They tend to be lighter birds with large combs, built for warm weather. The best known is the Leghorn, the bird behind most commercial white eggs. Others include the Ancona, Minorca, Andalusian and Sicilian Buttercup. A few crested breeds such as the Polish and Houdan also lay white eggs, and so do Hamburgs and Lakenvelders.

Do white eggs change color over the season?

Not much, which is one nice thing about them. Since there is no pigment layer to thin out, white eggs stay white all year. The bigger changes you will notice are in size and shell quality. Young pullets lay small eggs at first. Older hens tend to lay fewer, larger eggs with thinner shells. In hot weather, shells on any breed can get thinner because hens eat less.

What you trade for white eggs

Many white egg breeds are active, flighty and good at foraging. They often lay well and eat a little less than heavy breeds. On the other hand, they are usually less cuddly, more likely to fly over a short fence, and their big single combs can get frostbite in very cold areas. If you want white eggs in a cold climate, give them a dry, well-vented coop.

White egg myths

  • White eggs are bleached. They are not. The shell grows white.
  • White eggs are less nutritious. Shell color has no link to what is inside.
  • White earlobes always mean white eggs. It is a rough rule that often works for Mediterranean breeds, but there are plenty of exceptions.
  • White eggs come from factory hens only. Plenty of backyard breeds lay white eggs, and the eggs are just as fresh as any other.

If you want a mix of white and colored eggs in one carton, the colorful egg breeds guide pairs well with a few white layers.

Common questions about white eggs

Why are store eggs mostly white in the US?

Large egg farms often use white egg hybrids because they are efficient layers. It is about production, not quality.

Can a white egg layer suddenly lay brown eggs?

No. A hen does not switch colors. If you find a brown egg from a white layer flock, another hen laid it, or the egg picked up stains.

Are white eggs easier to candle?

Yes. With no pigment, light passes through more easily, so it is easier to see inside when you candle eggs for hatching.
299:
How chickens lay blue eggs

Blue eggs are not dyed on the outside like brown ones. The blue pigment, biliverdin, is added while the shell is forming, so the color runs all the way through. Crack a blue egg and the inside of the shell is blue too. That is the quickest way to tell a true blue egg from a pale green one, since green and olive eggs usually show blue inside with a brown layer on top.

The gene behind it

Blue shells come from a single gene, often called the blue egg gene or oocyan. It is dominant. A hen needs only one copy to lay blue eggs, and a bird with two copies passes it on to all of her chicks. This is why crossing a blue egg breed with a white egg breed can still produce blue layers, and crossing with a brown egg breed gives green or olive.

Breeds that lay blue eggs

  • Ameraucana, an American breed developed for blue eggs, with a beard, muffs and a pea comb.
  • Araucana, often rumpless and tufted. The tuft gene can be lethal in pairs, so they are harder to breed.
  • Cream Legbar, a crested bird whose chicks can be sexed by down color at hatch.
  • Whiting True Blue, a production-style blue layer.

Easter Eggers can lay blue too, but their eggs might also be green, olive or even tinted, depending on their mix.

Does blue fade?

Blue tends to stay steadier than brown, since it is part of the shell rather than a coating. Some hens still lay a little paler late in the season or as they age. The first egg a pullet lays is often one of the brightest.

Blue egg myths

Blue eggs are not lower in cholesterol or higher in nutrients. That claim gets passed around a lot, but shell color does not change the inside. Another myth is that any hatchery bird sold as an Ameraucana will lay blue. Many of those are Easter Eggers, which may lay green.

Common questions about blue eggs

Why is my blue egg turning green?

If the hen carries brown egg genes too, a light brown layer can sit over the blue and make it look green. Her eggs will look that way from the start.

Are blue eggs smaller?

Many blue egg breeds lay medium eggs, a little smaller than big production brown layers. It varies by line.

Can I hatch blue egg layers from blue eggs?

Yes, but the chicks only lay blue if they inherit the gene. Hatching from a blue layer crossed with a non-blue rooster can give mixed results.
301:
Where green eggs come from

There is no green pigment in a chicken egg. A green egg is a blue egg with a light brown coating on top. The blue goes all the way through the shell, and the brown sits on the outside. Mix the two and your eye sees green. A pale coating gives a minty or sage shell. A heavier coating pushes it toward olive.

Test it yourself

Crack a green egg and look at the inside of the shell. It will usually be blue. That tells you the hen has the blue egg gene and also some brown egg genetics. If you gently scrub the outside of some green eggs, a bit of the brown can even rub away, leaving a bluer patch.

Breeds that lay green eggs

Green layers are usually crosses rather than standard breeds. The most common is the Easter Egger, a mixed bird that carries the blue egg gene. Some lay blue, but many lay green in shades that range from pale mint to sea green. The Olive Egger is bred by crossing a blue layer with a dark brown layer, and lighter-coated hens from those crosses lay green. The Isbar is a Swedish breed known for green to mossy eggs.

Why you cannot predict the exact shade

Because green comes from two separate traits, the shade depends on how much blue and how much brown each hen inherited. Two sisters from the same hatch can lay very different greens. If you buy chicks sold as green layers, expect a range, and maybe the odd blue or tinted egg.

How green eggs change through the year

The blue part stays fairly steady. The brown coating is the part that shifts. Like brown eggs, the brown layer often fades over a long laying season or with age. So a hen that lays olive-green in spring might lay a lighter, bluer green by late summer. After a molt, the color often deepens again.

Green egg myths

  • Green eggs are spoiled or unsafe. No. Green shells are normal. A green ring around a cooked yolk is a different thing, caused by overcooking.
  • Green egg hens are a pure breed. Most are crosses, so looks and egg shade vary.
  • Green eggs taste different. The inside is the same as any other egg.

Common questions about green eggs

What chicken lays the greenest eggs?

There is no single answer, because shade varies hen to hen. Easter Eggers and Olive Eggers are the most common choices.

Do green eggs hatch green egg layers?

Some chicks will lay green and some will not, depending on what genes they get from each parent.

When do Easter Eggers start laying?

Many start somewhere around five to seven months old, depending on season and line.
302:
What a cream egg really is

Cream eggs sit between white and light brown. The shell is white underneath, like every chicken egg, with just a faint wash of brown pigment over the top. Some cream eggs look ivory or buttery, and some look like the palest tan. If you hold one next to a white egg, the difference is easy to see. Next to a typical brown egg, it looks almost white.

Why the color is so light

Brown pigment goes on near the end of shell formation. Hens that lay cream eggs carry genetics for only a small amount of it. The bloom, the thin protective coating on a fresh egg, can also soften the color and add a creamy or chalky look. Washing the egg removes the bloom and can make the shell look slightly different.

Breeds that often lay cream eggs

The Silkie is the classic cream layer, with small eggs that range from cream to lightly tinted. Faverolles often lay pale tinted or cream eggs. Some Sussex hens and a few other heritage breeds lay cream to light brown, depending on line. Expect variation. Within a single breed, one hen might lay cream and another a light brown.

How cream eggs change

Since cream is a very thin brown coating, it can fade toward white over a busy laying season or as a hen gets older. Some cream layers drift toward off-white by late summer. Many come back a shade darker after their molt and winter rest.

Cream eggs and broody hens

A lot of cream egg breeds, Silkies above all, go broody often. A broody hen stops laying while she sits. So if your cream eggs dry up in spring, check whether a hen has claimed a nest box. It is normal behavior, not a health problem.

Myths about cream eggs

  • Cream eggs are old eggs. No. A fresh egg can be cream. Age does not change shell color.
  • Cream means the hen is short on calcium. Not by itself. Calcium affects shell strength, not color. If cream eggs also feel thin or rough, then look at diet and health.
  • Cream eggs are a separate breed group. Cream is just a light point on the brown scale.

Common questions about cream eggs

Are Silkie eggs good to eat?

Yes. They are small, so many people use two in place of one large egg in recipes.

Why are my cream eggs getting whiter?

That is often normal fading over the laying season. If the shells also get thin or soft, look at feed and calcium.

Can cream egg hens lay brown eggs later?

A hen's color stays in the same range for life. It may get a little darker after a rest, but it will not jump to dark brown.
310:
What tinted eggs are

"Tinted" is the word keepers and breed standards use for eggs that are not quite white and not quite brown. Think pale beige, light cream or a faint pinkish tan. Under the color, the shell is white, like every chicken egg. A hen that lays tinted eggs adds only a light brown coating at the end of shell formation.

Tinted, cream and pink, what is the difference?

Mostly the eye of the beholder. These names describe points along the same light brown range. Some people call a warm tint pink. Others call a yellow-leaning tint cream. The genetics behind them are similar, with small amounts of brown pigment and, in some breeds, a heavy bloom that changes how the color looks.

Breeds that often lay tinted eggs

Many heritage and fancy breeds fall in this range. Sussex hens often lay tinted to light brown eggs. Brahmas commonly lay light brown to tinted. Some Cochins lay tinted eggs too. Silkies and Faverolles are other common examples. Expect a spread of shades even within one breed, since lines and individual hens differ.

Why tinted eggs vary so much

When the brown coating is this thin, small changes show up clearly. A hen that is laying every day may lay a paler egg than one laying every other day. Hot weather and stress can wash out color for a few weeks. Older hens often lay lighter eggs than they did as pullets. And after the molt, color may return a little stronger.

Using tinted eggs in a mixed carton

Tinted eggs fill the gap between white and brown, so they make a carton look more varied. If you want a rainbow carton, pair a tinted layer with a blue layer, a dark brown layer and an olive layer. The olive egg guide explains how to get the green end of the spectrum.

Myths about tinted eggs

  • Tinted eggs are dirty. The color is in the coating, not on top of it. Real dirt washes off. Pigment mostly does not.
  • Tinted means a mixed breed. Many purebred heritage breeds are expected to lay tinted eggs.
  • Tinted eggs are weaker. Shell strength depends on calcium and age, not color.

Common questions about tinted eggs

Is a tinted egg the same as a light brown egg?

Close. Tinted is usually lighter than what most people call light brown, but the line between them is fuzzy.

Why do some tinted eggs look pink?

A warm tone in the pigment plus a heavy bloom can make the shell look pinkish, especially in soft light.

Do tinted eggs come from older hens?

Not necessarily. Some breeds lay tinted eggs at any age, although many brown layers fade toward a tint as they get older.
311:
How hens lay dark brown eggs

A dark brown egg starts out white, like every other chicken egg. In the last stage of shell formation, the hen's shell gland adds a coat of brown pigment. Breeds known for dark eggs simply add a lot more of it. The deepest layers produce eggs that look like milk chocolate or even close to dark chocolate. Crack one open and the inside of the shell is still pale, because the color is only on the outside.

Breeds known for dark eggs

  • Marans are the best known. Some lines lay very dark chocolate eggs, while hatchery stock is often lighter.
  • Welsummers lay a rich terracotta brown, often with darker speckles.
  • Barnevelders lay a deep brown egg, sometimes with a matte finish.
  • Penedesencas, a Spanish breed, are known for very dark reddish brown eggs.

Egg darkness varies a lot by line, so if color is your goal, buy from a breeder who selects for it and ask to see eggs from the parent flock.

Why dark eggs get lighter

This is the biggest surprise for new Marans keepers. Dark layers often lay their richest eggs at the start of a laying cycle, then fade as the season goes on. The hen has a limited supply of pigment, and laying often spreads it thinner. Color usually comes back after the molt or a winter break. Age matters too. Many hens lay darker eggs in their first year or two than later on. Stress, heat and illness can also lighten eggs for a while.

The coating can rub off

On very dark eggs, part of the color sits in the outer layer and bloom. A fresh egg can smudge if handled while still damp, and washing can lift a little color. That is normal and does not mean anything is wrong with the egg.

Dark egg myths

  • Darker eggs are more nutritious. The shell color has nothing to do with the yolk or white.
  • Feeding certain foods darkens shells. Diet affects yolk color, not shell color. Genetics sets the shell shade.
  • All Marans lay dark eggs. Many hatchery Marans lay medium brown. Line and selection matter.

Hatching dark eggs

Very dark shells make candling harder. Use a bright light in a dark room, and give it a few extra days before deciding an egg is not developing. The hatch date calculator helps you track timing.

Common questions about dark brown eggs

Which chicken lays the darkest eggs?

Well-bred Marans, especially from lines selected for egg color, are usually the darkest. Penedesencas can be very dark too.

Why did my Marans start laying lighter eggs?

Fading through the laying season is normal. Color often comes back after the molt.

Do dark eggs have thicker shells?

Not because of the color. Shell thickness comes from the hen's health, age and calcium intake.
313:
Why some eggs look pink

Pink eggs are not a separate color in the genetic sense. They are light brown eggs with a warm undertone, and often a heavy bloom that gives them a soft, dusty look. Under that thin outer layer, the shell is white. In daylight one egg might look pink, and under a kitchen light it can look beige. That is part of the charm, and part of why the label varies so much.

The role of the bloom

The bloom, also called the cuticle, is a thin coating the hen puts on the egg just before laying. It helps seal the pores. On some hens it is thick enough to look chalky or frosted, and on a light brown egg it can shift the color toward pink or lilac. If you wash or wipe a pink egg, it may look more tan afterward. That is the bloom coming off, not the pigment.

Breeds whose eggs often look pink

Pink tones show up in several breeds that lay light brown or tinted eggs. Keepers often mention Plymouth Rocks, Orpingtons and Sussex. Some Easter Eggers lay a pinkish egg instead of blue or green, because they did not inherit the blue egg gene. No breed reliably lays pink eggs every time, so think of pink as a happy bonus.

How pink eggs change over time

Because the color is a light coating, pink eggs often fade toward beige or cream over a long laying season. Older hens tend to lay paler eggs. After the molt, the color may warm up again. A hen that was laying pink can go through a stretch of plain tan eggs, and that is normal.

Getting more pink eggs in your carton

There is no feed or trick that turns eggs pink. Your best bet is to keep several light brown layers and see which hens throw the pinkest eggs. If you hatch, keeping eggs from those hens can nudge future birds in that direction, though there are no guarantees.

Pink egg myths

  • Pink eggs mean a sick hen. No. A healthy hen can lay pink eggs. Watch for soft or rough shells instead.
  • Pink eggs come from one special breed. Several breeds can lay them, and individual hens vary.
  • Pink means the egg is blood stained. Blood shows up as streaks or spots, not an even tint.

Common questions about pink eggs

Are pink eggs safe to eat?

Yes. The inside is exactly like any other egg.

Why does my pink egg look tan after washing?

You washed off some of the bloom, which was adding the pink look. The pigment underneath is light brown.

Do pink egg hens lay pink their whole life?

Their eggs stay in the same light brown range, but the pink tone may come and go with the seasons and with age.

How olive eggs get their color

An olive egg is a blue egg wearing a brown coat. The blue pigment runs all the way through the shell. The brown is laid down on the outside at the end. Put a fairly heavy brown coat over blue and you get olive, a deeper and earthier shade than the minty green of a light coating. Crack an olive egg and the inside of the shell is blue, which proves it.

How Olive Eggers are made

An Olive Egger is not a standard breed. It is a cross, usually between a blue egg layer and a dark brown egg layer. A common pairing is a Marans or Welsummer with an Ameraucana, Cream Legbar or other blue layer. The blue egg gene is dominant, so if the blue parent carries two copies, every daughter lays a blue-based egg, and the brown parent adds the coating. When the blue parent carries only one copy, some daughters lay brown instead.

Breeds and crosses that lay olive eggs

  • First generation crosses of a dark brown layer such as the Marans with a blue layer such as the Ameraucana.
  • Some Easter Eggers, which can carry both blue and brown egg genes.
  • Back crosses, where an Olive Egger is bred back to a dark brown layer to push the egg darker.

Why olive is so variable

Shade depends on how much blue and how much brown a hen inherited. A cross with a very dark Marans parent tends to give darker olive than one with a lighter brown parent. Sisters can lay noticeably different shades. Over a busy laying season, the brown coat often thins, so olive eggs can drift toward green. After the molt, they often deepen again.

Olive egg myths

  • Olive Eggers breed true. They do not. Hatching eggs from two Olive Eggers gives mixed results, including blue, green, olive and brown layers.
  • Olive eggs taste different. Shell color has no effect on the inside.
  • You can tell an Olive Egger by its feathers. Their look depends on the parents and can vary a lot.

Common questions about olive eggs

What is the best cross for dark olive eggs?

Many keepers use a dark egg Marans paired with a blue layer that carries two copies of the blue gene. The darker the brown parent, the darker the olive tends to be.

Can a rooster's breed affect egg color?

Yes. Both parents pass on egg color genes, even though roosters do not lay. A rooster from a dark egg line can darken his daughters' eggs.

Why is my olive egg turning green?

The brown coating usually fades over the laying season. The blue underneath stays, so the egg looks greener.
